An experiment measured the lifetime $T$ of a high-speed tau lepton in the laboratory frame as a function of its speed $v$.

| $v$ ($\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$) | $\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$ | $T$ ($\times10^{-13}$ s) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.00 | 1.06 | 3.08 |
| 1.50 | 1.15 | 3.35 |
| 2.00 | 1.34 | 3.89 |
| 2.50 | 1.81 | 5.25 |
| 2.75 | 2.50 | 7.26 |

Using a graph of $T$ against $\gamma$, determine the lifetime of the tau lepton in its rest frame.
questions.answer:
Time dilation gives $T=\gamma T_0$, so the gradient of the line of best fit is $T_0$. Using two well separated points on the line, for example $(1.20,\ 3.48)$ and $(2.40,\ 6.96)$ (in $10^{-13}$ s):
$$T_0=\frac{6.96-3.48}{2.40-1.20}\times10^{-13}=2.9\times10^{-13}\ \text{s}$$

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. Calculate the component of its initial velocity perpendicular to the field.
questions.answer: $v_\perp=8.0\times10^6\sin70^\circ=7.5\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. Calculate the component of its initial velocity parallel to the field.
questions.answer: $v_\parallel=8.0\times10^6\cos70^\circ=2.7\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. Outline why the electron moves in a helical path.
questions.answer: The perpendicular velocity component experiences a magnetic force at right angles to it, producing uniform circular motion, while the parallel component experiences no force and stays constant. The combination is a helix.

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. The magnetic flux density is 0.015 T. Calculate the radius of the loops of the helix.
questions.answer: $qv_\perp B=\dfrac{mv_\perp^2}{r}$, so $r=\dfrac{mv_\perp}{qB}=\dfrac{9.109\times10^{-31}\times7.5\times10^6}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.015}=2.8\times10^{-3}$ m

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. The magnetic flux density is 0.015 T. Calculate the distance between adjacent loops of the helix.
questions.answer:
Period of the circular motion: $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}=\dfrac{2\pi\times9.109\times10^{-31}}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.015}=2.38\times10^{-9}$ s

Distance advanced in one period: $p=v_\parallel T=8.0\times10^6\cos70^\circ\times2.38\times10^{-9}=6.5\times10^{-3}$ m

*Note: the school gets $6.2\times10^{-3}$ m because it rounded the period down to $2.3\times10^{-9}$ s.*

questions.question: A student uses the apparatus shown to measure the magnetic flux density $B$ of a magnet. A rectangular coil of $N$ turns, width $w$, length $L$ and mass $M$ hangs from one arm of a balance with equal arms, its lower end in a uniform field perpendicular to the plane of the coil. The system is first balanced with no current. When a current $I$ flows, a mass $m$ must be added to the other side to rebalance it. Derive an expression for the magnitude of $B$.
questions.answer:
Only the bottom side (length $w$, $N$ conductors) gives a vertical magnetic force: $F=NBIw$.

The arms are equal (length $\ell$), so the change in torque due to the field is balanced by that of the added weight:
$$NBIw\,\ell=mg\,\ell\ \Rightarrow\ B=\frac{mg}{NIw}$$

questions.question: A student uses the apparatus shown to measure the magnetic flux density $B$ of a magnet. A rectangular coil of $N$ turns, width $w$, length $L$ and mass $M$ hangs from one arm of a balance with equal arms, its lower end in a uniform field perpendicular to the plane of the coil. The system is first balanced with no current. When a current $I$ flows, a mass $m$ must be added to the other side to rebalance it. Why is the expression for $B$ independent of the length $L$ of the coil?
questions.answer: The forces on the two vertical sides are horizontal, equal in size and opposite in direction (their currents flow in opposite directions), so they cancel and produce no change in the balance. Only the horizontal side in the field contributes.

questions.question: Two identical bar magnets hang from identical springs, each with its south pole inside a solenoid. The two solenoids are connected by conducting wires. Magnet A is displaced so that it oscillates vertically, moving into and out of its coil. Magnet B then starts to oscillate, with increasing amplitude. Using physics principles, account for the increase in the amplitude of B's oscillation.
questions.answer:
- As A oscillates, the flux through its solenoid changes continually, so by Faraday's law an alternating emf is induced. By Lenz's law the current opposes A's motion.
- The solenoids form one closed circuit, so the same alternating current flows through B's solenoid.
- This current makes a changing magnetic field that exerts an alternating force on magnet B, at the frequency of A's oscillation.
- The two mass–spring systems are identical, so this driving frequency equals B's natural frequency. Resonance occurs: each push adds energy in phase with B's motion, so its amplitude builds up.
- The energy comes from A (whose oscillation dies down), consistent with conservation of energy.

questions.question: A monochromatic source of wavelength $\lambda$, a narrow single slit, a double slit and a screen are arranged as shown, and light and dark bands form on the screen. The screen is 3.2 m from the double slit and the slit separation is 0.39 mm. The graph shows the intensity on the screen against distance from its centre. Determine the wavelength of the light.
questions.answer:
Adjacent maxima are about 0.60 cm apart.
$$\lambda=\frac{d\,\Delta x}{L}=\frac{0.39\times10^{-3}\times0.60\times10^{-2}}{3.2}=7.3\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}\ (730\ \text{nm})$$

questions.question: A monochromatic source of wavelength $\lambda$, a narrow single slit, a double slit and a screen are arranged as shown, and light and dark bands form on the screen. The source is red. It is replaced by a blue source. Predict what (if anything) happens to the separation of the bright fringes. Justify your answer.
questions.answer: The fringes move closer together. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, and the fringe spacing $\Delta x=\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$ is proportional to $\lambda$.

questions.question: A monochromatic source of wavelength $\lambda$, a narrow single slit, a double slit and a screen are arranged as shown, and light and dark bands form on the screen. A polarising filter is placed over each of the two slits, as shown. With the planes of polarisation of the filters parallel, the bands are still seen. When one filter is rotated through 90°, there are no dark bands and the screen is evenly illuminated. Explain why.
questions.answer: Each filter transmits only the component of the electric field oscillating along its own plane of polarisation. With the filters parallel, the waves from the two slits have parallel electric fields, so where they arrive half a wavelength out of step they cancel, giving dark bands. With the filters at 90°, the two electric fields are perpendicular. Perpendicular vibrations cannot cancel each other whatever their phase difference, so there is no destructive (or constructive) interference in intensity: the intensities simply add and the screen is evenly lit.

questions.question: In the 19th and 20th centuries our understanding of the nature of light changed, as debates about its wave and particle nature were challenged by experimental observations. Use this as an example to explain how scientists test and validate models.
questions.answer:
Scientists test a model by deriving predictions from it and comparing them with observation. Agreement supports it; disagreement means it must be refined or replaced.

**Two competing models.** Newton's corpuscle model and Huygens' wave model could both explain reflection and refraction, so these observations could not decide between them. The models made different predictions elsewhere.

**Testing.** Young's double slit experiment produced interference fringes, and diffraction was observed; waves predict these and Newton's particles do not. Foucault found light slower in water, as the wave model predicted. The wave model was accepted, and was strengthened when Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves travelling at $c$ and Hertz detected them.

**Anomalies.** Classical wave theory predicted that a black body would emit ever more energy at short wavelengths (the ultraviolet catastrophe), contrary to experiment. Planck matched the data by proposing energy exchanged in quanta, $E=hf$. In the photoelectric effect there is a threshold frequency, emission is immediate and $K_{max}$ depends on frequency not intensity, none of which a wave model predicts.

**New model, new test.** Einstein proposed photons, predicting $K_{max}=hf-\phi$. Millikan's careful measurements confirmed this linear relationship, validating it.

**Refinement.** Interference still needs waves, so neither model was simply discarded: light is described as having wave–particle duality. This shows that models are provisional, are accepted for how well they explain and predict evidence, and are revised when new reproducible observations conflict with them.

questions.question: In 1897 J. J. Thomson measured the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron. With the aid of an annotated diagram, describe how Thomson's experiment can be performed.
questions.answer:
Set up an evacuated discharge tube: a high voltage accelerates cathode rays from the cathode through a slit in the anode, between parallel plates, to a fluorescent screen. Coils outside the tube give a magnetic field at right angles to both the beam and the electric field (diagram).

1. With both fields on, adjust them until the beam is undeflected. The forces balance, $qE=qvB$, so $v=\dfrac{E}{B}$, where $E=V/d$.
2. Switch off the electric field. The beam now follows a circular arc of radius $r$ in the magnetic field alone, with $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Measure $r$ from the deflection.
3. Combine the two:
$$\frac{q}{m}=\frac{v}{Br}=\frac{E}{B^2r}$$

All of $E$, $B$ and $r$ are measurable. Thomson obtained the same large value of $q/m$ with different cathode materials and gases, showing that the particles are a common constituent of atoms.

questions.question: In 1913 Niels Bohr proposed a model of the hydrogen atom. Describe Bohr's model and explain how it accounted for the formation of spectral lines.
Outline TWO shortcomings of Bohr's model of the atom.
questions.answer: First, it works only for hydrogen and other one-electron ions; it cannot predict the spectra of larger atoms. Second, it cannot explain the different intensities of the spectral lines. (Others: it does not explain the splitting of lines in a magnetic field or their fine structure, and it gives no reason why the allowed orbits do not radiate.)

questions.question: Calculate the wavelength of the violet H-delta emission line of hydrogen, produced by a transition from the sixth to the second energy level.
questions.answer:
$$\frac1\lambda=R\left(\frac1{2^2}-\frac1{6^2}\right)=1.097\times10^7\times\left(\tfrac14-\tfrac1{36}\right)$$
$$\lambda=4.10\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}\ (410\ \text{nm})$$

questions.question: A carbon-12 atom contains 6 protons and 6 neutrons in its nucleus and has a mass of 12.000 u. Calculate the mass defect of one carbon-12 atom in atomic mass units, assuming the mass of the electrons is negligible.
questions.answer:
Mass of the separate nucleons: $6\times1.673\times10^{-27}+6\times1.675\times10^{-27}=2.0088\times10^{-26}$ kg

Mass of carbon-12: $12.000\times1.661\times10^{-27}=1.9932\times10^{-26}$ kg

$\Delta m=1.56\times10^{-28}$ kg $=\dfrac{1.56\times10^{-28}}{1.661\times10^{-27}}=0.094$ u

questions.question: The graph shows the decay of an unknown radioactive isotope. Use the graph to determine the decay constant of the isotope in s$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
The count rate falls from 850 s$^{-1}$ to 425 s$^{-1}$ in about 3.8 days, so $t_{1/2}=3.8\times86400=3.28\times10^5$ s.
$$\lambda=\frac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{0.693}{3.28\times10^5}=2.1\times10^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}$$

questions.question: A radioactive isotope is an alpha emitter whose daughter nuclide is polonium-218. Write a nuclear equation for the decay.

Unpolarised light reflected from water is horizontally polarised. The windscreen of a speed boat is a polariser with its axis at $30^\circ$ to the vertical. By what percentage is the intensity of the reflected light seen by the driver reduced?
questions.answer: The angle between the light's (horizontal) polarisation and the axis is $60^\circ$. By Malus' law $I = I_{max}\cos^2 60^\circ = 0.25 I_{max}$, a 75% reduction.

questions.question: Hole 12 at a golf course is on a circular green between a lake and a sand trap. The map shows distances from the tee, which is at the same elevation as the hole. A golfer hits the ball in line with the hole at $47.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $42.5^\circ$ above the ground. Where does the ball land?
questions.answer: Time of flight $t = \dfrac{2(47.8\sin 42.5^\circ)}{9.8} = 6.59\ \text{s}$; range $= 47.8\cos 42.5^\circ \times 6.59 = 232\ \text{m}$, which is in the sand trap.

questions.question: The radius of the Moon's orbit is $3.84 \times 10^{8}$ m, the mass of the Moon is $7.34 \times 10^{22}$ kg and the mass of the Earth is $5.98 \times 10^{24}$ kg. At what distance from the centre of the Earth does a lunar spacecraft experience no net gravitational force from the Earth and Moon?
questions.answer: $\dfrac{M_E}{r^2} = \dfrac{M_M}{(d-r)^2}$ gives $\dfrac{r}{d-r} = \sqrt{M_E/M_M} = 9.03$, so $r = \dfrac{9.03}{10.03}\times 3.84\times10^{8} = 3.46 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m}$.

questions.question: A rectangular coil of wire with sides 2.0 cm and 5.0 cm lies in a plane at $30^\circ$ to a magnetic field of 20.0 T, as shown. What is the magnetic flux through the coil?
questions.answer: The field makes $60^\circ$ with the normal to the coil: $\Phi = BA\cos\theta = 20.0 \times (0.020\times 0.050)\times\cos 60^\circ = 0.010\ \text{Wb}$. (The paper printed the unit as W; flux is measured in webers.)

questions.question: A stream of electrons is generated in a vacuum tube as shown. What is the direction of the magnetic field at point $P$?
questions.answer: Electrons move from cathode to anode (to the right), so conventional current in the tube is to the left. By the right-hand grip rule the field below this current is out of the page.

questions.question: An aeroplane at an altitude of 500 m is moving horizontally at $160\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ when a small object falls from it. Which describes the effect of including air resistance, compared with ignoring it, on the object's motion until it hits the ground?
questions.answer: Drag reduces the downward acceleration (longer time of flight) and reduces the horizontal velocity (shorter horizontal displacement). The vertical displacement is unchanged.
options: Time of flight is longer and horizontal displacement is shorter
Time of flight is shorter and horizontal displacement is shorter
Horizontal displacement is longer and vertical acceleration is smaller
Vertical displacement is shorter and vertical acceleration is smaller

questions.question: Two satellites are in circular orbits around the Earth. The first is $R$ metres from the centre of the Earth and has orbital speed $V$. The second is $4R$ metres from the centre. What is the orbital speed of the second satellite?
questions.answer: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, so quadrupling $r$ halves $v$.

questions.question: How much work is done on a proton accelerated between two charged plates with a potential difference of 1 kV?
A satellite of mass $6.30 \times 10^{3}$ kg orbits the Earth at an altitude of $1.88 \times 10^{4}$ km. Its gravitational potential energy is closest to:
5 cm of a conductor carrying a current of 0.35 A runs through a 1.3 T magnetic field directed into the page, as shown. What is the magnitude of the force on this length of conductor?
questions.answer: The conductor lies in the plane of the page, so it is perpendicular to the field whatever its angle in the page: $F = BIl = 1.3\times0.35\times0.05 = 0.023\ \text{N}$.

questions.question: The hydrogen-$\alpha$ line of the Balmer series occurs at 656.3 nm. In the spectrum of a star it is recorded at 686.2 nm. Which of the following is true?
questions.answer: The observed wavelength is longer (red shift), so the star is moving away.
options: The star is blue-shifted and moving away from Earth
The star is blue-shifted and moving towards Earth
The star is red-shifted and moving towards Earth
The star is red-shifted and moving away from Earth

questions.question: The trace of a sine wave on an oscilloscope is shown. What is the frequency of the wave?
questions.answer: The period is about 2.3 ms (about 4 cycles in 9 ms), so $f = 1/T \approx 440\ \text{Hz}$.

questions.question: A doughnut-shaped spacecraft with outer radius 48.6 m rotates to provide artificial gravity for its occupants in deep space. What period of rotation gives an artificial gravity of $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ at the outer radius?
questions.answer: $a = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2} \Rightarrow T = 2\pi\sqrt{48.6/9.8} = 14.0\ \text{s}$.

questions.question: The transformer in a laptop charger has 2400 turns in the primary coil and 400 turns in the secondary coil. The laptop draws 4.2 A when charging. What is the current in the primary coil?
questions.answer: $I_p = I_s\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = 4.2\times\dfrac{400}{2400} = 0.70\ \text{A}$.

questions.question: A laser of wavelength 536 nm is shone through a pair of small slits in a card. On a wall 5.54 m away, the bright spots are 3.3 cm apart. What is the separation of the slits?
questions.answer: $d = \dfrac{\lambda L}{\Delta y} = \dfrac{536\times10^{-9}\times5.54}{0.033} = 9.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}$.

questions.question: The spaceship shown has a proper length of 86.0 m and is observed from Earth to be travelling at $2.7 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What length does the observer on Earth measure?
questions.answer: $l = l_0\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = 86.0\sqrt{1-0.9^2} = 37.5\ \text{m}$. (Option C was printed with unit 'ms'.)

questions.question: The acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface is $g$. A planet has three times the mass and twice the radius of the Earth. What is the acceleration due to gravity at its surface?
Michelson and Morley performed an experiment to detect the motion of the Earth through the luminiferous aether. The result of the experiment showed that:
questions.answer: The null result provided no evidence for the aether; it could not confirm it, but did not by itself prove it does not exist.
options: The Earth was moving at a constant speed through the aether
The existence of the aether could not be confirmed
The Earth was not moving through the aether

questions.question: A magnet is dropped down a copper pipe with its north pole facing down and its acceleration is recorded. It is then dropped down the same pipe with its south pole facing down. Which best describes the acceleration of the magnet in each case (north pole down; south pole down)?
questions.answer: By Lenz's law the induced eddy currents oppose the relative motion whichever pole leads, so the acceleration is less than $g$ in both cases.

questions.question: A car is driven around a curve of radius 25.0 m at a constant speed of $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the acceleration of the car.
questions.answer: $a = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \dfrac{20^2}{25.0} = 16\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, directed towards the centre of the curve.

questions.question: A car is driven around a curve of radius 25.0 m at a constant speed of $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. If the driver has a mass of 68 kg, calculate the net force on the driver.
questions.answer: $F = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{68\times20^2}{25.0} = 1.1\times10^{3}\ \text{N}$ (1088 N), directed towards the centre of the curve.

questions.question: In a double slit experiment, two slits, each 100 $\mu$m wide and separated by 600 $\mu$m, are placed in front of a blue laser of wavelength 380 nm. The interference pattern is observed on a screen 2.4 m away. Calculate the spacing between the (single-slit) Fraunhofer diffraction minima.
questions.answer: Single-slit minima: $w\sin\theta = m\lambda$ with $\sin\theta \approx y/L$, so the spacing is $\Delta y = \dfrac{\lambda L}{w} = \dfrac{380\times10^{-9}\times2.4}{100\times10^{-6}} = 9.1\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}$. (The central maximum is twice this wide.)

questions.question: In a double slit experiment, two slits, each 100 $\mu$m wide and separated by 600 $\mu$m, are placed in front of a blue laser of wavelength 380 nm. The interference pattern is observed on a screen 2.4 m away. Calculate the number of interference maxima visible within the central diffraction maximum.
questions.answer:
Interference maxima are spaced $\Delta y = \dfrac{\lambda L}{d} = \dfrac{380\times10^{-9}\times2.4}{600\times10^{-6}} = 1.52\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}$.

The first diffraction minimum is at $9.12\times10^{-3}$ m, i.e. at order $m = d/w = 6$, so the $m = \pm6$ maxima are missing.

Visible orders are $m = -5$ to $+5$: **11 maxima**.

questions.question: In a double slit experiment, two slits, each 100 $\mu$m wide and separated by 600 $\mu$m, are placed in front of a blue laser of wavelength 380 nm. The interference pattern is observed on a screen 2.4 m away. Describe any changes that would be observed if the blue laser were replaced with a red laser.
questions.answer:
Red light has a longer wavelength (and the pattern is red).

- Diffraction minima are at $y = m\lambda L/w$, so they move further apart: the diffraction envelope is wider.
- Interference maxima are spaced $\lambda L/d$ apart, so the fringes are further apart.
- The number of fringes within the central diffraction maximum is unchanged (11), since it depends only on $d/w$.

questions.question: A velocity selector consists of parallel plates producing an electric field $E$ inside a magnetic field $B$, as shown. A charged particle entering it experiences both electric and magnetic forces; when they balance, the particle continues straight through. Derive an expression for the velocity of a particle that passes straight through.
questions.answer:
The electric force on a charge $q$ is $F_E = qE$ (down the page for $+q$, towards the negative plate). The magnetic force is $F_B = qvB\sin 90^\circ = qvB$ (up the page, by the right-hand rule).

For no deflection $qvB = qE$, so $v = \dfrac{E}{B}$.

questions.question: A velocity selector consists of parallel plates producing an electric field $E$ inside a magnetic field $B$, as shown. A charged particle entering it experiences both electric and magnetic forces; when they balance, the particle continues straight through. A particle that would pass straight through has its positive charge replaced by an equal negative charge, with all other properties and both fields unchanged. Describe the effect of the fields on its path.
questions.answer: It also passes straight through undeflected. Both the electric and magnetic forces reverse direction (electric now up the page, magnetic down), but their magnitudes $qE$ and $qvB$ are still equal, so they cancel. The condition $v = E/B$ does not depend on the charge.

questions.question: An astronaut doing maintenance on a spaceship in orbit above the Earth uses a spanner with a 45 cm shaft to tighten a nut, which requires a torque of 5.0 N m to be fully tightened. Calculate the force required if the astronaut applies it perpendicular to the spanner shaft.
questions.answer: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$, so $F = \dfrac{\tau}{r\sin 90^\circ} = \dfrac{5.0}{0.45} = 11\ \text{N}$.

questions.question: An astronaut doing maintenance on a spaceship in orbit above the Earth uses a spanner with a 45 cm shaft to tighten a nut, which requires a torque of 5.0 N m to be fully tightened. The force needed to tighten the nut when applied perpendicular to the shaft is instead applied at $75^\circ$ to the shaft. How much torque is applied to the nut?
questions.answer: $F = 5.0/0.45 = 11.1$ N, so $\tau = rF\sin75^\circ = 0.45\times11.1\times\sin75^\circ = 4.8\ \text{N m}$.

questions.question: Describe the changes in the kinetic and potential energy of an orbiting spaceship as it fires its engines to move to a higher orbit.
questions.answer:
The engines do work on the spaceship, increasing its total mechanical energy $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$.

- Gravitational potential energy $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ **increases** (becomes less negative) as work is done against gravity.
- In the new, higher orbit the kinetic energy $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ is **smaller** (the orbital speed is lower).

For a move from $r = R$ to $2R$: $\Delta U = +\dfrac{GMm}{2R}$, $\Delta K = -\dfrac{GMm}{4R}$ and $\Delta E = +\dfrac{GMm}{4R}$, supplied by the engines.

*Note: the school solution's working gives $\Delta K = -GMm/R$; the correct value is $-GMm/(4R)$.*

questions.question: Distinguish between escape velocity and orbital velocity, including formulae for both in your answer.
questions.answer:
**Orbital velocity** is the speed needed for a circular orbit of radius $r$: gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force, $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v_o = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$. The object stays bound, with total energy $K + U = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r} < 0$.

**Escape velocity** is the minimum speed at distance $r$ for an object (without further thrust) to move infinitely far away, arriving with zero speed: $\tfrac12 mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = 0$, so $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}$. The object is no longer bound (total energy zero).

$v_e = \sqrt2\,v_o$; for speeds between them (launched tangentially) the orbit is elliptical.

questions.question: An electron is accelerated to $0.9999c$ in a particle accelerator. Calculate its relativistic mass.
An electron is accelerated to $0.9999c$ in a particle accelerator. Calculate the electron's relativistic momentum.

A positron is the antiparticle of the electron, with the same properties except for a charge of $+1$. When a positron collides with an electron they annihilate and produce two photons. Calculate the energy released, taking both particles to be essentially at rest.
questions.answer: The rest mass of both particles is converted to energy: $E = 2m_ec^2 = 2\times9.109\times10^{-31}\times(3.00\times10^{8})^2 = 1.64\times10^{-13}\ \text{J}$ (1.02 MeV).

questions.question: Justify how Einstein's mass–energy equivalence equation can be used to explain phenomena such as the energy produced by the Sun.
questions.answer:
$E = mc^2$ states that mass and energy are equivalent; because $c^2$ is very large, a small loss of mass corresponds to a very large amount of energy.

In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium (overall $4\,{}^1_1\text{H} \to {}^4_2\text{He} + 2e^+ + 2\nu$). The products have less mass than the reactants. This mass defect $\Delta m$ is released as energy $E = \Delta mc^2$ (kinetic energy of products and photons).

The enormous number of fusion reactions each second accounts for the Sun's power output, so the equation quantitatively explains the source of its energy.

questions.question: Outline one piece of evidence that supports Einstein's theory of special relativity.
questions.answer:
**Muon decay.** Muons are produced by cosmic rays high in the atmosphere and travel at close to $c$. Their mean lifetime at rest is only about 2.2 $\mu$s, so without relativity very few should reach the ground.

Far more are detected at sea level than this predicts (e.g. Frisch and Smith, 1963). In the Earth's frame the moving muon's lifetime is dilated, $t = \dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$ (in the muon's frame, the distance is length-contracted), and the number detected agrees with this prediction.

questions.question: A wireless charger is used to recharge the battery of a mobile phone; the arrangement is shown. Explain the operation of the charger when charging the phone.
questions.answer:
- The charger contains a primary coil supplied with **alternating** current.
- This current produces a continually changing magnetic field around the coil.
- The phone, placed on the charger, has a secondary coil close to and aligned with the primary, so part of the changing field passes through it: the flux $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ through the secondary changes.
- By Faraday's law an emf $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ is induced in the secondary; in the closed circuit this drives an alternating current whose field, by Lenz's law, opposes the change in flux.
- The phone's circuit board rectifies the AC to DC (and regulates the voltage) to charge the battery.

Energy is therefore transferred from charger to phone through the changing magnetic field, with no electrical contact, like a transformer: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$ in the ideal case. In practice, with no iron core there is flux leakage, plus resistive and eddy current heating, so efficiency is less than 100%; keeping the coils close and aligned reduces these losses.

questions.question: A simple device for investigating the photoelectric effect is shown. When light of sufficient energy hits the cathode, electrons are ejected towards the anode. The voltage of the supply can be varied until no current is measured at the ammeter; this is the stopping voltage. Calculate the maximum initial speed of the electrons leaving the cathode if the stopping voltage is 4.9 V.
questions.answer: $\tfrac12 m v^2 = qV$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times1.602\times10^{-19}\times4.9}{9.109\times10^{-31}}} = 1.3\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question: A simple device for investigating the photoelectric effect is shown. When light of sufficient energy hits the cathode, electrons are ejected towards the anode. The voltage of the supply can be varied until no current is measured at the ammeter; this is the stopping voltage. The device is used to investigate the relationship between the type of metal at the cathode and the stopping voltage. Write a suitable hypothesis for this investigation.
questions.answer: For light of a given frequency above threshold, a cathode metal with a larger work function will give a smaller stopping voltage.

questions.question:
A simple device for investigating the photoelectric effect is shown. When light of sufficient energy hits the cathode, electrons are ejected towards the anode. The voltage of the supply can be varied until no current is measured at the ammeter; this is the stopping voltage.

The following data was collected for a zinc cathode.

| photon frequency ($\times 10^{15}$ Hz) | stopping voltage (V) |
|---|---|
| 1.00 | no current detected |
| 1.25 | 0.87 |
| 1.50 | 1.90 |
| 1.75 | 2.94 |
| 2.00 | 3.97 |
| 2.25 | 5.01 |

Plot this data on a graph with a line of best fit.
questions.answer:
Plot stopping voltage (vertical axis) against frequency (horizontal axis), with labelled axes and units, a title and a straight line of best fit extended to the frequency axis. The line has gradient $\approx 4.14\times10^{-15}$ V s ($= h/e$) and horizontal intercept $\approx 1.04\times10^{15}$ Hz. The 1.00 point (no current) is below threshold and is not plotted as a data point.

*Note: the school paper gave the frequencies as $\times10^{14}$ Hz, which would imply a Planck constant ten times too small; they have been corrected to $\times10^{15}$ Hz.*

questions.question:
A simple device for investigating the photoelectric effect is shown. When light of sufficient energy hits the cathode, electrons are ejected towards the anode. The voltage of the supply can be varied until no current is measured at the ammeter; this is the stopping voltage.

The following data was collected for a zinc cathode.

| photon frequency ($\times 10^{15}$ Hz) | stopping voltage (V) |
|---|---|
| 1.00 | no current detected |
| 1.25 | 0.87 |
| 1.50 | 1.90 |
| 1.75 | 2.94 |
| 2.00 | 3.97 |
| 2.25 | 5.01 |

Using a graph of this data, calculate the work function of zinc.
questions.answer:
The line of best fit crosses the frequency axis at the threshold frequency $f_0 = 1.04\times10^{15}$ Hz.

$\phi = hf_0 = 6.626\times10^{-34}\times1.04\times10^{15} = 6.9\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ (4.3 eV).

*Note: the school paper gave the frequencies as $\times10^{14}$ Hz, which would imply a Planck constant ten times too small; they have been corrected to $\times10^{15}$ Hz.* *The school's answer of $7.0\times10^{-20}$ J is too small by a factor of ten.*

questions.question:
A simple device for investigating the photoelectric effect is shown. When light of sufficient energy hits the cathode, electrons are ejected towards the anode. The voltage of the supply can be varied until no current is measured at the ammeter; this is the stopping voltage.

The following data was collected for a zinc cathode.

| photon frequency ($\times 10^{15}$ Hz) | stopping voltage (V) |
|---|---|
| 1.00 | no current detected |
| 1.25 | 0.87 |
| 1.50 | 1.90 |
| 1.75 | 2.94 |
| 2.00 | 3.97 |
| 2.25 | 5.01 |

Explain how the quantum model of light accounts for the results of this experiment.
questions.answer:
In the quantum model light consists of photons, each of energy $E = hf$, and one photon gives all its energy to one electron.

- An electron needs at least the work function $\phi$ to escape. If $hf < \phi$ no electrons are emitted whatever the intensity, which explains why no current is detected at $1.00\times10^{15}$ Hz (below the threshold $f_0 = \phi/h \approx 1.04\times10^{15}$ Hz).
- Above threshold the surplus becomes kinetic energy: $K_{max} = hf - \phi$.
- The stopping voltage satisfies $eV_s = K_{max}$, so $V_s = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{\phi}{e}$: a straight line, as observed, with gradient $h/e$ and intercept set by zinc's work function.

A wave model, in which energy depends on intensity and can accumulate, cannot explain the threshold frequency or this dependence on frequency.

questions.question: Explain, using a series of annotated diagrams or a step-by-step description through one rotation, how a small DC motor operates.
questions.answer:
**Components:** a coil (armature) in the magnetic field of a pair of magnets (stator), connected to a DC supply through a split-ring commutator and brushes.

1. **Coil parallel to the field:** current flows in opposite directions in the two sides, so by $F = BIl$ they experience forces in opposite directions (one up, one down). This gives maximum torque $\tau = nIAB$.
2. **Rotating towards perpendicular:** the forces stay the same size but their perpendicular distance from the axis shrinks, so $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$ ($\theta$ between the field and the normal to the coil) decreases.
3. **Coil perpendicular to the field:** torque is zero; the brushes cross the gaps in the split ring and momentum carries the coil past.
4. **Just past:** the commutator has swapped the connections, reversing the current in the coil. The side now on each side of the motor again feels a force in the original sense, so the torque continues in the same direction.

This repeats every half turn, giving continuous rotation.

questions.question: If the shaft of a single-coil DC motor is turned by an external torque it acts as a generator. Sketch the output voltage of this DC generator against the angle of the shaft for one complete rotation.
questions.answer: A full-wave rectified sine curve: two positive humps per rotation, falling to zero every $180^\circ$ (where the commutator swaps connections). The graph shown takes $0^\circ$ as the position with the coil perpendicular to the field (zero emf).

questions.question: A simple pendulum consists of a bob of mass $m$ on a massless string of length $L$ fixed at a pivot $P$. When displaced and released it swings with periodic motion, and its period (for small angles) is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$. An investigation aims to estimate the acceleration due to gravity $g$ using a simple pendulum. Write a procedure to collect appropriate data from the pendulum to meet this aim.
questions.answer:
1. Clamp a string with a small dense bob firmly at the top. Measure $L$ from the pivot to the centre of the bob with a metre rule.
2. Displace the bob by a small angle (less than about $10^\circ$) and release it without pushing, so it swings in one plane.
3. Using a stopwatch, time 10 complete oscillations, timing from the lowest point; divide by 10 to get $T$.
4. Repeat at least three times for the same length and average.
5. Repeat for at least five different lengths (e.g. 0.2 m to 1.0 m), keeping the bob and release angle the same.
6. Record $L$, the times, $T$ and $T^2$ in a table, then graph $T^2$ against $L$.

*Note: the school paper printed the period as $T=\sqrt{L/g}$, omitting the factor $2\pi$; it is corrected here.*

questions.question: A simple pendulum consists of a bob of mass $m$ on a massless string of length $L$ fixed at a pivot $P$. When displaced and released it swings with periodic motion, and its period (for small angles) is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$. An investigation aims to estimate the acceleration due to gravity $g$ using a simple pendulum. Show how the equation can be rearranged so the data can be analysed graphically to obtain a value for $g$.
questions.answer:
Squaring: $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}L$.

A graph of $T^2$ (vertical) against $L$ (horizontal) is a straight line through the origin with gradient $\dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}$, so $g = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{\text{gradient}}$.

*Note: the school paper omitted the $2\pi$ from the period formula, so its answer (gradient $1/g$) is wrong.*

questions.question: Which statement is true as you move from left to right on the electromagnetic spectrum shown?
questions.answer: From radio waves to gamma rays frequency and photon energy ($E=hf$) increase while wavelength decreases.

questions.question: A car experiences a force of $1.40 \times 10^{3}$ N from the road on its rotating tyres. If the tyres have a diameter of 45 cm, what is the magnitude of the torque on a tyre?
questions.answer: $\tau = rF = 0.225\times1.40\times10^{3} = 315\ \text{N m}$.

questions.question: Which scenario results in no net force from the field stated?
questions.answer: A magnetic force $F = qvB\sin\theta$ requires motion, so a stationary charge experiences none. (A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field would also feel none, but A is always true.)
options: A stationary charged particle placed in a magnetic field
A stationary charged particle placed in an electric field
A moving charged particle placed in a magnetic field
A moving charged particle placed in an electric field

questions.question: Which row correctly identifies the orbit type with (short orbital period; large altitude; used for mapping surface terrain)?
questions.answer: Low (near Earth) orbits have short periods and are used for terrain mapping; geostationary orbits are at large altitude.

questions.question: A current-carrying conductor experiences a force when placed in a uniform magnetic field. This is known as:
questions.answer: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is the motor effect.

questions.question: Which correctly matches each model of light with an experiment that supported it (light is a particle; light is a wave)?
questions.answer: The photoelectric effect supports the particle (photon) model; double slit interference supports the wave model.
options: Young's double slit; Young's double slit

questions.question: A student attaches a tennis ball to a 1.0 m string and swings it in a vertical circle. Which best describes the energy of the ball as it moves from the bottom to the top of its path?
questions.answer: Kinetic energy is converted into gravitational potential energy, and work is done on the ball (by gravity, and by the student in maintaining the motion).
options: Its energy changes and work is done on the ball
Its energy changes and total work is a constant
Its energy remains the same and work is done on the ball
Its energy remains the same and total work is a constant

questions.question: Two identical current-carrying conductors are placed parallel to each other. Which of the following will **not** increase the magnitude of the force between them by a factor of 4?
questions.answer: $F/l = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1I_2}{2\pi r}$. Option D gives $\tfrac12\times\tfrac12\times8 = 2$ times the force.
options: Doubling the current in both wires
Doubling the current in one wire and halving the distance between the wires
Decreasing the distance between the wires by a factor of 4
Halving the current in both wires and decreasing the distance between the wires by a factor of 8

questions.question: Which core design (shown) would best minimise heating due to eddy currents?
questions.answer: Eddy currents circulate in planes perpendicular to the changing flux (the coil's axis). Insulating layers must lie parallel to the flux so they cut across those loops, as in design C.

questions.question: Which was NOT a contribution made by Maxwell to ideas in physics?
questions.answer: Maxwell's work was theoretical electromagnetism; he did no experiments on the photoelectric effect (which was not discovered by Planck).
options: He was able to calculate the speed of light accurately
He proposed that light was self-propagating electromagnetic radiation
He predicted an endless spectrum of electromagnetic radiation
He did follow-up experiments to analyse the photoelectric effect discovered by Planck

Which graph shows the relationship between the energy of a photon (y-axis) and its wavelength (x-axis)?
questions.answer: $E = hc/\lambda$: inversely proportional.

questions.question: An archer shoots at a bullseye at the same height as the arrow's release. In the 70.0 m event she shoots horizontally and misses the centre of the target. She then shoots horizontally at the same speed in the 50.0 m event. Which is the expected outcome?
questions.answer: The shorter horizontal distance takes less time, so the second arrow falls less.
options: Both arrows hit the same spot just below the bullseye and the second has a shorter time of flight
The first arrow hits lower than the second and both have the same time of flight
The first arrow hits lower than the second and the second has a shorter time of flight
The second arrow hits lower than the first and both have the same time of flight

questions.question: How did Newton's particle theory of light explain refraction?
questions.answer: Newton proposed that particles are attracted into the denser medium, changing their direction (and increasing their speed).
options: Stronger forces within the refracting medium changed the direction of the light particles as they entered it
The refracting medium was so dense compared with air that the particles were forced to slow down
The particles scattered because the medium's particles were closer together than air particles
It showed that the angle of incidence equals the angle of refraction

questions.question: A current-carrying conductor (current into the page) is in a magnetic field directed up and to the right, as shown. Which represents the direction of the force on the conductor?
questions.answer: The force is perpendicular to both $I$ and $B$; by the right-hand rule $\vec{I}\times\vec{B}$ points down and to the right.

questions.question: A particle with a charge of magnitude $2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ C travels horizontally into the electric field between two plates, as shown. What can be concluded about its charge and the work done on it by the field?
questions.answer: It deflects towards the lower-potential plate, so it is positive. It starts midway (85 V) and reaches 50 V: $W = q\Delta V = 2.0\times10^{-4}\times35 = 7.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}$.

questions.question: A DC motor is set up as shown. Which row of graphs represents the flux through the area WXYZ and the force on wire WX through one revolution, starting from the position shown?
questions.answer: The coil starts parallel to the field, so flux starts at zero and varies sinusoidally. The force on WX has constant magnitude, and its direction swaps when the commutator reverses the current.

questions.question: A golfer hits three golf balls from a cliff top, following the paths shown. Which statement about the balls as they are hit is correct?
questions.answer: They reach different heights (different vertical velocities) and so have different flight times, yet the same range, so their horizontal velocities also differ.
options: Each has the same initial velocity
Each has the same initial horizontal velocity
Each has the same initial vertical velocity
None of the velocities are the same

questions.question: Starship *Alpha* travels at $0.9c$ past an identical starship *Beta*, which is at rest. A cabin boy on *Alpha* and a cook on *Beta* each measure the time for the other ship to pass their window. Who measures the longer time?
questions.answer: The situation is symmetric: each sees the other ship contracted by the same factor and moving at the same speed.
options: The measured times cannot be compared

questions.question: A water rocket on the Moon ($m_{Moon} = 7.35 \times 10^{22}$ kg, $r_{Moon} = 1.74 \times 10^{6}$ m) is travelling vertically at $22\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at 1.9 s after launch, about 21 m above the surface. Explain whether it would escape the Moon's gravitational field if the thrust stops then.
questions.answer:
$v_{esc} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times6.67\times10^{-11}\times7.35\times10^{22}}{1.74\times10^{6}}} = 2.37\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

The rocket's $22\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is far less than this, so it would not escape; it would rise a little further and fall back.

questions.question: Bob sets up a frictionless snooker table, not knowing that his floor is tilted by $5.0^\circ$ (side view shown). He hits a frictionless ball from corner Z at $1.10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $50.0^\circ$ from the long side ZY, and it curves into the pocket at Y (top view shown). Calculate the net acceleration of the ball.
questions.answer: Only the component of gravity down the slope acts: $a = g\sin 5.0^\circ = 0.85\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, down the slope (towards side ZY).

questions.question: Bob sets up a frictionless snooker table, not knowing that his floor is tilted by $5.0^\circ$ (side view shown). He hits a frictionless ball from corner Z at $1.10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $50.0^\circ$ from the long side ZY, and it curves into the pocket at Y (top view shown). Calculate the time for the ball to reach pocket Y.
questions.answer:
Up-slope component: $u_y = 1.10\sin 50.0^\circ = 0.843\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $a_y = -0.854\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

$s_y = 0 = u_yt + \tfrac12 a_yt^2 \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{2(0.843)}{0.854} = 1.97\ \text{s}$.

*Note: the school's alternative method gives 2.1 s, an arithmetic error.*

questions.question: Bob sets up a frictionless snooker table, not knowing that his floor is tilted by $5.0^\circ$ (side view shown). He hits a frictionless ball from corner Z at $1.10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $50.0^\circ$ from the long side ZY, and it curves into the pocket at Y (top view shown). How far is pocket Y from the position where the ball was hit?
questions.answer: $s_x = u\cos\theta\, t = 1.10\cos 50.0^\circ\times1.97 = 1.4\ \text{m}$.

questions.question: The graph shows $Y = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - X^2/3^2}}$. Explain the significance of the shape of the graph for our understanding of time in the special theory of relativity.
questions.answer:
With $X$ as speed $v$ (in units of $10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so $c = 3$), $Y$ is the Lorentz factor in $t = \dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$ — the ratio of dilated time to proper time.

- The graph is nearly flat at $Y\approx1$ for low speeds: time dilation is negligible, so everyday experience suggests time is absolute.
- It rises steeply as $v$ approaches $c$ (beyond about $X = 2.5$): moving clocks run markedly slow relative to a stationary observer.
- $Y \to \infty$ as $v \to c$: time is relative, and an object with mass cannot reach $c$.

questions.question: The graph shows the peak wavelength of the radiation emitted by a black body at different temperatures. Using data points from the graph, show that it is consistent with Wien's law.
questions.answer:
Wien's law: $\lambda_{max} = \dfrac{b}{T}$, so $\lambda_{max}T$ should be constant ($b = 2.898\times10^{-3}\ \text{m K}$).

Reading points from the graph:

- $T = 400$ K, $\lambda \approx 7.2\ \mu$m: $b = 2.9\times10^{-3}$ m K
- $T = 800$ K, $\lambda \approx 3.6\ \mu$m: $b = 2.9\times10^{-3}$ m K

The product is constant (average $2.9\times10^{-3}$ m K) and agrees with the data-sheet value, so the graph is consistent with Wien's law.

questions.question: To test Newton's law of universal gravitation, Lucy places two 100 kg lead balls on a frictionless slide rod so each can move freely towards or away from the centre. A distance meter in the middle reflects light off the balls, and the apparatus rotates on a pivot in the horizontal plane. She aims to find the speed at which the gravitational force between the balls provides exactly the centripetal force. How would Lucy know when the force of gravity equals the centripetal force required?
questions.answer: The balls would neither slide in nor out: the distance meter would show a constant separation.

questions.question: To test Newton's law of universal gravitation, Lucy places two 100 kg lead balls on a frictionless slide rod so each can move freely towards or away from the centre. A distance meter in the middle reflects light off the balls, and the apparatus rotates on a pivot in the horizontal plane. She aims to find the speed at which the gravitational force between the balls provides exactly the centripetal force. Derive an expression for the speed $v$ of each ball in terms of $G$, the mass $m$ of a ball and its distance $r$ from the pivot.
questions.answer:
The balls are $2r$ apart and each moves in a circle of radius $r$: $\dfrac{Gm^2}{(2r)^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{Gm}{4r}} = \dfrac12\sqrt{\dfrac{Gm}{r}}$.

*Note: the paper states $v=\sqrt{Gm/r}$ with $r$ measured from the pivot; that omits the factor of $\tfrac12$, because the ball separation is $2r$.*

questions.question: To test Newton's law of universal gravitation, Lucy places two 100 kg lead balls on a frictionless slide rod so each can move freely towards or away from the centre. A distance meter in the middle reflects light off the balls, and the apparatus rotates on a pivot in the horizontal plane. She aims to find the speed at which the gravitational force between the balls provides exactly the centripetal force. The required speed of each ball is $v = \sqrt{Gm/(4r)}$, where $r$ is its distance from the pivot. Justify why Lucy would not observe any measurable results.
questions.answer:
Taking $r = 0.5$ m: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times100}{4\times0.5}} = 5.8\times10^{-5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, a period of about 15 hours.

The gravitational force (under $10^{-6}$ N) and the speed needed are far too small to produce or detect: tiny residual friction, air currents and vibration would swamp the effect.

questions.question: Muons created in the upper atmosphere are unstable and decay after 2.2 $\mu$s measured in their own frame. Muons travelling at $0.995c$ pass the top of a 2627 m mountain and reach the ground. Calculate the lifetime of the muons as measured by a stationary observer on the ground.

Muons created in the upper atmosphere are unstable and decay after 2.2 $\mu$s measured in their own frame. Muons travelling at $0.995c$ pass the top of a 2627 m mountain and reach the ground. Explain why many more muons reach the ground than classical physics would predict.
questions.answer:
Classically they would travel only $0.995c\times2.2\ \mu\text{s} \approx 660$ m before decaying, much less than 2627 m.

Relativity: in the ground frame their lifetime is dilated to 22 $\mu$s, so they can travel about 6.6 km and most reach the ground. (In the muon frame, the mountain is length-contracted to about 260 m.)

questions.question: Two objects of identical mass fall from the same altitude to the surface of a planet with no atmosphere. $m_1$ is moving too slowly to remain in orbit and follows a parabolic path down; $m_2$ starts from rest and falls straight down. Compare qualitatively their impact speeds, referring to energy changes.
questions.answer:
Both start at the same height, so both lose the same gravitational potential energy $\Delta U$ on the way to the surface, which becomes kinetic energy.

$m_1$ also has initial kinetic energy (from its orbital-direction velocity), while $m_2$ has none. So $K_{final} = K_{initial} + |\Delta U|$ is larger for $m_1$: **$m_1$ hits at a greater speed than $m_2$**.

questions.question: Most electric vehicles have a switch that changes a DC motor into a DC generator for braking, as shown. With reference to the law of conservation of energy, explain the difference between a DC motor and a DC generator.
questions.answer:
**Motor (drive):** the battery supplies current to the coil in the magnetic field; the motor effect produces a torque. Electrical energy is transformed into kinetic energy (plus heat). As the coil spins, a back emf opposes the supply, as required by Lenz's law, so mechanical output is paid for by electrical input.

**Generator (brake):** the moving car turns the coil, changing the flux through it and inducing an emf (Faraday). The induced current charges the battery. By Lenz's law this current produces a torque opposing the rotation.

Energy is conserved: the electrical (chemical) energy gained comes from the car's kinetic energy, so the coil and car slow down. The two devices have the same construction but transfer energy in opposite directions; neither creates energy.

questions.question: A spacecraft exploring a distant planet and its orbiting moon follows the dashed path shown (not to scale), using its rockets only to leave the planet's orbit. Identify where, on or near its path, the net gravitational force on the spacecraft could be zero.
questions.answer:
On the line joining the planet and the moon, between them (where the path passes between the two), at the point where $\dfrac{GM_p}{r_p^2} = \dfrac{GM_m}{r_m^2}$. This is much closer to the moon, since it is less massive.

*Note: the school also marked a point below the planet, away from the planet–moon line; the two forces cannot cancel there.*

questions.question: A spacecraft exploring a distant planet and its orbiting moon follows the dashed path shown (not to scale), using its rockets only to leave the planet's orbit. Describe how this model is useful in understanding satellite motion AND how it has limitations.
questions.answer:
**Useful:** it shows how the path curves under the gravitational fields of the planet and moon, changing direction towards whichever body dominates.

**Limitations:** it is not to scale (distances and sizes are wrong), shows the moon at a fixed position although it moves, assumes simple circular shapes, and shows no information about speed or the size of the forces.

The generator starts from the position shown (coil parallel to the field). Describe or sketch the graph of the generator's emf against time.

A stationary AC generator is connected to an ideal transformer as shown. The primary coil has 7 turns and the secondary 5 turns, as drawn.

Identify the transformer as step-up or step-down.
questions.answer: Step-down: the secondary (5 turns) has fewer turns than the primary (7 turns).

Given $\varepsilon_{max} = 2\pi fBA$, where $f$ is the frequency of rotation, calculate the maximum current reading on the galvanometer (treat the meter and secondary as having total resistance $R$).

A stationary AC generator is connected to an ideal transformer as shown. The primary coil has 7 turns and the secondary 5 turns, as drawn.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Magnetic field strength $B$ | $8.50 \times 10^{-2}$ T |

| Resistance of the secondary wire $R$ | $5.25\ \Omega$ |

The generator is changed to a DC generator by replacing the slip rings with a split ring commutator. What happens to the reading on the galvanometer?
questions.answer: It still oscillates. The primary receives pulsating DC, whose current is still changing, so the flux in the core changes and induces a varying emf in the secondary (at twice the frequency and with a different waveform).

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ is moving at constant velocity $v$ when a magnetic field of strength $B$ (into the page) is switched on, as shown. Show that the period of its circular motion is $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

$T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$.

questions.question: Calculate the period of circular motion of an electron in a magnetic field of $2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ T, with velocity perpendicular to the field.
questions.answer: $T = \dfrac{2\pi m_e}{eB} = \dfrac{2\pi\times9.109\times10^{-31}}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times2.0\times10^{-4}} = 1.8\times10^{-7}\ \text{s}$.

questions.question: The diagram shows the circular path of an electron in a magnetic field (into the page) during one period $T$. Describe and sketch the electron's path over the same time $T$ if the field strength were halved.
questions.answer: $r = mv/qB$ doubles and the period doubles to $2T$. So in time $T$ the electron, starting upwards and curving clockwise (to the right), covers a **semicircle of twice the original radius**.

questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength 545 nm is shone onto a diffraction grating with $1.2 \times 10^{3}$ lines per centimetre, as shown. Calculate the angle between the central maximum and the third-order bright spot.
questions.answer:
$d = \dfrac{1.0\times10^{-2}}{1.2\times10^{3}} = 8.33\times10^{-6}$ m.

$d\sin\theta = m\lambda$: $\theta = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3\times545\times10^{-9}}{8.33\times10^{-6}}\right) = 11^\circ$.

questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength 545 nm is shone onto a diffraction grating with $1.2 \times 10^{3}$ lines per centimetre, as shown. Explain why this produces regions of bright and dark.
questions.answer:
Light diffracts at each slit, and the waves from the many slits (coherent sources) overlap at the screen after travelling different distances.

- Where the path difference between adjacent slits is a whole number of wavelengths ($d\sin\theta = m\lambda$), the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively: bright.
- At other angles they arrive out of phase and interfere destructively (e.g. a half-wavelength difference between adjacent slits): dark.

questions.question: Intensity against wavelength curves for black body radiation at various temperatures are shown. State Planck's two fundamental postulates used to explain the shape of black body radiation curves.
questions.answer:
1. The energy of the oscillators in the black body is quantised: $E = nhf$, where $n$ is a whole number.
2. Radiation is emitted or absorbed only in discrete packets (quanta) when an oscillator changes energy level: $\Delta E = hf$.

questions.question: Intensity against wavelength curves for black body radiation at various temperatures are shown. Explain how these postulates account for the experimental data at high temperatures.
questions.answer:
As temperature rises, more thermal energy is available, so more oscillators can reach higher quanta: intensity increases at all wavelengths and the peak shifts to shorter wavelength (higher frequency).

At very short wavelengths each quantum $hf$ is large compared with the typical thermal energy, so few oscillators can emit it and the intensity falls to zero instead of rising without limit as classical theory predicted.

questions.question: Unpolarised light of intensity $128\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ passes through three polarising filters. The axes of the first and third filters are at $0^\circ$. If the light leaving the third filter has intensity $16\ \text{W m}^{-2}$, calculate the angle $\theta$ through which the second filter is rotated.
questions.answer:
After filter 1: $I_1 = \tfrac12\times128 = 64\ \text{W m}^{-2}$.

After filter 2: $I_2 = 64\cos^2\theta$. After filter 3 (at angle $\theta$ to filter 2): $I_3 = I_2\cos^2\theta = 64\cos^4\theta$.

$16 = 64\cos^4\theta \Rightarrow \cos^2\theta = \tfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta = 45^\circ$.

questions.question: Students studying the photoelectric effect obtained the graph shown of maximum kinetic energy $K_{max}$ of photoelectrons against the frequency of incident light. Using the graph, determine the value the students would have obtained for Planck's constant.
questions.answer:
The line goes from about $(3.6\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}, 0)$ to $(7.5\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}, 2.0\ \text{eV})$.

$h = \text{gradient} = \dfrac{2.0\times1.602\times10^{-19}}{(7.5-3.6)\times10^{14}} \approx 8.3\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$ (higher than the accepted value).

questions.question: Students studying the photoelectric effect obtained the graph shown of maximum kinetic energy $K_{max}$ of photoelectrons against the frequency of incident light. Using the graph, determine the maximum wavelength of light that would cause photoelectrons to be emitted.
questions.answer: Threshold frequency $f_0 \approx 3.6\times10^{14}$ Hz, so $\lambda_{max} = c/f_0 \approx 8.3\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}$ (about 800–830 nm).

prev.question: Students studying the photoelectric effect obtained the graph shown of maximum kinetic energy $K_{max}$ of photoelectrons against the frequency of incident light. Using the graph, determine the value the students would have obtained for Planck's constant.
prev.answer:
The line goes from about $(3.6\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}, 0)$ to $(7.5\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}, 2.0\ \text{eV})$.

$h = \text{gradient} = \dfrac{2.0\times1.602\times10^{-19}}{(7.5-3.6)\times10^{14}} \approx 8.3\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$ (higher than the accepted value).

questions.question: The graph of $K_{max}$ against frequency for a metal of work function $\phi$ is shown dashed. Describe and sketch the line obtained for a metal with work function $\tfrac12\phi$.
questions.answer: The gradient ($h$) is unchanged, so the line is parallel to the original. $\phi \approx 1.9$ eV, so the new vertical intercept is about $-0.95$ eV and the threshold frequency halves to about $1.8\times10^{14}$ Hz.

questions.question: A simple DC motor drives a benchtop drill, with a series variable resistor to protect the coil windings: its resistance is large at start-up and is slowly lowered as the motor reaches operating speed. Explain improvements that can be made to motors to minimise issues with torque and back emf.
questions.answer:
**Background.** Torque $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$. A spinning coil experiences a changing flux, inducing a back emf that opposes the supply (Lenz's law): $I = (V - \varepsilon_{back})/R$. At start-up $\varepsilon_{back} = 0$ so current (and heating) is large; at speed, back emf reduces current and torque, limiting the speed. Back emf cannot be eliminated, as it is how energy is converted.

**Torque improvements**
- **Curved (radial) magnet poles** with a soft iron core: the field stays parallel to the plane of the coil over a large part of the rotation, so torque stays near $nIAB$.
- **Several coils at different angles** with a multi-segment commutator: the coil receiving current is always near the maximum-torque position, giving smoother, larger torque with no dead spots.
- **More turns / soft iron core / stronger magnets** (or electromagnets): raise $n$, $B$ and hence torque. Note these also raise back emf at a given speed.

**Managing back emf and its effects**
- **Starting resistance** (the variable resistor, or electronic speed control) limits the large start-up current and is reduced as back emf builds.
- **Variable field electromagnets:** a strong field at start gives high torque; weakening it at speed reduces back emf, allowing a higher speed.
- **Laminated armature core:** reduces eddy currents induced by the same changing flux, reducing heating and the opposing torque.
- **Cooling and low-resistance windings** protect against overheating when the drill stalls and back emf drops.

questions.question:
An observatory monitored the brightness of a distant star P3682 and found regular dips caused by an exoplanet passing in front of it (first graph, time in Earth days). The star's mass is $7.96 \times 10^{30}$ kg and its continuous spectrum is shown in the second graph. Astronomers established these conditions for such an exoplanet to sustain human life:

| Property | Required range |
|---|---|
| Orbital radius of planet | 0.5 – 2.5 times Earth's orbital radius ($1.50 \times 10^{11}$ m) |
| Orbital speed of planet | 2 – 80 $\text{km s}^{-1}$ |
| Temperature of central star | 4000 – 6000 K |

Assess whether humans would be able to live on this exoplanet.
questions.answer:
**Period** (spacing of dips): $T \approx 495$ days $= 4.28\times10^{7}$ s.

**Orbital radius** (Kepler): $r = \left(\dfrac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3} = 2.9\times10^{11}$ m $\approx 1.9$ Earth orbital radii: within range.

**Orbital speed:** $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = 4.3\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1} = 43\ \text{km s}^{-1}$: within range.

**Star temperature** (Wien): peak $\lambda \approx 580$ nm, $T = \dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{580\times10^{-9}} \approx 5000$ K: within range.

**Judgement:** on these three criteria the planet is a candidate for habitation. The data alone cannot show it is habitable, since atmosphere, water, surface temperature, mass/gravity and radiation are unknown, and travel there would be impractical.

*Note: the paper's table gave the orbital radius range in 'Earth radii'; it must mean Earth orbital radii, as the teacher acknowledged.*

questions.question: A $10\ \text{g}$ ball rolls off the edge of a $1\ \text{m}$ tall table at $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. How far from the edge of the table does the ball land?
questions.answer: Vertical: $s=\tfrac12gt^2$, so $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times1}{9.8}}=0.452\ \text{s}$. Horizontal: $x=vt=2\times0.452=0.90\ \text{m}=90\ \text{cm}$ (B). The mass is irrelevant.

questions.question: A conductor (a sliding bar) moves to the left through a uniform magnetic field directed out of the page, along rails that are joined by a wire at the right-hand end, as shown. In which direction does the current flow in the external circuit?
questions.answer: As the bar moves left, the area of the circuit (between the bar and the right-hand end) increases, so the flux out of the page through the circuit increases. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes this by producing a field **into** the page inside the loop, which requires a **clockwise** current (C).

questions.question: Two planets, A and B, orbit the same star. Planet A has an orbital radius of $2\times10^{8}\ \text{m}$ whilst Planet B has an orbital radius of $6\times10^{9}\ \text{m}$. Planet A's mass is $3\times10^{25}\ \text{kg}$ and it has an orbital period of $15$ ooshwucks (a measurement of time on Planet A). What is the orbital period of Planet B in ooshwucks?
questions.answer: Kepler's third law for planets orbiting the same star: $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}=\text{constant}$, so $$T_B=T_A\left(\frac{r_B}{r_A}\right)^{3/2}=15\times\left(\frac{6\times10^{9}}{2\times10^{8}}\right)^{3/2}=15\times30^{1.5}=2465$$ ooshwucks (B). The mass of the planet is irrelevant, and the unit of time does not matter since only a ratio is used.

questions.question: An electron travelling at $3\times10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to the right enters an electric field of strength $10\ \text{N C}^{-1}$ and is deflected. A magnetic field is then set up with direction into the page, acting over the distance of the electric field. This causes the electron to now travel in a straight line. What was the magnetic field strength?
questions.answer: For a straight path the electric and magnetic forces balance: $qE=qvB$, so $B=\dfrac Ev=\dfrac{10}{3\times10^{7}}=3.33\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}$ (A).

questions.question: An electron travelling to the right enters an electric field and is deflected. A magnetic field directed **into the page** is then set up over the same region, which causes the electron to travel in a straight line. What was the direction of the electric field?
questions.answer: For the electron (negative charge) moving to the right in a field into the page, $\mathbf F=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$: $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ is upward for a positive charge, so the magnetic force on the electron is **downward**. For a straight path the electric force on the electron must be **upward**. Since the electron is negative, the electric force is opposite to the field, so the electric field points **down** (D).

questions.question: A rollercoaster manufacturer wants to design their perfectly circular rollercoaster loop (diameter $10\ \text{m}$) such that the passengers will feel weightless once they reach the top of the rollercoaster. At what speed (in $\text{m s}^{-1}$) should the rollercoaster be travelling at the top of the loop for this to occur?
questions.answer:
Passengers feel weightless when the normal force is zero, so gravity alone provides the centripetal force at the top: $mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v=\sqrt{gr}=\sqrt{5g}$ with $r=5\ \text{m}$ (B).

*Note:* the paper asks for the speed at which the rollercoaster *enters* the loop, but its key ($\sqrt{5g}$) is the speed required at the top. The entry speed would be $\sqrt{25g}=5\sqrt g\approx15.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (from $\tfrac12mv_b^2=\tfrac12mv_t^2+mg(10)$), which is not among the options, so the question has been reworded to ask for the speed at the top.

questions.question: What is the altitude of a geostationary satellite (above Earth's surface)?
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite has $T=24\ \text{h}=86\,400\ \text{s}$. From $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}=\dfrac{GM}{4\pi^2}$: $$r=\left(\frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3}\approx4.22\times10^{7}\ \text{m}\ (42{,}200\ \text{km})$$ from the *centre* of the Earth. The altitude above the surface is $r-R_E\approx42{,}200-6{,}400\approx3.6\times10^{4}\ \text{km}$, i.e. option D. ($42{,}230\ \text{km}$ is the orbital radius, not the altitude.)

questions.question: The wires connecting to Mary's household are $240\ \text{V}$ AC with $3.6\ \text{A}$ of current running in them. Her phone charger has a non-ideal step-down transformer inside. If her phone requires $30\ \text{V}$ to charge, what is the most likely current output of the charger?
questions.answer: For an ideal transformer $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$: $I_s=\dfrac{240\times3.6}{30}=28.8\ \text{A}$. A non-ideal transformer loses some power (eddy currents, resistive heating, incomplete flux linkage), so the output power and current are *less* than ideal: $I_s<28.8\ \text{A}$, and the only option below this is $28\ \text{A}$ (B).

questions.question: A projectile is fired from the ground at an angle of $45^\circ$ to the horizontal and hits the ground $20\ \text{m}$ away. Find the maximum height of the projectile.
questions.answer: $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}=\dfrac{u^2}{g}=20$, so $u^2=196$ and $u_y^2=\dfrac{u^2}{2}=98$. Maximum height $h=\dfrac{u_y^2}{2g}=\dfrac{98}{19.6}=5\ \text{m}$ (D). (Alternatively $h=\dfrac{R\tan\theta}{4}=5\ \text{m}$.)

questions.question: A single-turn coil of wire is placed in a uniform magnetic field $B$ (directed downward) at right angles to the plane of the coil as shown in the diagrams. The coil is then rotated in a clockwise direction about the dashed axis as shown. Which of the following shows the direction of current flow in the coil as it begins to rotate?
questions.answer: The field is perpendicular to the plane of the coil, so the flux is a maximum. As the coil begins to rotate, the component of the coil's area perpendicular to $B$ decreases ($\Phi=BA\cos\theta$), so the downward flux *decreases*. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes this by producing a field in the same (downward) direction through the coil, which is a **clockwise** current when viewed from above. This matches option A.

questions.question: A stationary observer on Earth looks at a ship flying past at $0.9c$ with a clock on it. What curious observation does the stationary observer make about the clock on the ship?
options: The clock moves slower than clocks on Earth.
The clock moves faster than clocks on Earth.
The clock was periodically appearing and disappearing.
questions.answer: Time dilation: moving clocks run slow as observed from a different inertial frame, $t=\dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$ (B).

questions.question: Which gauge boson carries the weak nuclear force?
questions.answer: The weak force is mediated by the $W^+$, $W^-$ and $Z^0$ bosons (D). Gluons carry the strong force and photons carry the electromagnetic force; the Higgs boson is associated with giving particles mass.

questions.question: Which of the following was a limitation of the Bohr model?
options: It couldn't explain Hydrogen's emission spectra.
It couldn't explain why electrons do not emit EMR in orbit
It couldn't explain the emission spectra of atoms with multiple electrons in their valence shell.
It couldn't explain why few alpha particles deflected by angles > 90° in the Geiger-Marsden experiment
questions.answer: The Bohr model successfully explained the hydrogen emission spectrum (so A is not a limitation), but it could not explain the spectra of atoms with more than one electron (C), the relative intensities of lines, or the splitting of lines (Zeeman effect). Alpha scattering (D) was explained by Rutherford's nuclear model, and Bohr simply *postulated* that orbiting electrons do not radiate.

questions.question: What is the absolute magnitude of a star?
options: The apparent magnitude of a star measured from a distance of 10 parsecs.
The apparent magnitude of a star measured from Earth.
The apparent brightness of a star measured from a distance of 1 parsec.
The total energy released from a star during one cycle.
questions.answer: Absolute magnitude is the apparent magnitude a star would have if it were placed at a standard distance of $10$ parsecs from the observer, which allows the true luminosities of stars to be compared (A).

questions.question: What did Maxwell define the propagation of electromagnetic waves as?
options: Mutually propagating electric and magnetic fields parallel to each other.
Adjacent particles having completely elastic collisions to transfer energy.
Mutually propagating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other.
Many electrons travelling at the speed of light with energy, $E = hf$.
questions.answer: Maxwell predicted that a changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field and vice versa, so an electromagnetic wave consists of self-propagating electric and magnetic fields that are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (C).

questions.question: Wilhelm Hallwachs set up a gold leaf electroscope as shown (UV light is incident on the metal cap) to investigate the photoelectric effect. What did he observe when the metal cap was positively charged?
options: The gold leaf did not move.
The gold leaf collapsed onto the metal stem.
questions.answer: A positively charged cap with the gold leaf already repelled outwards: UV light can free photoelectrons from the metal, but they are attracted back to the positively charged surface, so no net charge is lost and the leaf does not move (A). (Had the cap been negatively charged, the emitted electrons would leave and the leaf would collapse.)

questions.question: What is the role of magnetic fields in a synchrotron?
questions.answer: The magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to its velocity, so it does no work and cannot change its speed. In a synchrotron the magnets bend the beam around the ring (they *direct* the charged particles), while electric fields in the RF cavities accelerate them (C).

questions.question: The graph shows the continuous blackbody spectrum of a star, Star XLR8 (flux per unit wavelength against wavelength from $400\ \text{nm}$ to $800\ \text{nm}$, with a peak at about $450\ \text{nm}$). Make an educated guess of the colour of Star XLR8.
questions.answer: By Wien's law, $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac bT$, the peak at about $450\ \text{nm}$ (blue) corresponds to $T\approx\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{450\times10^{-9}}\approx6400\ \text{K}$, with more blue light than red across the visible range. The star appears blue (blue-white) (D).

questions.question: A student shot monochromatic light with a wavelength of exactly $656\ \text{nm}$ at a sample of hydrogen gas in a dark room. What did they observe behind the hydrogen sample through a spectroscope, and what electron transition occurred?
options: One black line on a continuous background; $n=2$ to $n=4$
One black line on a continuous background; $n=2$ to $n=3$
One faint bright line on a black background; $n=3$ to $n=2$
One faint bright line on a black background; $n=4$ to $n=2$
questions.answer: The source is monochromatic, so the only light that can reach the spectroscope is at $656\ \text{nm}$: there is no continuous background, which rules out options A and B (a dark absorption line requires a continuous spectrum). The $656\ \text{nm}$ line is the red Balmer H-$\alpha$ line, with photon energy $\Delta E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=1.89\ \text{eV}=13.6\left(\dfrac1{2^2}-\dfrac1{3^2}\right)$, corresponding to the $n=3\leftrightarrow n=2$ transition. The student sees a single faint bright line on a black background (C).

questions.question: An astronaut from Earth travelled to a planet $10$ light years away at a speed of $0.995c$. He stays there for $10$ years to relax and then returns to Earth at the same speed. What is the age gap now between him and his twin sister to the nearest year?
questions.answer:
Earth frame: each leg takes $\dfrac{10}{0.995}=10.05$ years, so the sister ages $2\times10.05+10=30.1$ years.

Astronaut: $\gamma=\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-0.995^2}}=10.0$, so the travelling time is $\dfrac{20.1}{10.0}=2.0$ years, plus the $10$ years at the planet: $12.0$ years.

Age gap $=30.1-12.0\approx18$ years, with the **sister older** (C).

questions.question: An $800\ \text{kg}$ F1 car travels on a rough banked track (inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal) in circular motion, at its maximum speed around the corner. State ALL the forces acting on the car, and state the direction of the net force.

An $800\ \text{kg}$ F1 car travels on a rough banked track (inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal) in circular motion at its maximum speed. If the radius of the track is $100\ \text{m}$ and the coefficient of friction of the track is $0.30$, find the maximum speed at which the car can travel around the track.
questions.answer:
At maximum speed friction acts down the slope with $F_{\text{fric}}=\mu N$.

Vertical (no acceleration): $N\cos\theta=mg+\mu N\sin\theta\ \Rightarrow\ N(\cos\theta-\mu\sin\theta)=mg$.

Horizontal (centripetal): $N\sin\theta+\mu N\cos\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\ \Rightarrow\ N(\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta)=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

Dividing: $$v_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{gr(\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta)}{\cos\theta-\mu\sin\theta}}=\sqrt{\frac{9.8\times100\times(\sin30^\circ+0.30\cos30^\circ)}{\cos30^\circ-0.30\sin30^\circ}}=32\ \text{m s}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: Below is a DC motor with a $5$-turn square coil of side length $4\ \text{cm}$, external magnetic field strength of $2\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}$ and constant current of $25\ \text{A}$.
