In the position shown, the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field. Calculate the torque experienced by the coil and state which direction it will rotate.
questions.answer: With the plane of the coil parallel to the field the torque is a maximum: $$\tau=nBIA=5\times(2\times10^{-3})\times25\times(0.04\times0.04)=4\times10^{-4}\ \text{N m}.$$ The coil rotates **anti-clockwise** (as seen in the diagram, from the direction of the motor effect forces on the two sides of the coil).

questions.question: Identify the purpose of a DC motor, and explain how it functions (no need to explain the split-ring commutator).
questions.answer:
**Purpose:** a DC motor converts electrical energy into kinetic (mechanical, rotational) energy.

**How it works:** current from the DC supply flows through the armature coil, which sits in the magnetic field of the permanent magnets. By the motor effect ($F=nBIl\sin\theta$) a force acts on each of the two sides of the coil perpendicular to the field. Because the current flows in opposite directions along the two sides, the forces are in opposite directions (one up, one down), and together they produce a torque on the coil, so it rotates about its axle.

questions.question: Compare a split-ring commutator to a slip ring.
questions.answer:
**Split-ring commutator (DC motors/generators):** a ring split into two halves, each connected to one end of the coil, with brushes touching it. Every half turn, as the coil passes the vertical position, the contacts swap which half touches which brush, so the **direction of the current in the coil reverses**. This keeps the torque in the same direction, so the motor spins continuously in one direction (in a DC generator it converts the alternating induced current into a direct current).

**Slip rings (AC generators/alternators):** two complete, unbroken rings, each permanently connected to one end of the coil, with brushes touching them. They provide a continuous connection that does **not** reverse the current, so the current in the external circuit alternates (AC) as it does in the coil.

**Contrast:** a split-ring commutator reverses the connection every half-rotation (producing DC); slip rings maintain the same connection (producing AC).

**Similarity:** both transfer current between the rotating coil (armature) and the stationary external circuit through brushes.

questions.question: A student was about to start a DC motor, but the teacher suggested they use a variable resistor before starting it. Why did the teacher suggest this?
questions.answer:
A spinning motor coil cuts the magnetic field, so by Faraday's law an EMF is induced in it that opposes the supply voltage (Lenz's law). This is the **back EMF**, which is proportional to the speed of rotation and reduces the net voltage across the coil: $I=\dfrac{V_{\text{supply}}-\varepsilon_{\text{back}}}{R}$.

When the motor is first started it is at rest, so the back EMF is zero and the current is $I=\dfrac{V_{\text{supply}}}{R}$, which is very large because the resistance of the coil is small. This very large starting current could overheat and damage the coil or overload the supply.

A variable resistor in series (set to a high resistance at the start) limits the starting current. As the motor speeds up and the back EMF increases, the resistance can be reduced.

questions.question: Satvik Gupta is in a hot air balloon at rest on a $10\ \text{m}$ tall platform. It starts rising vertically at a constant acceleration of $2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Satvik stops the burner after $5$ seconds, and immediately throws his English text horizontally at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (in his frame of reference) which impacts the ground sometime later. At what height off the ground did Satvik throw his English text?
questions.answer: $s_y=u_yt+\tfrac12a_yt^2=0+\tfrac12(2)(5)^2=25\ \text{m}$ above the platform, so the height above the ground is $25+10=35\ \text{m}$.

questions.question: Satvik Gupta is in a hot air balloon at rest on a $10\ \text{m}$ tall platform. It starts rising vertically at a constant acceleration of $2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Satvik stops the burner after $5$ seconds, and immediately throws his English text horizontally at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (in his frame of reference). Determine the initial velocity of the English text as viewed from the ground.
questions.answer:
At the moment of the throw the balloon (and so the text) is moving upward: $v_y=u_y+a_yt=0+(2)(5)=10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ upward.

Initial velocity from the ground: $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ horizontally and $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ upwards, so $$|v|=\sqrt{10^2+20^2}=22\ \text{m s}^{-1},\qquad\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{10}{20}=27^\circ$$ above the horizontal.

questions.question: Satvik Gupta throws his English text from a height of $35\ \text{m}$ above the ground. As viewed from the ground, its initial velocity is $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ horizontally and $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ upwards. Determine the time of flight and range of the English text.
questions.answer: Vertical (taking up as positive): $s_y=u_yt+\tfrac12a_yt^2$, so $-35=10t-4.9t^2$, i.e. $4.9t^2-10t-35=0$: $$t=\frac{10+\sqrt{100+686}}{9.8}=3.9\ \text{s}.$$ Range: $x=u_xt=20\times3.88=78\ \text{m}$.

questions.question: Satvik Gupta throws his English text from a height of $35\ \text{m}$ with an initial velocity (as viewed from the ground) of $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ horizontally and $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ upwards. It lands $3.88\ \text{s}$ later. Determine the velocity of the English text on impact.
questions.answer:
$v_x=20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. $v_y=u_y+at=10-9.8\times3.88=-28.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (downward).

$|v|=\sqrt{20^2+28.0^2}=34\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $\theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{28.0}{20}=54^\circ$ below the horizontal.

questions.question: Satvik Gupta is in a hot air balloon rising vertically at $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ when he stops the burner (so the balloon and its contents are then in free fall) and throws his English text horizontally from a height of $35\ \text{m}$. If the landing platform is removed so that Satvik also lands on the ground, what is the time difference between himself and the English text impacting the ground?
questions.answer: **Zero.** After the burner stops, both Satvik (with the balloon) and the text have the same initial vertical velocity ($10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ up), the same vertical acceleration ($g$ downward) and start from the same height. Horizontal motion does not affect the vertical motion, so they reach the ground at the same time.

questions.question: Early electric generators were often very simple. A hand-operated version is a metal disc rotated between the poles of a magnet by a handle, with Brush X touching the metal axle and Brush Y touching the rim of the disc (Brush Y is at the bottom). The diagram shows the metal disc viewed from the handle, rotating anti-clockwise, with the lower part of the disc in a region of uniform magnetic field (out of the page). Describe the eddy currents that form on the metal disc, and explain why they form.
questions.answer:
As the disc rotates, the part of the disc moving into and out of the magnetic field has a **changing magnetic flux** through it. By **Faraday's law**, an EMF is induced in the metal, and because the disc is a conductor this drives circulating **eddy currents** (small loops of current that swirl within the disc, as drawn in the answer image: two loops of opposite sense side by side, which flow together through the central region towards the rim at Brush Y).

By **Lenz's law**, the eddy currents flow in the direction that produces magnetic fields opposing the change in flux that causes them (and, by the motor effect, they exert a force that opposes the rotation).

questions.question: In a hand-operated generator (a metal disc rotating in a magnetic field, with Brush X touching the axle and Brush Y touching the rim of the disc), explain which direction current will flow in the external circuit (X to Y or Y to X).
questions.answer: The eddy currents in the two regions of the disc swirl in opposite senses, so where the loops meet they converge near the centre-line of the disc and flow along the metal disc together, down towards the rim at Brush Y. The EMF therefore drives current through the disc towards Y and then round the external circuit (the globe) back to the axle: current flows from **Y to X** in the external circuit.

questions.question: Briefly explain two strategies used to increase the efficiency of transformers.
questions.answer:
1. **Use a soft iron core**: it has a high magnetic permeability, so it increases the flux linkage between the primary and secondary coils (less flux is lost), which makes more of the input power available at the output.
2. **Laminate the iron core** (thin insulated sheets): this breaks up the paths available to the eddy currents induced in the core, reducing their size, which reduces resistive (heat) energy losses and so increases efficiency.

(Other accepted strategies: wrapping the primary and secondary coils on top of each other for greater flux linkage; using thick, low-resistance wire and cooling fins to reduce resistive heating.)

questions.question: An electron is shot at $4\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal from the lower plate into the electric field between two infinitely long parallel plates $5\ \text{cm}$ apart. The top plate is at $0\ \text{V}$ (negative) and the bottom plate is at $10\ \text{V}$ (positive). Find the acceleration experienced by the electron.
questions.answer: $E=\dfrac Vd=\dfrac{10}{0.05}=200\ \text{V m}^{-1}$. The only significant force is the electric force: $ma=qE$, so $$a=\frac{qE}{m}=\frac{1.602\times10^{-19}\times200}{9.109\times10^{-31}}=3.5\times10^{13}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$$ directed **downward** (the electron is attracted to the positive plate, opposite to the field direction).

questions.question: An electron is shot at $4\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal from the lower (positive, $10\ \text{V}$) plate into the electric field between two infinitely long parallel plates $5\ \text{cm}$ apart. The top plate is at $0\ \text{V}$. The electron's acceleration is $3.5\times10^{13}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ downward. Determine the velocity of the electron upon impact and which plate it hits.
questions.answer:
$u_x=4\times10^{6}\cos30^\circ=3.46\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (constant) and $u_y=4\times10^{6}\sin30^\circ=2.0\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ upward.

**Which plate?** The greatest height the electron could reach is $\dfrac{u_y^2}{2a}=\dfrac{(2\times10^6)^2}{2\times3.52\times10^{13}}=0.057\ \text{m}=5.7\ \text{cm}>5\ \text{cm}$, so it reaches the top plate: it hits the **negative (top, $0\ \text{V}$) plate**.

**Velocity on impact:** $v_y^2=u_y^2-2ad=(2\times10^6)^2-2(3.52\times10^{13})(0.05)=4.83\times10^{11}$, so $v_y=6.9\times10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ upward.

$$|v|=\sqrt{(3.46\times10^6)^2+(6.9\times10^5)^2}=3.5\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1},\qquad\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{6.9\times10^5}{3.46\times10^6}=11^\circ$$ above the horizontal. (Check by energy: the electron loses $10\ \text{eV}$ of its $45.5\ \text{eV}$ kinetic energy, giving $v=3.5\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.)

*Note:* the paper's solution finds the same speed, but its angle ($2.1^\circ$) comes from subtracting $\Delta v_y=\sqrt{2qV/m}$ from $u_y$, which is not valid (the energy change is $\tfrac12m(v_y^2-u_y^2)$, not $\tfrac12m(\Delta v_y)^2$); the correct angle is about $11^\circ$.

questions.question:
A student conducts an experiment using a photoelectric cell. Light is shone through a grid onto a metal surface. The metal is at earth potential and the grid is at $100\ \text{V}$, so that any electrons emitted from the surface produce a current in the external circuit. The student shines light sources of different photon energies onto the metal surface, with equal intensities, and records the current flowing for each.

| Photon energy (eV) | Photo-current ($\mu$A) |
|---|---|
| 0.50 | 0 |
| 0.90 | 0 |
| 1.20 | 0.5 |
| 1.70 | 2.8 |
| 1.75 | 4.0 |
| 1.90 | 8.0 |
| 2.20 | 9.2 |
| 2.50 | 9.4 |

Describe the straight line of best fit through the points in the region where the photo-current varies the most with photon energy (give its gradient and where it meets the photon-energy axis).
questions.answer: The steep region is between about $1.6$ and $1.9\ \text{eV}$ (points $(1.70, 2.8)$, $(1.75, 4.0)$ and $(1.90, 8.0)$). The best-fit line through these rises from the photon-energy axis at about $1.6\ \text{eV}$ to about $10\ \mu\text{A}$ at about $1.95\ \text{eV}$: gradient $\approx\dfrac{10}{0.35}\approx30\ \mu\text{A eV}^{-1}$ (the red line in the answer image).

questions.question: In a photoelectric cell experiment, the line of best fit through the steep region of the photo-current against photon energy graph meets the photon-energy axis at about $1.6\ \text{eV}$ (points $(1.70,2.8)$, $(1.75,4.0)$, $(1.90,8.0)$ $\mu$A, with no current for photon energies of $0.9\ \text{eV}$ or less). From the line, estimate the minimum energy (work function) for photoelectric emission.
questions.answer: Photoelectrons are only emitted when the photon energy is at least the work function, $hf\ge\phi$. The photocurrent is zero below this threshold, so the work function is where the line meets the photon-energy axis: $\phi\approx1.6\ \text{eV}$.

questions.question: In a photoelectric cell experiment, the photo-current against photon energy graph (with equal-intensity light sources) has a steep section with a gradient of about $30\ \mu\text{A eV}^{-1}$ meeting the photon-energy axis at $1.6\ \text{eV}$. The experiment is repeated, but the intensities of the light sources are doubled. Predict the results of this new experiment by describing the new line.
questions.answer: The new line starts at the same point on the photon-energy axis ($1.6\ \text{eV}$, since the work function is a property of the metal and does not depend on intensity), but it has **double the gradient** (about $60\ \mu\text{A eV}^{-1}$). So it is steeper and lies to the left of the first line (the blue line in the answer image), and the maximum (saturation) current is also doubled.

questions.question: In a photoelectric cell experiment, the experiment is repeated with the intensities of the light sources doubled, and the photo-current against photon energy graph then has twice the gradient of the original line, starting from the same threshold energy. Justify this.
questions.answer: Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons arriving per second (each photon's energy $hf$ is unchanged). Each photon with energy above the work function releases at most one photoelectron, so twice as many photons release twice as many electrons per second. The photocurrent (charge per second) therefore doubles at each photon energy, which doubles the gradient. The threshold energy is unchanged because it depends only on the metal's work function.

questions.question: Explain how analysing stellar spectra can inform us about the characteristics of stars.
questions.answer:
**Surface temperature.** The *continuous blackbody spectrum* of a star peaks at a wavelength that depends on its surface temperature (Wien's law, $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac bT$): a hotter star has its peak at a shorter wavelength (blue stars are hotter than red stars). The relative strengths of particular absorption lines also depend on temperature, which is used to classify stars into spectral classes (O, B, A, F, G, K, M).

**Chemical composition.** The *absorption spectrum* of a star shows dark lines at wavelengths that match the emission/absorption lines of particular elements (e.g. hydrogen, helium, calcium) in the cooler outer atmosphere of the star. Identifying the pattern of lines identifies which elements are present.

**Velocity and rotation.** The wavelengths of the *absorption lines* are Doppler shifted relative to their laboratory values: a shift to longer wavelengths (red-shift) means the star is moving away, and to shorter wavelengths (blue-shift) means it is moving towards us (radial velocity). The lines are also *broadened* for a rapidly rotating star, because one side is approaching and the other receding.

questions.question: Match each type of radioactive decay (alpha, beta, gamma) to the ionising and penetrating powers: (i) high ionising power, low penetrating power; (ii) medium ionising power, medium penetrating power; (iii) low ionising power, high penetrating power.
questions.answer:
(i) **Alpha** — high ionising power, low penetrating power.

(ii) **Beta** — medium ionising power, medium penetrating power.

(iii) **Gamma** — low ionising power, high penetrating power.

questions.question: Explain the different ionising and penetrating powers of the three types of radioactive decay (alpha, beta and gamma).
questions.answer:
Ionising power depends on how strongly the radiation interacts with atoms along its path (by electrostatic forces), and so on the charge and mass of the radiation. Penetrating power is inversely related: the more an emission ionises, the faster it loses energy.

- **Alpha particles** (${}^4_2\text{He}$ nuclei) are relatively massive and have a charge of $+2$, so they interact very strongly with atoms and strip electrons readily (high ionising power). They lose their energy over a very short distance, so they have low penetrating power (stopped by paper or a few cm of air).
- **Beta particles** (electrons) have much less mass and a charge of $-1$, so they ionise less (medium) and penetrate further (stopped by a few mm of aluminium).
- **Gamma rays** are high-energy photons with no mass and no charge, so they interact only rarely with atoms (low ionising power) and pass through large distances of material (high penetrating power; reduced by thick lead or concrete).

questions.question: Carbon-14 decays into Nitrogen-14. Give a complete equation to show this decay.
questions.answer: This is beta-minus decay (a neutron changes into a proton, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino): $${}^{14}_{6}\text{C}\rightarrow{}^{14}_{7}\text{N}+{}^{\ 0}_{-1}e+\bar\nu_e.$$

questions.question: Calculate the energy released from the decay of Carbon-14 to Nitrogen-14 in MeV if the mass of Carbon-14 $=14.00421\ \text{u}$, Nitrogen-14 $=14.00307\ \text{u}$ and an electron $=0.00055\ \text{u}$.
questions.answer:
Mass defect: $\Delta m=m_{\text{reactants}}-m_{\text{products}}=14.00421-(14.00307+0.00055)=0.00059\ \text{u}$.

$E=\Delta mc^2=0.00059\times931.5\ \text{MeV}=0.55\ \text{MeV}$.

questions.question: A student found a skull and measured its age using Carbon-14 dating. The half-life of Carbon-14 is $5{,}730$ years. He measured the mass of Carbon-14 in the skull to be $1.45\ \text{g}$. If the skull initially had $92.8\ \text{g}$ of Carbon-14 in it, find the age of the skull.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{N}{N_0}=\left(\dfrac12\right)^n$: $\dfrac{1.45}{92.8}=\dfrac1{64}=\left(\dfrac12\right)^n$, so $n=6$ half-lives. Age $=6\times5730=34{,}380$ years ($\approx3.4\times10^4$ years).

questions.question: Unpolarised light rays of intensity $I_0$ pass through two polarising filters $P_1$ and $P_2$ to a light detector. The filters are originally aligned so that they produce the maximum amount of light, then filter $P_2$ is slowly rotated through $180^\circ$. Sketch a graph showing how the intensity of the light at the detector, $I$, changes as $P_2$ rotates from $0$ to $180^\circ$.
questions.answer: The unpolarised light is reduced to $\dfrac{I_0}{2}$ by $P_1$. Then by Malus' law $I=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle by which $P_2$ has been rotated. The graph has a $\cos^2\theta$ shape: it starts at the maximum $\dfrac{I_0}{2}$ at $0^\circ$, falls to zero at $90^\circ$, and returns to $\dfrac{I_0}{2}$ at $180^\circ$.

questions.question: Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ passes through two polarising filters $P_1$ and $P_2$ to a light detector. $P_2$ is rotated to a position so that no light reaches the detector (it is at $90^\circ$ to $P_1$). Without moving $P_1$ or $P_2$, a third polariser filter ($P_{1.5}$) is inserted between $P_1$ and $P_2$ at an angle of $30^\circ$ from $P_1$. Explain using calculations or diagrams why the light intensity at the detector is no longer zero.
questions.answer:
After $P_1$: $I_1=\dfrac{I_0}{2}$.

Through $P_{1.5}$ (at $30^\circ$ to $P_1$): $I_{1.5}=I_1\cos^230^\circ=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\times\dfrac34=\dfrac38I_0$.

$P_2$ is now at $90^\circ-30^\circ=60^\circ$ to $P_{1.5}$: $I_2=I_{1.5}\cos^260^\circ=\dfrac38I_0\times\dfrac14=\dfrac{3}{32}I_0$.

So the intensity at the detector is $\dfrac3{32}I_0\ne0$: the middle filter rotates the plane of polarisation of the light, so some component of the light is now parallel to the axis of $P_2$.

questions.question: Many attempts have been made to measure the speed of light, some horrendous like Galileo approximating the speed of light to $3400\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, and some better ones today which can measure the speed of light to $9$ significant figures. Contrast a HISTORICAL method to a CONTEMPORARY method of measuring the speed of light.
questions.answer:
**Historical method: Fizeau's toothed wheel (1849).** A beam of light was passed through a gap in a rotating toothed wheel, travelled a long distance ($\approx8.6\ \text{km}$) to a mirror, and was reflected back to the wheel. The speed of rotation was increased until the returning light was blocked by the next tooth. Then the time for the round trip $t=\dfrac{2d}{c}$ equals the time for the wheel to turn from a gap to a tooth (a known fraction of a revolution), so $c=\dfrac{2d}{t}$. Result: $c\approx3.15\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (uncertainty of several percent).

**Contemporary method: laser interferometry / electronic distance meter.** The frequency $f$ of a stable laser (measured against an atomic clock) and its wavelength $\lambda$ (measured by interferometry, counting fringes) are measured, and $c=f\lambda$. Since 1983 the metre has been *defined* from the speed of light, which is fixed at $299\,792\,458\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Contrast:** the historical method relied on mechanical apparatus, human observation of the light being blocked, and a long path through air, giving a low precision (about 1–5%). The contemporary method uses lasers, electronic detectors and atomic-clock time standards, giving a precision of about one part in $10^9$, and uses a much more compact apparatus. Both use the relationship between distance (or wavelength) and time (or frequency) for light.

questions.question: The early 1900s saw significant development to our understanding of the atom. De Broglie made a significant prediction about the particle-wave duality. Explain what his prediction was and support that prediction with ONE piece of experimental evidence.
questions.answer:
De Broglie proposed that, just as light behaves as both a wave and a particle, **matter also has a wave nature**: all particles of momentum $p=mv$ have an associated matter wave of wavelength $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}$.

**Evidence: the Davisson–Germer experiment (1927).** A beam of electrons accelerated through a known potential difference was fired at a nickel crystal. The scattered electrons were detected at different angles, and a strong peak in the intensity of scattered electrons was observed at $50^\circ$. This is an interference/diffraction pattern: the atoms of the crystal act as a diffraction grating (Bragg diffraction), and the wavelength calculated from the diffraction angle matched de Broglie's $\lambda=\dfrac h{mv}$ for the electrons ($\approx0.165\ \text{nm}$). (G. P. Thomson's electron diffraction through thin metal foil, which produced ring patterns like X-rays, is another example.)

questions.question: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a $50\ \text{g}$ tennis ball travelling at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Then explain why we do not observe everyday objects such as tennis balls to show wave properties.
questions.answer:
$\lambda=\dfrac h{mv}=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{0.050\times20}=6.6\times10^{-34}\ \text{m}$.

Wave properties such as diffraction and interference are only observable when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the gaps or obstacles the wave meets (about $10^{-10}\ \text{m}$ for atoms). The ball's wavelength is far smaller than the size of any object or gap it could pass through (even an atomic nucleus is about $10^{-15}\ \text{m}$), so no diffraction or interference effects could ever be detected: because $h$ is so small and the momentum of everyday objects so large, their wavelength is immeasurably small.

questions.question: Explain how de Broglie was able to derive Bohr's third postulate: \"the angular momentum ($mvr$) of electrons in orbit about a nucleus is quantised as $\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, where $n$ is a whole number.\" In your answer, use a diagram to illustrate the case for $n=4$.
questions.answer:
De Broglie treated an orbiting electron as a matter wave. For the orbit to be stable the wave must form a **standing wave**, so the circumference of the orbit must hold a whole number of wavelengths (otherwise the wave would interfere destructively with itself): $$n\lambda=2\pi r.$$ Substituting the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda=\dfrac h{mv}$: $$\frac{nh}{mv}=2\pi r\ \Rightarrow\ mvr=\frac{nh}{2\pi},$$ which is Bohr's third postulate: the angular momentum is quantised in whole-number multiples of $\dfrac h{2\pi}$.

For $n=4$: $4\lambda=2\pi r$, i.e. exactly four wavelengths fit around the orbit (see the diagram).

questions.question:
Consider the electric field between two parallel plates, shown in the diagram (the top plate is positive and the bottom plate is negative, so the field points downwards).

Which particle, fired horizontally from the left and moving into the field, would experience the greatest electric force upwards?
questions.answer: The field points down, so the force on a negative charge is upward (alpha particles and protons are positive and are pushed down). $F=qE$, and the $\text{O}^{2-}$ ion carries $2e$ compared with $e$ for the electron, so it feels the greatest upward force.

questions.question:
The diagram (not to scale) shows two identical satellites orbiting a planet. The orbital radius of satellite X is $r$. Satellite Y is $2r$ from the planet's centre.

How would the gravitational potential energy of satellite Y change if it was moved into the same orbit as X?
options: It would increase by a factor of 2.
It would decrease by a factor of 2.
It would increase by a factor of 4.
It would decrease by a factor of 4.
questions.answer: $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. At $2r$, $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$; at $r$, $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. The potential energy becomes twice as negative, i.e. it decreases by a factor of 2 (B).

questions.question:
A $50\ \text{g}$ mass is rotating at 25 revolutions per minute at $15\ \text{cm}$ from the centre of a turntable.

How would the angular velocity of this mass change if it continued to rotate with the same frequency, but was moved to a position $20\ \text{cm}$ from the centre?
options: The angular velocity would be 1.5 times greater.
The angular velocity would decrease by one third.
The angular velocity would decrease by two thirds.
The angular velocity would not change.
questions.answer: Angular velocity $\omega=2\pi f$ depends only on the frequency of rotation, not on the radius, so it does not change (D). Only the linear speed $v=\omega r$ changes.

questions.question: Which option best displays the directions of the centripetal force and instantaneous velocity of a satellite orbiting the Earth?
questions.answer: The centripetal (gravitational) force points towards the centre of the Earth, and the instantaneous velocity is along the tangent to the orbit, i.e. perpendicular to the force. Only D shows both.

questions.question: Which option identifies the characteristics of the motion of a charged particle when it is injected into a uniform magnetic field?
options: The vertical velocity is greater than the horizontal velocity.
Both the net velocity and acceleration are constant.
It has constant horizontal motion and uniformly accelerated vertical motion.
It has constant vertical motion and uniformly accelerated horizontal motion.
questions.answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work: the speed is constant, and (with a constant-magnitude force) so is the magnitude of the acceleration, although their directions keep changing and the path is a circle/helix. Options C and D describe parabolic motion in a uniform electric field or gravitational field, and A has no basis. B is the best available choice (note: the paper's option B is only strictly correct for the magnitudes of velocity and acceleration).

questions.question:
A projectile is launched directly upwards.

Which pair of graphs best displays how the horizontal velocity ($v_x$, left) and vertical velocity ($v_y$, right) change over time? (Dashed lines show the graphs; the solid line is the time axis.)
questions.answer: With only gravity acting (no air resistance) the horizontal velocity stays constant, so the $v_x$ graph is a horizontal line, while the vertical velocity changes uniformly at $-g$: a straight line of negative gradient that passes through zero at the top of the flight and becomes negative on the way down. Graph A is the only pair with constant $v_x$ and a single straight line of negative gradient for $v_y$ (B has a V-shape, which would be speed rather than velocity; C and D have a changing $v_x$).

questions.question:
The diagram shows a polarising filter which has its polarising axis vertical and an analyser which has its polarising axis at an angle $\theta$ to the first.

What value for angle $\theta$ will allow only $30\%$ of the light intensity incident on the analyser to pass through the analyser?
questions.answer: Malus' law: $I=I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$, so $\cos^2\theta=0.30$, $\cos\theta=0.5477$, $\theta=56.8^\circ\approx57^\circ$ (C).

questions.question:
Three parallel current-carrying wires are set up as shown, each carrying $150\ \text{A}$ (in the directions shown). Wire X is $3d$ from wire Y, and wire Z is $d$ from wire Y. The net force on wire Y due to the other two wires is $F$.

What will happen to the force on Y if the currents in X and Z are each halved, but the distances stay the same?
options: It will decrease by a factor of 4 to $F/4$.
questions.answer: The force per unit length on Y from each wire is $\dfrac{\mu_0 I_Y I}{2\pi r}$, which is proportional to the current in the other wire. Y is attracted to Z (parallel currents) and repelled by X (opposite currents), so both forces act in the same direction (towards Z) and add. Halving $I_X$ and $I_Z$ halves each force, so the net force halves to $F/2$ (A). $I_Y$ is unchanged.

questions.question:
The figure shows a vehicle travelling in a horizontal circle at constant speed on a frictionless banked track.

Which arrow, A, B, C or D, represents the direction of the normal force on the vehicle?
questions.answer: The normal force acts perpendicular to the surface of the track and away from it, which is arrow A. (D is the weight, B is the horizontal net/centripetal force direction.)

questions.question:
A transformer with 1200 turns in the primary coil and 300 turns in the secondary coil has a current of $1.75\ \text{A}$ in the secondary coil (the current drawn from it).

If the transformer is ideal, what is the current in the primary coil?
questions.answer: $\dfrac{I_p}{I_s}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$, so $I_p=1.75\times\dfrac{300}{1200}=0.4375\approx0.438\ \text{A}$ (B).

questions.question: In one of Thomson's experiments in 1897 he accelerated electrons to a speed of $2.65\times10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What is the de Broglie wavelength of these electrons?

Two spaceships Alpha and Delta are travelling towards each other, with velocities relative to space of $0.8c$ (Alpha) and $0.6c$ (Delta) as shown.

If Alpha sent a beam of light to Delta, what would the velocity of the light be when it reaches Delta?
questions.answer: By Einstein's second postulate the speed of light in a vacuum is the same, $c$, for all inertial observers regardless of the motion of the source or the observer. The light travels at $1.0c$ as measured by Delta (A).

questions.question:
The diagram shows an experiment set up to demonstrate the photoelectric effect. Light is directed onto a metal plate (cathode) and the photocurrent is measured using the ammeter.

If the frequency of the light is increased, what effect will this have?
options: The number of electrons emitted from the metal plate will increase.
The maximum photoelectron kinetic energy will increase.
questions.answer: $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$: increasing $f$ increases the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons (C), and hence the stopping potential also increases (so B is wrong). The number of electrons emitted and the photocurrent depend on the light intensity (number of photons), not frequency.

questions.question: When pushing on a very heavy door to close it, which of the following describes how to achieve maximum torque?
options: The force should be applied at right angles to the door at the smallest distance possible from the hinge.
The force should be applied at $45^\circ$ to the door at the smallest distance possible from the hinge.
The force should be applied at right angles to the door at the middle distance between the outer edge of the door and the hinge.
The force should be applied at right angles to the door at the largest distance possible from the hinge.
questions.answer: $\tau=rF\sin\theta$ is maximised when $\sin\theta=1$ (force at $90^\circ$ to the door) and $r$ is as large as possible (at the outer edge, furthest from the hinge) (D).

questions.question:
Monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$ strikes a double slit and produces bright and dark fringes on a screen. Light from slit $S_1$ travels along path $P_1$ and light from slit $S_2$ travels along path $P_2$ to produce the bright fringe shown in the diagram.

What is the difference in length between $P_1$ and $P_2$?
questions.answer: For a bright fringe (constructive interference) the path difference must be a whole number of wavelengths, $m\lambda$, which rules out B and D. From the diagram the fringe shown is the second-order bright fringe ($m=2$), so the path difference is $2\lambda$ (C), as given in the school's answer.

questions.question:
A coil in a simple DC motor rotates through $360^\circ$ within a uniform magnetic field. Initially the normal to the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field lines.

Which graph best shows how the magnetic flux through the coil varies over time through one rotation?
questions.answer: $\Phi=BA\cos\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the normal and the field. Initially $\theta=90^\circ$ so $\Phi=0$; the flux then rises to a maximum, falls through zero to a negative maximum (the coil faces the other way) and returns to zero after $360^\circ$. This is a sine curve starting at zero (A).

questions.question:
James Chadwick discovered the neutron by observing its properties in an experiment like the one in the diagram: alpha particles from a polonium source strike substance X, which emits neutrons; the neutrons strike substance Y, which emits protons that are detected.

What is substance Y?
questions.answer: Substance X is beryllium (it emits neutrons when struck by alpha particles). Neutrons are uncharged so are not detected directly, but they knock protons out of a hydrogen-rich material, paraffin wax, and the protons are detected (D).

questions.question:
A charged particle $q$ enters a uniform magnetic field $B$ at velocity $v$. The particle follows a circular path of radius $r$ as shown.

If the velocity was doubled, what other change could be made to keep the radius the same?
questions.answer: $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$. Doubling $v$ doubles $r$, so $q$ (or $B$) must be doubled to restore the original radius. Doubling the charge (A) works; the other options make $r$ larger or leave it the same as doubled.

questions.question:
The diagram shows an attempt to measure the speed of light by passing a beam through a toothed wheel and observing reflections from a distant mirror.

Which person is this experiment attributed to?
questions.answer: A rotating toothed wheel with a distant mirror was Fizeau's method (1849). Galileo used lanterns, Romer used Jupiter's moons, and Michelson used a rotating octagonal mirror.

questions.question:
The diagram shows the intensity versus wavelength for spectra of light from sources X and Y.

Which option best compares the temperatures of the two bodies?
options: Source X has a higher temperature because its peak wavelength is shorter than Y's.
Source X has a higher temperature because the intensity at its peak wavelength is higher than Y's.
Source X has a higher temperature because the total area under its graph is greater than Y's.
Source Y has a higher temperature because its peak intensity is at a longer wavelength than that of X.
questions.answer: By Wien's law $\lambda_{\max}=b/T$, a shorter peak wavelength means a higher temperature. X peaks at about 800 nm compared with about 1500 nm for Y, so X is hotter (A).

questions.question: What is a geostationary satellite?
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite has an orbital period equal to the Earth's rotational period (24 hours), and it orbits in the plane of the equator in the same direction as the Earth rotates, at an altitude of about $36\,000\ \text{km}$. As a result it stays above the same point on the Earth's surface.

questions.question: State one important function of a geostationary satellite.
questions.answer: Telecommunications (e.g. satellite TV and phone relay). Other acceptable uses: weather observation or oceanography.

questions.question: During the 1971 mission to the Moon, astronaut Alan Shepard hit a golf ball on level, flat ground. The Moon has a mass of $7.342\times10^{22}\ \text{kg}$ and a radius of $1737.4\ \text{km}$. Find the acceleration due to gravity on the Moon.

On the Moon (where $g=1.62\ \text{m s}^{-2}$) astronaut Alan Shepard hit a golf ball that landed $40.0\ \text{m}$ from where it was hit, on level flat ground. The ball was launched at an angle of $35.0^\circ$ to the horizontal. Determine the initial launch speed of the ball.
questions.answer:
Vertical: $\Delta y=0$ at landing, so $0=u\sin35^\circ\,t-\tfrac12(1.62)t^2$, giving $t=\dfrac{2u\sin35^\circ}{1.62}$.

Horizontal: $40.0=u\cos35^\circ\,t=\dfrac{2u^2\sin35^\circ\cos35^\circ}{1.62}$.

$$u^2=\frac{40.0\times1.62}{2\sin35^\circ\cos35^\circ}=\frac{64.8}{0.9397}=68.96,\qquad u\approx 8.30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$
(The school's solution gives $8.31\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, a rounding difference.)

questions.question: On the Moon ($g=1.62\ \text{m s}^{-2}$) a golf ball is launched at $35.0^\circ$ to the horizontal with an initial speed of $8.31\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from level ground. What is the maximum height above ground level reached by the golf ball?
questions.answer:
At the top $v_y=0$ with $u_y=8.31\sin35^\circ=4.77\ \text{m s}^{-1}$:
$$0=u_y^2-2gs\ \Rightarrow\ s=\frac{4.77^2}{2\times1.62}=\frac{22.7}{3.24}=7.00\ \text{m}$$

questions.question:
Students carried out an experiment to determine the relationship between the radius and velocity for a $55\ \text{g}$ mass moving with uniform circular motion. The centripetal force was kept constant for each variation in radius. The time for 10 complete cycles was measured. The results are shown in the table.

| Radius of path (cm) | Time for 10 cycles (s) |
|---|---|
| 10 | 4.3 |
| 20 | 6.1 |
| 30 | 7.3 |
| 40 | 8.5 |
| 50 | 9.5 |
| 60 | 10.1 |

They were asked to use all the results to determine the magnitude of the constant centripetal force. List and explain the steps of the analysis required to calculate the centripetal force. (You are not required to calculate the force.)
questions.answer:
1. Use the model $F_c=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, which rearranges to $v^2=\dfrac{F_c}{m}\,r$. Since $F_c$ and $m$ are constant, $v^2$ is directly proportional to $r$.
2. Because there are several data sets, use graphical analysis so that all results are combined.
3. Convert the data: find the period $T=\dfrac{\text{time for 10 cycles}}{10}$ and convert each radius to metres ($r$ in m).
4. Calculate the linear speed for each trial using $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$, then square it to get $v^2$.
5. Plot a graph of $v^2$ (vertical axis) against $r$ (horizontal axis) and draw a line of best fit.
6. Find the gradient of the line of best fit, which equals $\dfrac{F_c}{m}$.
7. Calculate $F_c=\text{gradient}\times m$, ensuring that the mass is in kilograms ($0.055\ \text{kg}$).
Mercury. Its perihelion ($46\times10^6$ km) and aphelion ($69.8\times10^6$ km) differ the most in proportion, giving the largest eccentricity, $\dfrac{69.8-46}{69.8+46}\approx0.21$.

questions.question:
The table displays data from the 8 planets in our solar system.

| | Mercury | Venus | Earth | Mars | Jupiter | Saturn | Uranus | Neptune |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mass ($\times10^{24}$ kg) | 0.33 | 4.87 | 5.97 | 0.642 | 1898 | 568 | 86.8 | 102 |
| Diameter (km) | 4879 | 12,104 | 12,756 | 6792 | 142,984 | 120,536 | 51,118 | 49,528 |
| Density (kg/m$^3$) | 5427 | 5243 | 5514 | 3933 | 1326 | 687 | 1271 | 1638 |
| Length of day (hours) | 4222.6 | 2802 | 24 | 24.7 | 9.9 | 10.7 | 17.2 | 16.1 |
| Orbital period (days) | 88 | 224.7 | 365.2 | 687 | 4331 | 10,747 | 30,589 | 59,800 |
| Average distance from Sun ($\times10^6$ km) | 57.9 | 108.2 | 149.6 | 227.9 | 778.6 | 1433.5 | 2872.5 | 4495.1 |
| Perihelion ($\times10^6$ km) | 46 | 107.5 | 147.1 | 206.6 | 740.5 | 1352.6 | 2741.3 | 4444.5 |
| Aphelion ($\times10^6$ km) | 69.8 | 108.9 | 152.1 | 249.2 | 816.6 | 1514.5 | 3003.6 | 4545.7 |

At what distance from the Sun is Mars travelling with its greatest orbital velocity? Which of Kepler's laws did you use to answer this?
questions.answer: Mars travels fastest at its closest point to the Sun, the perihelion, $206.6\times10^6\ \text{km}$. This follows from Kepler's second law (law of equal areas): the line joining the planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so the planet must move faster when it is closer to the Sun.

questions.question: The mass of the Sun is $2.00\times10^{30}\ \text{kg}$. The mass of Mercury is $0.33\times10^{24}\ \text{kg}$ and its average distance from the Sun is $57.9\times10^{6}\ \text{km}$. What is the average gravitational force between the Sun and Mercury?

A satellite is in a stable low Earth orbit with a constant speed and altitude. The controller of the satellite wants to move it to a higher orbit. On-board rockets are fired to increase the speed of the satellite and, when the new orbit is reached, the rockets are fired to reduce the speed. Use your understanding of relevant physical principles to explain this sequence of events.
questions.answer:
To move to a higher orbit the satellite must gain gravitational potential energy. By conservation of energy this comes from chemical energy in the rocket fuel, which is converted into kinetic energy of the satellite. The rocket works by Newton's third law: the exhaust gases are pushed backwards, and they push the rocket forwards with an equal and opposite force. By Newton's second law ($F=ma$) the unbalanced force speeds the satellite up, so it moves outwards to a higher altitude (gaining potential energy as it climbs and losing some speed).

At the new radius the orbital speed required for a circular orbit, $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, is less than that of the lower orbit. So once the new altitude is reached the satellite is moving too fast for a circular orbit there, and the rockets are fired against the direction of motion. By Newton's second law this force decelerates the satellite to the lower orbital speed needed for a stable circular orbit at the larger radius.

questions.question: Explain why electrical energy is transmitted over large distances at very high AC voltages and low currents.
questions.answer:
Electrical energy is transmitted as AC because AC can easily be stepped up or down using transformers.

For a given power $P=IV$, a higher voltage means a lower current. The power lost as heat in the transmission lines of resistance $R$ is $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$, so a lower current greatly reduces the power lost (halving the current reduces the loss to a quarter). Reducing line loss makes the transmission more efficient, so more of the generated energy reaches consumers. Step-up transformers at the power station raise the voltage for transmission and step-down transformers lower it again for safe use in homes.

questions.question:
A charged particle, particle X, is moving perpendicular to a uniform electric field (field lines pointing to the right, particle moving down the page). Another charged particle, particle Y, is moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field (field into the page). The particles are identical in charge (positive) and mass and have the same initial velocity.

Outline ONE similarity and ONE difference between the behaviours of the particles in the fields.
questions.answer:
Similarity: both particles experience a force that acts perpendicular to their initial velocity, so both are deflected to the right and follow curved paths.

Difference: the shape of the path. In the electric field the force has constant magnitude and direction so X follows a parabola; in the magnetic field the force is always perpendicular to the velocity so Y moves in a circle at constant speed. (Also: the electric force does work on X, increasing its speed, whereas the magnetic force does no work on Y.)

questions.question:
A positively charged particle X moves perpendicular to a uniform electric field, and an identical particle Y moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The two particles have identical charge, mass and initial velocity.

If the initial velocity of each particle was doubled, what effect would this have on the motion in each field?
questions.answer:
Particle X: the force $F=qE$ does not depend on speed, so the acceleration is unchanged. But with double the speed the particle spends only half the time in the field, so it is deflected less: the parabolic path becomes flatter (less curved).

Particle Y: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ gives $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$, so the radius is proportional to $v$. The radius of the circular path doubles.

questions.question:
A motor uses a coil with 40 turns that has dimensions of $30.0\ \text{cm}\times20.0\ \text{cm}$, as shown in the diagram. A current of $1.5\ \text{A}$ flows through the coil in the direction shown (A to B along the top side). The coil is vertical (in the plane of the page) and is in a magnetic field of $5.1\times10^{-2}\ \text{T}$ directed down the page as shown.

What is the magnitude and direction of the magnetic force exerted on side AB?
questions.answer:
Side AB is perpendicular to the field ($\theta=90^\circ$), with length $0.300\ \text{m}$ and 40 turns:
$$F=nBIL\sin\theta=40\times5.1\times10^{-2}\times1.5\times0.300=0.918\ \text{N}\approx9.2\times10^{-1}\ \text{N}$$
Direction: using the right-hand rule (current to the right, field down the page) the force is into the page.

questions.question:
A motor uses a coil with 40 turns that has dimensions of $30.0\ \text{cm}\times20.0\ \text{cm}$ (AB = $30.0\ \text{cm}$). A current of $1.5\ \text{A}$ flows through the coil in the direction shown (A to B along the top side). The coil is vertical (in the plane of the page) in a magnetic field of $5.1\times10^{-2}\ \text{T}$ directed down the page as shown, i.e. parallel to the plane of the coil.

What is the magnitude and direction of the torque experienced by the coil in this position?
questions.answer:
The area is $A=0.300\times0.200=0.0600\ \text{m}^2$. The normal to the coil is perpendicular to the field ($\theta=90^\circ$), which is the position of maximum torque:
$$\tau=nIAB\sin\theta=40\times1.5\times0.0600\times5.1\times10^{-2}=0.18\ \text{N m}$$
Direction: side AB is forced into the page and side CD out of the page, so the coil rotates with AB moving into the page and CD coming out.

questions.question: A coil in a simple DC motor starts with its plane parallel to a uniform magnetic field and rotates because of the applied torque. What would happen to the magnitude of the torque as the coil rotates through $90^\circ$?
questions.answer: The torque falls to zero. After $90^\circ$ the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, so $\sin\theta=0$ in $\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$ (the forces on the sides are then along the same line and produce no turning effect).

questions.question:
A circular loop of wire is dropped vertically to fall through a magnetic field (into the page) as shown in the diagram. The plane of the coil is always perpendicular to the field lines. In Fig. 1 the loop is entering the field, a current flows in the direction shown and the coil experiences a force in the direction opposite to its motion. However, when the coil is entirely inside the field, Fig. 2, there is no current and no opposing force.

Use your understanding of Faraday's law and Lenz's law to explain this scenario.
questions.answer:
In Fig. 1 the coil is entering the field, so the magnetic flux through it ($\Phi=BA$) is changing (increasing). By Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, an emf is induced, and since the loop is a closed circuit a current flows. By Lenz's law the induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change in flux (here producing a field out of the page, anticlockwise as seen), and the resulting magnetic force on the current in the field opposes the motion of the loop (a retarding force, consistent with conservation of energy).

In Fig. 2 the loop is entirely inside the uniform field, so the flux through it is constant and $\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=0$. By Faraday's law there is no induced emf, so no current flows, and therefore there is no magnetic force opposing the motion: the loop falls without this retarding force.

questions.question:
A student placed lens B over lens A and noted that the intensity of light passing through was reduced in the region where the lenses overlap (Figure 1). Lens B was then rotated (Figure 2), and it was noted that even less light passed through.

Explain the observations made by the student.
questions.answer:
Both lenses are polarising filters. Light passing through lens A becomes plane polarised along the transmission axis of A. When this passes through lens B, whose axis is at an angle $\theta$ to that of A, only the component of the electric field along B's axis is transmitted. By Malus' law the transmitted intensity is $I=I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$, which is less than $I_{\max}$ for $\theta\neq0$, so the overlap region is darker (Figure 1).

In Figure 2, rotating B increased the angle $\theta$ between the two axes (towards $90^\circ$), so $\cos^2\theta$ decreased and less light was transmitted, giving a darker overlap region.

questions.question: A transformer in a laptop charger converts $240\ \text{V}$ AC into $6.0\ \text{V}$ AC. When the charger is plugged into the laptop there is an output current of $500\ \text{mA}$. The charger has an energy efficiency of $90\%$. Calculate the input current to the transformer in the charger.
questions.answer:
Output power: $P_{out}=V_sI_s=6.0\times0.500=3.0\ \text{W}$.

Efficiency $=\dfrac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}=0.90$, so $P_{in}=\dfrac{3.0}{0.90}=3.33\ \text{W}$.

$$I_p=\frac{P_{in}}{V_p}=\frac{3.33}{240}=1.4\times10^{-2}\ \text{A}\ (14\ \text{mA})$$

questions.question: Calculate the energy of a photon of light which is emitted when an electron in an excited hydrogen atom transitions from level 5 down to level 2.
questions.answer:
Rydberg equation:
$$\frac1\lambda=R\left(\frac1{n_f^2}-\frac1{n_i^2}\right)=1.097\times10^{7}\left(\frac1{2^2}-\frac1{5^2}\right)=2.304\times10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}$$
$$\lambda=4.34\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}$$
$$E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{4.34\times10^{-7}}=4.58\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}\ (2.86\ \text{eV})$$
Note: the school's solution gives $4.52\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ ($2.7\ \text{eV}$), which is a calculation error; the correct value is $4.58\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$.

questions.question: A diffraction grating has 2000 lines per cm. It was placed between a monochromatic light source and a screen at a distance $D$. A student shone monochromatic light at the grating and found a first-order maximum at an angle of $7.5^\circ$ to the central maximum. Find the wavelength of the light source. Express your answer in nanometres.
questions.answer:
Slit spacing: $d=\dfrac{1\times10^{-2}}{2000}=5.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$.

$d\sin\theta=m\lambda$ with $m=1$: $\lambda=5.0\times10^{-6}\times\sin7.5^\circ=6.53\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}\approx653\ \text{nm}$ (about $650\ \text{nm}$).

questions.question: A diffraction grating is placed between a monochromatic light source and a screen at a distance $D$. If the distance $D$ between the screen and the diffraction grating was decreased, what would happen to the distance between the maxima on the screen?
questions.answer: The spacing between the maxima would decrease. The angles of the maxima are fixed by $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$, and the separation on the screen is about $D\tan\theta$, which is proportional to $D$.

questions.question: The graph shows the intensity vs wavelength for 3 black bodies at different temperatures. Black body radiation curves could not be explained using classical wave mechanics. What new interpretation did Max Planck introduce to explain the shape of the curves?
questions.answer: Planck proposed that the energy of the radiation emitted (by the oscillating atoms in the body) is quantised: it can only be emitted or absorbed in discrete packets (quanta), $E=hf$, rather than continuously.

questions.question: The graph shows the intensity vs wavelength (wavelength in $\mu\text{m}$) for 3 black bodies at different temperatures. Use Wien's law to estimate the temperature of the hottest of the three bodies.
questions.answer:
The hottest body has the shortest peak wavelength (the tallest curve), with $\lambda_{\max}\approx0.8\ \mu\text{m}=0.8\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$.
$$T=\frac{b}{\lambda_{\max}}=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{0.8\times10^{-6}}=3.6\times10^{3}\ \text{K}\ (\approx4000\ \text{K to 1 s.f.})$$

questions.question: Describe how Einstein used Planck's interpretation to explain the existence of the threshold frequency in the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer:
Einstein extended Planck's idea of quantised energy by proposing that light itself consists of particles (photons), each carrying a quantum of energy $E=hf$. When a photon strikes the metal surface, its entire energy is transferred to a single electron (a one-photon, one-electron interaction).

Part of this energy is used to free the electron from the metal; the minimum energy needed is the work function $\phi$. Any remaining energy appears as the kinetic energy of the ejected electron: $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$.

If the light has a frequency below the threshold frequency $f_0=\dfrac{\phi}{h}$, each photon has less energy than $\phi$, so it cannot free an electron, no matter how intense the light (many photons cannot combine their energy). If $f>f_0$, a photon has enough energy to eject an electron immediately, and the excess energy $hf-\phi$ becomes its kinetic energy.

questions.question:
Muons are unstable subatomic particles that decay into electrons and neutrinos with a mean lifetime of $2.2\ \mu\text{s}$. They are produced when cosmic rays bombard the upper atmosphere about $11.4\ \text{km}$ above the Earth's surface, and they travel very close to the speed of light relative to the Earth.

Explain how observations of these muons can be used as evidence to support Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity of both length contraction and time dilation.
questions.answer:
Without relativity: at (say) $v=0.999c$ a muon would travel only $s=vt=0.999\times3.0\times10^{8}\times2.2\times10^{-6}\approx660\ \text{m}$ before decaying, so almost none would reach the ground $11.4\ \text{km}$ away. In fact many more muons are detected at the Earth's surface than this predicts, which is evidence for relativistic effects.

Earth frame (time dilation): the muon's lifetime of $2.2\ \mu\text{s}$ is its proper time $t_0$. For an observer on Earth it is dilated:
$$t=\frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}=\frac{2.2\times10^{-6}}{\sqrt{1-0.999^2}}=49\ \mu\text{s}$$
The time needed to travel $11.4\ \text{km}$ is $t=\dfrac{11.4\times10^{3}}{0.999\times3.0\times10^{8}}=38\ \mu\text{s}$, which is less than $49\ \mu\text{s}$, so many muons survive to reach the ground.

Muon frame (length contraction): in the muon's frame its lifetime is only $2.2\ \mu\text{s}$, but the atmosphere moves past it at $0.999c$ and the $11.4\ \text{km}$ is contracted:
$$L=L_0\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}=11.4\times10^{3}\times\sqrt{1-0.999^2}=510\ \text{m}$$
The time to cover $510\ \text{m}$ is $\dfrac{510}{0.999\times3.0\times10^{8}}=1.7\ \mu\text{s}$, which is less than $2.2\ \mu\text{s}$, so the muon reaches the surface before decaying.

Both frames agree that the muon reaches the ground, with time dilation (Earth frame) and length contraction (muon frame) accounting for it, supporting Einstein's special relativity.

questions.question: An oil drop of mass $1.177\times10^{-15}\ \text{kg}$ falls vertically into the evacuated space between two parallel charged plates, which are $2.00\ \text{cm}$ apart. The oil drop is negatively charged. The voltage is altered so that it slows the oil drop until it is stationary. When the potential difference between the plates is $72.0\ \text{V}$, the oil drop stops moving. How many excess electrons are on the oil drop?
questions.answer:
When stationary the electric force balances the weight: $qE=mg$ with $E=\dfrac{V}{d}$.
$$q=\frac{mgd}{V}=\frac{1.177\times10^{-15}\times9.8\times2.00\times10^{-2}}{72.0}=3.20\times10^{-18}\ \text{C}$$
$$n=\frac{q}{e}=\frac{3.20\times10^{-18}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=20\ \text{electrons}$$

questions.question: An experiment with a similar approach (suspending charged oil drops between charged plates) was used by Robert Millikan. What did he conclude from his investigation?
questions.answer: The charge on each oil drop was always a whole-number multiple of a fundamental unit of charge, so charge is quantised, and the smallest unit is the charge on the electron, $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}$.

questions.question: JJ Thomson performed an investigation (1897) that determined the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron using the apparatus shown. Outline his procedure and how he derived the relationship $\dfrac{q}{m}=\dfrac{E}{rB^2}$.
questions.answer:
Procedure:
1. A high potential difference between the cathode C and anode A of the discharge tube produced a beam of cathode rays (electrons), collimated by slits and seen as a glowing spot on the phosphorescent screen at the end of the tube.
2. A magnetic field $B$ (from current-carrying coils) was applied perpendicular to the beam in the region between plates D and E. The beam was deflected in a circular arc, and the radius of curvature $r$ was found from the position of the spot on the screen.
3. An electric field $E$ was then applied between the plates D and E, adjusted so that the electric force exactly cancelled the magnetic force and the beam returned to its undeflected position.

Derivation:
Magnetic force provides the centripetal force in step 2: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{q}{m}=\dfrac{v}{rB}$. (1)

With the fields balanced in step 3: $qE=qvB\ \Rightarrow\ v=\dfrac{E}{B}$. (2)

Substituting (2) into (1): $$\frac{q}{m}=\frac{E/B}{rB}=\frac{E}{rB^2}$$
(Note: the school's sample answer mislabels the electrodes: the cathode is C and the anode A.)

questions.question:
Figure 1 (black body radiation curves at different temperatures) and Figure 2 (waves passing through a double slit, with interference maxima and minima) illustrate two pieces of experimental evidence.

Which model of light does the evidence in each figure support?
questions.answer: Figure 1 is black body radiation, which could only be explained by Planck's quantum (particle) model; Figure 2 is double-slit interference, which supports the wave model.

questions.question:
The graph shows the activity of Indium-116 as a function of time.

What is the half-life and decay constant of this isotope?
questions.answer: The activity falls from 160 to 80 disintegrations/s (half of the initial value) at about 13 s, so $t_{1/2}\approx 13$ s. Then $\lambda=\dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}=\dfrac{0.693}{13}\approx 0.053\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.question:
Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ passes through two polarising filters in turn, and the intensity of the transmitted light is then measured to be $\dfrac{I_0}{4}$.

What is the angle between the transmission axes of the two polarising filters?
questions.answer:
The first filter transmits half of the unpolarised light: $I_1=\dfrac{I_0}{2}$. By Malus' law $I_2=I_1\cos^2\theta$, so $\dfrac{I_0}{4}=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta$, $\cos^2\theta=\dfrac12$, $\theta=45^\circ$.
(Note: the original wording said the filters were 'crossed', which would give zero intensity; that word has been removed.)

questions.question:
A square coil carrying a current of 1 A, with sides of 10 cm and 50 turns, is free to pivot about point P in a uniform magnetic field of 1.2 T (field direction from the S pole to the N pole of the magnets, i.e. horizontal). The end-on view shows the coil's plane making an angle of $60^\circ$ with the horizontal field.

When the coil is at the angle shown, what is the torque on the coil?
questions.answer:
$\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the field and the normal to the coil. The plane is at $60^\circ$ to the field, so the normal is at $30^\circ$.
$\tau=50\times1\times(0.10)^2\times1.2\times\sin30^\circ=0.3\ \text{N m}$.

questions.question: An alpha particle is fired at a thin piece of gold foil and passes close to a gold nucleus. As it approaches the gold nucleus, which one of the following is true about the electric potential energy of the system and the magnitude of the momentum of the alpha particle?
questions.answer: Both are positively charged, so the repulsive electric force does negative work on the approaching alpha particle: the electric potential energy of the system increases and the alpha particle's kinetic energy, and hence its momentum, decreases.

questions.question:
A radioactive nucleus is formed by $\beta^-$ decay. The nucleus then decays by $\alpha$ decay.

Which graph of nucleon number $N$ plotted against proton number $Z$ shows the $\beta^-$ decay followed by $\alpha$ decay?
questions.answer: In $\beta^-$ decay a neutron becomes a proton: $Z$ increases by 1 and the nucleon number is unchanged (arrow to the right). In $\alpha$ decay $Z$ decreases by 2 and $N$ by 4 (arrow to the lower left, ending at $Z$ down 2, $N$ down 4). Only graph B shows this.

questions.question:
A student is investigating the force between two parallel current-carrying wires of equal length. With a particular experimental setup, the student measures a force of $F$ newtons.

Which of the following changes to the experiment would produce the force described?

| | Change to experimental design | Force produced |
|---|---|---|
| A | reverse the direction of one of the currents | $F/2$ |
| B | double the length of one wire | $F$ |
| C | double each current | $2F$ |
| D | halve the distance between the wires | $4F$ |
options: Reverse the direction of one of the currents: force $F/2$
Double the length of one wire: force $F$
Halve the distance between the wires: force $4F$
questions.answer: $\dfrac{F}{l}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1I_2}{r}$, where $l$ is the length over which the wires overlap. Doubling the length of one wire does not change the overlapping length, so the force stays $F$. Reversing a current reverses the force direction but not its size (so not $F/2$); doubling each current gives $4F$; halving the distance gives $2F$.

questions.question: Which of the following is a contribution that Schrodinger made to the current model of the atom?
options: Postulated that electrons exist as standing waves with quantised angular momentum which explains their unusual stability.
Developed a mathematical model called matrix mechanics to simultaneously determine the position and momentum of a particle.
Developed a mathematical model called wave mechanics which can be used to describe the likelihood of finding an electron in a certain position.
Proposed that no two electrons in the same quantum system can simultaneously have the same set of four quantum numbers.
questions.answer: Schrodinger developed wave mechanics, whose wave function gives the probability of finding an electron at a given position. (A is Bohr/de Broglie, B is Heisenberg, D is Pauli.)

questions.question:
The length and height of a train carriage are measured to be $L=5$ m and $H=2.5$ m respectively by an observer at rest with respect to the carriage.

Another observer measures the length $L'$ and height $H'$ of the same carriage as it moves past him at a speed of $v=0.8c$ (along its length) as shown in the diagram.

Which of the following correctly describes this observer's measurements?
questions.answer: Length contraction occurs only along the direction of motion: $L'=L\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}=5\times0.6=3$ m. The height is perpendicular to the motion and is unchanged: $H'=2.5$ m.

questions.question:
A rider in the "rotor" at an amusement park finds herself stuck with her back to the wall as the floor gradually falls away while the rotor reaches its optimum safe speed (diagram shown).

Which diagram correctly shows the forces acting on her?
questions.answer: Vertically she does not accelerate, so friction (up) balances her weight (down). Horizontally the wall's normal force points towards the axis and provides the centripetal force. There is no outward force on her (centrifugal force is not a real force). Diagram A.

questions.question:
The electrical substation at Carlingford contains a number of transformers as part of the electricity supply to local households, schools and businesses (they step the high transmission voltage down).

Which of the following diagrams provides a model for these transformers?
questions.answer: A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary than the primary (primary on the right with more turns in B and D). Eddy currents in the core are reduced by laminating it with the laminations parallel to the flux path (the sheets lying in the plane of the core loop, 'vertical laminations') so the eddy-current loops are cut. Only D has both features.

questions.question:
To safely negotiate curved sections of road at some critical speed, roads are usually banked, as shown (road inclined at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, car on the incline).

Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A component of the normal reaction force provides the frictional force, parallel to the inclined plane of the road.
At speeds lower than the critical speed, the car will tend to slide up the inclined plane of the road, while the frictional force acts down the plane.
A component of the normal reaction force provides the centripetal force, directed towards the centre of the curved section of the road.
At speeds greater than the critical speed, the car will tend to slide down the inclined plane of the road, while the frictional force acts up the plane.
questions.answer: On a banked road the horizontal component of the normal reaction (together with any friction component) provides the net force directed towards the centre of the curve, i.e. the centripetal force. (Below the critical speed the car tends to slide down the incline and friction acts up it; above it, the car tends to slide up and friction acts down.)

questions.question:
The diagram shows a screenshot from a simulation of the photoelectric effect. The voltage has been adjusted to the value with the smallest magnitude so that there is no current between the cathode and anode. The light has wavelength 210 nm and the voltage reading is $-1.59$ V.

Using the information provided in the diagram, the work function of the metal is:
questions.answer: At the stopping voltage $K_{\max}=1.59$ eV. Photon energy $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{1240\ \text{eV nm}}{210\ \text{nm}}=5.91$ eV. Then $\phi=E-K_{\max}=5.91-1.59=4.32$ eV.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows satellite A in an elliptical orbit around Earth. The velocity of satellite A at two locations, X and Y, is shown using vectors. Figure 2 shows satellite B in a circular orbit around Earth. The velocity of satellite B at two locations P and Q is also shown using vectors.

Which of the following correctly describes the work done by the force of gravity on satellite A as it moves between positions X and Y, and the work done on satellite B as it moves between positions P and Q?
questions.answer: In the elliptical orbit the speed (kinetic energy) differs at X and Y (the vectors have different lengths), so gravity does non-zero work between them. In the circular orbit the speed is constant and gravity is always perpendicular to the motion, so the work done is zero.

questions.question:
An electromagnetic brake is shown, with the disc rotating in a clockwise direction.

Which of the following correctly describes the eddy current at X and the vector quantity Y, as shown on the diagram?
options: Eddy current clockwise; Y is a force
Eddy current clockwise; Y is a torque
Eddy current anticlockwise; Y is a force
Eddy current anticlockwise; Y is a torque
questions.answer: The field between the poles passes through the disc (from the N pole to the S pole, away from the viewer). The disc material at X is moving out of the region of strong field, so the flux through it is decreasing; by Lenz's law the eddy current flows to oppose this loss, i.e. clockwise (to produce a field in the same direction as the decreasing field). Y is a force: the magnetic force on the eddy current opposes the motion (Lenz's law), which brakes the disc.

questions.question:
Consider the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram with 4 star groups labelled A, B, C and D (A: main sequence, B: red giants, C: supergiants, D: white dwarfs).

Identify the star groups where the following predominantly occur:

(i) p-p chain reaction: $4\,{}^1_1\text{H}\rightarrow{}^4_2\text{He}+2\,{}^{\ 0}_{+1}e+2\nu+2\gamma$

(ii) Triple-alpha reaction: ${}^4_2\text{He}+{}^4_2\text{He}\rightarrow{}^8_4\text{Be}+\gamma$ and ${}^4_2\text{He}+{}^8_4\text{Be}\rightarrow{}^{12}_6\text{C}+\gamma$
options: p-p chain: A; triple-alpha: A and C
p-p chain: D; triple-alpha: B and C
p-p chain: A; triple-alpha: B and C
p-p chain: D; triple-alpha: A and C
questions.answer: The p-p chain (hydrogen fusion) is the main energy source of main sequence stars (A). The triple-alpha process (helium fusion) occurs in post-main-sequence stars: red giants (B) and supergiants (C).

questions.question:
Two satellites, A and B, of equal mass $m$, orbit the Earth at altitudes of $R$ and $3R$ respectively, where $R$ is the radius of the Earth.

Which row of the table is a correct comparison of the satellites' gravitational potential energy $U$ and orbital velocity $v$?
questions.answer: The orbital radii (from Earth's centre) are $r_A=2R$ and $r_B=4R$. $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ so $\dfrac{U_A}{U_B}=\dfrac{r_B}{r_A}=2$. $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$ so $\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}=\sqrt{\dfrac{4R}{2R}}=\sqrt2$.

questions.question:
In a famous magic trick, a magician stands inside a metal ring attached to a lightweight curtain. The magician throws the ring into the air (1), and is momentarily hidden by the curtain (2). When the curtain falls down again, the magician has been replaced by a rabbit (3).

Which of the following graphs is consistent with the predicted emf induced by the movement of the ring in the Earth's magnetic field?
questions.answer: While the ring is in free flight in the (essentially uniform) Earth's field with its orientation unchanged, the magnetic flux through it does not change, so by Faraday's law the induced emf is zero. (The graph with emf constant at zero.)

questions.question:
Two rollercoaster designs are frictionless and identical in shape everywhere except between positions $x_1$ and $x_2$. Between these positions, rollercoaster A has a hill of height $H$, whereas on rollercoaster B the cart leaves the track and flies through the air before landing safely on the other side. In both designs the cart starts from rest at height $H$ as shown.

Which of the following correctly describes the maximum height that the carts in rollercoaster A and B reach between positions $x_1$ and $x_2$?
options: A: equal to H; B: equal to H
A: equal to H; B: less than H
A: less than H; B: equal to H
A: less than H; B: less than H
questions.answer: In A the cart can just reach the top of the hill at height $H$ (all its energy is potential there). In B the cart leaves the track as a projectile with a horizontal velocity component, which remains at the top of its flight, so some energy is still kinetic and it cannot reach height $H$: its maximum height is less than $H$.

questions.question:
A probe is launched vertically upwards from the surface of a planet of radius $R$ with speed equal to three quarters of the escape speed for that planet.

In terms of $R$, what is the maximum height, from the surface of the planet, reached by the probe? Ignore air resistance.
questions.answer: $v_{esc}^2=\dfrac{2GM}{R}$, so $v^2=\dfrac{9}{16}\cdot\dfrac{2GM}{R}=\dfrac{9GM}{8R}$. Energy conservation: $\tfrac12v^2-\dfrac{GM}{R}=-\dfrac{GM}{r}$, so $\dfrac{9GM}{16R}-\dfrac{GM}{R}=-\dfrac{7GM}{16R}=-\dfrac{GM}{r}$, giving $r=\dfrac{16}{7}R$. Height $=r-R=\dfrac97R$.

questions.question: The two spectra shown (A: a smooth, unbroken band of colours from red to violet; B: a dark background with a few discrete coloured lines) are of different types. Name the two types of spectra.
questions.answer: A: continuous (black body) spectrum. B: (line) emission spectrum.

questions.question: The image shows a continuous spectrum (A) and a line emission spectrum (B). Describe how these two spectra can be produced and observed in a science classroom.
questions.answer:
Continuous spectrum: pass a current through an incandescent (tungsten) filament lamp so it heats up and glows; its light contains all wavelengths (alternatively, view sunlight reflected from a white surface).
Emission spectrum: apply a high voltage across a discharge (spectral) tube containing a low-pressure gas (e.g. hydrogen); the excited atoms emit light only at specific wavelengths.
Observation: view each light source through a diffraction grating (or a spectroscope); different wavelengths are diffracted to different angles, spreading the light into its spectrum.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a "light clock", in which light travels from an emitter to a mirror a distance $L_0$ and back along the same path to a detector.

Write down an expression for the time, $t_0$, taken by light to travel from the emitter to the mirror and back, as measured by an observer in the same reference frame as the clock.

In a thought experiment, an observer with a light clock (distance $L_0$ between emitter/detector and mirror) observes a second, identical light clock moving at speed $v$ to the right (the diagram shows the light's path in the moving clock). Explain why the observer will see light take longer to travel from the emitter to the mirror and back on the moving clock than the time it takes light to travel this path in a stationary clock.
questions.answer: The speed of light is the same, $c$, in all inertial frames, so light moves at $c$ in both the observer's clock and the moving clock. In the observer's frame the moving clock moves sideways while the light is travelling, so the light follows a longer diagonal path (up to the mirror and down to the displaced detector) than the straight path $2L_0$ in the stationary clock. Using $t=\dfrac{d}{c}$ with the same $c$ but a greater distance, the observer measures a longer time between emission and detection (a longer 'tick') for the moving clock.

questions.question: In a thought experiment, an observer sees a light clock moving at speed $v$ take longer for light to travel from the emitter to the mirror and back than an identical stationary light clock. Name the effect predicted by this thought experiment.
questions.answer: Time dilation.

questions.question: Describe ONE way in which time dilation has been validated experimentally.
questions.answer:
Muon experiment (Rossi and Hall, 1941): muons are produced by cosmic rays in the upper atmosphere and have a rest lifetime of only $2.2\ \mu$s. Travelling at about $0.994c$, they should on average decay before reaching low altitude, yet far more were detected at the lower altitude (Denver) than predicted without relativity. The result is explained by time dilation: in Earth's frame the muons' lifetime is lengthened, so more survive.
(Alternative: Hafele and Keating, 1971, flew atomic clocks around the world on aircraft; compared with clocks left on the ground, the moving clocks showed a time difference consistent with the predictions of special relativity.)

questions.question: Outline the key features of the Rutherford model of the atom.
questions.answer: A small, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre contains nearly all the mass of the atom; negatively charged electrons orbit the nucleus at a distance; the atom is mostly empty space. (There are no neutrons in Rutherford's model.)

questions.question: Explain how the Bohr model of the atom overcomes an identified limitation of the Rutherford model of the atom.
questions.answer:
Limitation: in Rutherford's model the orbiting electrons are accelerating (centripetal acceleration) so, according to classical electromagnetism, they should continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, making the atom unstable; the model also cannot explain the discrete line spectra of hydrogen.
Bohr postulated that electrons orbit in fixed, stationary, quantised energy levels (shells) in which they do not radiate energy, so they do not spiral in. When an electron drops from a higher level to a lower level it emits a photon of energy $E=hf$ equal to the difference in energy of the levels, which explains the discrete frequencies of the emission lines.

questions.question:
Electrons of different velocities are passed through a hole in plate A. A potential difference $V$ between plates A and B produces an electric field $\vec E$; after the electrons enter the gap they slow down and stop at a stopping distance $d$ (diagram). The results are:

| Electron velocity, $v$ (m s$^{-1}$) | Stopping distance, $d$ ($\mu$m) | Square of electron velocity, $v^2$ (m$^2$ s$^{-2}$) |
|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 1.9 | |
| 2000 | 8 | |
| 3000 | 17 | |
| 4000 | 31 | |
| 5000 | 46 | |

Complete the last column of the table.

Electrons of different velocities enter the gap between two plates and slow to a stop. The squares of the electron velocities and stopping distances are:

| $v^2$ (m$^2$ s$^{-2}$) | $1\times10^{6}$ | $4\times10^{6}$ | $9\times10^{6}$ | $1.6\times10^{7}$ | $2.5\times10^{7}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $d$ ($\mu$m) | 1.9 | 8 | 17 | 31 | 46 |

Plot a graph of stopping distance against the square of the electron velocity and draw the line of best fit.
