questions.answer: Plot $d$ ($\mu$m) on the vertical axis against $v^2$ (with the multiplier inside the units, e.g. $\times10^{6}$ m$^2$ s$^{-2}$) on the horizontal axis, with labelled axes and units, a suitable linear scale using most of the grid, all five points plotted accurately, and a straight line of best fit through the points (passing close to the origin). The graph is a straight line.

questions.question: An electron of mass $m$ and charge magnitude $q$ enters a uniform electric field of strength $E$ with velocity $v$ directed against the field's force, and slows to a stop after a distance $d$. Derive an expression for the relationship between the electron's velocity and the stopping distance in terms of the mass and charge of the electron and the electric field strength.
questions.answer:
Work done by the electric force equals the change in kinetic energy: $W=Fd=qEd=\Delta K=\tfrac12mv^2$.
So $\tfrac12mv^2=qEd$, giving $v^2=\dfrac{2qEd}{m}$, or $d=\dfrac{m}{2qE}v^2$.

questions.question:
Electrons of mass $9.1\times10^{-31}$ kg and charge magnitude $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C enter a uniform electric field (between plates A and B, with electrons moving from A towards B) and stop after distance $d$. The relationship is $d=\dfrac{m}{2qE}v^2$. The measurements of $d$ against $v^2$ lie on a straight line through the points $(2.5\times10^{6}\ \text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2},\ 5\ \mu\text{m})$ and $(2.25\times10^{7}\ \text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2},\ 42\ \mu\text{m})$ (best-fit line; e.g. $v^2=2.5\times10^{7}$ gives $d=46\ \mu$m).

Use the graph to determine the magnitude and direction of the electric field $\vec E$ between the plates.
questions.answer:
Gradient of the $d$ against $v^2$ graph $=\dfrac{m}{2qE}$:
$\text{gradient}=\dfrac{(42-5)\times10^{-6}}{(22.5-2.5)\times10^{6}}=1.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{s}^2\text{m}^{-1}$.
$E=\dfrac{m}{2q\times\text{gradient}}=\dfrac{9.1\times10^{-31}}{2\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times1.85\times10^{-12}}\approx1.5\ \text{N C}^{-1}$ (V m$^{-1}$).
Direction: the electrons are decelerated, so the force on them points back towards A. Since the electron is negative, the field points the opposite way: towards B, i.e. to the right (in the direction the electrons were moving).

questions.question:
Auroras are caused by charged particles ejected from the Sun as part of the solar wind. When the charged particles come close to the Earth they spiral inwards around the Earth's magnetic field lines (diagram shows a positively charged hydrogen nucleus following a helical path as the field lines converge towards the pole).

With reference to the force(s) on the hydrogen nucleus, explain the motion of the charged particle when it is close to the Earth but before it reaches the atmosphere.
questions.answer:
The moving hydrogen nucleus (a charged particle) experiences a magnetic force $F=qvB\sin\theta$ that is perpendicular to both its velocity and the field (right-hand rule for a positive charge).
- The component of velocity parallel to the field produces no magnetic force, so the particle keeps moving along the field line towards the Earth.
- The component of velocity perpendicular to the field gives a force perpendicular to the velocity, which acts as a centripetal force, so the particle moves in a circle of radius $r=\dfrac{mv_\perp}{qB}$.
The combination of uniform motion along the field line and circular motion about it gives the helical (spiral) path.
As the particle moves towards the pole the field gets stronger, so $r\propto1/B$ decreases and the spiral tightens. The converging field also gives a force component opposing the motion along the field (magnetic mirror effect), reducing the pitch of the helix. Gravity and radiation losses have only a negligible effect on the particle's path here, and there is no atmosphere yet to slow it.

questions.question: A positively charged hydrogen nucleus from the solar wind spirals around the Earth's magnetic field lines towards the pole. Outline qualitatively how the motion of an electron from the solar wind would differ from the motion of a hydrogen nucleus once it reaches the Earth's magnetic field.
questions.answer: The electron has the opposite charge, so the magnetic force is in the opposite direction: it spirals around the field line in the opposite sense (clockwise rather than anticlockwise as seen along the field) while still spiralling in towards the pole. Its charge-to-mass ratio is much larger (mass about $\tfrac{1}{1836}$ of a proton), so for the same speed $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$ is much smaller: it follows a much tighter helix.

questions.question:
A toy car with a DC motor is connected to a 9 V battery. A child switches on the car while it is held in the air and the motor starts to spin freely. The car is then placed on some grass and starts to move. As grass gets caught in the axle of the wheels, the motor stops spinning. The child picks up the car and switches off the motor.

Describe the changes to back emf that occur in the motor during this time, for each stage: (i) car switched off; (ii) switched on and held in the air; (iii) moving on grass; (iv) stationary on grass; (v) switched off.
questions.answer:
(i) Switched off (before starting): the motor is not spinning, so there is no back emf (and no supply emf).
(ii) Switched on and spinning freely in the air: the back emf, produced by the coil rotating in the magnetic field, rises from zero to a large steady value, a little less than the 9 V supply (it varies periodically with the rotation). The net emf is small, so the current is small.
(iii) Moving on grass: the load makes the motor slow down, so the back emf decreases significantly; the net emf and current increase (more power delivered).
(iv) Stationary on grass: the motor is not turning, so the back emf is zero; the current is then at its maximum (risking overheating).
(v) Switched off: no rotation, so the back emf is zero.

questions.question:
In an experiment to measure the charge of an electron, a student allows tiny oil drops to enter the space between two horizontal plates connected to a variable voltage supply (plates 7.71 mm apart). With no potential difference between the plates the student watches a drop fall at a constant speed of $0.0313$ mm s$^{-1}$.

Describe the forces acting on the oil drop as it falls (as in a free body diagram), including their directions and relative sizes.
questions.answer: Two forces act: the weight of the drop (gravity) acting downwards, and the drag force (air resistance) acting upwards. As the speed is constant, the net force is zero, so they are drawn as arrows of equal length (equal magnitude) in opposite directions.

questions.question: In an oil drop experiment the oil drop has captured one or more electrons and is negatively charged. A potential difference is applied across two horizontal plates until the oil drop is stationary. Name the two forces now acting on the oil drop.
questions.answer: The electric force (due to the electric field between the plates) acting upwards on the negatively charged drop, and the gravitational force (weight) acting downwards.

questions.question: In a Millikan-style experiment, an oil drop of mass $2.93\times10^{-15}$ kg is held stationary between two horizontal plates 7.71 mm apart when the potential difference between the plates is 346 V. Calculate the electric charge of the oil drop.
questions.answer:
The drop is stationary, so the electric force equals the weight: $qE=mg$ with $E=\dfrac{V}{d}$.
$q=\dfrac{mgd}{V}=\dfrac{2.93\times10^{-15}\times9.8\times7.71\times10^{-3}}{346}=6.4\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}$ (magnitude; the drop is negative).

questions.question: A student carrying out Millikan's oil drop experiment obtains the following charges on the oil drops investigated: $9.6\times10^{-19}$ C, $12.8\times10^{-19}$ C and $3.2\times10^{-19}$ C. State how these results support Millikan's conclusion.
questions.answer: Each charge is an integer multiple of the elementary charge $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C ($6e$, $8e$ and $2e$ respectively), which supports Millikan's conclusion that charge is quantised and the electron carries a fixed minimum charge.

questions.question: The graph shows the binding energy per nucleon as a function of nucleon number. Using this diagram, account for the release of energy in fission and fusion reactions.
questions.answer:
Binding energy per nucleon is a measure of how tightly the nucleons are bound; the energy equivalent of the mass defect is $E=\Delta mc^2$. The curve rises to a maximum near iron-56 (about 8.8 MeV per nucleon).
Fusion: light nuclei (below Fe-56) join to form a heavier nucleus with a higher binding energy per nucleon. The product is more tightly bound and has less mass per nucleon than the reactants, so mass is converted to energy, which is released.
Fission: a heavy nucleus (above Fe-56) splits into two medium-mass nuclei, which have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus. The products have a total mass less than the reactant, and the mass defect is released as energy.

questions.question:
Consider one of the reactions in the proton-proton chain reaction: ${}^2_1\text{H}+{}^1_1\text{H}\rightarrow{}^3_2\text{He}+\gamma$.

The binding energy per nucleon for deuterium (${}^2_1\text{H}$) is 1.1 MeV and for helium-3 (${}^3_2\text{He}$) is 2.6 MeV. Calculate the energy released in this reaction.
questions.answer:
Total binding energy of ${}^3_2$He $=3\times2.6=7.8$ MeV; of ${}^2_1$H $=2\times1.1=2.2$ MeV; of ${}^1_1$H $=0$ (a single proton).
Energy released = BE(products) $-$ BE(reactants) $=7.8-2.2-0=5.6$ MeV.

questions.question: The diagram shows a model of nuclear fission (a neutron strikes a uranium-235 nucleus, which splits and releases three neutrons; one escapes and two go on to strike further uranium-235 nuclei, each releasing two or three neutrons). Relate this model to the concepts of controlled and uncontrolled chain reactions.
questions.answer:
The model shows a neutron striking a ${}^{235}$U nucleus to initiate fission, releasing about 2-3 neutrons (and energy) per fission (neutron multiplication). One neutron escapes without causing further fission, while the other two each cause another fission.
Uncontrolled chain reaction: on average more than one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission (multiplication factor $k>1$, supercritical), so the number of fissions and the rate of energy release grow exponentially. This is what the model shows, with two neutrons from the first fission initiating new fissions.
Controlled chain reaction: on average exactly one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission ($k=1$, critical), so the reaction proceeds at a steady rate. The model would represent this if only one neutron were left to cause a further fission and the others were absorbed (e.g. by control rods) or escaped.

questions.question:
Some of the energy levels in a mercury atom are: $n=4$: $-2.50$ eV; $n=3$: $-5.90$ eV; $n=2$: $-12.6$ eV; $n=1$: $-28.4$ eV.

List all the possible downward electron transitions that can occur in a mercury atom (initially in the $n=1$ level) after a successful collision with an incoming 22.5 eV photon. Justify your reasoning.
questions.answer:
Energy absorbed from $n=1$: $-28.4+22.5=-5.9$ eV, which is exactly the $n=3$ level. So the electron is excited to $n=3$ (22.5 eV $=28.4-5.9$ eV; it cannot reach $n=4$, which needs 25.9 eV, and a photon is absorbed only if its energy matches a level difference).
From $n=3$ it can then de-excite by the downward transitions: $3\rightarrow2$, $2\rightarrow1$, and directly $3\rightarrow1$.

questions.question: Mercury atom energy levels include $n=2$: $-12.6$ eV and $n=1$: $-28.4$ eV. A mercury lamp is used to produce light which is filtered so that only the wavelength produced by the $n=2$ to $n=1$ transition remains. Calculate the wavelength of the photon that strikes a potassium plate.
questions.answer:
Photon energy $\Delta E=28.4-12.6=15.8$ eV $=15.8\times1.602\times10^{-19}$ J.
$\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{15.8\times1.602\times10^{-19}}=7.85\times10^{-8}\ \text{m}=78.5$ nm.

questions.question: Light of photon energy 15.8 eV is shone onto a potassium metal plate whose work function is 2.00 eV. Calculate the maximum velocity of any electrons liberated from the potassium plate. Ignore relativistic effects.

A student standing in the rain on a windless day measures the velocity of raindrops to be $v_{RG}$ directly downwards. Another student travelling on a train moving with velocity $v_{TG}$ to the left relative to the ground observes that the apparent direction the rain is arriving from is $\theta^\circ$ to the vertical. Construct an equation which relates $v_{TG}$, $v_{RG}$ and the angle $\theta$.
questions.answer: Relative to the train the rain has horizontal speed $v_{TG}$ (towards the train's rear) and vertical speed $v_{RG}$, so $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v_{TG}}{v_{RG}}$.

questions.question: Light from stars appears to arrive at an angle to its true direction because of the Earth's motion around the Sun, just as rain appears to arrive at an angle $\theta$ to the vertical for a moving train where $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v_{train}}{v_{rain}}$. The largest shift in the apparent position of a star (near the poles) is $0^\circ0'20.5''$. The distance from Earth to the Sun is $r=1.5\times10^{11}$ m and the Earth's orbital period is $T=365.25$ days. Showing all working, determine the speed of light from this information.
questions.answer:
Orbital speed of Earth: $v_E=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi\times1.5\times10^{11}}{365.25\times24\times3600}=2.99\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
By analogy with the rain, the Earth's velocity plays the role of the train and light the role of the rain: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v_E}{c}$ so $c=\dfrac{v_E}{\tan\theta}=\dfrac{2.99\times10^{4}}{\tan(20.5'')}=\dfrac{2.99\times10^{4}}{9.94\times10^{-5}}\approx3.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question:
In the future an artificial "ringworld" is built around a newly discovered star (Neos): a thin cylinder of radius $R$ completely encircling Neos (Figure 1). The Sun is a G-class star; Neos is an A-class star (Figure 2, a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram on which Neos is about 10 times as luminous as the Sun). Inhabitants live on the inner face of the cylinder, which rotates at speed $v$; the radius is chosen so that the intensity of light on the inner surface is the same as on Earth.

Data: Earth's distance from the Sun $r_E=1.5\times10^{11}$ m; mass of Neos $4.0\times10^{30}$ kg; surface area of a sphere $4\pi r^2$.

Show, with working, that the intensity of light on the surface of the ringworld will be the same as the intensity on Earth if the radius of the ringworld is $R=4.7\times10^{11}$ m.
questions.answer: From the HR diagram Neos has luminosity $L_N\approx10L_{Sun}$. Intensity obeys an inverse square law, $I=\dfrac{L}{4\pi r^2}$. Equal intensities: $\dfrac{10L_{Sun}}{4\pi R^2}=\dfrac{L_{Sun}}{4\pi r_E^2}$, so $R=\sqrt{10}\,r_E=\sqrt{10}\times1.5\times10^{11}=4.7\times10^{11}$ m.

questions.question:
In the future an artificial "ringworld" is built around a newly discovered star (Neos): a thin cylinder of radius $R$ completely encircling Neos (Figure 1). The Sun is a G-class star; Neos is an A-class star (Figure 2, a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram on which Neos is about 10 times as luminous as the Sun). Inhabitants live on the inner face of the cylinder, which rotates at speed $v$; the radius is chosen so that the intensity of light on the inner surface is the same as on Earth.

Data: Earth's distance from the Sun $r_E=1.5\times10^{11}$ m; mass of Neos $4.0\times10^{30}$ kg; surface area of a sphere $4\pi r^2$.

Identify how the electromagnetic radiation experienced by the inhabitants of the ringworld will be different from that they would experience on Earth.
questions.answer: Neos is an A-class star, hotter than the Sun (G-class). By Wien's law $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac{b}{T}$ the peak wavelength of its radiation is shorter, so the inhabitants would receive more ultraviolet (and bluer light) than on Earth.

questions.question:
In the future an artificial "ringworld" is built around a newly discovered star (Neos): a thin cylinder of radius $R$ completely encircling Neos (Figure 1). The Sun is a G-class star; Neos is an A-class star (Figure 2, a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram on which Neos is about 10 times as luminous as the Sun). Inhabitants live on the inner face of the cylinder, which rotates at speed $v$; the radius is chosen so that the intensity of light on the inner surface is the same as on Earth.

Data: Earth's distance from the Sun $r_E=1.5\times10^{11}$ m; mass of Neos $4.0\times10^{30}$ kg; surface area of a sphere $4\pi r^2$.

Calculate the escape velocity for an object at a distance $R=4.7\times10^{11}$ m from Neos.
questions.answer: $v_{esc}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times6.67\times10^{-11}\times4.0\times10^{30}}{4.7\times10^{11}}}=3.4\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question:
In the future an artificial "ringworld" is built around a newly discovered star (Neos): a thin cylinder of radius $R$ completely encircling Neos (Figure 1). The Sun is a G-class star; Neos is an A-class star (Figure 2, a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram on which Neos is about 10 times as luminous as the Sun). Inhabitants live on the inner face of the cylinder, which rotates at speed $v$; the radius is chosen so that the intensity of light on the inner surface is the same as on Earth.

Data: Earth's distance from the Sun $r_E=1.5\times10^{11}$ m; mass of Neos $4.0\times10^{30}$ kg; surface area of a sphere $4\pi r^2$.

Explain how rotating the ring can provide the sensation of weight for the inhabitants and determine the speed, $v$, at which the ring should spin to produce artificial gravity that will mimic that experienced on the surface of Earth ($R=4.7\times10^{11}$ m).
questions.answer:
An inhabitant moves in a circle with the ring, so a net centripetal force towards the centre is needed. The ring's floor provides this as a normal force acting inwards (through the inhabitant's feet), and this normal force is what is felt as weight. To feel the same weight as on Earth, $N=mg$, so the centripetal acceleration must be $9.8$ m s$^{-2}$:
$N=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}=mg\ \Rightarrow\ v=\sqrt{Rg}=\sqrt{4.7\times10^{11}\times9.8}=2.1\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
(The gravitational attraction of Neos, about $GM/R^2\approx0.0012$ m s$^{-2}$, is negligible.)

questions.question:
In the future an artificial "ringworld" is built around a newly discovered star (Neos): a thin cylinder of radius $R$ completely encircling Neos (Figure 1). The Sun is a G-class star; Neos is an A-class star (Figure 2, a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram on which Neos is about 10 times as luminous as the Sun). Inhabitants live on the inner face of the cylinder, which rotates at speed $v$; the radius is chosen so that the intensity of light on the inner surface is the same as on Earth.

Data: Earth's distance from the Sun $r_E=1.5\times10^{11}$ m; mass of Neos $4.0\times10^{30}$ kg; surface area of a sphere $4\pi r^2$.

The 'top down' view shows the ring rotating anticlockwise about Neos. Draw the trajectory (path) taken by an inhabitant who accidentally steps off the side of the ring at position X (at the bottom of the ring). Explain why the trajectory you have drawn is correct.
questions.answer: The inhabitant leaves along a straight line tangent to the ring at X, in the direction they were moving just before stepping off (to the right at X for anticlockwise rotation), as shown. Their speed ($2.1\times10^{6}$ m s$^{-1}$) is far greater than the escape velocity at that distance ($3.4\times10^{4}$ m s$^{-1}$), so they are not bound to Neos; gravity from Neos is negligible and barely bends the path (strictly a hyperbola), and the person never returns. Once off the ring there is no centripetal force, so by Newton's first law the person continues in a straight line.

questions.question: Electrons with a velocity of $0.70c$ pass through a double slit and form an interference pattern. Show that the momentum of the electrons is $p=2.7\times10^{-22}$ kg m s$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
Relativistic momentum: $p=\dfrac{m_0v}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}=\dfrac{9.109\times10^{-31}\times0.70\times3\times10^{8}}{\sqrt{1-0.70^2}}=\dfrac{1.913\times10^{-22}}{0.714}=2.7\times10^{-22}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$.
(The school's solution wrote $0.695$ inside the root; with $0.70c$ the factor is $\sqrt{1-0.49}=0.714$ and the result is the same to 2 s.f.)

questions.question:
Electrons with velocity $0.70c$ (momentum $p=2.7\times10^{-22}$ kg m s$^{-1}$) pass through a double slit with slit separation $d=220$ nm and arrive at a screen to form the interference pattern shown. The intensity is graphed against the angle $\theta$ from the centre axis. The maximum marked X is the third-order maximum (the 0th, 1st and 2nd order maxima are obscured by direct transmission of the electron beam). 

De Broglie proposed that matter exhibits wave-like properties according to $\lambda=\dfrac hp$. Describe how the data from this experiment provides qualitative evidence to support this proposal.
questions.answer: The electrons form an interference (diffraction) pattern of alternating maxima and minima on the screen. Interference and diffraction are wave properties, so the electrons (particles) are behaving as waves.

questions.question:
Electrons with velocity $0.70c$ (momentum $p=2.7\times10^{-22}$ kg m s$^{-1}$) pass through a double slit with slit separation $d=220$ nm and arrive at a screen to form the interference pattern shown. The intensity is graphed against the angle $\theta$ from the centre axis. The maximum marked X is the third-order maximum (the 0th, 1st and 2nd order maxima are obscured by direct transmission of the electron beam). 

De Broglie proposed that matter exhibits wave-like properties according to $\lambda=\dfrac hp$. Explain how the data from this experiment provides quantitative evidence to support this proposal.
questions.answer:
De Broglie's prediction: $\lambda=\dfrac hp=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{2.7\times10^{-22}}=2.5\times10^{-12}$ m.
Experimental value: for a double slit, $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, and for small angles $\lambda=\dfrac{d\theta}{n}$. From the graph the third-order maximum (n = 3) is at $\theta\approx3.3\times10^{-5}$ rad, so $\lambda=\dfrac{220\times10^{-9}\times3.3\times10^{-5}}{3}=2.4\times10^{-12}$ m.
The wavelength measured from the interference pattern agrees with the de Broglie wavelength to within about 5%, so the data quantitatively supports de Broglie's relationship.

questions.question: A 1 kg explosive device is fired at an angle of $60^\circ$ with a speed of $30$ m s$^{-1}$ into the air. Air resistance is negligible. Determine the maximum height $H$ reached by the device.
questions.answer: Initial vertical velocity $v_y=30\sin60^\circ=26$ m s$^{-1}$. At the top $v=0$: $v^2=v_y^2+2aH$, so $H=\dfrac{0-26^2}{2\times(-9.8)}=34$ m.

questions.question:
A 1 kg explosive device is fired at $60^\circ$ with a speed of $30$ m s$^{-1}$. At its maximum height it explodes into two pieces (A and B), each of mass $0.5$ kg. Piece A has zero velocity immediately after the explosion. Assume air resistance is negligible.

Apply conservation of momentum and conservation of energy to calculate the mass defect due to the conversion of chemical energy to other forms of energy during the explosion.
questions.answer:
At the top the device moves horizontally with $v_x=30\cos60^\circ=15$ m s$^{-1}$ (vertical velocity is zero).
Momentum (the explosion forces are internal and much greater than gravity): $m v_x=m_Av_A+m_Bv_B$, $1\times15=0+0.5v_B$, so $v_B=30$ m s$^{-1}$ horizontally (it has no vertical momentum).
Kinetic energy before: $\tfrac12(1)(15)^2=112.5$ J. After: $\tfrac12(0.5)(30)^2+0=225$ J.
The extra 112.5 J comes from chemical energy, i.e. from mass converted to energy: $\Delta m=\dfrac{E}{c^2}=\dfrac{112.5}{(3\times10^{8})^2}=1.25\times10^{-15}$ kg.

questions.question: Which of the following factors about a rocket would affect the rocket's escape velocity?
questions.answer: Escape velocity $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}$ depends only on the mass of the planet and the distance from its centre, not on the mass or initial velocity of the rocket (D).

questions.question: Millikan measured the magnitude of the electron charge by balancing an upwards force with a gravitational force on a small oil drop. A student performed this experiment so that an oil drop of charge $9.6\times10^{-19}$ C was held stationary in an electric field of $1.0\times10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}$. What is the electrical force acting on the oil drop?
Which of the following is considered a piece of evidence for the Big Bang Theory?
questions.answer: The cosmic microwave background radiation is the cooled remnant of radiation released when atoms formed about 380 000 years after the Big Bang, and is key evidence for the theory (B).
options: The presence of antimatter in the universe.
The existence of the four fundamental forces.

questions.question: The diagrams show possible force vectors that could act on objects moving in uniform circular motion on a flat corner and on a banked curve. Identify the letter(s) that match the vector(s) that provide centripetal force in both situations.
questions.answer: On the flat corner the centripetal (centre-seeking) force is the friction force $R$ pointing towards the centre of the circle. On the banked curve the horizontal vector $N$ points towards the centre of the circular path, so it is the (net) force providing the centripetal force (A).
options: Flat corner: R; Banked curve: N
Flat corner: R + S; Banked curve: N
Flat corner: R; Banked curve: N + M
Flat corner: R + Q; Banked curve: N + L

questions.question: Which of the following most correctly describes Newton's and Huygens' models of light?
questions.answer: Newton proposed a corpuscular model (small massive particles obeying Newton's laws); Huygens proposed a wave model in which each point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that propagate forward (C).
options: Newton: light consists of small particles that have mass but do not obey the laws of physics. Huygens: light consists of waves that do not have mass but obey all laws of physics.
Newton: each point on a wave behaves as a point source for new waves to form. Huygens: light consists of particles that do not have mass, but obey all laws of physics.
Newton: light consists of small particles that have mass and obey the laws of physics. Huygens: each point on a wave behaves as a point source for waves in the direction of propagation.
Newton: light consists of waves that do not have mass but obey all laws of physics. Huygens: light consists of particles that have mass and obey the laws of physics.

questions.question: A graph can be used to represent the energies of satellites at different heights above the surface. Which graph correctly shows the kinetic, gravitational potential and total energies of a satellite as the orbital radius of the satellite changes?
questions.answer: For a circular orbit $E_k=\frac{GMm}{2r}$, $U=-\frac{GMm}{r}$ and $E_{total}=-\frac{GMm}{2r}=-E_k$. So the kinetic energy is positive and decreasing, the gravitational potential energy is negative and twice as large in magnitude as the total energy (which is negative, equal in magnitude to $E_k$); all curves flatten as $r$ increases. Only graph B shows this (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows the energy levels of hydrogen with four different electron transitions highlighted (A, B, C, D). Which of the transitions shown corresponds to an emitted photon of wavelength 486 nm?
questions.answer: $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{(6.626\times10^{-34})(3.0\times10^8)}{486\times10^{-9}}=4.09\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}=2.55$ eV. The transition $n=4\to n=2$ gives $-0.85-(-3.40)=2.55$ eV, which is transition A (A).

questions.question: Lightning storms can create highly accelerated electrons that in turn create gamma photons as a result of the high acceleration. N-13 is then produced when a gamma photon strikes an N-14 nucleus and removes a neutron: $\gamma+{}^{14}_{7}\text{N}\rightarrow{}^{13}_{7}\text{N}+{}^{1}_{0}n$, with masses ${}^{14}\text{N}=14.00307$ u, ${}^{13}\text{N}=13.00574$ u, ${}^{1}n=1.00867$ u. Calculate the energy, in MJ, that is absorbed in this reaction.

Polarised light of intensity $I_0$ passes through a polarising filter $P_1$ with the same plane of polarisation as the incoming light. The light then passes through a filter $P_2$ that is able to be rotated. What is the light intensity at the detector when the angle between the planes of polarisation of $P_1$ and $P_2$ is $30^\circ$?
questions.answer: Malus' law: $I=I_{max}\cos^2\theta=I_0\cos^230^\circ=0.75\,I_0$ (C).

questions.question: The graph shows current and back emf against time in a DC motor that is starting up from stationary. Why does the current decrease as the back emf increases?
questions.answer: As the coil spins faster, the back emf (Lenz's law) increases and opposes the supply voltage. The net voltage across the motor, $V_{supply}-\varepsilon_{back}$, falls, so the current $I=\dfrac{V_{net}}{R}$ decreases (A).
options: Net voltage across the motor decreases as the motor speeds up.
Resistance in the circuit becomes greater as more current flows.
Overall voltage across the motor increases as the motor speeds up.
Back emf causes a decrease in the supply emf as the motor speeds up.

questions.question:
The diagram shows components of an AC induction motor. A student wrote out the correct steps explaining its operation but not in order:

1. Causes a change in flux to be experienced by the squirrel cage bars.
2. Alternating current is supplied to the electromagnets in the stator.
3. A rotating magnetic field forms.
4. The squirrel cage generates a magnetic field that interacts with the rotating magnetic field to create a force, and thus a torque.
5. An emf is induced and thus a current in the bars.

Order the steps so they correctly explain the operation of an AC induction motor.
questions.answer: AC supplied to the stator (2) produces a rotating magnetic field (3), which causes a change in flux through the squirrel cage bars (1); an emf and current are induced in the bars (5); the current-carrying bars generate their own field that interacts with the rotating field, producing a force and torque (4): 2, 3, 1, 5, 4 (C).

questions.question: The diagram shows the current, measured in amperes, running through two parallel wires. The definition of the SI unit of the ampere is based upon the forces acting between two parallel wires with current running through them. Newton's third law of motion is related to the definition of the ampere for which reason?
questions.answer: Official key: D. By Newton's third law the forces on the two wires are equal in magnitude, so a single force per unit length, $\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$, defines the ampere; it depends on the length of wire considered and the separation (D). (Option A states only that the forces are equal and does not link to the quantities used in the definition.)
options: Forces acting on each wire are of the same magnitude.
The force between the two wires is only related to the current in the wires.
The direction of the force between the two wires changes depending on the direction of the current flow.
The equal force between the two wires depends on the length of the wire and the distance between the wires.

questions.question: At one point on the Earth's surface, at a distance of $R$ from the centre of the Earth, the gravitational field strength is measured as $9.76\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$. Which of the following is closest to Earth's gravitational field strength at a distance of $2R$ above the surface of the Earth at that point?
questions.answer: A height of $2R$ above the surface is a distance $3R$ from the centre. $g\propto\dfrac1{r^2}$, so $g=\dfrac{9.76}{3^2}=1.08\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$ (A).

questions.question: The table shows some of the laws used by Maxwell to explain the features of EM waves: Faraday's Law — oscillating magnetic fields produce an electric field; Ampere's Law — oscillating electric fields produce a magnetic field; Gauss' Law — electric charges produce a field that radiates outward, the electric flux being related to the size of the charge. Identify which option correctly matches the law to the feature of electromagnetic waves that is explained by that law.
questions.answer: A changing magnetic field produces an electric field (Faraday) and a changing electric field produces a magnetic field (Ampere); together these regenerate each other, so the wave is self-propagating without a medium (C).
options: Gauss' Law: electromagnetic waves are self-propagating.
Ampere's Law: the strength of an electromagnetic wave is related to the size of the oscillating charge.
Faraday's Law and Ampere's Law: electromagnetic waves are self-propagating.
Faraday's Law: electric and magnetic fields are produced at 90° to each other and 90° to the direction of propagation.

questions.question: Quasar 3C446 has a brightness that changes rapidly over time. The quasar is moving away from Earth at a speed of $0.704c$. Scientists observe the changes to the quasar's brightness over a $20$ hour time interval in a laboratory on Earth. What is the time interval of the observation period from the quasar's frame of reference?
questions.answer: The quasar's frame measures the proper time $t_0$; the Earth-frame time is dilated: $t=\dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$. $\sqrt{1-0.704^2}=0.7102$, so $t_0=20\times0.7102=14.204$ hours (C).

questions.question: Which of the following diagrams most correctly shows the conservation of energy that occurs during the release of a photoelectron during the photoelectric effect?
questions.answer: The photon energy is shared between the work function (energy needed to free the electron) and the maximum kinetic energy: $hf=K_{max}+\phi$ (D).

questions.question: A photoelectric circuit is set up using caesium (Cs) metal. A student plotted the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons against incoming light frequency for the caesium metal (graph). What is the approximate value for the cutoff frequency and work function of the caesium metal?
questions.answer:
The line crosses the frequency axis at $5\times10^{14}$ Hz (the cutoff frequency, where $K_{max}=0$) and the $K_{max}$ axis at $-2$ eV. Since $K_{max}=hf-\phi$, the vertical intercept is $-\phi$, so $\phi=+2$ eV (B). (Check: slope $=\frac{2\ \text{eV}}{5\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}}$ gives $h\approx6.4\times10^{-34}$ J s.)

*The school's answer key gives D, which is incorrect: the graph reaches $K_{max}=2$ eV at $10\times10^{14}$ Hz (not a cutoff there), and the work function is positive.*
options: Cutoff frequency $5\times10^{14}$ Hz; work function $-2$ eV
Cutoff frequency $5\times10^{14}$ Hz; work function $2$ eV
Cutoff frequency $10\times10^{14}$ Hz; work function $-4$ eV
Cutoff frequency $10\times10^{14}$ Hz; work function $4$ eV

questions.question: All rocks on Earth contain uranium-235. Over a long period of time the uranium-235 decays into other nuclides. If a sample of rock contains $5\%$ of the original amount of uranium-235 after a period of $4.5\times10^{6}$ years, calculate the decay constant for uranium-235.
questions.answer: $N_t=N_0e^{-\lambda t}\Rightarrow0.05=e^{-\lambda t}$. $t=4.5\times10^6\times365\times24\times3600=1.419\times10^{14}$ s. $\lambda=\dfrac{-\ln0.05}{1.419\times10^{14}}=\dfrac{2.996}{1.419\times10^{14}}=2.111\times10^{-14}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ (C).

questions.question: Mars has a radius of $3.40\times10^{6}$ m and a period of rotation on its axis of $8.86\times10^{4}$ s. Two satellites are in orbit around Mars. Satellite A has an altitude of $1.15\times10^{6}$ m and a period of $9314$ s. Satellite B is used to continually monitor the activity of a particular volcano. What is the altitude of satellite B?
questions.answer:
To monitor one volcano continuously, B must be areostationary: its period equals Mars' rotation period, $8.86\times10^4$ s. Kepler's third law: $\dfrac{r_A^3}{T_A^2}=\dfrac{r_B^3}{T_B^2}$ with $r_A=1.15\times10^6+3.40\times10^6=4.55\times10^6$ m.
$$r_B^3=\frac{(4.55\times10^6)^3(8.86\times10^4)^2}{9314^2}=8.52\times10^{21}\Rightarrow r_B=2.043\times10^7\ \text{m}.$$
Altitude $=2.043\times10^7-3.40\times10^6=1.70\times10^7$ m (C).

questions.question: A wire $2.0$ cm long is placed perpendicular to the magnetic field of a magnet that is placed on an electronic balance. The balance is zeroed with the magnet on it and no current flowing through the wire. The graph shows how the mass readings on the balance changed as the current in the wire was increased. What is the magnetic field of the magnet?
questions.answer:
The gradient is $\dfrac{0.42\ \text{g}}{7\ \text{A}}=0.06\ \text{g A}^{-1}=6\times10^{-5}\ \text{kg A}^{-1}$. The force on the magnet (reaction) is $F=BIl$, so $\dfrac FI=Bl$ and $\dfrac{mg}{I}=Bl$:
$$B=\frac{(6\times10^{-5})(9.8)}{0.020}=0.0294\ \text{T (B)}.$$

questions.question: The diagram shows a simple DC motor connected to an input power source. The coil is square with all sides $6.0$ cm in length, and there are $60$ loops in the coil. The coil is supplied with a current of $1.5$ A and is placed in a magnetic field of strength $0.50$ T. Calculate the maximum torque in the coil.
questions.answer:
$A=(0.060)^2=3.6\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$. The torque is greatest when the coil is parallel to the field ($\theta=90^\circ$ in $\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ measured from the normal):
$$\tau_{max}=nIAB=60\times1.5\times3.6\times10^{-3}\times0.50=0.162\approx0.16\ \text{N m}.$$

questions.question: A simple DC motor has a coil of $n$ loops, area $A$, carrying current $I$ in a magnetic field $B$, so that the torque is $\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$. Justify TWO adjustments that could be made to the motor to increase the torque in the coil.
questions.answer:
$\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$, so the torque is directly proportional to each of $n$, $I$, $A$ and $B$.

1. **Increase the number of loops $n$ in the coil** (more wire turns): each loop experiences the same force, so the total force on the coil and the torque ($\tau\propto n$) increase.
2. **Use stronger magnets (increase $B$)** or **increase the current $I$** (e.g. with a higher supply voltage): the force on each side of the coil $F=nBIl$ increases, so torque increases ($\tau\propto B$ or $\tau\propto I$).

questions.question: A person throws a ball which is projected at a speed of $40\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $15^\circ$ above the horizontal. The ball leaves the thrower at $2.10$ m above the ground. Calculate the time of flight if the ball is caught at the same height as thrown.
questions.answer:
$u_y=40\sin15^\circ=10.35\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $a_y=-9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Returning to the same height, $s_y=0$:
$$0=u_yt+\tfrac12a_yt^2\Rightarrow t=\frac{2u_y}{9.8}=\frac{2(10.35)}{9.8}=2.1\ \text{s}.$$

questions.question: A person throws a ball at $40\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $15^\circ$ above the horizontal and the ball is caught at the same height as thrown after $2.11$ s. The person catching the ball is standing $90$ m from the thrower at the same level. Determine how much closer or further away the catcher must move in order to catch the ball.
questions.answer: $u_x=40\cos15^\circ=38.64\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Range $=u_xt=38.64\times2.113=81.6$ m. The catcher is at $90$ m, so they must move $90-81.6=8.4$ m **closer** to the thrower.

questions.question: Io is a moon of Jupiter which can be observed from Earth going into and coming out of eclipses as it moves in and out of Jupiter's shadow. Ole Romer is credited with an early attempt to calculate the speed of light. He obtained a value of $200\,000\ \text{km s}^{-1}$. His method involved using the time difference between the predicted time period of an eclipse of Io and the actual time period, measured when the Earth is closest to Jupiter and again when the Earth is furthest from Jupiter. He assumed that the time difference was related to the extra distance that light had to travel. Justify why Romer's measurements of the speed of light were inaccurate.
questions.answer: The speed was calculated from $c=\dfrac{\text{extra distance}}{\text{time difference}}$, where the extra distance is about the diameter of Earth's orbit. At Romer's time the size of Earth's orbit (the Earth–Sun distance) was not accurately known, so the distance used was wrong. Timing of the eclipses was also imprecise with the instruments of the day. The resulting error in the distance and time difference gave an inaccurate (too low) value for $c$.

questions.question: Muons are particles created in the upper atmosphere, around $10$ km above the Earth. In a lab on Earth, muons have a mean lifetime of $2.20\times10^{-6}$ s. The speed of muons as they move towards Earth is $2.997\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Explain, using both qualitative and quantitative ideas, how muons show evidence of length contraction.
questions.answer:
**Without relativity:** the distance a muon travels in one mean lifetime is $d=vt=(2.997\times10^8)(2.20\times10^{-6})=659$ m, far less than the $10$ km to the surface, so almost no muons should reach the ground.

**With relativity (muon's frame):** muons are in fact detected at the Earth's surface in large numbers. In the muon's frame its lifetime is $2.20\ \mu$s, but the Earth-to-atmosphere distance is length-contracted:
$$L=L_0\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}=10\,000\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2.997\times10^8}{3.00\times10^8}\right)^2}=447\ \text{m}.$$
Since $447\ \text{m}<659$ m, the muon can cover the contracted distance within its lifetime. The observation of muons at the surface therefore provides evidence for length contraction (equivalently, time dilation in the Earth frame).

questions.question: A simple DC single coil motor has a constant current through the coil and rotates with constant speed. A student measures the torque provided by the coil at a range of different angular positions (graph shows data points at about $0^\circ,15^\circ,25^\circ,35^\circ,45^\circ$ with a torque of $10$ N m at $45^\circ$). Note that the coil starting position is NOT necessarily shown in the diagram. Complete the graph to show the torque of the motor between $0$–$180$ degrees and justify the trend of the graph you have drawn.
questions.answer:
For the coil, $\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$. Since $n$, $I$, $A$ and $B$ are all constant (fixed coil, steady current, permanent magnet), $\tau\propto\sin\theta$ and the graph is a sine curve.

- At $\theta=0^\circ$ the torque is $0$ (the coil is perpendicular to the field, so the forces on its two sides act along the same line), as the data show.
- Using the data at $45^\circ$: $10=\tau_{max}\sin45^\circ\Rightarrow\tau_{max}=\dfrac{10}{\sin45^\circ}=14.1\approx14$ N m, reached at $\theta=90^\circ$ where $\sin\theta=1$ (the field is parallel to the plane of the coil).
- The torque then decreases as $\sin\theta$ decreases, symmetric about $90^\circ$ since $\sin\theta=\sin(180^\circ-\theta)$, and returns to $0$ at $180^\circ$.
- The graph rises at a decreasing rate to the peak at $90^\circ$, then falls at an increasing rate to zero at $180^\circ$.

questions.question: Laser light passes through a diffraction grating that has $600$ slits per mm. The central maximum and the two first-order maxima are shown on a screen that is $1.20$ m from the grating. If the two first-order maxima are $30^\circ$ apart, calculate the wavelength of the light used.
questions.answer:
$d=\dfrac1{600\times1000}=1.667\times10^{-6}$ m. Each first-order maximum is at $\theta=\dfrac{30^\circ}2=15^\circ$ from the central maximum. $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$ with $m=1$:
$$\lambda=(1.667\times10^{-6})\sin15^\circ=4.3\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=430\ \text{nm}.$$

questions.question: The patterns produced by a double slit and a diffraction grating can be projected onto a flat screen for qualitative analysis. A student used two identical lasers, and projected a double slit pattern and a diffraction grating pattern onto a screen so they were side by side. An image of the double slit pattern is shown. Contrast the main features of the double slit and diffraction patterns the student observed.
questions.answer:
- **Width/sharpness of maxima:** the double slit pattern has wide, blurry bright bands; the diffraction grating pattern has narrow, sharp, bright spots/lines.
- **Brightness:** the grating maxima are brighter and more intense (many slits contribute), whereas the double slit bands are dimmer.
- **Spacing:** for the same wavelength the grating maxima are spread much further apart (larger angles) than the double slit fringes, which are closely spaced.
- **Intensity pattern:** the double slit pattern has an intensity that decreases gradually away from the centre (diffraction envelope), with dark/bright bands of roughly equal width; the grating's maxima are all of similar intensity, with wide dark regions between them.

questions.question: The diagram shows a simplified model of magnetic braking used in cars. The metal brake disc is surrounded by an electromagnet that can be switched on and off. Electromagnetic induction can be used to explain why magnetic braking slows the car. Use this theory to explain how magnetic braking works.
questions.answer: When the electromagnet is switched on, the spinning metal disc moves through its magnetic field, so the magnetic flux through sections of the disc changes. By **Faraday's law**, $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, an emf is induced in the disc, which drives circulating **eddy currents** in the metal. By **Lenz's law** the eddy currents create their own magnetic fields whose polarity opposes the change in flux (the motion) that produced them. The interaction of these fields with the electromagnet's field produces a force on the disc opposing its rotation. This braking force slows the disc and hence the wheel and car.

questions.question: Under magnetic braking the car decreases in velocity and the metal brake disc increases in temperature. Use the law of conservation of energy to explain these observations.
questions.answer: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed, so the total energy is constant. As the car slows, its kinetic energy ($\frac12mv^2$) decreases. This energy is transformed: the eddy currents flowing in the resistive metal disc dissipate energy as heat (resistive/Joule heating, $P=I^2R$), so the thermal energy of the disc increases and its temperature rises. The loss of kinetic energy equals the gain in thermal energy.

questions.question: The image shows significant events in the formation of the Universe (temperature against time elapsed since the Big Bang: forces unified, radiation dominates, protons and antiprotons form, electrons and positrons form, atoms form, galaxies form, stars form). By considering the importance and role of the fundamental forces, outline the process by which atoms formed in the early Universe.
questions.answer:
- In the first instant all four forces were unified and only energy existed. As the Universe expanded and cooled the forces separated (gravity first, then the strong nuclear force, then the weak and electromagnetic forces), and energy was converted to matter: fundamental particles (quarks, leptons, bosons) formed.
- Between about $10^{-6}$ s and $1$ s the **strong nuclear force** bound quarks together (mediated by gluons) to form hadrons: protons and neutrons.
- From about 3 to 20 minutes, at lower temperatures the strong nuclear force bound protons and neutrons into small nuclei (nucleosynthesis of hydrogen-2, helium and a little lithium).
- Atoms formed only about $380\,000$ years after the Big Bang when the Universe had cooled to about $3000$ K, and the **electromagnetic force** attracted electrons into orbit around the positively charged nuclei, forming neutral atoms.

questions.question: Two satellites, A and B, are in orbit above the Earth. Satellite A is used to take images of the weather over different continents, while Satellite B is a communications satellite. Justify each satellite as either a LEO (low Earth orbit) or GEO (geostationary) based on their uses and features of their orbit.
questions.answer:
**Satellite A (weather imaging) is in LEO.** A low orbital radius allows close, high-quality imaging of the surface, and a short period (about 90 minutes, roughly 16 orbits per day, $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ is high) means it can cover many different continents/parts of the surface over a day.

**Satellite B (communications) is in GEO.** To keep a constant link with fixed ground antennas, it must stay above the same point on Earth. This requires an orbit above the equator with a period of 24 h (matching Earth's rotation), at an altitude of about $36\,000$ km, from which it also 'sees' nearly half of the Earth's surface.

questions.question: Use the Standard Model to describe the structure of the helium-4 atom.
questions.answer:
Helium-4 (${}^4_2\text{He}$) has a nucleus of **2 protons and 2 neutrons**, surrounded by **2 electrons**.

- Protons and neutrons are **hadrons (baryons)**, not fundamental. A proton is made of **two up quarks and one down quark** ($+\frac23+\frac23-\frac13=+1$); a neutron is made of **one up quark and two down quarks** ($+\frac23-\frac13-\frac13=0$). So the nucleus has 6 up and 6 down quarks in total.
- The **strong nuclear force**, carried by **gluons** (gauge bosons), binds the quarks together within each nucleon and binds nucleons into the nucleus.
- The two **electrons** are fundamental particles (leptons) with charge $-1$ each; they orbit the nucleus, held by the electromagnetic force (carried by photons). Their charge balances the $+2$ of the nucleus, so the atom is neutral.

questions.question: Scenario 1 shows observations made by two people when a ball is thrown vertically upright by a person in a train carriage moving at constant velocity at non-relativistic speeds. Scenario 2 shows observations that could be made by two people when a pulse of light is shone vertically upwards towards a mirror on the roof of a train moving at a constant relativistic speed. Explain the observations that the two observers (on the train and at the station) would make in EACH situation.
questions.answer:
**Scenario 1 (non-relativistic ball).**
- *Observer on the train:* the ball and the observer share the same horizontal velocity, so there is no relative horizontal motion; the ball goes straight up and down, accelerating at $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ downwards.
- *Observer at the station:* the ball has the train's horizontal velocity as well as its vertical velocity. No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity is constant while the vertical motion is accelerated by gravity: the path is a parabola (projectile motion). Both observers agree on the vertical motion and the time of flight.

**Scenario 2 (light, relativistic speed).**
- *Observer on the train:* the light pulse goes straight up and back down a distance $2L$ at speed $c$, taking time $t_0=\dfrac{2L}{c}$ (the proper time).
- *Observer at the station:* the train moves while the light travels, so the light follows a longer diagonal (triangular) path. By Einstein's postulate the speed of light is $c$ in all inertial frames, so the same speed over a longer distance takes longer: $t>t_0$. This is time dilation, $t=\dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$ — the station observer measures the train's clock running slow.

The difference between the scenarios: in Scenario 1 speeds add (Galilean relativity) and time is the same for both observers, whereas in Scenario 2 the speed of light is invariant, so time must differ between frames.

questions.question: The diagram shows a simplified diagram of the transmission of electricity from a power station to a substation: a generator ($100$ MW at $10$ kV) feeds transformer $T_1$ (output $500$ kV), transmission wires of resistance $R_T=3.0\ \Omega$, and transformer $T_2$ (output $50$ kV) feeding the substation. The current in the transmission lines is $200$ A. Analyse the diagram quantitatively and qualitatively to describe the method of transmission of electricity from a generator (power station) to a substation (suburban area a substantial distance away) with minimal energy loss.
questions.answer:
**Power lost in the wires is $P_{loss}=I^2R$**, so to minimise loss the current in the transmission line must be as small as possible. Since $P=VI$, for a given power a high voltage means a low current.

- **Step-up transformer $T_1$:** raises the voltage from $10$ kV to $500$ kV (ratio $\frac{N_s}{N_p}=\frac{500}{10}=50$). For $P=100$ MW, the line current is $I=\dfrac{P}{V}=\dfrac{100\times10^6}{500\times10^3}=200$ A (the primary current is $\dfrac{100\times10^6}{10\times10^3}=10\,000$ A).
- **Loss in the line:** $P_{loss}=I^2R=(200)^2(3.0)=1.2\times10^5$ W $=120$ kW, only $0.12\%$ of the $100$ MW. If the power were transmitted at $10$ kV, the current would be $10\,000$ A and the loss $I^2R=(10\,000)^2(3.0)=3.0\times10^8$ W, more than the power generated.
- **Step-down transformer $T_2$:** reduces the voltage from $500$ kV to $50$ kV (and further reductions occur at suburban substations) for safe distribution to consumers; the current rises correspondingly ($V_pI_p=V_sI_s$ for an ideal transformer), but only after the long-distance transmission.
- **Transformer efficiency:** transformers also dissipate energy; losses are minimised using laminated soft-iron cores (reducing eddy currents), low-resistance windings, and an efficient core design so flux linkage is high.

questions.question: Atomic models develop as scientists suggest solutions to the limitations of a previous model. However, all atomic models have their own limitations. Analyse this idea in terms of Rutherford's and Bohr's atomic models.
questions.answer:
**Rutherford's model:** based on the gold-foil scattering experiment, in which most alpha particles passed straight through but a few were deflected through large angles. He proposed a small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the atom's mass, with electrons orbiting in the mostly empty space around it.
*Limitations:* an orbiting electron is accelerating (centripetal acceleration), so according to classical electromagnetism it should continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, making atoms unstable. The model also could not explain the discrete line emission spectra of elements, or how electrons are arranged.

**Bohr's model (solution):** Bohr kept the nucleus but proposed that electrons orbit only in certain stationary states (quantised angular momentum) with fixed energies without radiating; an electron emits or absorbs a photon only when it jumps between levels, $E=hf=E_i-E_f$. This explained the stability of atoms and the Balmer series/line spectra of hydrogen.
*Limitations:* it only works for hydrogen (single-electron) atoms; it cannot explain spectra of multi-electron atoms, the relative intensities of spectral lines, or the splitting of lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect); and it gives no reason why only certain orbits are allowed (later explained by de Broglie's matter waves and Schrödinger's quantum model).

questions.question: A student was asked to construct a model to demonstrate the experiment used to develop Rutherford's model of the atom. He used the setup in the photograph — a suspended solid hoop with a heavy ball hanging on a string near the centre of the 'atom'. He then threw $100$ rice grains through the hoop and recorded how many passed through and how many were deflected by the ball. Assess the use of the student's modelling experiment to demonstrate the development of Rutherford's model.
questions.answer:
**Pros:** the model represents the key features of the experiment: moving particles (rice grains ≈ alpha particles) encountering a small, heavy, stationary obstacle (the ball ≈ nucleus) in otherwise open space (the hoop ≈ the atom). Most grains pass through the empty space and a few are deflected through a range of angles, as with Rutherford's observations; it is simple and visual, and it shows that large deflections require a small, dense, concentrated mass.

**Cons:** the rice grains travel at a much lower speed than alpha particles; far fewer particles are used than in the real experiment (millions of alpha particles); the ratio of the nuclear radius to the atomic radius is far larger in the model than in a gold atom (where it is about $10^{-5}$); there are multiple gold atoms (many layers) in the real foil, not a single one; and the repulsion between the positive alpha particles and positive nucleus (an electrostatic force acting at a distance) is not modelled — grains are only deflected by contact with the ball.

**Judgement:** overall it is an accessible, straightforward model that illustrates the key idea of the experiment (mostly empty space with a small, dense centre), although its limitations mean it cannot model the quantitative scattering results.

questions.question: The diagram shows the position of four stars, P, Q, X and Y on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Compare the production of energy and predicted future life cycle evolutionary path of these four stars.
questions.answer:
**Positions:** X is a hot, very luminous Main Sequence star (top left, O/B type); Y is a cool, dim Main Sequence star, a red dwarf (bottom right, M type); P is a red giant (cool but luminous, above the Main Sequence); Q is a red supergiant (cool and extremely luminous, top right).

**Energy production:**
- *Similarity:* all produce energy by nuclear fusion in their cores/shells.
- X and Y are on the Main Sequence and fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores. Difference: Y (low mass, low core temperature) uses the **proton–proton chain**, while X (high mass, high core temperature) mainly uses the **CNO cycle**, so X is far more luminous and burns its fuel much faster.
- P and Q are post-Main Sequence stars. P (red giant) fuses hydrogen in a shell around an inert helium core and then fuses helium into carbon/oxygen (triple-alpha process) in its core. Q, being more massive, has reached higher core temperatures and fuses progressively heavier elements in successive shells (carbon, neon, oxygen, silicon… up to iron).

**Future life cycle:**
- *Y* (red dwarf) will remain on the Main Sequence for trillions of years, then slowly become a white dwarf (it never becomes a red giant).
- *X* (massive) will leave the Main Sequence quickly (millions of years), become a red supergiant, then explode as a supernova leaving a neutron star or black hole.
- *P* (red giant, low/medium mass) will eject its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf.
- *Q* (red supergiant) has already evolved from a massive Main Sequence star like X, and will end in a supernova followed by a neutron star or black hole.

*Similarities:* X and Q both end in supernovae (high mass); P and Y both end as white dwarfs (low mass). *Difference:* high-mass stars have shorter lives and produce heavier elements.

questions.question:
The wave model predicts that during the photoelectric effect, light of any frequency should release electrons, as energy would eventually build up enough to release an electron from the metal surface. The table shows the light wave prediction and the observations that were made through experiments:

| Frequency ($\times10^{14}$ Hz) | Light as a wave prediction | Observations |
|---|---|---|
| 1.2 | Electrons emitted | No electrons emitted |
| 2.7 | Electrons emitted | No electrons emitted |
| 3.6 | Electrons emitted | Electrons emitted |
| 4.9 | Electrons emitted | Electrons emitted |

Explain why there is a difference in the prediction and observation.
questions.answer: The wave model treats light energy as continuous, so energy absorbed by the metal should accumulate over time until an electron is freed, regardless of frequency. The observations are explained by the **particle (photon) model**: light comes in discrete packets (photons) of energy $E=hf$, and each photon transfers all its energy to a single electron in a single interaction. If the photon energy is less than the work function ($hf<\phi$), the electron cannot escape, and no accumulation occurs however long the light shines. At $1.2$ and $2.7\times10^{14}$ Hz the photon energy is below the work function (below the threshold frequency), so no electrons are emitted; at $3.6$ and $4.9\times10^{14}$ Hz $hf>\phi$, so electrons are emitted with $K_{max}=hf-\phi$.

questions.question: Describe another example of where wave theory and the observations do not match for the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer:
**Intensity and kinetic energy:** wave theory predicts that increasing the intensity (amplitude) of the light would increase the energy delivered, so the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons would increase. In experiments, increasing the intensity only increases the *number* of electrons emitted (photocurrent); the maximum kinetic energy depends only on the light's frequency ($K_{max}=hf-\phi$). 

(Alternatively: wave theory predicts a time delay while energy builds up before emission, but electrons are emitted instantaneously — in less than $10^{-9}$ s — when light of sufficient frequency strikes the surface.)

questions.question: A stone of mass $m$ is thrown upward at $25^\circ$ to the horizontal. At the instant the stone reaches its highest point, why is the vertical component of the velocity zero?
questions.answer: Official key: C. Gravity is the only force, so the net force is always $mg$ downwards and the acceleration is $g$ (A and D are false). Gravity has slowed the vertical motion until the vertical component of kinetic energy has been converted to gravitational potential energy, so $v_y=0$ at the top (the horizontal component of velocity, and its kinetic energy, remain). B is a true statement but does not explain why $v_y=0$.
options: The acceleration of the stone at that instant is zero.
The net force acting upon the stone at that instant has magnitude $mg$.
The stone's kinetic energy has been converted to gravitational potential energy.
The stone has no net force acting on it at the highest point.

questions.question: A spacecraft travels from point X to point Y in the Earth's gravitational field along the path shown. Which of the following is equal to the work done by gravitational force on the spacecraft along the given path?
questions.answer: Official key: A. Gravity is a conservative force, so the work it does depends only on the end points, not the path, and equals the change in gravitational potential energy between X and Y (in magnitude; $W_g=-\Delta U$). The change in kinetic energy would equal the net work only if gravity were the only force (the spacecraft may use thrust), and gravity does work on the spacecraft since it has a component along the displacement.
options: The change in gravitational potential energy between points X and Y.
The change in kinetic energy between points X and Y.
The change in total mechanical energy between points X and Y.
No work is done by the gravitational force between points X and Y.

questions.question: Which of the following quantities does NOT affect the magnitude of the escape velocity?
questions.answer: $v_{esc}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}$ depends on $G$, the planet's mass $M$ and radius $r$, but not on the mass of the projected object (B).
options: The mass of the object being projected.

questions.question: When white light is passed through a gas:
questions.answer: The gas absorbs photons whose energies match transitions between its energy levels, leaving dark lines at those wavelengths in the otherwise continuous spectrum: an absorption spectrum (C).
options: all the light is absorbed by the gas.
electrons are energised and produce light.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the term redshift in astronomical studies?
questions.answer: Light from a galaxy receding from us is shifted towards longer wavelengths (lower frequencies), i.e. towards the red end of the spectrum (B).
options: The time when a star moves from the main sequence to be a red giant.
The increase in wavelength of the light from a distant galaxy moving away from Earth.
The red filter used by astronomers to analyse the light from the distant stars.
The increase in frequency of the light from a distant galaxy moving away from us.

questions.question: In the emission spectrum of neon (Ne) shown, which lines represent the highest energy light?
questions.answer: $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so the shortest wavelength lines have the highest photon energy. These are the lines nearest 400 nm (A).

questions.question: An FM radio station transmits at a frequency of 102.8 MHz. What is the energy of each photon emitted by the transmitter?

The life cycle of a star after the protostar period depends on the size or mass of the star. A particular star is the same size as the Sun. What is the order of stages, after the protostar, in the life cycle of this star?
questions.answer: A Sun-sized star leaves the main sequence to become a red giant (not a supergiant, which is for high-mass stars), ejects its outer layers as a planetary nebula leaving a white dwarf, which eventually cools to a black dwarf (D).
options: Main sequence, red supergiant, white dwarf, black dwarf.
Main sequence, red giant, black dwarf, white dwarf.
Main sequence, red supergiant, black dwarf, white dwarf.
Main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the properties of a red giant and a white dwarf relative to the Sun?
questions.answer: A red giant is cooler than the Sun (red) but, because of its enormous surface area, much more luminous. A white dwarf is hot (white) but tiny, so its luminosity is far lower than the Sun's (A).
options: Red giant: surface temperature lower, luminosity higher. White dwarf: surface temperature higher, luminosity lower.
Red giant: surface temperature lower, luminosity higher. White dwarf: surface temperature lower, luminosity higher.
Red giant: surface temperature higher, luminosity higher. White dwarf: surface temperature lower, luminosity lower.
Red giant: surface temperature higher, luminosity lower. White dwarf: surface temperature lower, luminosity higher.

questions.question: The graph shows how the gravitational potential energy $U$ of a mass $m$ depends on $r$. The mass is projected vertically upwards from the Earth's surface, $R_E$. At a certain distance $R$ from the centre of the Earth, the total energy of the body may be represented by a point on the line XY. Five points A, B, C, D and E have been marked on this line. Which row correctly identifies the point(s) which could represent the total energy of the mass in each scenario?
questions.answer: Total energy $E=U+K$. At the top of the trajectory the mass is momentarily at rest, $K=0$, so $E=U$: the point on the line XY that lies on the $U$ curve, which is B. While falling, the mass is moving so $K>0$ and $E>U$, so its energy is above B; and since it was projected so as to rise and return, it is bound ($E<0$), so it must lie between B and the $E=0$ axis, which is C. D and E are at or above zero total energy (an escaping mass) and could not fall back (B).
options: Top of trajectory: A; falling towards the Earth: C
Top of trajectory: B; falling towards the Earth: C
Top of trajectory: A; falling towards the Earth: D and E
Top of trajectory: B; falling towards the Earth: D and E

questions.question: A mass at the end of a string is suspended from a fixed point O. The mass is in contact with the cone and moves in a horizontal circle on the inside of a cone at a constant speed. If the tension in the string is $T$ and the normal force by the cone is $N$, which of the following gives the centripetal force on the bob?
questions.answer: Official key: C. The net horizontal force (towards the centre of the circle) is the centripetal force. The tension acts along the string at angle $\alpha$ to the vertical, so its horizontal component towards the axis is $T\sin\alpha$. The normal force from the cone surface is perpendicular to the cone wall; with $\beta$ as marked in the diagram its horizontal component towards the axis is $N\cos\beta$. So $F_c=T\sin\alpha+N\cos\beta$ (C).

questions.question: A toy car is released from rest at a height $h$ on a frictionless track. The car goes around the circular loop of diameter $D$ without leaving the track. What is the minimum possible value of the height $h$ required for the car to remain on the track while going around the loop?
questions.answer:
At the top of the loop the car just stays on the track when the normal force is zero, so $mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\Rightarrow v^2=gR$ where $R=\dfrac D2$. Conserving energy from release to the top of the loop (height $2R=D$):
$$mgh=mg(2R)+\tfrac12mv^2=2mgR+\tfrac12mgR=\tfrac52mgR\Rightarrow h=\tfrac52R=\tfrac{5D}{4}\ (\text{A}).$$

questions.question: Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ is incident on two ideal polarising sheets on top of each other. Initially the planes of polarisation of the sheets are perpendicular. What must be the angle between the direction of the sheets if the intensity of the transmitted light is one third the maximum intensity of the incident beam?
questions.answer: The first sheet transmits $\dfrac{I_0}{2}$ of unpolarised light. By Malus' law, $\dfrac{I_0}{3}=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta\Rightarrow\cos^2\theta=\dfrac23\Rightarrow\theta=35.3^\circ\approx35^\circ$ (C).

questions.question: The set-up for Young's double slit experiment is shown. The pattern of bright and dark bands is observed on the screen. Which one of the following actions will increase the distance, $\Delta x$, between the dark bands in this double slit interference pattern?
questions.answer: $\Delta x=\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$, so the band spacing is inversely proportional to the slit separation $d$. Decreasing $d$ increases $\Delta x$ (B); decreasing $L$ or $\lambda$ decreases it.
options: Decreasing the distance of separation between the slits.
Decreasing the distance between the slit and the screen.
Decreasing the wavelength of the light.

questions.question: An astronaut set out in a spaceship from Earth orbit to travel to a distant star in our galaxy. The spaceship travelled at a speed of $0.80c$. When the spaceship reached the star, the on-board clock showed the astronaut that the journey took 10 years. An identical clock remained on Earth. What time had elapsed on this clock when seen from the astronaut's spaceship?
questions.answer: The 10 years on the spaceship clock is the proper time $t_0$. The Earth clock reading is $t=\dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{1-0.80^2}}=\dfrac{10}{0.60}=16.7$ years (D).

questions.question: A horseshoe magnet rests on an electronic balance with a wire situated between the poles of the magnet. With no current in the wire, the reading on the balance is 142.0 g. With a current of 2.0 A in the wire in the direction XY, the reading on the balance changes to 144.6 g. What is the reading on the balance when there is a current of 3.0 A in the wire in the direction YX?
questions.answer: By Newton's third law the force on the magnet is equal and opposite to the force on the wire, $F=BIl$, so the change in reading is proportional to the current. With 2.0 A (XY) the reading increases by $2.6$ g. Reversing the current reverses the force, so with 3.0 A (YX) the reading decreases by $\dfrac{2.6}{2.0}\times3.0=3.9$ g: $142.0-3.9=138.1$ g (A).

questions.question: The primary coil of a transformer is connected to a 240 V AC power supply. Four identical lamps are connected to the secondary coil as shown. The lamps are rated 12 V and 24 W and are operating at normal brightness. If the transformer is not 100% efficient, what could be the possible value of the current that can be drawn from the power supply?
questions.answer: The four lamps (in parallel, 12 V each) use $4\times24=96$ W. For an ideal transformer, $V_pI_p=96\Rightarrow I_p=\dfrac{96}{240}=0.40$ A. Because the transformer is not 100% efficient (resistive heating, eddy currents, incomplete flux linkage), the input power must exceed 96 W, so $I_p>0.40$ A. Only 0.45 A qualifies (D).

questions.question: All stars emit radiation as black bodies. The radiation curves of intensity versus wavelength are plotted for two stars, Star A and Star B. The surface temperature of Star A is lower than the surface temperature of Star B. Which of the following graphs represents the distribution of radiation by Stars A and B?
questions.answer: The hotter star (B) emits more energy at every wavelength (its curve is above, enclosing a larger area, $\propto T^4$) and, by Wien's law $\lambda_{max}=\dfrac{b}{T}$, its peak is at a shorter wavelength than that of the cooler Star A. Only graph C has Star B as the higher curve with its peak to the left of Star A's (C).

questions.question: Two wires, A and B, are arranged as shown. Wire A is free to move vertically while wire B is fixed. Both wires carry equal currents of 100 A and both have a mass per unit length of $20.0\ \text{g m}^{-1}$. Determine the height which wire A is above wire B and the relative directions of the currents.
questions.answer:
Wire A floats above B, so the force on it must be upwards (repulsion), which requires currents in opposite directions. The magnetic force per unit length balances the weight per unit length:
$$\frac{\mu_0I^2}{2\pi r}=\frac mLg\Rightarrow\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times100^2}{2\pi r}=0.0200\times9.8\Rightarrow r=0.0102\ \text{m}\ (\text{C}).$$

questions.question: A metal rod is thrown in the air and acts as a projectile. Whilst in motion, the metal rod's long axis remains perpendicular to the Earth's magnetic field. Assume that air resistance is negligible and the Earth's magnetic field is pointing downwards and is uniform throughout the rod's trajectory. Which of the following graphs shows the variation of the emf induced between both ends of the rod with time?
questions.answer: The field is vertical, so only the horizontal component of the rod's velocity cuts the field lines (the vertical motion is parallel to $B$ and induces nothing). The horizontal velocity of a projectile is constant, so the induced emf $\varepsilon=Blv_x$ is constant (D).

questions.question: A game at a festival involves tossing a coin into a small dish mounted on a shelf. If the person can flick a coin into the small dish, they win a prize. Aidan flicks the coin with an initial speed of $u\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $60.0^\circ$ to the horizontal. When the coin leaves his hand, the horizontal distance between the coin and the dish is $2.80$ m and the vertical distance from his hand to the dish is $1.71$ m. Calculate the initial speed, $u$, required for Aidan to win a prize.
questions.answer:
Components: $u_x=u\cos60.0^\circ=\tfrac12u$, $u_y=u\sin60.0^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}u$.

Horizontal: $s_x=u_xt\Rightarrow 2.80=\tfrac12ut\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{5.6}{u}$.

Vertical: $s_y=u_yt-\tfrac12gt^2\Rightarrow1.71=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}ut-4.9t^2$.

Substituting $t=\dfrac{5.6}{u}$:
$$1.71=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}(5.6)-\frac{4.9(5.6)^2}{u^2}=4.850-\frac{153.7}{u^2}\Rightarrow u^2=\frac{153.7}{3.140}=48.9$$
$$u=7.00\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$

questions.question: Daniel suggests that if he flicks the coin so that the initial speed is greater, the coin will reach the dish more quickly and they can win prizes more efficiently. Explain why this is not the case and propose an additional change that would make his suggestion work.
questions.answer:
The time to travel the $2.80$ m horizontally is $t=\dfrac{s_x}{u\cos\theta}$. Increasing $u$ alone increases the horizontal component of velocity, but also the vertical component, so the coin follows a longer, higher path: it reaches the horizontal distance of the dish at a greater height (or overshoots), and so it no longer lands in the dish at height $1.71$ m. The suggestion does not work by itself.

To make it work, the launch angle must also be changed so that the trajectory still passes through the dish. Because the faster coin travels further horizontally for a given angle, the angle must be **decreased** (a flatter launch), which keeps the coin on target while the larger $u\cos\theta$ makes the flight time shorter.

*Note:* the school's sample answer proposed increasing the launch angle to reduce the range. That would bring the coin back to the dish, but it does not shorten the flight time (the horizontal component $u\cos\theta$ would be unchanged), so it does not meet Daniel's aim of a quicker flight.

questions.question: A binary star system consists of two stars, Star 1 (mass $M_1$, circular orbit of radius $r_1$) and Star 2 (mass $M_2$, radius $r_2$), which orbit a fixed point X. Both stars have the same angular speed of $4.98\times10^{-8}\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ about X. Explain why the centripetal force acting on both Stars 1 and 2 is the same.
questions.answer: The centripetal force on each star is provided by the gravitational attraction between the two stars. By Newton's third law, the gravitational forces the stars exert on each other are equal in magnitude (and opposite in direction), so the centripetal force on Star 1 equals the centripetal force on Star 2.

questions.question: In the binary star system (angular speed $4.98\times10^{-8}\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ about X), the distance of separation between the centres of the stars is $2.8\times10^{8}$ km. Given that Star 1 is three times heavier than Star 2, calculate $r_1$.
questions.answer:
Equal centripetal forces: $M_1r_1\omega^2=M_2r_2\omega^2\Rightarrow M_1r_1=M_2r_2$. With $M_1=3M_2$: $r_2=3r_1$.

The separation is $r_1+r_2=2.8\times10^{8}\ \text{km}=2.8\times10^{11}$ m, so $4r_1=2.8\times10^{11}$:
$$r_1=7.0\times10^{10}\ \text{m}$$

questions.question: In the same binary star system (angular speed $4.98\times10^{-8}\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$, $r_1=7.0\times10^{10}$ m, separation $2.8\times10^{11}$ m, $M_1=3M_2$), calculate the mass of Star 2.
questions.answer:
Gravity provides the centripetal force on Star 1: $\dfrac{GM_1M_2}{(r_1+r_2)^2}=M_1r_1\omega^2\Rightarrow M_2=\dfrac{r_1\omega^2(r_1+r_2)^2}{G}$:
$$M_2=\frac{(7.0\times10^{10})(4.98\times10^{-8})^2(2.8\times10^{11})^2}{6.67\times10^{-11}}=2.0\times10^{29}\ \text{kg}$$
(Kepler's third law gives the same result.)

questions.question: A beam of electrons is accelerated across the space between two parallel plates (potential difference $V$) and passes through a small opening. Derive an expression for the speed of a charged particle as it passes through the small opening.
questions.answer:
The particle (charge $q$, mass $m$) starts from rest and the work done by the electric field equals its gain in kinetic energy:
$$qV=\tfrac12mv^2-0\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{\frac{2qV}{m}}$$

questions.question: After passing through the opening, the electrons enter a uniform magnetic field directed into the page (see diagram). Describe the path of the electrons after they enter the uniform magnetic field.
questions.answer: The magnetic force on the electron is always perpendicular to its velocity. By the right-hand rule (reversed for the negative charge) it initially points downwards. It therefore acts as a centripetal force and the electron moves in a semicircular path, striking the lower grey plate $0.020$ m below the opening.

questions.question:
The potential difference between the plates is varied, and for each potential difference $V$ the magnetic field $B$ is varied so the beam strikes one of the grey plates at a distance of $0.020$ m from the opening:

| Potential difference (V) | Magnetic field (mT) | $B^2$ ($\times10^{-6}$ T$^2$) |
|---|---|---|
| 60.0 | 2.62 | |
| 70.0 | 2.78 | |
| 100.0 | 3.39 | |
| 110.0 | 3.54 | |
| 120.0 | 3.78 | |
