| 140.0 | 3.99 | |

The charge-to-mass ratio $q/m$ is the charge of a particle divided by its mass. Determine the quantities that should be graphed to yield a straight line from which the mass-to-charge ratio of an electron can be calculated, by completing the table.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow B=\dfrac{mv}{qr}$. Substituting $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2qV}{m}}$ (part a):
$$B^2=\frac{m^2}{q^2r^2}\cdot\frac{2qV}{m}=\frac{2m}{qr^2}\,V$$
So $B^2$ should be plotted on the vertical axis against $V$ on the horizontal axis: a straight line through the origin with gradient $\dfrac{2m}{qr^2}$.

Completed table ($B^2$ in $\times10^{-6}$ T$^2$): 6.86, 7.73, 11.49, 12.53, 14.29, 15.92.

questions.question: Plot the relevant data from (c) ($B^2$ against $V$) on a grid (potential difference 40–150 V, $B^2$ 4–17 $\times10^{-6}$ T$^2$) and draw a line of best fit.
questions.answer: Points are plotted as crosses with labelled axes with units, using most of the grid, and a straight line of best fit is drawn through the data (see graph). The gradient of the line is about $1.18\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}^2\text{V}^{-1}$.

questions.question: Using the line of best fit, calculate the charge-to-mass ratio of an electron.
questions.answer:
Choose two well-spaced points on the line (not data points), e.g. $(62.0\ \text{V},\ 7.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{T}^2)$ and $(130.0\ \text{V},\ 15.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{T}^2)$:
$$\text{gradient}=\frac{(15.0-7.0)\times10^{-6}}{130.0-62.0}=1.18\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}^2\text{V}^{-1}$$
Since gradient $=\dfrac{2m}{qr^2}$:
$$\frac qm=\frac{2}{r^2\times\text{gradient}}$$
The electrons strike the plate $0.020$ m from the opening, which is the diameter of the semicircle, so $r=0.010$ m:
$$\frac qm=\frac{2}{(0.010)^2(1.18\times10^{-7})}=1.7\times10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$$

questions.question: A simple DC motor is connected to a 6.00 V battery. The armature of the motor has a resistance of $4.00\ \Omega$ and consists of 40 turns. It rotates within an external magnetic field produced by radial magnets of strength $150\times10^{-3}$ T. Identify the direction of rotation of the motor as viewed from the eye and outline how this rotation is maintained during the operation of the motor.
questions.answer:
The motor rotates **clockwise** as viewed from the eye.

The rotation is maintained by the split-ring commutator, which reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half revolution (as the coil passes the vertical position) by changing the contact of each half of the ring with the brushes. This reverses the forces on the two sides perpendicular to the field at the right moment, so the torque stays in the same rotational direction and the coil spins continuously.

questions.question: The motor above (40 turns, $B=150\times10^{-3}$ T, current initially $1.50$ A, later constant at $0.35$ A) was noted to have a current that was initially $1.50$ A. The sides perpendicular to the magnetic field each experience a force of magnitude $2.10$ N initially when the motor was turned on. Determine the length of sides AB and CD.
questions.answer:
$F=nIlB\sin90^\circ$ with the initial current $I=1.50$ A:
$$l=\frac{F}{nIB}=\frac{2.10}{40\times1.50\times150\times10^{-3}}=0.23\ \text{m}$$
*Note:* the question page printed in the paper says "when the current became constant", whereas the marking guide says "initially when the motor was turned on". The solution (and this answer) uses the initial current of 1.50 A.

questions.question: In addition to the changes in current noted previously (initially $1.50$ A, decreasing to a constant $0.35$ A with no load), the students also noted that the potential difference across the armature of the motor was less than $6.00$ V. With the aid of calculations, account for the changes in the current and voltage across the armature and its significance to the law of conservation of energy.
questions.answer:
**Initially** the armature is stationary, so there is no back emf and $I=\dfrac VR=\dfrac{6.00}{4.00}=1.50$ A.

**As the motor speeds up**, the coil's changing flux linkage induces a back emf $\varepsilon_{back}=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ (Faraday's law), proportional to the rotation speed. By Lenz's law it opposes the supply emf (it opposes the change that produces it). The net emf driving current through the armature falls:
$$6.00-\varepsilon_{back}=IR$$
At the constant (maximum) speed, $I=0.35$ A, so the net potential difference across the armature resistance is $IR=0.35\times4.00=1.40$ V (less than $6.00$ V), and
$$\varepsilon_{back}=6.00-1.40=4.6\ \text{V}$$

**Conservation of energy:** if the induced emf aided the supply instead of opposing it, the current and speed would keep increasing and the motor would produce energy from nothing. Instead the supply power is shared: $P_{supply}=6.00\times0.35=2.10$ W, of which $I^2R=0.35^2\times4.00=0.49$ W is lost as heat in the coil and $\varepsilon_{back}I=4.6\times0.35=1.61$ W is converted to mechanical power. With no load this goes to friction and other losses, which is why a small residual current of $0.35$ A is still needed to maintain the speed.

questions.question: A group of Physics students investigated an AC generator. It has $N=150$ turns of wire in a square coil, in a magnetic field $B$. Show that the maximum emf, $\varepsilon_{max}$, can be described by $\varepsilon_{max}=2\pi fNBA$, where $f$ is the frequency, $N$ is the number of turns, $B$ is the magnetic field strength and $A$ is the area of the coil.
questions.answer:
Assume a uniform field and a coil rotating at constant angular speed $\omega$, with side length $l$ (along the axis) and width $w$ (so $A=lw$). Only the two sides of length $l$ cut the field lines. For one side moving at speed $v=\omega\dfrac w2$ at angle $\omega t$ to the field, the emf is $Blv\sin\omega t$. For two sides and $N$ turns:
$$\varepsilon=2NBl\left(\omega\frac w2\right)\sin\omega t=NBA\omega\sin\omega t$$
With $\omega=2\pi f$: $\varepsilon=2\pi fNBA\sin(\omega t)$. The emf is greatest when $\sin\omega t=1$:
$$\varepsilon_{max}=2\pi fNBA$$
(Equivalently, from Faraday's law with $\Phi=BA\cos\omega t$.)

questions.question: The generator has 150 turns in a $6.00$ cm wide square coil, in a field of strength $1.85\times10^{2}$ mT, and is rotated at $240$ rpm. Calculate the maximum emf produced by the generator using the above conditions.

The students then built their own AC generator and tested it at a constant speed. An induced emf versus time graph for this test is shown (peak emf 2.0 V, period 0.20 s). Sketch the output that is likely when the speed of rotation is doubled.
questions.answer:
Doubling the speed of rotation doubles the angular speed $\omega$, so:
- the **frequency doubles** (period halves to $0.10$ s), and
- the **maximum emf doubles** to $4.0$ V (since $\varepsilon_{max}=2\pi fNBA\propto f$).

The graph is a sine wave of amplitude $4.0$ V with peaks at $0.025$ s, $0.125$ s, ... (see graph).

questions.question: Owen builds a metal frame and slides it at a constant velocity of $0.500\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ across a uniform magnetic field (to the right). At $t=0$ the frame is at the position shown. The changes in magnetic flux linkage ($\Phi$) through the metal frame from the time it enters the magnetic field to $t=12.0$ s are shown in the graph. Calculate the value of the length, $L$.
questions.answer:
The 4.00 m high, 2.00 m wide section enters first, taking $\dfrac{2.00}{0.500}=4.0$ s, when $\Phi=20$ Wb:
$$\Phi=BA\Rightarrow20=B(4.00\times2.00)\Rightarrow B=2.5\ \text{T}$$
The $L$ m high, 1.00 m wide section then enters between $t=4$ s and $t=6$ s, adding $25-20=5$ Wb:
$$5=2.5\times(L\times1.00)\Rightarrow L=2\ \text{m}$$

questions.question: Complete the graph by drawing the changes in $\Phi$ through the metal frame from $t=12.0$ s to the time the entire metal frame leaves the magnetic field.
questions.answer: The frame is 3.00 m wide and the field region is 6.00 m wide, so at $t=12$ s the front edge is at the far edge of the field and the frame begins to leave. The changes mirror those when entering: the 2.00 m wide (4.00 m high) section leaves first from $t=12$ s to $t=16$ s, so $\Phi$ falls linearly from $25$ Wb to $5$ Wb; then the 1.00 m wide section leaves from $t=16$ s to $t=18$ s, so $\Phi$ falls linearly from $5$ Wb to $0$ (see graph).

questions.question: Edward then connected a light bulb across two points of the metal frame (see diagram). He repeats the experiment with the metal frame at the same initial velocity of $0.500\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to the right. Edward noted that an external force needed to be applied to the metal frame when it entered and left the magnetic field so that it would move across at constant speed. Explain the above observation.
questions.answer:
While the frame enters the field ($t=0$ to $6$ s) its magnetic flux linkage increases, so by Faraday's law an emf is induced. The light bulb completes the circuit, so a current flows. By Lenz's law the current is in the direction (anticlockwise) that produces a force opposing the motion that caused the change in flux. The current-carrying sides of the frame in the field therefore experience a magnetic force to the left, which would slow the frame. To keep the speed constant, an external force to the right must be applied so that the net force on the frame is zero.

Between $t=6$ s and $12$ s the frame is completely inside the uniform field, the flux does not change, no emf or current is induced and no external force is needed.

When the frame leaves ($t=12$ to $18$ s) the flux decreases, so again an emf and current are induced, and the Lenz's law force opposes the motion (again to the left), so an external force to the right is needed again. (The energy supplied by the external force is converted to electrical energy and dissipated in the bulb, in agreement with conservation of energy.)

questions.question: Blue light of frequency $6.25\times10^{14}$ Hz is shone onto the sodium photocathode of a photocell. The graph of the photoelectric current versus potential difference is shown. The threshold frequency for sodium is $5.50\times10^{14}$ Hz. Calculate the stopping potential, $V_0$, when blue light of frequency $6.25\times10^{14}$ Hz is shone onto the sodium photocathode of this photocell.
On the graph of photoelectric current versus potential difference for blue light, sketch the curve expected if the light is changed to ultraviolet with a lower intensity than the original.
questions.answer: Ultraviolet light has a higher frequency, so the photoelectrons have a greater maximum kinetic energy and a greater stopping potential: the curve starts at a more negative potential difference (larger $|V_0|$). The lower intensity means fewer photons per second and fewer electrons emitted, so the curve levels off at a lower saturation current (see graph).

questions.question: Discuss the significance of Maxwell's contribution to the development of our current understanding of the nature of light.
questions.answer:
- **Unification and equations:** Maxwell combined the laws of electricity and magnetism (Gauss's, Faraday's and Ampère's laws, with his addition of the displacement current) into a single set of equations. They showed that a changing magnetic field produces an electric field and a changing electric field produces a magnetic field, so an oscillating charge produces a self-propagating transverse electromagnetic wave that needs no medium.
- **Speed of light:** the equations predicted a wave speed $c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}\approx3.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, matching the measured speed of light, so Maxwell concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave. Because $c$ is fixed by $\mu_0$ and $\varepsilon_0$ it is independent of the motion of the source or observer, which led Einstein to the constancy of the speed of light and special relativity.
- **Predictions confirmed and later developments:** Maxwell predicted a spectrum of EM waves beyond visible light. Hertz produced and detected radio waves in 1887 and showed they reflect, refract, diffract, polarise and travel at the speed of light. Maxwell's wave theory explained Young's interference results and polarisation, while later experiments (the photoelectric effect, explained by Einstein) showed that light also has particle properties, leading to the quantum model.

Maxwell's work therefore established the wave nature of light as part of the electromagnetic spectrum and set the stage for relativity and quantum theory.

questions.question: After its initial launch, the Juno probe travelled around Earth and then entered Jupiter's atmosphere. The probe reached a maximum velocity of $7.36\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ as it went past the Earth at a height of 559 km above the surface. Using appropriate calculations, show that the probe was able to move away from the Earth and not be captured in orbit around it.
questions.answer:
The probe escapes if its speed exceeds the escape velocity at that height. The distance from Earth's centre is $r=6.371\times10^6+5.59\times10^5=6.930\times10^6$ m:
$$v_{esc}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM_E}{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(5.97\times10^{24})}{6.930\times10^6}}=1.07\times10^4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$
Since $v_{max}=7.36\times10^4\ \text{m s}^{-1}>v_{esc}$ (it also far exceeds the circular orbital speed $\sqrt{GM/r}=7.6\times10^3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$), the probe escapes Earth's gravity and is not captured in orbit.

questions.question: The Juno probe was launched from Earth and entered Jupiter's orbit, having a trip of 1796 days. It had an average velocity of $7.15\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Assuming there was no effect from gravitational fields, calculate the time difference between the two clocks, one based in the probe and the other in the laboratory on Earth.
questions.answer:
The Earth-based time is $t=1796\ \text{days}=1.552\times10^{8}$ s. The probe clock records the proper time $t_0=t\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$. With $v/c=2.383\times10^{-4}$ (so $v^2/c^2=5.68\times10^{-8}$, very small):
$$\Delta t=t-t_0\approx t\cdot\frac{v^2}{2c^2}=(1.552\times10^{8})(2.84\times10^{-8})=4.41\ \text{s}$$
The Earth clock is ahead by about $4.4$ s ($5.1\times10^{-5}$ days).

questions.question: A He-Ne laser of wavelength 632 nm directs the monochromatic beam onto a set of two parallel slits. A pattern from these slits has been projected onto a distant wall (see diagram). Explain the formation of the bright and dark regions in terms of the wave-like nature of light.
questions.answer: Light from each slit diffracts and the two waves overlap and interfere. Bright regions occur where the waves arrive in phase (constructive interference), where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, $m\lambda$ ($m=0,1,2,\dots$). Dark regions occur where the waves arrive out of phase (destructive interference), where the path difference is a half-integer number of wavelengths, $\left(m+\tfrac12\right)\lambda$.

questions.question: The teacher asks each student to estimate the difference between the length of the lines P1 and P2, which are the lines between the centre of each slit and the 6th bright spot. Calculate the difference in length between P1 and P2.
questions.answer:
The path difference to the $m$th bright band is $m\lambda$ (equal to $d\sin\theta$). For the 6th bright spot, $m=6$:
$$P_1-P_2=6\lambda=6\times632\times10^{-9}=3.79\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}=3.79\ \mu\text{m}$$

questions.question: Monochromatic light is now replaced with white light. Does this result in any changes in the pattern of the bands on the screen? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: Yes. White light is a mixture of all visible wavelengths. The position of the $m$th bright band is $y=\dfrac{m\lambda L}{d}$, so each wavelength produces its own set of bands with different spacing (longer wavelengths are spread further from the centre). All wavelengths are in phase at the centre ($m=0$), so the central maximum is white, but on either side the bands become coloured spectra (violet/blue nearest the centre, red furthest) that overlap and wash out at higher orders, instead of the evenly spaced bands of a single colour.

questions.question: The following flowchart represents a model of the scientific method used to show the relationship between theory and the evidence supporting it (Observation, Problem raised, New hypothesis, Experiment to test hypothesis, Collection of data, Analysis of results, Support for hypothesis or lack of support, New theory or law). Evaluate the role of thought experiments in the development of our current understanding of length and time.
questions.answer:
Thought experiments allowed Einstein to explore the consequences of his postulates (the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames and the speed of light in a vacuum is constant) before any experiment could test them, at the "new hypothesis" stage of the model. They showed that the classical idea of absolute time and length cannot be correct.

Example: a carriage moving past a platform with a light source at the centre. For an observer inside the carriage, light reaches both ends at the same time. For an observer on the platform, the rear of the carriage moves towards the light and the front moves away, and since the light travels at the same speed $c$ in both directions, it reaches the rear first. Events that are simultaneous in one frame are not in another, so time (and hence length) depends on the observer's motion. This led to the mathematical results of time dilation and length contraction, which were later confirmed by experiment.

*Evaluation:* thought experiments were essential for generating the hypotheses and revealing the logic of relativity, but they are not evidence by themselves; their value depends on being tested experimentally (data collection, analysis, support for the hypothesis).

questions.question: Describe two pieces of experimental evidence that support the concepts of length and time as developed through the thought experiments in (a).
questions.answer:
**1. Muon decay (time dilation and length contraction).** Muons are created about 10 km up in the atmosphere by cosmic rays, travel at about $0.98c$ and have a half-life of only $2.2\ \mu$s at rest, in which time they would travel only about 650 m. Yet large numbers reach the Earth's surface. In the Earth's frame the muons' time is dilated, so they survive much longer; in the muon's frame the distance to the ground is length-contracted to a much shorter distance. Both descriptions predict the observed number of muons at the surface.

**2. Hafele–Keating experiment (time dilation).** In 1971 atomic caesium clocks were flown around the world on commercial airliners (eastwards and westwards) and compared with a clock kept at the US Naval Observatory. The flown clocks showed small differences (nanoseconds) from the ground clock that agreed, within experimental error, with the predictions of special relativity (together with the gravitational effect from general relativity), confirming that moving clocks run slow.

questions.question: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram shows five stars A–E. Identify the stars that will evolve into white dwarfs.
questions.answer: Stars A and B. A (a Sun-like main-sequence star) and B (a red giant) have low to medium mass, so they will shed their outer layers and leave a white dwarf core. E is a high-mass main-sequence star and C a supergiant, which will end as supernovae, and D is already a white dwarf.

questions.question: Outline the two nuclear reactions that are occurring in Star B.
questions.answer:
Star B is a red giant, in which two fusion reactions occur:
- **Hydrogen shell burning:** hydrogen fuses to helium in a shell around the star's helium core; the helium produced sinks onto the core.
- **Helium fusion in the core:** the core is hot enough for helium nuclei to fuse into heavier nuclei, mainly carbon and oxygen (triple-alpha process).

questions.question: Energy can be produced in Star A and Star E by two nuclear processes: the proton–proton chain and the CNO cycle. Compare these two processes.
questions.answer:
**Similarity:** in both processes four hydrogen nuclei (protons) are fused into one helium-4 nucleus, releasing energy.

**Difference:** the CNO cycle uses carbon-12 as a catalyst (it facilitates the reaction but is regenerated), while the proton–proton chain has no catalyst.

**Which dominates:** the mass of the main sequence star determines this. Lower-mass stars with lower core temperatures (like Star A) use mainly the proton–proton chain. Higher-mass stars (like Star E) have a higher core temperature due to greater gravitational compression, which allows the CNO cycle to dominate.

questions.question: Astronomers combine mathematical models with observations to develop theories to describe the evolution of the observable universe. The Big Bang theory is the prevailing cosmological model that explains the origin and subsequent large-scale expansion of the universe. Describe how the careful observation of the electromagnetic radiation from various sources gave evidence in support of the Big Bang Theory.
questions.answer:
**Redshift of galaxies.** Observation of the visible light from distant galaxies showed that their spectral lines are shifted to longer wavelengths (lower frequencies), a redshift. The redshift is greater for more distant galaxies (Hubble, using distances determined from Cepheid variables), meaning all galaxies are moving away from each other, so the universe is expanding. Extrapolating backwards, all matter was once concentrated at a point, which supports the Big Bang theory. (The Steady State theory could also explain redshift, so redshift alone did not distinguish between the two.)

**Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR).** Radio telescopes (Penzias and Wilson) detected microwave radiation from all directions in space with a black-body spectrum corresponding to about $2.7$ K. This is the residual radiation from the early hot universe, released when atoms formed about 380 000 years after the Big Bang and cooled by expansion. Only the Big Bang theory predicted it, and later space telescopes (e.g. COBE) gave detailed measurements of its spectrum and tiny variations, giving strong support to the theory over the Steady State model.

questions.question: A charge of $0.7$ C is moving at an angle of $38^\circ$ to the vertical across magnetic field lines of strength $0.006$ T that are directed vertically down, at a velocity of $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. Ignoring any effects due to gravitational fields, the shape of the path that the charge would follow as it moves through this magnetic field would be:
questions.answer: The velocity has a component perpendicular to $\mathbf B$ (which gives circular motion) and a component parallel to $\mathbf B$ (which is unaffected by the field and gives constant drift along the field lines). Together they give a helix (C).

questions.question: A charge of $0.7$ C is moving at an angle of $38^\circ$ to the vertical across magnetic field lines of strength $0.006$ T that are directed vertically down, at a velocity of $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. Ignoring any effects due to gravitational fields, the magnitude of the force that the charge would experience as it passes through this magnetic field would be:
questions.answer: Only the component of velocity perpendicular to the field matters: $F=qvB\sin\theta=0.7\times6.2\times0.006\times\sin38^\circ=0.016$ N (B).

questions.question: A charge of $0.7$ C is moving at an angle of $38^\circ$ to the vertical across magnetic field lines of strength $0.006$ T that are directed vertically down, at a velocity of $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. Ignoring any effects due to gravitational fields, the magnitude of the vertical displacement that the charge would have travelled through after a time of $6$ seconds would be:
questions.answer: The vertical component of velocity is parallel to the (vertical) field, so it is unchanged: $v_\parallel=6.2\cos38^\circ=4.89$ m s$^{-1}$. Over $6$ s the vertical displacement is $4.89\times6=29.3$ m (D).

questions.question: A particle with a charge of $+0.6$ mC is moving vertically downward through free space with a velocity of $200$ m s$^{-1}$ when it encounters a uniform electric field of strength $20$ N C$^{-1}$ directed vertically downward. After the charge has moved through a distance of $15$ metres in a direction parallel to the field, the magnitude of the amount of work done on the charge would be:

A particle with a charge of $+0.6$ mC is moving vertically downward through free space with a velocity of $200$ m s$^{-1}$ when it encounters a uniform electric field of strength $20$ N C$^{-1}$ directed vertically downward. If the mass of the charge was $3$ grams, the magnitude of the change in velocity of the charge over this $15$ metre distance would be closest to:

A particle with a charge of $+0.6$ mC is moving vertically downward through free space with a velocity of $200$ m s$^{-1}$ when it encounters a uniform electric field of strength $20$ N C$^{-1}$ directed vertically downward. The mass of the particle is $3$ grams. If the electric field was now set up horizontally instead of vertically, the magnitude of the displacement of the particle $4$ seconds from the instant the particle entered the field would be closest to:
questions.answer:
The $200$ m s$^{-1}$ vertical velocity is unaffected, so the vertical displacement is $200\times4=800$ m. The field gives a horizontal acceleration $a=\frac{qE}m=4$ m s$^{-2}$, so the horizontal displacement is $\frac12(4)(4)^2=32$ m.

Displacement $=\sqrt{800^2+32^2}=800.6$ m (B).

questions.question: Two parallel wires are brought close to each other. Wire X has a current of $4$ A flowing through it and wire Y has a current of $6$ A flowing through it. Both currents are flowing in the same direction. From the information we can conclude that:
questions.answer: By Newton's third law the forces on the two wires are equal in magnitude, $\frac FL=\frac{\mu_0I_XI_Y}{2\pi d}$. Parallel currents in the same direction attract, so the force on X is directed towards Y (B).
options: the force on wire X is the same magnitude as the force on wire Y and is directed away from wire Y
the force on wire X is the same magnitude as the force on wire Y and is directed towards wire Y
the force on wire X is larger than the force on wire Y and is directed away from wire Y
the force on wire X is smaller than the force on wire Y and is directed towards wire Y

questions.question: Various charged and uncharged particles are sent through a magnetic field (into the page) as shown. Assuming that all the particles enter the field at the same velocity and the magnitude of the charges on the charged particles are the same, the most likely explanation for the paths that the particles take is that:
questions.answer:
Path II is undeflected, so that particle is neutral. For a positive particle moving to the right in a field into the page, $\mathbf F=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ is upward, so path I (curving up) is positive and path III (curving down) is negative.

The radius is $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$. With equal $v$, $|q|$ and $B$, a larger radius means a larger mass. Path I is nearly straight (large $r$), so its particle is more massive than path III's (B).
options: All the particles are positively charged.
Particle path I is positive and more massive than particle path III, which is negative.
Particle path I is positive and less massive than particle path III, which is negative.

questions.question: A proton moves through a magnetic field of strength $2$ T with a velocity of $150$ m s$^{-1}$ as shown (field into the page, velocity perpendicular to the field). The magnitude of the acceleration of the proton is closest to:

Two wires, one carrying a current of $2$ amps and the other carrying a current of $3$ amps, both of length $4$ m, cross each other perpendicularly: that is, they are $90$ degrees to each other. They are separated by a distance of $1$ cm at the point where they cross. The electromagnetic force between the wires is closest to:
questions.answer: The formula $\frac FL=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$ only applies to parallel wires. For perpendicular wires, the magnetic field of one wire at the other wire (crossing at the midpoints) acts either along the second wire (no force, since $\mathbf F=I\mathbf L\times\mathbf B$ with $\mathbf L\parallel\mathbf B$) or perpendicular to it with equal and opposite directions on the two halves, so the forces cancel. The net force is $0$ N (D).

questions.question:
A uniform electric field is set up between two parallel charged plates P and N as shown in the figure. There is a potential difference $V$ between P and N which are distance $d$ apart. The electric field provides a force $F$ on a small plastic sphere, which is carrying a positive charge $q$ and is on the point of moving from P to N. Assume that gravitational effects on the sphere are negligible.

In terms of $V$ and $q$: how much more electrical potential energy has the sphere on P than it has on N?
questions.answer: The potential energy difference is $\Delta U=qV$ (the sphere has $qV$ more energy at P).

questions.question:
A uniform electric field is set up between two parallel charged plates P and N. There is a potential difference $V$ between P and N which are distance $d$ apart. A small plastic sphere carrying a positive charge $q$ is on the point of moving from P to N. Assume that gravitational effects on the sphere are negligible.

In terms of $V$ and $q$: what must be the increase in the kinetic energy of the sphere as it moves from P to N?
questions.answer: All the lost potential energy becomes kinetic energy: $\Delta E_k=qV$.

questions.question:
A uniform electric field is set up between two parallel charged plates P and N. There is a potential difference $V$ between P and N which are distance $d$ apart. A small plastic sphere carrying a positive charge $q$ is on the point of moving from P to N. Assume that gravitational effects on the sphere are negligible.

In terms of $V$ and $q$: how much work is done by the electric field in moving the sphere from P to N?
questions.answer: The work done by the field equals the gain in kinetic energy: $W=qV$.

questions.question:
Two insulated brass plates, P and Q, stand vertically $12$ cm apart, and are connected as shown in the figure to a $720$ V supply. When a small positively charged sphere at the end of an insulating rod is placed as illustrated at the point X, $6.0$ cm from the plate P, the electrical force acting on it is $12$ mN to the left.

Specify fully the electric field strength between the plates.
questions.answer:
$E=\dfrac Vd=\dfrac{720}{0.12}=6000$ V m$^{-1}$ (N C$^{-1}$), uniform between the plates and directed from the positive plate P to the negative plate Q (to the right, as the school's answer gives).

*The question says the force on the positive sphere is to the left, but in the diagram P is positive, so the field, and the force on a positive charge, point to the right. The magnitudes in this question are not affected.*

questions.question:
Two insulated brass plates, P and Q, stand vertically $12$ cm apart, and are connected as shown in the figure to a $720$ V supply. When a small positively charged sphere at the end of an insulating rod is placed as illustrated at the point X, $6.0$ cm from the plate P, the electrical force acting on it is $12$ mN to the left.

What is the charge on the sphere?
questions.answer: $F=Eq\Rightarrow q=\dfrac FE=\dfrac{12\times10^{-3}}{6000}=2\times10^{-6}$ C.

questions.question:
Two insulated brass plates, P and Q, stand vertically $12$ cm apart, and are connected as shown in the figure to a $720$ V supply. When a small positively charged sphere at the end of an insulating rod is placed as illustrated at the point X, $6.0$ cm from the plate P, the electrical force acting on it is $12$ mN to the left.

The separation of the plates is increased to $16$ cm. What is now the magnitude of the electric force on the charged sphere?

Two insulated brass plates, P and Q, stand vertically $12$ cm apart, and are connected as shown in the figure to a $720$ V supply. When a small positively charged sphere at the end of an insulating rod is placed as illustrated at the point X, $6.0$ cm from the plate P, the electrical force acting on it is $12$ mN to the left.

With the plates again $12$ cm apart, the voltage selector on the power supply is adjusted. If the new force on the sphere is $1.6$ mN, what is now the potential difference across the plates?

A current-carrying loop of wire VWXYZ is placed in a magnetic field which is directed to the left, as indicated in the figure.

What is the direction of the magnetic force acting on section WX?
questions.answer: The cell's positive terminal (long plate) is at the top, so conventional current flows $V\to W\to X\to Y\to Z$. In WX the current is downward and the field is to the left. By $\mathbf F=I\mathbf L\times\mathbf B$ (right-hand rule), the force is **into the page**.

questions.question:
A current-carrying loop of wire VWXYZ is placed in a magnetic field which is directed to the left, as indicated in the figure.

What is the direction of the magnetic force acting on section XY?
questions.answer: Current flows from X to Y, i.e. downward and to the left. Only the component perpendicular to the field (the downward part) experiences a force, which for a downward current in a leftward field is **into the page**.

questions.question:
A current-carrying loop of wire VWXYZ is placed in a magnetic field which is directed to the left, as indicated in the figure.

What is the direction of the magnetic force acting on section YZ?
questions.answer: In YZ the current flows to the left, parallel to the field, so $\sin\theta=0$ and the force is **zero**.

questions.question: Two positive charges, identical in mass and charge, enter a uniform electric field. One charge enters the field with no velocity. The other charge enters the field with a velocity that is in the same direction as the field. Mathematically or otherwise, explain why the magnitude of the change in velocity of the moving charge will always be less than the change in velocity of the stationary charge after both have moved through the same distance in the field. In your answer you should compare the work done on both charges for this distance in the field.
questions.answer:
**Work.** The field is uniform, so the force on each charge is the same constant $F=qE$ whatever its speed, and each moves the same distance $s$ along the field. So the work done on each is the same, $W=qEs$ (equivalently $W=qV$ with $V=Es$), and each gains the same kinetic energy.

**Acceleration.** Since $F=qE$ is the same and the masses are the same, $a=\frac{qE}m$ is the same for both.

**Change in velocity.** For the charge starting at rest, $\frac12mv^2=W$, so $\Delta v=\sqrt{2W/m}$. For the moving charge with initial speed $u$:
$$\frac12mv^2-\frac12mu^2=W\Rightarrow\Delta v=v-u=\frac{2W}{m(v+u)}.$$
Since $u>0$ the denominator is larger than for the charge starting at rest (where it is $mv$), so $\Delta v$ is smaller. (Equivalently, the moving charge covers the distance in less time, so the same acceleration acts for a shorter time and produces a smaller change in velocity.)

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

What is the net force on each ion due to the electric and magnetic fields?
questions.answer: The ions travel in a straight line at constant velocity, so the net force is **zero** (the electric and magnetic forces are equal and opposite).

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

What must be the direction of the magnetic field?
questions.answer: The electric force on a positive ion is to the west, so the magnetic force must be to the east. Using $\mathbf F=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ with $\mathbf v$ downward and $\mathbf F$ to the east, the right-hand rule gives $\mathbf B$ **to the north**.

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

In terms of $q$, specify fully the electric force acting on each ion.
questions.answer: $F=qE=2.0\times10^4q$ newtons, directed to the west.

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

In terms of $q$ and $v$, the speed of the ions, specify fully the magnetic force on each ion.
questions.answer: $F=qvB=4.0\times10^{-3}qv$ newtons, directed to the east (opposite to the electric force).

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

Deduce the value for the speed $v$.
questions.answer: For no deflection $qvB=qE$, so $v=\dfrac EB=\dfrac{2.0\times10^4}{4.0\times10^{-3}}=5.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
In an experiment, two $50$ cm long sections of wire are mounted parallel to each other. They exert a repulsive force of $4\times10^{-6}$ N on each other when they each carry a current of $5$ A.

How far apart are the wires spaced?
questions.answer: $F=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1I_2l}{d}\Rightarrow d=\dfrac{(2\times10^{-7})(5)(5)(0.5)}{4\times10^{-6}}=0.625$ m.

questions.question:
In an experiment, two $50$ cm long sections of wire are mounted parallel to each other. They exert a repulsive force of $4\times10^{-6}$ N on each other when they each carry a current of $5$ A.

Are the currents in the wires in the same or opposite directions?
questions.answer: **Opposite** directions: parallel wires repel when the currents are in opposite directions.

questions.question: Using the formula for the force on a charge $q$ moving through a magnetic field $B$ with a velocity $v$, and simple kinematics and circuit theory, derive an expression for the force on a wire of length $l$ carrying a current $I$ in a magnetic field $B$. Show all the steps involved in your derivation.
questions.answer:
A charge $q$ moving at velocity $v$ at angle $\theta$ to the field experiences $F=qvB\sin\theta$.

Consider charge $q$ moving along a length $l$ of wire in time $t$, so $v=\dfrac lt$. Then
$$F=q\frac ltB\sin\theta=\frac qt\,lB\sin\theta.$$
Since current is the charge passing per unit time, $I=\dfrac qt$, so
$$F=BIl\sin\theta.$$

questions.question: Using the relationship between magnetic force and the resulting centripetal force that occurs when a charged particle moves perpendicularly through a uniform magnetic field, and for circular motion kinematics, $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$, show mathematically or otherwise that the period of rotation of the particle through the field is independent of its speed through the magnetic field.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}r$, so $qB=\dfrac{mv}r$.

Substituting $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}T$: $qB=\dfrac{m}{r}\cdot\dfrac{2\pi r}T=\dfrac{2\pi m}T$, so
$$T=\frac{2\pi m}{qB}.$$
The period depends only on $m$, $q$ and $B$, and $v$ (and $r$) cancel, so it is independent of speed.

questions.question: An electron is fired into a region of space where an electric field and a magnetic field are present. In the space below, sketch the orientation of these two fields if the electron is to pass through the region undeflected. (Ignore gravitational effects.)
questions.answer:
For no deflection the electric and magnetic forces on the electron must be equal and opposite, which needs $E=vB$ with the fields perpendicular to each other and to the velocity.

One arrangement (sketched): the electron moves to the right, $\mathbf B$ points into the page, and $\mathbf E$ points downward (top plate positive, bottom plate negative). The electric force on the electron is upward (opposite to $\mathbf E$) and the magnetic force $-e\,\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ is downward, so they can cancel.

Another valid answer: $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ both parallel (or antiparallel) to the electron's velocity. Then $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B=\mathbf 0$ so there is no magnetic force, and the electric force acts along the line of motion, so the electron is not deflected (it only speeds up or slows down).",answer_images=[f"{IMG}/a19.png"])

questions.question: Which of the following is constant for the entire flight of a projectile?
questions.answer: With air resistance ignored the only force is gravity, so the acceleration is constant ($g$ downward) (D). The height, speed and velocity all change during the flight.

questions.question: The following spectrum was observed during an experiment. Which type of spectrum is this?
questions.answer: A continuous background with dark lines at particular wavelengths is an absorption spectrum (C): the gas has absorbed light at the wavelengths corresponding to its energy-level transitions.

questions.question: A proton travels at a velocity of $0.5$ m s$^{-1}$ from right to left perpendicular to a magnetic field, $B$, of strength $2.0\times10^{-5}$ mT. The magnetic field is running vertically downwards. What is the size of the force that the particle will experience?
questions.answer:
$B=2.0\times10^{-5}\text{ mT}=2.0\times10^{-8}$ T, so $F=qvB=(1.602\times10^{-19})(0.5)(2.0\times10^{-8})=1.6\times10^{-27}$ N.

Direction: take the page with $x$ to the right, $y$ up and $z$ out of the page. Then $\mathbf v=-x$ (right to left) and $\mathbf B=-y$ (down), and for a positive charge $\mathbf F\propto\mathbf v\times\mathbf B=(-x)\times(-y)=+z$, i.e. out of the page (D).

questions.question: Neptune has a mass of $1.024\times10^{26}$ kg and radius of $2.46\times10^{7}$ m. What is the gravitational field strength on the surface of Neptune?

A group of scientists on Earth are observing a nearby star, Barnard's Star. They noticed that the peak wavelength of Barnard's Star's radiation is $925$ nm. What is the surface temperature of Barnard's Star?
questions.answer: Wien's law: $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac bT\Rightarrow T=\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{925\times10^{-9}}=3133$ K (A).

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the change in force between two parallel current carrying conductors, when one current decreases by a factor of four, and the separation distance halves?
questions.answer: $\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$. One current becomes $\frac14$ of its value (factor $\frac14$) and $d$ halves (factor $2$), so $F$ changes by $\frac14\times2=\frac12$: the force halves (B).
options: The force will increase by a factor of eight.
The force will remain the same.
The force will increase by a factor of two.

questions.question: A satellite $S_1$ is in a stable low-Earth orbit (LEO) and another satellite $S_2$ is in a stable geostationary orbit (GEO). Both satellites have the same mass. Which of the following is correct about the two satellites in orbit?
questions.answer: Orbital speed $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ is greater at the smaller radius, so $S_1$ (LEO) is faster. Gravitational potential energy $U=-\dfrac{GMm}r$ is negative and rises towards zero as $r$ increases, so the satellite in the larger (GEO) orbit, $S_2$, has the greater potential energy (B).
options: Greater orbital speed: $S_1$; greater gravitational potential energy: $S_1$
Greater orbital speed: $S_1$; greater gravitational potential energy: $S_2$
Greater orbital speed: $S_2$; greater gravitational potential energy: $S_1$
Greater orbital speed: $S_2$; greater gravitational potential energy: $S_2$

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the problem with using classical physics to predict the spectrum of light emitted by a heated body?
questions.answer: Classical (Rayleigh–Jeans) theory fitted the data at long wavelengths but predicted an intensity that grew without limit at short wavelengths (the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'), contrary to experiment (A). This is what led Planck to propose quantised energy.
options: Predictions of classical physics did not agree with experimental data for short wavelengths.
Prediction of classical physics did not agree with experimental data for long wavelengths.
Predictions of classical physics did not agree with experimental data due to poor experimentation.
Predictions of classical physics did not agree with experimental data as the predicted spectrum is continuous rather than discrete.

questions.question: A rectangular coil of area $40.0$ cm$^2$ and resistance $2.0\ \Omega$ is located in a uniform magnetic field $B=8.0\times10^{-4}$ T which is directed out of the page. The plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field as shown in the diagram. What is the magnitude of the emf induced in the coil when the strength of the magnetic field is doubled in a time of $1.0$ ms?
questions.answer: $\varepsilon=\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{A\,\Delta B}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{(40.0\times10^{-4})(8.0\times10^{-4})}{1.0\times10^{-3}}=3.2\times10^{-3}$ V (B). The resistance is not needed.

questions.question: Five square wire loops of side length $15$ cm are free to rotate within a magnetic field strength of $2.50\times10^{-4}$ T. A current of $3.00$ A is flowing through the coil. What is the torque on the coil when the plane of the coil is at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the magnetic field?
questions.answer:
The torque is $\tau=nIAB\sin\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the normal to the coil and the field. The plane of the coil is $30^\circ$ to the field, so the normal is at $\theta=60^\circ$ to the field (equivalently $\tau=nIAB\cos30^\circ$; the torque is a maximum when the plane is parallel to the field).

$\tau=(5)(3.00)(0.15^2)(2.50\times10^{-4})\sin60^\circ=8.44\times10^{-5}\times0.866=7.3\times10^{-5}$ N m (A).

*The paper's key gives B ($4.2\times10^{-5}$ N m), which comes from using $\sin30^\circ$ with the angle between the plane and the field; the correct answer is A.*

questions.question: Spacecraft 1 is launched with an initial speed $v$ and eventually enters a circular orbit near the Earth's surface. An identical spacecraft, Spacecraft 2, is launched from the same position with a launch speed of $2v$. Which of the following best describes the motion of Spacecraft 2? Ignore air resistance.
questions.answer: Spacecraft 1 enters a circular orbit near the surface, so $v=\sqrt{GM/r}\approx7.9$ km s$^{-1}$. The escape speed is $\sqrt2$ times this (about $11.2$ km s$^{-1}$), and $2v\approx15.8$ km s$^{-1}>v_{esc}$, so Spacecraft 2 has positive total energy and escapes Earth (D).
options: It will enter a circular orbit around the Earth with a shorter period than spacecraft 1.
It will enter a circular orbit around the Earth with a longer period than spacecraft 1.
It will travel in a parabolic path and return to the surface of the Earth.
It will leave the Earth and travel to outer space.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the energy of a photon is correct?
questions.answer: $E=hf$, so photon energy is proportional to frequency (C) (and inversely proportional to wavelength and period).
options: The energy of a photon is always the same.
The energy of a photon is proportional to its wavelength.
The energy of a photon is proportional to its frequency.
The energy of a photon is proportional to its period.

questions.question: Two parallel wires, both $4.00$ m long, are placed vertically on two identical frictionless trolleys on a horizontal surface. When the power supply is switched on, both wires have a current of $18.0$ A and the trolleys move away in opposite directions from each other with initial accelerations of $0.100$ m s$^{-2}$. The wires are $2.00$ mm apart. What is the mass of each trolley?
questions.answer: $F=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1I_2l}{d}=(2\times10^{-7})\dfrac{(18.0)^2(4.00)}{2.00\times10^{-3}}=0.1296$ N on each wire. For each trolley, $m=\dfrac Fa=\dfrac{0.1296}{0.100}=1.30$ kg (A).

questions.question: Which of the following statements best describes the speed of light in various media, including a vacuum?
questions.answer: Maxwell showed that electromagnetic waves travel at $v=\dfrac1{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}$, which depends only on the magnetic permeability and electric permittivity of the medium ($c=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$ in a vacuum) (D). It does not depend on the motion of the source.
options: The speed of light in a medium depends only on the relative motion between the medium and the light source.
The speed of light in a medium depends only on the mass density of the material.
The speed of light in a medium depends only on the temperature of the material.
The speed of light in a medium depends only on the magnetic and electrical properties of the medium.

questions.question: When a magnet is dropped through a coil, a voltage sensor will detect an induced voltage as shown. Which of the following is correct?
questions.answer: The magnet accelerates under gravity, so it moves faster as it leaves the coil than as it enters. The rate of change of flux (and so the emf, $\varepsilon=-N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$) is larger on exit, so the trough (B) has a greater magnitude than the peak (A): $A<B$ (C).
options: Peak and trough: $A=B$; the strength of the magnet is the same.
Peak and trough: $A=B$; the area of the coil is the same.
Peak and trough: $A<B$; the magnet speeds up as it falls through the coil.
Peak and trough: $A>B$; the coil heats up as the magnet falls.

questions.question: If the frequency of the electrical supply to an AC induction motor is increased, what happens to the speed of the rotor?
questions.answer: The rotating magnetic field of the stator turns at a rate set by the supply frequency, and the rotor follows it (slightly slower). Increasing the frequency increases the speed of the rotor (C).
options: It is increased in the opposite direction.

questions.question: A famous chef is using an electrical beater to make cake batter. As the batter thickens it creates friction causing the beaters to slow down. Which choice below best describes what happens to the current in the beaters' coils and the back emf in these coils as the beaters slow down?
questions.answer: The back emf is proportional to the speed of rotation, so it decreases as the beaters slow. The net emf across the coil, $V-\varepsilon_{back}$, increases, so the current $I=\dfrac{V-\varepsilon_{back}}R$ increases (B).

questions.question: A beam of monochromatic light is shone on a diffraction grating. The second-order bright fringes are found at $25^\circ$ to the incident beam as shown in the diagram. What is the highest order of bright fringe that can be observed?
questions.answer: $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$: $\dfrac\lambda d=\dfrac{\sin25^\circ}2=0.2113$. The maximum order has $\sin\theta\le1$: $m\le\dfrac d\lambda=4.73$, so the highest order seen is the $4^{th}$ (C).

questions.question: A simple generator consists of a coil with $N=100$ turns and an area of $100$ cm$^2$ in a uniform magnetic field of $B=0.5$ T. Originally it has a frequency of $50.0$ Hz and produces the first voltage output (as a function of time). Another experiment was carried out by changing some of the variables and the result is shown in Diagram A. Given that the scale of both diagrams are the same, which of the specifications in the table could produce the voltage output described by Diagram A?
questions.answer: The peak emf is $\varepsilon_{max}=2\pi fNBA$. Diagram A has the same period as the original (same number of cycles on the same scale), so $f$ is unchanged ($50$ Hz), and twice the amplitude, so $NBA$ must double. Only option A does this ($N$ doubled, everything else the same). B and C halve the period; D quadruples the amplitude (A).

questions.question: Kirsten is travelling in a spacecraft towards Mars at $0.6c$ relative to Earth and Mars. When the spacecraft is halfway between Earth and Mars, Kirsten sends a radio signal towards Earth and Mars as shown in the diagram. Given that the distance between the surface of Earth and Mars is $3.69\times10^{11}$ m (measured from Earth), how long would it take until the radio signal reaches the surface of Earth and Mars respectively (in Earth and Mars' frame of reference)?
questions.answer: In the Earth–Mars frame the signal travels at $c$ in both directions (the speed of light is independent of the motion of the source), and each planet's surface is $\frac12(3.69\times10^{11})=1.845\times10^{11}$ m from the spacecraft at the instant of emission. So $t=\dfrac{1.845\times10^{11}}{3.00\times10^8}=615$ s for each (D).

questions.question:
A proton and an electron are accelerated from one charged parallel plate to the opposite plate. The plates have a potential difference of $650$ V and are separated by a distance of $5$ cm. The initial positions of the proton and electron are shown.

Find the final kinetic energy of both the electron and proton given that they were both initially at rest.
questions.answer:
The work done by the field equals the change in kinetic energy: $\Delta K=W=qV$. Both particles have a charge of magnitude $e$ and cross the same potential difference, so
$$K_f-0=(1.602\times10^{-19})(650)=1.04\times10^{-16}\text{ J}$$
for **both** the electron and the proton.

questions.question:
A proton and an electron are accelerated from one charged parallel plate to the opposite plate. The plates have a potential difference of $650$ V and are separated by a distance of $5$ cm. The initial positions of the proton and electron are shown.

Quantitatively compare the accelerations of both particles as they move between the two charged plates.
questions.answer:
$E=\dfrac Vd=\dfrac{650}{0.05}=1.3\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$, and $a=\dfrac{F}m=\dfrac{qE}m$.

Proton: $a=\dfrac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(13\,000)}{1.673\times10^{-27}}=1.25\times10^{12}$ m s$^{-2}$ (towards the negative plate, to the right).

Electron: $a=\dfrac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(13\,000)}{9.109\times10^{-31}}=2.29\times10^{15}$ m s$^{-2}$ (towards the positive plate, to the left).

The forces are equal in size, but the proton is much more massive, so its acceleration is smaller by a factor of $\dfrac{m_p}{m_e}\approx1840$ (the electron's is about $1.8\times10^3$ times larger), and the accelerations are in opposite directions.

questions.question: State Einstein's two postulates for his theory of special relativity.
questions.answer:
1. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference (all inertial frames are equivalent).
2. The speed of light in a vacuum is the same constant, $c$, for all observers in inertial frames, regardless of the motion of the source or the observer.

questions.question: Outline experimental evidence that validated the prediction of length contraction.
questions.answer: Muon decay: muons are produced about $10$ km up in the atmosphere and have a very short half-life, so at their speed (close to $c$) they would be expected to decay long before reaching the ground if the Earth-frame distance were the distance travelled. More muons than expected are detected at the surface. In the muon's frame of reference the atmosphere is length-contracted ($L=L_0\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$), so the distance the muon travels is much shorter and it survives long enough to reach the surface. (In the Earth frame the same result is explained by time dilation.)

questions.question: Monochromatic light passes through a double slit $1.25\ \mu$m apart. The $1^{st}$ order maximum is observed to be $28^\circ$ from the central maximum as shown in the diagram. Determine the wavelength of the monochromatic light used.
questions.answer: $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$: $(1.25\times10^{-6})\sin28^\circ=(1)\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=5.87\times10^{-7}$ m ($587$ nm).

questions.question: Monochromatic light passes through a double slit. Explain the formation of the interference pattern on the screen.
questions.answer:
Each slit acts as a source of coherent, in-phase circular (diffracted) waves, and the waves from the two slits overlap and **superpose** on the screen.

*Bright fringes:* at points where the path difference between the waves from the two slits is a whole number of wavelengths, $m\lambda$ ($m=0,1,2,\dots$), the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively, giving maxima of intensity (the central maximum is at $m=0$).

*Dark fringes:* where the path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths, $\left(m+\frac12\right)\lambda$, the waves arrive in antiphase and interfere destructively, giving minima.

The alternating bright and dark bands (fringes) result.

questions.question:
Charged particles A and B move into a magnetic field and move along different circular paths as shown (the field for A is out of the page, the field for B is into the page).

A student observes the diagrams and states that A and B are both negatively charged. Evaluate this statement.
questions.answer: The statement is **incorrect**. For A the field is out of the page and it moves clockwise; at the top of its path it moves to the right and the centripetal force is downwards, towards the centre. The right-hand rule ($\mathbf F=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$) gives a downward force for a **positive** charge here. For B (field into the page, anticlockwise motion, moving left at the top with the force downwards) the same rule again gives a positive charge. Both particles are positively charged.

questions.question:
Charged particles A and B move into a magnetic field and move along different circular paths as shown (the field for A is out of the page, the field for B is into the page).

Particle A is more massive than particle B. Explain how it is possible for the radii of their paths in the fields to be identical.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}r$, so $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

Particle A has the larger mass, but its radius can still equal that of B if the ratio $\dfrac{mv}{qB}$ is the same, for example if A has a larger charge (greater $q$), a lower speed, or is in a stronger magnetic field.

questions.question:
A $975$ kg spacecraft is returning to Earth from a space mission. It will be placed into a geostationary orbit around the Earth before landing on the surface. The diagram shows a possible path of the spacecraft as it approaches the Earth (point A is $5.5\times10^7$ m from the centre of the Earth and point B is in the geostationary orbit). Assume no air resistance for the entire journey of the spacecraft. (Take $M_E=6.0\times10^{24}$ kg.)

Calculate the orbital speed of the spacecraft when it is in the geostationary orbit at point B.
questions.answer:
A geostationary orbit has a period of $24$ h $=86\,400$ s. By Kepler's third law,
$$\frac{r^3}{T^2}=\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}\Rightarrow r=\left[\frac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.0\times10^{24})(86\,400)^2}{4\pi^2}\right]^{1/3}=4.23\times10^7\text{ m}.$$
$$v=\frac{2\pi r}T=\frac{2\pi(4.229\times10^7)}{86\,400}=3.08\times10^3\text{ m s}^{-1}.$$

questions.question:
A $975$ kg spacecraft is returning to Earth from a space mission. It will be placed into a geostationary orbit around the Earth before landing on the surface. The diagram shows a possible path of the spacecraft as it approaches the Earth (point A is $5.5\times10^7$ m from the centre of the Earth and point B is in the geostationary orbit). Assume no air resistance for the entire journey of the spacecraft. (Take $M_E=6.0\times10^{24}$ kg.)

Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy of the spacecraft as it moves from point A to point B.
questions.answer: $$\Delta U=U_f-U_i=-GMm\left(\frac1{r_f}-\frac1{r_i}\right)=-(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.0\times10^{24})(975)\left(\frac1{4.229\times10^7}-\frac1{5.5\times10^7}\right)=-2.1\times10^9\text{ J}.$$

questions.question:
A $975$ kg spacecraft is returning to Earth from a space mission. It will be placed into a geostationary orbit around the Earth before landing on the surface. The diagram shows a possible path of the spacecraft as it approaches the Earth (point A is $5.5\times10^7$ m from the centre of the Earth and point B is in the geostationary orbit). Assume no air resistance for the entire journey of the spacecraft. (Take $M_E=6.0\times10^{24}$ kg.)

Explain what happens to the total energy of the spacecraft as it moves from point A to point B.
questions.answer: The total (mechanical) energy of the spacecraft stays **constant**: only gravity acts (no thrusters or air resistance), so by conservation of energy $U+K$ is unchanged. The gravitational potential energy decreases by $2.1\times10^9$ J as it moves closer to the Earth, and the kinetic energy increases by the same amount.

questions.question:
A $975$ kg spacecraft is returning to Earth from a space mission. It will be placed into a geostationary orbit around the Earth before landing on the surface. The diagram shows a possible path of the spacecraft as it approaches the Earth (point A is $5.5\times10^7$ m from the centre of the Earth and point B is in the geostationary orbit). Assume no air resistance for the entire journey of the spacecraft. (Take $M_E=6.0\times10^{24}$ kg.)

After a while in the geostationary orbit, the spacecraft turns on its thrusters momentarily to reduce its speed to $2.5\times10^3$ m s$^{-1}$. It then begins its descent to the surface as shown. Calculate the speed of the spacecraft just before it hits the surface at point C. (Radius of the Earth $=6.371\times10^6$ m.)
questions.answer:
Conservation of energy from the geostationary radius ($r_i=4.229\times10^7$ m, $v_i=2.5\times10^3$ m s$^{-1}$) to the surface ($r_f=6.371\times10^6$ m):
$$-\frac{GMm}{r_f}+\frac12mv_f^2=-\frac{GMm}{r_i}+\frac12mv_i^2$$
$$v_f^2=v_i^2+2GM\left(\frac1{r_f}-\frac1{r_i}\right)=(2.5\times10^3)^2+2(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.0\times10^{24})\left(\frac1{6.371\times10^6}-\frac1{4.229\times10^7}\right)=1.13\times10^8$$
$$v_f=1.1\times10^4\text{ m s}^{-1}.$$

questions.question:
A straight metal rod sits on two parallel metal rails spaced $d$ m apart. The rails sit perpendicular to the table and the spacing between the rails ($d$) can be adjusted. The rails can be fixed into place once it is adjusted. The apparatus sits within a magnetic field directed into the page with adjustable strength ($B$). The power source supplies an adjustable voltage ($V$) and a current of magnitude $I$ runs through the metal rod as shown.

The metal rod was observed to be stationary. What force(s) are acting on the metal rod?
questions.answer: The weight of the rod, $F_g=mg$, acts downwards. The current is to the right and the field is into the page, so the magnetic force $F=BId$ on the rod is upwards. The rod is stationary, so these two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction (friction is ignored).

questions.question:
A straight metal rod sits on two parallel metal rails spaced $d$ m apart. The rails sit perpendicular to the table and the spacing between the rails ($d$) can be adjusted. The rails can be fixed into place once it is adjusted. The apparatus sits within a magnetic field directed into the page with adjustable strength ($B$). The power source supplies an adjustable voltage ($V$) and a current of magnitude $I$ runs through the metal rod as shown.

A group of students wanted to find the mass of the metal rod. Explain how the variable(s) could be changed and measured to allow them to calculate the mass. Friction can be ignored.
questions.answer:
For the rod to be held stationary, $F_B=F_g$: $BId=mg$, so
$$B=\frac{mg}d\cdot\frac1I.$$
*Method:* fix the rail separation $d$ (and measure it). Change the current $I$ by changing the supply voltage $V$ (measuring $I$ with an ammeter), and for each current adjust the magnetic field until the rod is just stationary and record $B$ (e.g. with a Hall probe). Plot $B$ against $\dfrac1I$: the graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient $\dfrac{mg}d$, so $m=\dfrac{\text{gradient}\times d}g$.

questions.question:
Samantha is riding in a car on a roller-coaster. Their combined mass equals $245$ kg. As shown in the diagram, it can be assumed that the track is circular near the points A (the top of a hill) and B (the bottom of a dip) with radii $35$ m and $65$ m respectively; B is $5.5$ m below A.

Consider Samantha and the car as a single object. On the diagram, draw and label all the forces acting on the single object using a solid line. Use a dotted line to show the resultant force acting on the single object.
questions.answer: At A two forces act on the car and rider: the weight $F_g=mg$ downwards and the normal force $N$ from the track upwards. The car moves in a circle with its centre below A, so the resultant force (dotted) is downwards, towards the centre, with magnitude $mg-N=\frac{mv^2}r$. So $F_g>N$.

questions.question:
Samantha is riding in a car on a roller-coaster. Their combined mass equals $245$ kg. As shown in the diagram, it can be assumed that the track is circular near the points A (the top of a hill) and B (the bottom of a dip) with radii $35$ m and $65$ m respectively; B is $5.5$ m below A.

Due to safety reasons, the rollercoaster was designed such that the passengers would NOT feel 'weightless' at point A. Calculate the maximum speed at which Samantha could be moving at point A.
questions.answer:
At A, $F_c=F_g-N$. The passengers feel weightless when $N=0$, so the maximum speed has $F_c=F_g$:
$$\frac{mv^2}r=mg\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{rg}=\sqrt{35\times9.8}=18.5\ldots\approx19\text{ m s}^{-1}.$$
Samantha must be moving at less than about $19$ m s$^{-1}$ at A.

questions.question:
Samantha is riding in a car on a roller-coaster. Their combined mass equals $245$ kg. As shown in the diagram, it can be assumed that the track is circular near the points A (the top of a hill) and B (the bottom of a dip) with radii $35$ m and $65$ m respectively; B is $5.5$ m below A.

Assume that the car is travelling at the speed calculated in (b) ($v_A=\sqrt{35\times9.8}$ m s$^{-1}$) and there is no friction and no driving force on the car after point A. Calculate the speed of the car when it reaches point B, $5.5$ m below point A.
questions.answer:
Conservation of energy: $K_f=K_i-\Delta U$, with $\Delta U=mg(-5.5)$:
$$\frac12v_B^2=\frac12(18.5\ldots)^2+(9.8)(5.5)\Rightarrow v_B^2=343+107.8=450.8$$
$$v_B=21.2\approx21\text{ m s}^{-1}.$$

questions.question:
Samantha is riding in a car on a roller-coaster. Their combined mass equals $245$ kg. As shown in the diagram, it can be assumed that the track is circular near the points A (the top of a hill) and B (the bottom of a dip) with radii $35$ m and $65$ m respectively; B is $5.5$ m below A.

Calculate the normal force acting on Samantha and the car at point B (using the speed from part (c)).
questions.answer:
At the bottom of the dip the centre of the circle is above the car, so $F_c=N-F_g$:
$$N=\frac{mv^2}r+mg=\frac{(245)(450.8)}{65}+(245)(9.8)=1699+2401=4.1\times10^3\text{ N}.$$

The wire's field through the loop is into the page (below a wire carrying current to the right) and is stronger nearer the wire.

**A (rotation about Y):** the flux $\Phi=BA\cos\theta$ varies sinusoidally, so the emf is a sinusoid with one complete cycle during one rotation, starting from zero. At the start the flux (into the page) is a maximum and is decreasing, so by Lenz's law the induced current is **clockwise** (to produce a field into the page); after half a rotation it reverses to anticlockwise.

**B (parallel to the wire):** the field at the loop does not change, so the flux is constant and the emf is **zero** (direction not relevant).

**C (moving away):** the flux into the page decreases (the field weakens with distance), so an emf is induced to oppose this, producing a field into the page: **clockwise**. The rate of change of flux (and the emf) is largest at the start and decays as the loop moves further away (the field falls off as $1/r$).

questions.question:
A group of students set up the experiment shown to study the photoelectric effect. They shone light of varying wavelengths onto different metal surfaces and measured the stopping voltage. Using the stopping voltage, they were able to measure the work function for each metal surface they tested. The results are: caesium $2.1$ eV, barium $2.5$ eV, calcium $2.9$ eV, magnesium $3.7$ eV, beryllium $5.0$ eV.

Using data from the table, draw a graph on the grid of the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron against frequency of the incident light for calcium.
questions.answer:
$K_{\max}=hf-\phi$ is a straight line of gradient $h=4.14\times10^{-15}$ eV s $\left(6.626\times10^{-34}\text{ J s}\right)$ with a vertical intercept of $-\phi=-2.9$ eV and a frequency (horizontal) intercept at the threshold frequency
$$f_0=\frac\phi h=\frac{2.9}{4.14\times10^{-15}}=7.0\times10^{14}\text{ Hz}.$$
(Only the part with $K_{\max}\ge0$, i.e. $f\ge f_0$, is physical; the rest is the extrapolation to the intercept.)

questions.question:
A group of students set up the experiment shown to study the photoelectric effect. They shone light of varying wavelengths onto different metal surfaces and measured the stopping voltage. Using the stopping voltage, they were able to measure the work function for each metal surface they tested. The results are: caesium $2.1$ eV, barium $2.5$ eV, calcium $2.9$ eV, magnesium $3.7$ eV, beryllium $5.0$ eV.

If monochromatic light of wavelength $400$ nm is incident on each of the metal surfaces, how many of them would exhibit the photoelectric effect? Show all working.
questions.answer:
The photon energy is
$$E=\frac{hc}\lambda=\frac{(6.626\times10^{-34})(3.00\times10^8)}{400\times10^{-9}}=4.97\times10^{-19}\text{ J}=\frac{4.97\times10^{-19}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=3.10\text{ eV}.$$
The photoelectric effect occurs only for metals with $\phi<3.10$ eV: caesium ($2.1$), barium ($2.5$) and calcium ($2.9$). Magnesium ($3.7$ eV) and beryllium ($5.0$ eV) do not. So **three** metals exhibit the photoelectric effect.

questions.question: The students noticed that when light of a certain wavelength was shone on a metal surface, no electrons are emitted. They then increased the intensity of this light and still did not detect any electrons. Explain the students' observations and state whether this supports light being a wave or particle.
questions.answer:
Electrons are emitted only if the frequency of the light is above the threshold frequency of the metal ($f>f_0=\phi/h$), however intense the light is. Each photon has energy $E=hf$ and each electron absorbs one photon: if $hf<\phi$ a single photon does not have enough energy to eject an electron, and increasing the intensity only increases the number of photons, not the energy of each, so still no electrons are emitted.

This supports the **particle (photon) model** of light. The wave model predicts that a sufficiently intense light of any frequency would eventually give the electrons enough energy to escape.

questions.question:
A group of physics students made a simple AC generator in class. It had $150$ turns of wire in a $6.00$ cm wide square coil that was placed in a magnetic field of strength $1.85\times10^{2}$ mT. They connected the handle to a motor which rotated with a frequency of $4.00$ Hz and used the electricity produced to power a light globe.

Given that $\varepsilon=2\pi nBAf$, calculate the emf produced by the generator.

A group of physics students made a simple AC generator in class. It had $150$ turns of wire in a $6.00$ cm wide square coil that was placed in a magnetic field of strength $1.85\times10^{2}$ mT. They connected the handle to a motor which rotated with a frequency of $4.00$ Hz and used the electricity produced to power a light globe.

The students removed the motor and turned the handle themselves, maintaining a constant speed of rotation. They noticed the force required to turn the handle varied as the coil rotated. They also noticed that the light bulb glowed brightest when the force required was greatest and went out when the force required was virtually zero. Explain these observations using Lenz's Law and the Law of Conservation of Energy.
questions.answer:
The induced emf is $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$. The rate of change of flux (and so the emf and the induced current) is greatest when the plane of the coil is **parallel** to the field (the coil sides are cutting across the field lines fastest) and zero when the plane is **perpendicular** to the field (the flux is at a maximum but is momentarily not changing). The globe therefore glows brightest when the emf is a maximum and goes out when the emf is zero.

By Lenz's law, the induced current produces a magnetic field (and a motor-effect torque on the coil) that opposes the change in flux that causes it, that is, it opposes the rotation. This opposing torque is largest when the current is largest, so the force needed to turn the handle at constant speed is greatest when the bulb is brightest, and is almost zero when the induced current is zero.

By conservation of energy, the electrical energy dissipated in the globe must come from the work done turning the handle (mechanical energy). When the electrical power output is greatest, the mechanical work needed per second is greatest; when no current flows, no electrical energy is produced and virtually no force is needed. If Lenz's law were reversed (the induced current assisted the motion), energy would be created from nothing.

questions.question:
A group of scientists have created an unknown particle, particle X. They designed an experiment to identify this particle. Particle X was placed stationary between oppositely charged plates A and B (separated by $0.165$ m) as shown. The plates were charged such that particle X would exit with a speed of $0.55c$.

Calculate the acceleration experienced by particle X if it took $2$ ns to reach plate B.
questions.answer: From rest, $s=ut+\frac12at^2$: $0.165=\frac12a(2\times10^{-9})^2\Rightarrow a=8.25\times10^{16}$ m s$^{-2}$.

questions.question:
Particle X, travelling at a constant speed of $0.55c$, then enters a uniform magnetic field and moves in a circle as shown.

When particle X is at rest, it has a mean lifetime of $2.6\times10^{-8}$ s. Find the mean lifetime of particle X measured by the scientists as the particle travelled in circular motion inside the magnetic field.
questions.answer: Time dilation: $t=\dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}=\dfrac{2.6\times10^{-8}}{\sqrt{1-0.55^2}}=3.1\times10^{-8}$ s.

questions.question:
Particle X, travelling at a constant speed of $0.55c$, then enters a uniform magnetic field and moves in a circle as shown.

Show that the radius of the circular motion is given by $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$.
questions.answer: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}r$. Dividing by $v$ and rearranging, $qB=\dfrac{mv}r$, so $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.question:
The scientists changed the magnetic field strength ($B$) and measured the radius of particle X's motion ($r$) in their frame of reference. They then presented the results as the graph of $r$ against $\dfrac1B$ shown (particle X travels at $0.55c$).

Use the graph to determine the distance travelled by particle X in one cycle of the circular motion in the particle's frame of reference when the magnetic field strength is $0.238$ T.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac1B=\dfrac1{0.238}=4.2$ T$^{-1}$. From the graph, $r=1.08$ m in the scientists' frame, so the distance travelled in one cycle in their frame is $L_0=2\pi(1.08)=6.79$ m.

In the particle's frame of reference this length is contracted: $L=L_0\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}=6.79\times\sqrt{1-0.55^2}=6.79\times0.835=5.7$ m.

questions.question:
The scientists changed the magnetic field strength ($B$) and measured the radius of particle X's motion ($r$) in their frame of reference. They then presented the results as the graph of $r$ against $\dfrac1B$ shown (particle X travels at $0.55c$).

The scientists suspect that particle X is one of the particles listed in the table:

| Particle | Charge (C) | Mass (kg) |
|---|---|---|
| Pion | $+1.602\times10^{-19}$ | $2.49\times10^{-28}$ |
| Kaon | $-1.602\times10^{-19}$ | $8.79\times10^{-28}$ |
| D | $+1.602\times10^{-19}$ | $3.33\times10^{-27}$ |

Use the gradient of the graph to find the charge to mass ratio and predict what particle X might be.
questions.answer:
From (c), $r=\dfrac{mv}q\cdot\dfrac1B$, so the gradient of $r$ against $\frac1B$ is $\dfrac{mv}q$. Using two points on the line of best fit, $(3.94,\,1.02)$ and $(4.69,\,1.20)$:
$$\text{gradient}=\frac{1.20-1.02}{4.69-3.94}=0.24\text{ T m}.$$
With $v=0.55c=1.65\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$: $\dfrac mq=\dfrac{0.24}{1.65\times10^8}\Rightarrow\dfrac qm=6.9\times10^8$ C kg$^{-1}$.

Charge to mass ratios: pion $\dfrac{1.602\times10^{-19}}{2.49\times10^{-28}}=6.4\times10^8$; kaon $1.8\times10^8$; D $4.9\times10^7$ C kg$^{-1}$. Particle X is closest to the **pion** (and its curvature in the figure is consistent with a positive charge).

questions.question:
A wind turbine runs a $150$ kW generator with an output voltage of $1000$ V. The voltage is increased by a transformer $T_1$, with a ratio of primary turns to secondary turns of $1:10$, and transmitted to a town $5$ km away through power lines with a total resistance of $2\ \Omega$. Another transformer $T_2$, with a ratio of primary turns to secondary turns of $40:1$, reduces the voltage before it is delivered for commercial use.

Analyse the electrical data of the transformers and power lines and explain how the efficiency of this transmission process can be increased. Your analysis should include both qualitative and quantitative information.
questions.answer:
**Current design.** $T_1$ is a step-up transformer: $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}\Rightarrow V_s=10\times1000=10\,000$ V. The power is $P=VI$, so the line current is $I=\dfrac{150\times10^3}{10\,000}=15$ A.

Power lost in the lines: $P_{loss}=I^2R=(15)^2(2)=450$ W. The efficiency of transmission is
$$\frac{150\,000-450}{150\,000}=99.7\%.$$
(Equivalently the voltage drop along the lines is $IR=30$ V, so $9970$ V reaches $T_2$.) $T_2$ steps this down by $40:1$ to about $250$ V, with a current of about $600$ A, available for use.

**Why stepping up helps (qualitative).** For a given power, a higher voltage means a lower current, and the losses in the lines depend on $I^2R$. Stepping the voltage up before transmission therefore greatly reduces energy lost as heat; stepping it back down at the town gives a safe, usable voltage and a large current.

**Increasing efficiency.**
