questions.question: In a photoelectric effect experiment the voltage applied across the photocell is increased until the photocurrent just falls to zero; this is the stopping voltage. Explain how the stopping voltage is related to the electrons' kinetic energy.
questions.answer: The applied voltage sets up an electric field that opposes the motion of the emitted photoelectrons towards the collector, so the field does negative work on each electron as it crosses the potential difference $V$: $W=qV=eV$. When the voltage is increased to the stopping voltage, the work done by the field on even the most energetic electrons equals their maximum kinetic energy on leaving the surface, so none reach the collector and the photocurrent just falls to zero. Hence $K_{max}=eV_{stop}$: the stopping voltage is the lowest applied voltage at which no photocurrent is recorded, and it is a direct measure of the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

questions.question:
In a photoelectric effect experiment the stopping voltage $V$ was measured for light of different frequencies $f$:

| $f$ ($\times10^{14}$ Hz) | 6.0 | 7.0 | 7.5 | 8.0 | 9.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $V$ (V) | 0.16 | 0.52 | 0.72 | 0.88 | 1.35 |

Use a line of best fit through the graph of $V$ against $f$ to determine the work function in eV, as well as Planck's constant.
questions.answer:
From $K_{max}=hf-\phi$ and $K_{max}=eV$: $V=\dfrac hef-\dfrac\phi e$. A graph of $V$ against $f$ is a straight line with gradient $\dfrac he$ and vertical intercept $-\dfrac\phi e$.

**Gradient** of the best-fit line: $\dfrac{1.35-0.16}{(9.0-6.0)\times10^{14}}\approx3.9\times10^{-15}\ \text{V s}$ (a least-squares line through all five points gives $3.93\times10^{-15}$), so
$$h=e\times\text{gradient}=1.602\times10^{-19}\times3.93\times10^{-15}\approx6.3\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}.$$
**Work function.** The line meets the frequency axis ($V=0$) at the threshold frequency $f_0\approx5.7\times10^{14}$ Hz (equivalently its vertical intercept is about $-2.2$ V), so
$$\phi=hf_0=6.3\times10^{-34}\times5.65\times10^{14}\approx3.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}\approx2.2\ \text{eV}.$$
(Values read from a hand-drawn line of best fit are acceptable within a reasonable range: the school's sample gives $h\approx6.5\times10^{-34}$ J s and $\phi\approx2.3$ eV.)

questions.question: In a photoelectric effect experiment the stopping voltage was measured for light of different frequencies. Amy repeats the same procedure. This time she doubles the intensity of the incident light and produces a new graph of stopping voltage against frequency which is identical to the first one. Use the appropriate model of light to account for this observation.
questions.answer:
The observation is explained by the **photon (quantum) model** of light: light consists of photons each carrying energy $E=hf$, and each photoelectron is released by the absorption of a single photon, so $K_{max}=hf-\phi$.

Doubling the intensity at a given frequency means twice as many photons arrive per second, but each photon still has the same energy $hf$. So twice as many electrons are released (a larger photocurrent), but the maximum kinetic energy of each electron, $K_{max}=hf-\phi$, depends only on the frequency of the light (and the work function of the metal), not on the intensity. As the stopping voltage is given by $eV_{stop}=K_{max}$, the stopping voltage at each frequency is unchanged, which is why the graph is identical to the first. (The wave model, in which more intense light would give electrons more energy, cannot explain this.)

questions.question: A ball is thrown from $S$ at an angle to the horizontal as shown in the diagram. $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are different positions along the ball's trajectory. Which row of the table best represents the velocity and acceleration of the ball at $X$, $Y$ and $Z$?
questions.answer: The velocity of the ball is always tangent to its path (up and to the right at $X$, horizontal at $Y$, down and to the right at $Z$; it is not zero at $Y$ because the horizontal component is constant). Ignoring air resistance the only force is gravity, so the acceleration is $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ vertically downward at every point. This is row A.

questions.question: James Clerk Maxwell made significant contributions to physics. Which of the following did Maxwell NOT contribute to our understanding of physics?
questions.answer: Maxwell's equations unified electricity and magnetism, predicted electromagnetic waves and gave their speed ($c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$). The existence of electromagnetic waves was experimentally validated by Hertz (who produced and detected radio waves with an induction coil), not by Maxwell.
options: Unifying electricity and magnetism through equations
Predicting the existence of electromagnetic waves
Predicting the velocity of electromagnetic waves
Validating the existence of electromagnetic waves

questions.question: An electromagnet is attached to the bottom of a light train which is travelling from left to right, as shown. When a large current is passed through the coils of the electromagnet, the train slows down as a direct result of the law of conservation of energy. In which of the following devices is the law of conservation of energy applied in the same way?
questions.answer: The moving electromagnet induces eddy currents in the rail; by Lenz's law these produce a magnetic field that opposes the relative motion between the magnet and the rail, so the train slows (its kinetic energy is transferred to electrical, then thermal, energy). An induction motor works in the same way: the rotating magnetic field induces currents in the rotor (or axle) whose fields oppose the relative motion between rotor and field, so the rotor is dragged round to reduce that relative motion.

questions.question: In an experiment, alpha particles were fired into a thin sheet of beryllium. Unknown radiation was detected. Which of the results below provides the strongest evidence that the unknown radiation is not gamma radiation?
questions.answer: Gamma radiation and neutrons are both uncharged (so neither is deflected by an electric or magnetic field), both are highly penetrating, and both can knock protons out of paraffin. The photoelectric effect is the distinguishing test: gamma photons have energy well above the work function of a metal and will eject photoelectrons, while neutrons will not.
options: The unknown radiation could not be deflected by an electric field.
The unknown radiation had a very high penetrating power.
The unknown radiation caused protons to be ejected from a block of paraffin.
The unknown radiation could not produce the photoelectric effect.

questions.question: A student swings a $20$ g metal ball on the end of a $1.10$ m length of string around his body at a constant angular velocity of $4\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. The string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal, as shown. What is the magnitude of the centripetal force acting on the ball?
questions.answer:
The ball moves in a horizontal circle of radius $r=1.10\cos30^\circ=0.953$ m. The centripetal force is the net (horizontal) force:
$$F_c=m\omega^2r=0.020\times(4\pi)^2\times0.953=3.0\ \text{N}.$$
(This is not the tension in the string, which acts along the string.)

questions.question: Geiger and Marsden carried out an experiment to investigate the structure of the atom. Which diagram best represents the model corresponding to the results that they obtained?
questions.answer: Almost all alpha particles passed straight through, but a very small number were deflected through large angles (some almost straight back). This led Rutherford to the nuclear model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space containing the electrons. Diagram A shows a small central nucleus with a few large-angle deflections; the diagrams with a uniformly filled sphere (the plum-pudding model) or with no deflection do not fit the results.

questions.question: When electromagnetic radiation shines on metals, photoelectrons may be emitted. The maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons is plotted against radiation frequency for four metals as shown in the graph. Electromagnetic radiation of wavelength $167$ nm shines upon an unknown metal and the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is found to be $4.0\times10^{-19}$ J. Based on this information, what is the unknown metal?
questions.answer:
$$f=\frac c\lambda=\frac{3.00\times10^8}{167\times10^{-9}}=1.80\times10^{15}\ \text{Hz},\qquad K_{max}=\frac{4.0\times10^{-19}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=2.5\ \text{eV}.$$
On the graph the point $(1.80\times10^{15}\ \text{Hz},\,2.5\ \text{eV})$ lies on the line for Be (the line furthest to the right, i.e. with the highest threshold frequency of the three close lines).

questions.question: A proton, p$^+$, enters an electric field between two parallel charged plates (100 V on the top plate, 0 V on the bottom plate, $20$ cm apart) with an initial horizontal velocity of $u\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. After two microseconds, the proton's velocity is in the direction $45^\circ$ from the horizontal. What is the magnitude of the velocity at two microseconds?
questions.answer:
The field is vertical, so it does not change the horizontal component of velocity, which stays $u$. At $45^\circ$ to the horizontal the vertical component must also equal $u$, so
$$v=\sqrt{u^2+u^2}=\sqrt2\,u\approx1.4u.$$
The field strength and plate voltage are not needed.

questions.question: A radioisotope, $X$, undergoes $\beta^-$ decay. On the grid of number of neutrons against atomic number shown, which choice represents the product of the decay?
questions.answer:
In $\beta^-$ decay a neutron changes into a proton: $n\to p^++e^-+\bar\nu$. The daughter nuclide therefore has the atomic number increased by 1 and the neutron number decreased by 1: one square to the right and one square down on the grid. That is $Q$.

(School error: the marking guide's explanation says the nuclide "loses 1 proton and gains 1 neutron" (which describes $\beta^+$ decay, product $P$), but the school's own answer sheet gives $Q$, which is correct.)

questions.question: The gravitational potential energy of a mass positioned at $X$ in the gravitational field of Earth is $U_X$, and for the same mass positioned at $Y$ is $U_Y$. The diagram is drawn to scale (distances are measured from the centre of Earth). What is the value of $\dfrac{U_X}{U_Y}$?
questions.answer:
From the scale diagram $r_X=2.8$ cm and $r_Y=4.2$ cm. Since $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}\propto-\dfrac1r$,
$$\frac{U_X}{U_Y}=\frac{r_Y}{r_X}=\frac{4.2}{2.8}=1.5.$$

questions.question: Three identical parallel wires $W_1$, $W_2$ and $W_3$ are positioned as shown, each carrying a current of the same magnitude in the direction indicated ($W_1$ down, $W_2$ up, $W_3$ down). $W_1$ and $W_2$ are a distance $d$ apart, and $W_2$ and $W_3$ are a distance $2d$ apart, with $W_3$ to the right. If the wire $W_1$ exerts a force on wire $W_2$ of $F$, then what is the magnitude and direction of the total, resultant force on $W_2$?
questions.answer: For parallel wires $\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1I_2}{r}$, so with equal currents and lengths, $F\propto\dfrac1r$. $W_1$ and $W_2$ carry opposite currents, so they repel: $W_1$ pushes $W_2$ to the right with force $F$. $W_3$ is twice as far away, so its force on $W_2$ has magnitude $\tfrac12F$; $W_3$ and $W_2$ also carry opposite currents, so $W_3$ pushes $W_2$ to the left. The net force is $F-\tfrac12F=\tfrac12F$ to the right.

questions.question:
The radioactive decay of thorium-232 is $^{232}_{90}\text{Th}\to{}^{228}_{88}\text{Ra}+{}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$. Using the information in the table below, what is the energy released as a result of this decay?

| Nucleus or particle | Mass (u) |
|---|---|
| $^{232}_{90}$Th | 232.038055 |
| $^{228}_{88}$Ra | 228.031070 |
| $^{4}_{2}$He | 4.001506 |

Three identical spaceships are near each other at a given time. An astronaut on ship $A$, sitting on a platform on Earth, observes the lengths of the two other spaceships, ship $B$ and ship $C$, as they pass by Earth at $0.75c$ and $0.94c$, respectively, as shown in the diagram (all three travelling in the same direction). What would the astronauts on the two passing ships observe?
questions.answer:
Length contraction depends on the relative speed between the observer and the object: the faster the relative speed, the shorter the object appears.

Astronaut on $B$: $A$ moves past at $0.75c$, while $C$ moves relative to $B$ at only $\dfrac{0.94c-0.75c}{1-0.94\times0.75}=0.64c$. $A$ is moving faster relative to $B$, so $A$ appears shorter than $C$.

Astronaut on $C$: $A$ moves past at $0.94c$ while $B$ moves relative to $C$ at $0.64c$, so $A$ appears shorter than $B$.

Hence $A$ is shorter in both cases (option D). (The school used the Galilean $0.19c$ for the relative speed, which gives the same conclusion.)
options: Astronaut on ship $B$: length of $A$ > length of $C$; astronaut on ship $C$: length of $A$ > length of $B$
Astronaut on ship $B$: length of $A$ > length of $C$; astronaut on ship $C$: length of $A$ < length of $B$
Astronaut on ship $B$: length of $A$ < length of $C$; astronaut on ship $C$: length of $A$ > length of $B$
Astronaut on ship $B$: length of $A$ < length of $C$; astronaut on ship $C$: length of $A$ < length of $B$

questions.question:
The table contains information related to two moons orbiting Mars.

| Moon | Mass (kg) | Orbital radius (m) | Orbital velocity (km s$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deimos | $1.476\times10^{15}$ | $2.35\times10^{7}$ | $1.35$ |
| Phobos | $1.066\times10^{16}$ | $9.38\times10^{6}$ | — |

The orbital velocity of Phobos can be determined by using data selected from this table. What is the orbital velocity of the moon Phobos?
questions.answer:
For orbits about the same body, $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, so $rv^2=GM$ is constant (the moons' own masses do not matter). Then
$$v_P=v_D\sqrt{\frac{r_D}{r_P}}=1.35\times\sqrt{\frac{2.35\times10^{7}}{9.38\times10^{6}}}=2.14\ \text{km s}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: The emission spectra from a selection of metals (Mg, Al, Cu, Li) and an unknown mixture of metals are shown within the visible waveband in the figure. What metals are in the unknown mixture?
questions.answer: Compare distinctive lines: the mixture has the lines at about 540 nm (Mg) and 720 nm (Al), but not the distinctive lines of Cu (about 553 nm) or Li (about 648 nm). The mixture therefore contains aluminium and magnesium.

questions.question: What is the wavelength, in metres, of a photon emitted from a hydrogen atom when an electron in the $n=2$ level makes a transition to the $n=1$ level?
questions.answer: Rydberg formula: $\dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)=1.097\times10^7\left(\dfrac1{1^2}-\dfrac1{2^2}\right)=8.23\times10^6\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda=1.22\times10^{-7}$ m.

questions.question: Which of the following ideal transformers could be used to convert an input voltage of $40$ volts AC to an output voltage of $8$ volts AC? The number of turns on the two coils of each transformer is shown in the diagram (either coil may be used as the input).
questions.answer: $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}$, so $\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}=\dfrac{40}{8}=5$. The only transformer with a turns ratio of $5$ is C: the input is connected to the $30$-turn coil and the output taken from the $6$-turn coil (a step-down transformer). The others have ratios of $1.25$ (or $0.8$), $4.2$ (or $0.24$) and $10$ (or $0.1$).

questions.question: Three polarisers, $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$, were placed in between a light source and a light detector with their polarising axes aligned parallel, as shown in the first diagram. The light detector recorded a light intensity of $I$. Polariser $P_2$ and $P_3$ were then rotated clockwise, $30^\circ$ and $90^\circ$, respectively (second diagram). What light intensity did the light detector record?
questions.answer: Malus' law $I=I_{max}\cos^2\theta$ at each polariser. $P_1\to P_2$: the angle is $30^\circ$, so $I_2=I\cos^2 30^\circ=0.75I$. $P_2\to P_3$: $P_3$ is at $90^\circ$ and $P_2$ at $30^\circ$, so the angle between them is $60^\circ$: $I_3=0.75I\cos^260^\circ=0.1875I\approx0.19I$.

questions.question: The diagram shows some parts of a simple AC motor (a coil $WXYZ$ between the poles of a magnet). Which row of the table correctly describes the direction of the force acting on side $WX$ and the direction of the torque this produces on the coil?
questions.answer: With an alternating current the current in side $WX$ reverses every half cycle, so by $F=BIl$ the force on it reverses direction every $180^\circ$. As the coil also turns through $180^\circ$ in that time, the side that is passing the other pole now carries the reversed current, so the force on the sides always acts so as to turn the coil in the same sense: a motor needs torque in a continuous direction to keep turning, so the torque on the coil remains in a constant direction.
options: Force on $WX$: remains constant; torque on coil: remains constant
Force on $WX$: remains constant; torque on coil: reverses every $180^\circ$
Force on $WX$: reverses every $180^\circ$; torque on coil: remains constant
Force on $WX$: reverses every $180^\circ$; torque on coil: reverses every $180^\circ$

questions.question: In 1981, a German research team produced 5 atoms of the isotope bohrium-262 via the following nuclear reaction: $^{209}_{83}\text{Bi}+{}^{54}_{24}\text{Cr}\to{}^{262}_{107}\text{Bh}+{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$. Based on the graph of average binding energy per nucleon against mass number, which of the following choices best describes the nuclear process and energetics of this reaction?
questions.answer: Two nuclei combine into a larger nucleus, so the process is fusion (the emitted neutron is not counted as a second nucleus). The reactants ($A\approx209$ and $54$) and the product ($A=262$) lie on the right-hand, falling side of the binding energy curve, and the product ($A=262$) has a lower binding energy per nucleon than $^{209}$Bi, so the product is less stable than the reactants. Energy must therefore be put in for the reaction to proceed: it is endothermic (energy absorbed).

questions.question:
The light from an incandescent bulb passes through a transparent container of cold hydrogen gas before passing through a collimating slit, as shown in the diagram. The collimated light is incident on a digital spectrometer that measures the spectral intensity curve, which is shown on the graph (a smooth black-body curve with peak near $0.85\ \mu$m and small absorption dips at about $0.41$, $0.43$, $0.49$ and $0.66\ \mu$m).

Explain the absorption dips in the curve in terms of the Bohr model of the atom, with reference to the law of conservation of energy.
questions.answer:
The dips are caused by electrons in the cold hydrogen gas absorbing photons. In the Bohr model, electrons in the $n=2$ level (the Balmer series) absorb a photon of exactly the right energy to move to a higher orbit ($n=3,4,5,6$), which has higher energy. By conservation of energy the photon energy must equal the energy difference between the two levels:
$$E_{photon}+E_{i}=E_{f}\ \Rightarrow\ hf=E_f-E_i.$$
Only photons with these specific wavelengths are absorbed (and re-emitted in random directions), so the intensity of light reaching the spectrometer is reduced at these wavelengths, producing narrow dips in the continuous spectrum.

questions.question:
The light from an incandescent bulb passes through a transparent container of cold hydrogen gas before passing through a collimating slit, as shown in the diagram. The collimated light is incident on a digital spectrometer that measures the spectral intensity curve, which is shown on the graph (a smooth black-body curve with peak near $0.85\ \mu$m and small absorption dips at about $0.41$, $0.43$, $0.49$ and $0.66\ \mu$m).

Calculate the temperature of the incandescent globe.
questions.answer:
From Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{max}=\dfrac bT$. The peak of the curve is at $\lambda_{max}=0.85\times10^{-6}$ m, so
$$T=\frac{b}{\lambda_{max}}=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{0.85\times10^{-6}}=3.4\times10^{3}\ \text{K}\ (3409\ \text{K}).$$

questions.question:
The light from an incandescent bulb passes through a transparent container of cold hydrogen gas before passing through a collimating slit, as shown in the diagram. The collimated light is incident on a digital spectrometer that measures the spectral intensity curve, which is shown on the graph (a smooth black-body curve with peak near $0.85\ \mu$m and small absorption dips at about $0.41$, $0.43$, $0.49$ and $0.66\ \mu$m).

On the same graph, sketch the curve expected if the experiment is repeated with another incandescent globe radiating at a higher temperature. Assume the absorption dips are approximately the same height. Describe your sketch in words.

Thomas Young described an experiment where light was passed through two slits and the subsequent result was projected on to a screen. The diagram shows the results predicted by two different models: Prediction X (two bright bands on the screen, in line with the slits) and Prediction Y (a pattern of many alternating bright and dark fringes). Identify an assumption of EACH model that determines the results on the screen.
questions.answer: Prediction X (two bands, one behind each slit) corresponds to the assumption that light is a stream of particles (corpuscles) travelling in straight lines, so only the paths through the slits are lit. Prediction Y (a series of bright and dark fringes) corresponds to the assumption that light is a wave, so the light diffracts at each slit and the two waves interfere.

questions.question: Thomas Young described an experiment where light was passed through two slits and the subsequent result was projected on to a screen. The diagram shows the results predicted by two different models: Prediction X (two bright bands in line with the slits) and Prediction Y (alternating bright and dark interference fringes). How did Young's results help lead to the reconceptualisation of the model of light?
questions.answer: At the time, Newton's corpuscular (particle) model was the accepted model of light, which predicts two bright bands (Prediction X). Young passed light through two closely spaced narrow slits and observed an interference pattern of alternating bright and dark fringes on the screen (like Prediction Y). Interference (constructive and destructive superposition) is a wave phenomenon that particles in the corpuscular model cannot explain. Young's results therefore supported Huygens' wave model of light and challenged Newton's particle model, so the model of light was reconceptualised from particles to waves.

questions.question: Use the work of TWO scientists to explain how the combination of their experiments led to a better understanding of the electron.
questions.answer:
**J. J. Thomson** passed cathode rays through perpendicular electric and magnetic fields and adjusted them until the deflections cancelled, so that he could measure the charge-to-mass ratio $q/m$ of the particles. He found that it was the same whatever the cathode metal, showing that cathode rays are negatively charged particles (electrons) common to all matter, much lighter than atoms.

**G. P. Thomson** fired a beam of electrons at a thin metal foil (aluminium or gold) with a photographic plate behind it. He observed concentric diffraction rings like those produced by X-rays, which can only be produced by waves, and the spacings agreed with the crystal dimensions. This confirmed de Broglie's hypothesis that electrons behave like waves.

Together, J. J. Thomson's experiment showed that the electron is a particle with a definite charge-to-mass ratio, and G. P. Thomson's showed that it also has wave properties, giving a more complete (wave–particle duality) understanding of the electron.

questions.question:
Two solenoids are mounted on trays as shown. Each tray is suspended by identical strings of negligible mass to a fixed platform, such that each tray can swing freely. Each solenoid is connected to a galvanometer ($G_1$ and $G_2$), and the solenoid on tray 1 is also connected to an open switch and a battery. The total mass of tray 1 is twice that of tray 2. The solenoids are side by side with their axes aligned.

Explain what would be observed when the switch on tray 1 is closed. In your answer, refer to the current in each galvanometer and the movement of the trays until they reach their maximum displacement.
questions.answer:
**Tray 1.** When the switch is closed a steady current flows through solenoid 1 and $G_1$, so $G_1$ shows a continuous reading. Solenoid 1 becomes an electromagnet with a steady magnetic field, with its north pole at the end facing tray 2 (the right-hand end).

**Tray 2.** While the current in solenoid 1 rises from zero to its steady value, the magnetic flux through solenoid 2 (directed towards the right) increases. By Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, an emf is induced in solenoid 2. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the change in flux, so it produces a field directed to the left through solenoid 2: a north pole at its left-hand end (facing solenoid 1). This current flows through $G_2$ in the corresponding direction. Once the current in solenoid 1 is steady the flux no longer changes, so the emf and current fall to zero: $G_2$ gives only a brief flick.

**Motion.** For that brief time the facing ends of the two solenoids are both north poles, so they repel. The forces on the two trays are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction (Newton's third law), so the trays are pushed apart and swing away from each other. The force acts for the same time on each, so the impulse and momentum gained are equal and opposite: $m_1v_1=m_2v_2$ (total momentum stays zero), giving $\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}=\dfrac{m_2}{m_1}=\dfrac12$. Tray 2 (half the mass) therefore leaves with twice the speed of tray 1. Converting kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy ($\tfrac12v^2=gh$), the height gained is proportional to $v^2$, so tray 2 swings out further and rises to about four times the height of tray 1 before both trays momentarily stop (maximum displacement) and swing back.

questions.question:
A scientist was studying the radioactive decay of beryllium-11. His results are shown in the table below.

| Time (s) | Mass of beryllium-11 (g) | $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 32.6 | 0 |
| 7 | 21.8 | $-0.25$ |
| 13 | 16.1 | $-0.55$ |
| 20 | 11.4 | $-0.90$ |
| 24 | 9.3 | $-1.10$ |

Plot the results for time and $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ on a graph (time on the horizontal axis), including a suitable heading, labelled axes and a line of best fit. Describe the graph you would draw.
questions.answer:
A full-mark graph has: an appropriate descriptive heading (e.g. "Radioactive decay of beryllium-11: $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ against time"); time (s) on the $x$-axis and $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ on the $y$-axis, each labelled with units where relevant; a suitable scale so the points fill most of the grid (e.g. $x$ from 0 to 26 s and $y$ from $-1.2$ to $0$); the five points plotted accurately; and a straight line of best fit (drawn with a ruler) with a negative gradient passing close to all the points, as shown.

(Note: the $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ column is the data to plot. The masses in the middle column do not give exactly these values if $N_0$ is taken as the mass at $t=2$ s, so use the logarithm column as given.)

questions.question:
A scientist was studying the radioactive decay of beryllium-11. His results are shown in the table below.

| Time (s) | Mass of beryllium-11 (g) | $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 32.6 | 0 |
| 7 | 21.8 | $-0.25$ |
| 13 | 16.1 | $-0.55$ |
| 20 | 11.4 | $-0.90$ |
| 24 | 9.3 | $-1.10$ |

Use a graph of $\ln(N_t/N_0)$ against time to determine the decay constant of beryllium-11.
questions.answer:
From $N_t=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, $\ln\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}=-\lambda t$, so the gradient of the graph is $-\lambda$. Using two points on the line of best fit, e.g. $(4,-0.10)$ and $(22,-1.00)$:
$$\text{gradient}=\frac{-1.00-(-0.10)}{22-4}=-0.050\ \text{s}^{-1}\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=0.050\ \text{s}^{-1}.$$
(Equivalently, using the data points $(2,0)$ and $(24,-1.10)$: $\lambda=1.10/22=0.050\ \text{s}^{-1}$.)

questions.question: Outline a practical investigation to observe the emission spectra of gas discharge tubes.
questions.answer:
1. Clamp a gas discharge tube vertically in a retort stand.
2. Connect the output terminals of an induction coil to the electrodes of the gas discharge tube, and connect the input of the induction coil to a low-voltage DC power supply (through a switch or tapping key). The induction coil provides the high voltage needed to ionise the gas.
3. Turn off the room lights, switch on the power supply so the gas glows, and observe the light through a hand-held spectroscope (or diffraction grating).
4. Record (draw or photograph) the coloured emission lines seen, then repeat with other gases and compare the line patterns.

questions.question: Identify ONE potential hazard associated with performing gas discharge tube investigations, and outline ONE safe work practice which addresses this hazard.
questions.answer:
Hazard: the induction coil produces a very high voltage (risk of electric shock/electrocution). Safe work practice: only touch the circuit when the power supply is switched off (or use a tapping key so the circuit is on only briefly), and do not touch the electrodes or metal terminals while the apparatus is operating.

(Alternative: sparking can produce X-rays, so keep exposure short and keep a distance from the tube; or the tube becomes hot, so allow it to cool before handling.)

questions.question: Using de Broglie's hypothesis, calculate the wavelength of the electron in the first stationary state of the hydrogen atom if its speed is $2.188\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
$$\lambda=\frac hp=\frac h{mv}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{9.109\times10^{-31}\times2.188\times10^{6}}=3.325\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}\ (0.3325\ \text{nm}).$$
(The speed is only $0.0073c$, so relativistic effects are negligible.)

questions.question: Describe how de Broglie's hypothesis extended the work of Bohr in explaining the stability of electron orbits in the hydrogen atom.
questions.answer: Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus only in certain quantised "stationary states" in which they do not radiate energy, but he gave no reason why only those orbits were stable. De Broglie hypothesised that moving particles such as electrons have an associated matter wave, $\lambda=h/mv$. An electron in orbit must then form a standing wave around the orbit, which requires the circumference to be a whole number of wavelengths, $2\pi r_n=n\lambda_n$. Orbits that do not satisfy this would interfere destructively with themselves, so only the standing-wave orbits exist: this gives Bohr's quantised stationary states (and the condition $mvr=nh/2\pi$) and explains why the electron does not radiate unless it moves between these states.

questions.question:
Bubble chambers are used in conjunction with particle accelerators to photographically record the tracks of fast-moving charged particles. An intense magnetic field is applied at right angles to the path of the particles to deflect them according to their charge and momentum. The diagram shows a beam of protons travelling horizontally and entering a liquid hydrogen bubble chamber in a vertical magnetic field of $25.0$ mT. Examination of the photograph taken by the camera, as sketched, shows that the protons were deflected along a circular path of radius $0.280$ m.

Derive an expression for the velocity of a proton from the forces it experiences in this experiment.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force:
$$F_B=F_c\ \Rightarrow\ qvB=\frac{mv^2}{r}\ \Rightarrow\ v=\frac{qBr}{m}.$$

questions.question:
Bubble chambers are used in conjunction with particle accelerators to photographically record the tracks of fast-moving charged particles. An intense magnetic field is applied at right angles to the path of the particles to deflect them according to their charge and momentum. The diagram shows a beam of protons travelling horizontally and entering a liquid hydrogen bubble chamber in a vertical magnetic field of $25.0$ mT. Examination of the photograph taken by the camera, as sketched, shows that the protons were deflected along a circular path of radius $0.280$ m.

Calculate the velocity of a proton in the bubble chamber.

Bubble chambers are used in conjunction with particle accelerators to photographically record the tracks of fast-moving charged particles. An intense magnetic field is applied at right angles to the path of the particles to deflect them according to their charge and momentum. The diagram shows a beam of protons travelling horizontally and entering a liquid hydrogen bubble chamber in a vertical magnetic field of $25.0$ mT. Examination of the photograph taken by the camera, as sketched, shows that the protons were deflected along a circular path of radius $0.280$ m.

Outline TWO limitations of applying special relativity to the analysis of the motion of the protons in this experiment.
questions.answer:
1. The speed is too low for relativistic effects to matter. $v=6.70\times10^5\ \text{m s}^{-1}=0.0022c$, so the Lorentz factor is $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}=1.0000025$, effectively 1; the classical result is accurate and relativity makes no measurable difference.
2. Special relativity applies only to inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference. The protons move in a circle, so they are constantly accelerating (centripetal acceleration), and the frame of a proton is not an inertial frame.

(School note: the solution writes $6.70\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ in this part, a typo for $6.70\times10^5$ m s$^{-1}$; $0.0022c$ corresponds to $6.7\times10^5$.)

questions.question: The graph shows the vertical displacement of a projectile throughout its trajectory on Earth (the maximum height is $17.6$ m and the horizontal range is $60.0$ m, landing at the same height it was launched from). Calculate the initial velocity of the projectile (magnitude and direction).
questions.answer:
**Vertical:** at the maximum height $v_y=0$ at $s_y=17.6$ m. Using $v_y^2=u_y^2+2a_ys_y$ with $a_y=-9.8$:
$$u_y=\sqrt{2\times9.8\times17.6}=18.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}.$$
**Time of flight:** by symmetry, $t=\dfrac{2u_y}{g}=\dfrac{2\times18.57}{9.8}=3.79$ s.

**Horizontal:** $u_x=\dfrac{s_x}{t}=\dfrac{60.0}{3.79}=15.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

**Initial velocity:**
$$u=\sqrt{u_x^2+u_y^2}=\sqrt{15.83^2+18.57^2}=24\ \text{m s}^{-1},\qquad\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{18.57}{15.83}=50^\circ\ \text{above the horizontal}.$$

questions.question: A Molniya orbit is an inclined, highly elliptical orbit with a period of 12 hours, designed to provide communications and remote sensing coverage over high latitudes. The diagram shows the orbit, with $P$ the satellite's position at its greatest distance from Earth. Account for the changes in velocity of the satellite as it completes one orbit from position $P$.
questions.answer:
The total energy of the satellite, $E=U+K$ with $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, is constant. As the satellite falls from $P$ towards Earth its gravitational potential energy decreases (becomes more negative), so by conservation of energy its kinetic energy and speed increase, reaching the maximum at the closest point (perigee). As it moves back out towards $P$, kinetic energy is converted back into potential energy and the speed decreases to its minimum at $P$.

In addition, the gravitational force is not parallel to the satellite's velocity (except at $P$ and perigee), so it continually changes the direction of the satellite's velocity. Since both the speed and the direction change throughout the orbit, the velocity (a vector) is continuously changing.

questions.question: The g-lite was designed to provide light to remote locations that do not have access to electricity. It uses a lowering mass to drive a generator (through a pulley) to illuminate a light globe. Explain the factors that affect the maximum brightness of the light globe. Use mathematical models to support your answer.
questions.answer:
The brightness depends on the electrical power delivered to the globe, which depends on the emf induced in the generator and the resistance of the circuit. There are two parts: the turning system and the generator.

**Turning system (rate at which the generator is turned)**

- *Mass:* a larger mass gives a larger weight, $F_g=mg$, so a larger torque on the pulley and a faster rotation of the generator, and so a higher emf and brightness.
- *Pulley radius:* the torque is $\tau=rF=rmg$, so a larger radius gives more torque on the generator; but a larger radius also has a larger circumference ($C=2\pi r$), so the mass must fall further per rotation (and the lamp runs for a shorter time).
- *Friction* in the pulley or axle reduces the rotation rate and so reduces the brightness.

**Generator**

The induced emf is $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=-N\dfrac{\Delta(BA\cos\theta)}{\Delta t}$, so the emf increases with:

- stronger magnets (larger $B$);
- a larger coil area $A$;
- more turns $N$ on the coil;
- faster rotation (a shorter time $\Delta t$ for each change of flux).

**Circuit resistance:** thicker coil wire and thicker connecting wires have a lower resistance, so by $V=IR$ (and $P=VI=I^2R$) a larger current flows for the same emf and the globe is brighter.

A larger emf and current therefore give a greater power to the globe and so a greater maximum brightness.

questions.question:
A charged particle, $q_1$, is accelerated from rest between oppositely charged plates $X$ and $Y$ (a distance $d$ apart), before entering a uniform magnetic field (into the page) occupying a square region of side $d$, as shown in the first diagram. The particle strikes plate $Y$ at point $P$, a vertical distance $s$ from its entry point into the magnetic field. Ignore the effect of gravity.

The experiment is repeated with an apparatus that is twice the size (plates $2d$ apart and a field region of side $2d$), as shown in the second diagram. The voltage between the plates and the magnetic flux are the same. An identical particle, $q_2$, is accelerated from rest between the oppositely charged plates, before entering the uniform magnetic field.

Compare the work done on $q_1$ and $q_2$. Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
The work done on $q_1$ and $q_2$ is the same.

*Electric field:* the work done is $W=qV$. The particles are identical (same $q$) and the potential difference $V$ is the same, so the work done by the electric field is the same for both.

*Magnetic field:* the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity (the particle moves in a circular path), so $W=F_\parallel s=0$ for both particles: no work is done by the magnetic field.

So the total work done is the same.

questions.question:
A charged particle, $q_1$, is accelerated from rest between oppositely charged plates $X$ and $Y$ (a distance $d$ apart), before entering a uniform magnetic field (into the page) occupying a square region of side $d$, as shown in the first diagram. The particle strikes plate $Y$ at point $P$, a vertical distance $s$ from its entry point into the magnetic field. Ignore the effect of gravity.

The experiment is repeated with an apparatus that is twice the size (plates $2d$ apart and a field region of side $2d$), as shown in the second diagram. The voltage between the plates and the magnetic flux are the same. An identical particle, $q_2$, is accelerated from rest between the oppositely charged plates, before entering the uniform magnetic field.

Compare the vertical distances travelled by $q_1$ and $q_2$ in the magnetic field.
questions.answer:
From (a) the work done by the electric field is the same, so the particles enter the magnetic field with the same speed: $qV=\tfrac12mv^2\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{2qV/m}$.

In the magnetic field $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$, i.e. $r\propto\dfrac1B$ for identical particles with the same speed.

The same magnetic flux $\Phi=BA$ is spread over an area $A$ that is four times as large ($(2d)^2$ instead of $d^2$), so $B=\Phi/A$ and $B_2=\tfrac14B_1$. Therefore $r_2=4r_1$.

The particle completes a semicircle and strikes plate $Y$ a vertical distance $s=2r$ from its entry point, so $s_2=4s_1$: $q_2$ travels four times the vertical distance of $q_1$.

questions.question:
A $500$ g metal rod is allowed to slide along a pair of parallel metal rails, $30$ cm apart and tilted at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. The rails are connected to a DC power supply and switch, which results in a current of $2.8$ A passing through the rod. The apparatus is in a uniform magnetic field of $2.5$ T which is horizontal, directed out of the strong magnet (perpendicular to the plane containing the rails' horizontal direction and the rod), as shown.

What is the force, including its direction, acting on the rod solely due to the magnetic field?
questions.answer:
The rod is horizontal and perpendicular to the field, so
$$F=BIl\sin\theta=2.5\times2.8\times0.30\times\sin90^\circ=2.1\ \text{N}.$$
By the right-hand rule the force is perpendicular to both the rod and the field: it acts vertically upward (not up the rails).

questions.question:
A $500$ g metal rod is allowed to slide along a pair of parallel metal rails, $30$ cm apart and tilted at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. The rails are connected to a DC power supply and switch, which results in a current of $2.8$ A passing through the rod. The apparatus is in a uniform magnetic field of $2.5$ T which is horizontal, directed out of the strong magnet (perpendicular to the plane containing the rails' horizontal direction and the rod), as shown.

Calculate the initial acceleration of the rod along the rails.
questions.answer:
Weight: $F_g=mg=0.500\times9.8=4.9$ N downward. The magnetic force is $2.1$ N upward, so the net vertical force is $4.9-2.1=2.8$ N downward.

The rod can only accelerate along the rails (inclined at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal), so the component of this vertical force along the rails is
$$F_{net}=2.8\sin60^\circ=2.4\ \text{N}.$$
$$a=\frac{F_{net}}{m}=\frac{2.42}{0.500}=4.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}\ \text{down the rails}.$$

questions.question:
A $500$ g metal rod is allowed to slide along a pair of parallel metal rails, $30$ cm apart and tilted at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. The rails are connected to a DC power supply and switch, which results in a current of $2.8$ A passing through the rod. The apparatus is in a uniform magnetic field of $2.5$ T which is horizontal, directed out of the strong magnet (perpendicular to the plane containing the rails' horizontal direction and the rod), as shown.

The experiment is repeated with the switch open. Explain why the acceleration of the rod is different with the switch open.
questions.answer:
With the switch open no current flows through the rod, so the magnetic force on it is zero. The only force along the rails is then the component of the weight:
$$a=\frac{mg\sin60^\circ}{m}=9.8\sin60^\circ=8.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}\ \text{down the rails}.$$
This is greater than the $4.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ with the switch closed, because with the switch closed the upward magnetic force opposes part of the weight and reduces the net force down the rails.

questions.question: A spaceship travels to a distant star at a constant speed, $v$. When it arrives, $17.6$ years have passed on Earth but $9.2$ years have passed for an astronaut on the spaceship. What is the distance to the star, as measured by an observer on Earth?
questions.answer:
The astronaut's time is the proper time, $t_0=9.2$ y, and the Earth time is $t_v=17.6$ y: $t_v=\dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$, so
$$\frac vc=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{t_0}{t_v}\right)^2}=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{9.2}{17.6}\right)^2}=0.8524.$$
In Earth's frame the trip takes $17.6$ y, so the distance is
$$s=vt=0.8524c\times17.6\ \text{y}=15.0\ \text{light-years}.$$

questions.question: A car of mass $1000\ \text{kg}$ follows a circular road of radius $r$ at velocity $v$, and its centripetal force is $F_c$. A truck of mass $3000\ \text{kg}$ goes around the same corner. In order for the centripetal force to be the same for both the truck and the car:
options: The truck's speed must be $\dfrac v3$.
The truck's speed must be the same as the car.
questions.answer: $F_c=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. For the same $F_c$ and $r$: $3m\,v_T^2=m v^2$, so $v_T^2=\dfrac{v^2}{3}$ and $v_T=\dfrac{v}{\sqrt3}$ (A).

questions.question: A ball is thrown horizontally from the top of a cliff, and it hits the ground with a range $R$ from the base of the cliff. A second ball is thrown horizontally from the top of the same cliff at three times the speed. What is the range of the second ball?
questions.answer: The vertical motion is independent of the horizontal motion, so both balls take the same time $t$ to fall the height of the cliff. $R=ux\,t$, so with horizontal speed $3u_x$ the range is $3u_xt=3R$ (C).

questions.question: A square loop of wire of side length $0.15\ \text{m}$ is placed in a uniform magnetic field of $5.2\ \text{T}$. The side view shows the plane of the loop making an angle of $60^\circ$ with the field lines. Calculate the magnetic flux, $\Phi$, through the loop.
questions.answer:
Area $A=0.15^2=0.0225\ \text{m}^2$. The angle between the field and the *plane* of the loop is $60^\circ$, so the angle between the field and the normal to the loop is $30^\circ$.

$\Phi=BA\cos\theta=5.2\times0.0225\times\cos30^\circ=0.101\ \text{Wb}$ (B), equivalently $BA\sin60^\circ$.

questions.question: A boy throws a ball upwards from the roof of a moving car (which moves at constant velocity) and then catches it when the car has travelled $100\ \text{m}$ down the road. He throws the ball up again and it goes vertically four times higher than before. How far has the car travelled this time when he catches it again?
questions.answer: Four times the height needs twice the vertical launch speed ($h=\dfrac{v^2}{2g}$), so the time of flight $t=\dfrac{2v}{g}$ doubles. The car moves at constant speed, so in twice the time it travels twice as far: $2\times100=200\ \text{m}$ (B).

questions.question: An electron released from rest from the negative plate strikes the positive plate at a speed of $5.50\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The separation of the plates is $3.0\times10^{-2}\ \text{m}$. Calculate the potential difference, $V$, between the two plates.
questions.answer: Work done by the field equals the kinetic energy gained: $qV=\tfrac12mv^2$, so $$V=\frac{mv^2}{2q}=\frac{9.11\times10^{-31}\times(5.50\times10^{6})^2}{2\times1.6\times10^{-19}}=86.1\ \text{V}\approx8.6\times10^{1}\ \text{V}$$ (B). The separation is not needed.

questions.question: A wire of length $0.300\ \text{m}$ sits in a $2.50\ \text{T}$ magnetic field (directed into the page) in Position X, as shown. The wire carries a current of $1.80\ \text{A}$. The wire, which stays in the plane of the page, is then rotated $45.0^\circ$ to Position Y. Calculate the *change* in the magnitude of the force acting on the wire after it rotates from X to Y.
questions.answer: $F=BIL\sin\theta$. The field is directed into the page and the wire lies in the plane of the page, so the wire is perpendicular to the field in *both* positions ($\theta=90^\circ$). Rotating the wire within the page does not change the angle. $F=2.50\times1.80\times0.300=1.35\ \text{N}$ in both positions, so the change is $0\ \text{N}$ (A).

questions.question: The diagram shows a square coil rotating in a magnetic field at one instant in its rotation. The plane of the coil makes an angle of $35^\circ$ with the field lines. The square coil consists of $15$ turns of wire and has dimensions $0.25\ \text{m}\times0.25\ \text{m}$. A current of $I=3.25\ \text{A}$ flows through it. The external magnetic field is $B=1.20\ \text{T}$. Calculate the magnitude of the torque, $\tau$, on the coil at the angle shown.
questions.answer: The torque is a maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, so with $\theta=35^\circ$ between the plane and the field: $$\tau=nIAB\cos35^\circ=15\times3.25\times(0.25)^2\times1.20\times\cos35^\circ=3.00\ \text{N m}$$ (C).

questions.question: Two very long parallel wires, X and Y, separated by a distance $d$, have a force per unit length between them of $5.5\times10^{-5}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$. Wire X carries a current of $2\ \text{A}$ and Wire Y carries a current of $3\ \text{A}$, as shown in the diagram. What is the separation, $d$, between the two wires?
questions.answer: $\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$, so $$d=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi(F/l)}=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2\times3}{2\pi\times5.5\times10^{-5}}=2.2\times10^{-2}\ \text{m}\approx2\ \text{cm}$$ (B).

questions.question: A coil of wire is placed in a magnetic field (directed into the page) so that the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the direction of the field. The strength of the magnetic field is then varied, as shown in the graph of $B$ against time (constant for $0$–$2\ \text{s}$, decreasing steadily to zero at $4\ \text{s}$, increasing steadily to about half its original value at $6\ \text{s}$, then constant). Which of the following graphs correctly shows the EMF induced across the coil?
questions.answer: By Faraday's law $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, so the EMF is proportional to (minus) the gradient of the $B$–$t$ graph. $0$–$2\ \text{s}$: $B$ constant, so $\varepsilon=0$. $2$–$4\ \text{s}$: $B$ decreases steadily, so a constant EMF of one sign. $4$–$6\ \text{s}$: $B$ increases at about half the rate, so a constant EMF of the opposite sign and about half the magnitude. $6$–$8\ \text{s}$: $B$ constant, so $\varepsilon=0$. This is graph D.

questions.question: A square coil of conducting wire with sides of length $W$ is moved at constant speed $v$ left to right through a uniform magnetic field which is directed into the page and has width $W$, as shown below. From the point where the coil enters the magnetic field until the point where it leaves it, which description best describes the direction of the current induced in the coil?
questions.answer: While the coil enters the field, the flux into the page increases. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes this, producing a field out of the page, so the current is **anti-clockwise**. Because the coil is exactly as wide as the field, it begins to leave as soon as it is fully inside, so the flux then decreases. The induced current now produces a field into the page, so it is **clockwise**. The answer is D.

questions.question: A satellite of mass $m$ is travelling in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around a planet of mass $M$. If the satellite is moved to a new circular orbit where its kinetic energy is now $25\%$ larger, then the radius of the new circular orbit will be:
questions.answer: For a circular orbit $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $K=\tfrac12mv^2=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, i.e. $K\propto\dfrac1r$. $K'=1.25K$ gives $r'=\dfrac{r}{1.25}=\dfrac{4r}{5}$ (B).

questions.question: The net force on a car (mass $m$, constant speed $v$) at the top of a circular hump-back bridge of radius $r$ is compared with the net force on a satellite (mass $m$, orbital speed $v$, orbital radius $r$) in a circular orbit around Earth (mass $M$). Which of the following correctly represents the net force in both situations?
questions.answer: In uniform circular motion the **net** force is the centripetal force $\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ in both cases. For the car at the top of the bridge, $mg-N=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ (the net force is $\frac{mv^2}{r}$, not $mg$). For the satellite, gravity alone is the net force and $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The answer is A.

questions.question: A red (wavelength $610\ \text{nm}$) laser pointer emits $0.5\ \text{mW}$ of light. How many photons per second are being emitted by the laser pointer?
questions.answer: Energy per photon $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{610\times10^{-9}}=3.26\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. Photons per second $=\dfrac{P}{E}=\dfrac{0.5\times10^{-3}}{3.26\times10^{-19}}=1.5\times10^{15}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ (A).

questions.question: Plane-polarised light is incident normally on a polariser which is able to rotate in the plane perpendicular to the light. In Diagram 1, the intensity of the incident light is $8\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ and the transmitted intensity of light is $2\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. Diagram 2 shows the polariser rotated $90^\circ$ from the orientation in Diagram 1. In Diagram 2, what is the new transmitted intensity?
questions.answer: Malus' law: $I=I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$. Diagram 1: $2=8\cos^2\theta$, so $\cos^2\theta=\dfrac14$ and $\theta=60^\circ$. Rotating the polariser through $90^\circ$ makes the angle $30^\circ$ (or $150^\circ$), so $I=8\cos^230^\circ=8\times\dfrac34=6\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ (C). (Equivalently, $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$, so the two intensities add to $8$.)

questions.question: An observer notes that the second-hand on a stopwatch is four times slower on a passing spacecraft. What is the velocity of the spacecraft?
questions.answer: Time dilation: $t=\gamma t_0$ with $\gamma=4$. $\gamma=\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}=4$, so $1-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}=\dfrac1{16}$ and $v=c\sqrt{\dfrac{15}{16}}=0.968c\approx0.97c$ (D).

questions.question: The spectrum of an object was measured and graphed (intensity against wavelength, from $200\ \text{nm}$ to $800\ \text{nm}$, with a maximum at about $340\ \text{nm}$). Which of the following best represents the temperature of this object?
questions.answer: The peak of the graph is at $\lambda_{\max}\approx340\ \text{nm}$. By Wien's law, $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac bT$ with $b=2.898\times10^{-3}\ \text{m K}$: $$T=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{340\times10^{-9}}=8.5\times10^{3}\ \text{K}$$ (B, $8{,}524\ \text{K}$).

questions.question: What is the magnitude of the relativistic momentum of a proton travelling at half the speed of light?

At two separate times, two charged particles approach a current-carrying wire and follow the trajectories depicted in the diagram below. (The current in the wire flows to the left; Particle A passes above the wire and Particle B below it.) Determine the charge of each particle.
options: A: positively charged; B: positively charged
A: positively charged; B: negatively charged
A: negatively charged; B: positively charged
A: negatively charged; B: negatively charged
questions.answer:
The current flows to the left. By the right-hand rule the magnetic field is **into the page above** the wire and **out of the page below** it.

Particle A (above) is moving to the left at its closest point and is deflected upward (away from the wire), so the force is up. For a positive charge, $\mathbf F=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ with $\mathbf v$ to the left and $\mathbf B$ into the page would be downward, so A must be **negative**.

Particle B (below) is moving to the right at its closest point and is deflected downward. For a positive charge, $\mathbf v$ to the right and $\mathbf B$ out of the page gives a downward force, so B is **positive**. The answer is C.

questions.question: The range of a projectile on a horizontal surface is given by $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin(2\theta)}{g}$, where $R$ is the range, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, $u$ is the initial speed and $\theta$ is the angle of the projectile to the horizontal. Which of the following changes would increase the range of the projectile to $2R$?
questions.answer: $R\propto u^2$, so to double $R$ the speed must be multiplied by $\sqrt2$ (D). Doubling $u$ gives $4R$; doubling $g$ halves $R$; changing $\theta$ from $30^\circ$ to $45^\circ$ multiplies $R$ by $\dfrac{\sin90^\circ}{\sin60^\circ}=1.15$ only.

questions.question: Two experiments are conducted using a photoelectric cell where the applied voltage is varied, and the resultant photocurrent is measured by the ammeter. The results of both experiments are shown in the following graphs. In Experiment A, three curves have different stopping potentials but the same saturation (maximum) photocurrent. In Experiment B, three curves have the same stopping potential but different saturation photocurrents. Which would be the correct interpretation of these experiments?
options: A: three different frequencies of light; B: three different intensities of the same frequency of light
A: three different intensities of the same frequency of light; B: three different frequencies of light
A: three different intensities of the same frequency of light; B: three different metals
A: three different frequencies of light; B: three different metals
questions.answer:
The stopping voltage (where the photocurrent falls to zero) depends on the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$, so it depends on the frequency (and the metal) but not the intensity. The saturation current depends on the number of photoelectrons per second, which is proportional to the light intensity.

Experiment A has different stopping potentials, so the frequency (or metal) varies, and with the same saturation current the intensity is unchanged: three different frequencies. Experiment B has the same stopping potential (same frequency and metal) but different saturation currents: three different intensities of the same frequency. The answer is A.

questions.question: Muons are particles created in the upper atmosphere by cosmic ray collisions and travel towards the ground at $0.98c$. Of all the muons detected at an altitude of $10\ \text{km}$, only $1$ in $45{,}000$ were predicted to reach ground level with the rest decaying due to their short lifetime of $2.2\ \mu\text{s}$. However, it was measured that $1$ in $8$ were able to be detected at ground level. Explain how this provides evidence to support Einstein's Special Theory of relativity. (Calculations are not required.)
questions.answer:
Even moving at $0.98c$, most muons created in the upper atmosphere are expected to decay before travelling $10\ \text{km}$ to the ground because of their short lifetime (the classical prediction is only $1$ in $45{,}000$ surviving).

As a consequence of his two postulates, Einstein predicted time dilation: the time for an event occurring in a moving frame of reference is longer when measured by an external observer. For an observer on the ground, the lifetime of the (fast-moving) muons is therefore longer, so they survive for longer and travel further, and more muons are able to reach the ground. (From the muon's frame of reference, the distance to the ground is length-contracted, so it is shorter and fewer muons decay on the way.)

The much larger fraction detected at the ground ($1$ in $8$ instead of $1$ in $45{,}000$) matches the prediction of time dilation, and so supports Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity.

questions.question: When light is incident on Europium metal, photoelectrons are emitted. The graph below shows how the measured kinetic energy of the photoelectrons changes when different wavelengths of light are incident on the metal. Using the graph, determine the work function of Europium.
questions.answer:
Choose a data point on the graph, e.g. $\lambda=310\ \text{nm}$, $K_{\max}=1.5\ \text{eV}$.

$K_{\max}=hf-\phi=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}-\phi$, so $\phi=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}-K_{\max}$.

$\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{310\times10^{-9}\times1.6\times10^{-19}}=4.0\ \text{eV}$

$\phi=4.0-1.5=2.5\ \text{eV}$ (or $\approx4.0\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$).

questions.question: For any metal there is a maximum wavelength of light after which no photoelectrons are emitted. Use Einstein's explanation of the photoelectric effect to explain why no electrons are emitted if the wavelength is greater than this maximum.
questions.answer:
Einstein proposed that light is made of photons, each with energy $E=hf=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$. When light is incident on a surface, all the energy of one photon is transferred to a single electron. The electron uses part of this energy to escape from the metal by overcoming the electrostatic attraction of the metal (the work function, $\phi$), and the remaining energy is its maximum kinetic energy: $hf=\phi+K_{\max}$, or $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$.

Electrons are only emitted if the energy of a photon is at least the work function: $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\ge\phi$. This minimum photon energy corresponds to a maximum wavelength $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac{hc}{\phi}$ (where $K_{\max}=0$). If the wavelength is greater than $\lambda_{\max}$, each photon has less energy than $\phi$, so no electron can be released, no matter how intense the light (many low-energy photons cannot combine their energy).

questions.question: Explain why, from an observer's point of view, an object with mass would not be able to accelerate to the speed of light, $c$, in a vacuum.
questions.answer: In order for conservation of momentum to hold in all inertial frames of reference, Einstein redefined momentum as $p_v=\dfrac{m_0v}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$. As $v\to c$, $p_v\to\infty$. The impulse is $I=\Delta p=p_f-p_i=p_v$ when starting from rest ($p_i=0$), so an infinite impulse would be required to increase an object's speed to the speed of light. It is not possible to apply an infinite impulse to an object: as the velocity increases, an ever-increasing force ($F=\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$) would be required to change the momentum, or the effect of a constant force would change the velocity less and less (with the acceleration asymptotically reducing to zero). Equivalently, an infinite amount of work/energy would be needed, since $E^2=(pc)^2+(m_0c^2)^2\to\infty$ as $v\to c$. This limit on the speed of an object with mass is a consequence of Einstein's postulates of special relativity.

questions.question: As a thought experiment, Observer A is on a train travelling at a velocity of $v=0.9c$ compared to Observer B. Observer A shines a laser beam towards a mirror at the front of the train, a distance of $2.3\ \text{m}$. The light beam reflects off the mirror and returns to a timing device on the laser. According to observer A, how long would it take for the light beam to complete this journey?
questions.answer: For Observer A the train is at rest and the light travels $2\times2.3=4.6\ \text{m}$ at $c$: $$t_0=\frac dv=\frac{2\times2.3}{3.0\times10^{8}}=1.53\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}.$$

questions.question: As a thought experiment, Observer A is on a train travelling at a velocity of $v=0.9c$ compared to Observer B. Observer A shines a laser beam towards a mirror at the front of the train, a distance of $2.3\ \text{m}$. The light beam reflects off the mirror and returns to a timing device on the laser. According to Observer A the journey takes $1.53\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}$. According to Observer B, how long would it take for the light beam to complete this journey?
questions.answer: Observer A measures the proper time $t_0=1.53\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}$ (both events happen at the same place on the train). Observer B measures the dilated time: $$\gamma=\frac1{\sqrt{1-0.9^2}}=2.294,\qquad t=\gamma t_0=2.294\times1.53\times10^{-8}=3.52\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}.$$

questions.question: As a thought experiment, Observer A is on a train travelling at a velocity of $v=0.9c$ compared to Observer B. The laser and the mirror at the front of the train are $2.3\ \text{m}$ apart according to Observer A. According to observer B, what is the distance he would measure between the laser and the mirror?
questions.answer: The $2.3\ \text{m}$ is the proper length $L_0$ (measured in the train's rest frame). Observer B sees length contraction along the direction of motion: $$L=L_0\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}=2.3\sqrt{1-0.9^2}=1.0\ \text{m}.$$

prev.question: As a thought experiment, Observer A is on a train travelling at a velocity of $v=0.9c$ compared to Observer B. Observer A shines a laser beam towards a mirror at the front of the train, a distance of $2.3\ \text{m}$. The light beam reflects off the mirror and returns to a timing device on the laser. According to Observer A the journey takes $1.53\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}$. According to Observer B, how long would it take for the light beam to complete this journey?
prev.answer: Observer A measures the proper time $t_0=1.53\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}$ (both events happen at the same place on the train). Observer B measures the dilated time: $$\gamma=\frac1{\sqrt{1-0.9^2}}=2.294,\qquad t=\gamma t_0=2.294\times1.53\times10^{-8}=3.52\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}.$$

questions.question: In the 1840s, French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau performed an experiment to measure the speed of light using a rotating toothed cogwheel. He shone an intense light source at a mirror and broke up the light beam with a rotating toothed cogwheel. He adjusted the speed of rotation of the wheel until the reflected light beam could no longer be seen returning through the gaps in the cogwheel. The diagram below shows a similar experiment: the rotating toothed cogwheel has $250$ teeth and $250$ gaps of the same width, and the distance between the rotating toothed cogwheel and the mirror is $500\ \text{m}$. Determine the minimum rotation speed of the cogwheel that would completely block the returning light.
questions.answer:
The light travels to the mirror and back: $t=\dfrac{2\times500}{3.0\times10^{8}}=3.33\times10^{-6}\ \text{s}$.

To block the returning light, in this time the wheel must turn so that a tooth replaces the gap the light passed through, i.e. through half of one tooth-and-gap cycle. There are $250+250=500$ equal teeth and gaps, so the wheel turns through $\dfrac{2\pi}{500}\ \text{rad}$: $$\omega=\frac{2\pi/500}{3.33\times10^{-6}}\approx3.77\times10^{3}\ \text{rad s}^{-1}.$$ (Directly: $\omega=\dfrac{\pi c}{500\times500}=3.77\times10^3\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.)

questions.question: In a Fizeau-type experiment in air the minimum rotation speed of the toothed cogwheel that completely blocks the returning light was measured. The same experiment is performed again but this time a $500\ \text{m}$ long rectangular tank of pure water is added between the cogwheel and the mirror. The new minimum rotation speed of the toothed cogwheel that would completely block the returning light is $2830\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$, which is lower than the one measured in air. What conclusion about the speed of light in water can be made from this observation?
questions.answer: A lower rotation speed means the light takes longer to travel to the mirror and back (a longer time for the wheel to turn from a gap to a tooth). So the speed of light is **lower in water than in air**.

questions.question: A Fizeau-type experiment shows that light travels more slowly in water than in air, which provides evidence for Huygens' model of light. Describe one other observation or experimental evidence that supports Huygens' model.
questions.answer: The double-slit experiment (Young's experiment) shows the wave nature of light, as predicted by Huygens' model, through the observation of an interference pattern on a screen behind the slits. The dark and bright fringes can only occur if light is a wave (superposition of waves from the two slits, with constructive and destructive interference). (Diffraction and polarisation are also accepted as evidence; each cannot be explained by Newton's particle model.)

prev.question: In a Fizeau-type experiment in air the minimum rotation speed of the toothed cogwheel that completely blocks the returning light was measured. The same experiment is performed again but this time a $500\ \text{m}$ long rectangular tank of pure water is added between the cogwheel and the mirror. The new minimum rotation speed of the toothed cogwheel that would completely block the returning light is $2830\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$, which is lower than the one measured in air. What conclusion about the speed of light in water can be made from this observation?
prev.answer: A lower rotation speed means the light takes longer to travel to the mirror and back (a longer time for the wheel to turn from a gap to a tooth). So the speed of light is **lower in water than in air**.

questions.question: DC motors are used in electric trains because they can combine high starting torques with the ability to provide regenerative braking. When a DC motor is connected to a voltage source the armature current starts high and then falls as the speed of the vehicle reaches a steady value as shown in the graph below (current falls from $I_{\max}$ to zero as the speed rises to a constant value). Explain why the current starts at a specific maximum value $I_{\max}$ then falls to zero as the motor increases its speed.
questions.answer:
$I_{\max}$ is determined by the physical constraints of the system, i.e. the voltage supplied to the coil and the resistance of the coil: $I_{\max}=\dfrac{V_{\text{supply}}}{R_{\text{coil}}}$ (when the motor is at rest, there is no back EMF).

As the motor spins, its coil rotates in an external magnetic field and, by Faraday's law, an EMF is generated in the coil, in the opposite direction to the voltage supplied to the coil (Lenz's law). This is the back EMF, $\varepsilon_{\text{back}}$, so $V_{\text{coil}}=V_{\text{supply}}-\varepsilon_{\text{back}}$.

By Ohm's law, the overall current in the coil is $I_{\text{coil}}=\dfrac{V_{\text{supply}}-\varepsilon_{\text{back}}}{R_{\text{coil}}}=I_{\max}-\dfrac{\varepsilon_{\text{back}}}{R_{\text{coil}}}$.

As the motor's speed of rotation increases, $\varepsilon_{\text{back}}$ increases too and $I_{\text{coil}}$ decreases from its maximum value of $\dfrac{V_{\text{supply}}}{R_{\text{coil}}}$. Eventually, $\varepsilon_{\text{back}}$ reaches the value of $V_{\text{supply}}$ and $I_{\text{coil}}=0$ (in practice, a small current remains to overcome friction and load).

questions.question: A helium neon laser, which emits light of wavelength $\lambda=632\ \text{nm}$, is shone through a diffraction grating with $120\ \text{lines/cm}$. It is placed $L=5.00\ \text{m}$ away from a screen. Determine the separation between the slits in the grating.
questions.answer: $d=\dfrac1{120\ \text{lines/cm}}=\dfrac1{120\times10^{2}\ \text{lines/m}}=8.3\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}$ ($=8.3\times10^{-3}\ \text{cm}$).

questions.question: A helium neon laser, which emits light of wavelength $\lambda=632\ \text{nm}$, is shone through a diffraction grating. For the $3^{\text{rd}}$ order maximum to occur, what is the additional distance or \"path difference\" that the light must have travelled from one slit on the grating to the screen compared to the adjacent slit?
questions.answer:
For a maximum, the path difference between light from adjacent slits is a whole number of wavelengths: $m\lambda=3\times632\ \text{nm}=1.90\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$.

*Note:* the school's working uses $620\ \text{nm}$ and gets $1.86\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$; with the given $\lambda=632\ \text{nm}$ the path difference is $1.90\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$.

questions.question: A helium neon laser, which emits light of wavelength $\lambda=632\ \text{nm}$, is shone through a diffraction grating with $120\ \text{lines/cm}$ (slit separation $d=8.3\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}$). It is placed $L=5.00\ \text{m}$ away from a screen. What is the distance on the screen between the central maximum and the $3^{\text{rd}}$ order maximum?
questions.answer:
$d\sin\theta=m\lambda$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{3\times632\times10^{-9}}{8.3\times10^{-5}}=0.0228$ and $\theta=1.31^\circ$.

On the screen, $\tan\theta=\dfrac xL$, so $x=L\tan\theta=5.00\times\tan1.31^\circ=0.114\ \text{m}$ ($11.4\ \text{cm}$).

questions.question: Explain how the stator in an AC induction motor generates torque in the rotor.
questions.answer:
- The stator of an AC induction motor is usually made of $3$ pairs of electromagnets, each opposite pair being connected to one phase of a three-phase current generator. This setup creates a **rotating magnetic field** within the cavity of the stator, where the rotor is placed.
- The rotor consists of several metallic bars connected at the ends by two metallic plates.
- The rotating $B$ field within the stator creates a **change in magnetic flux** through the metallic bars of the rotor. By **Faraday's law**, an emf is induced in the bars ($\varepsilon=-\dfrac{\Delta\Phi_B}{\Delta t}$). As the rotor is a closed conductor, induced **eddy currents** flow in the bars and through the connecting end plates.
- By **Lenz's law**, these eddy currents flow in a direction such that the $B$ field they create opposes the change in flux that induced them in the first place.
- The eddy currents in the bars are in the external $B$ field of the stator, so each bar experiences a **force** due to the motor effect ($F=BIl\sin\theta$).
- Currents in opposite bars of the rotor flow in opposite directions, so the forces on them are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, creating a **torque** on the rotor.
- This torque makes the rotor turn in the **same direction** as the rotation of the $B$ field in the stator: as a consequence of Lenz's law, the rotor tries to catch up with the rotating $B$ field to minimise (counter) the change in flux it experiences.

questions.question: A charged particle of mass $6.0\times10^{-7}\ \text{kg}$ is travelling at an initial velocity of $2.5\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The particle enters a perpendicular electric field of $7.5\times10^{4}\ \text{N C}^{-1}$ (between the plates shown, directed from the top plate to the bottom plate), and follows the trajectory shown below: it is deflected $0.0040\ \text{m}$ towards the bottom plate while travelling $0.34\ \text{m}$ horizontally. Calculate the magnitude of the charge on the particle.
questions.answer:
Treat the motion like a projectile (ignore gravity).

Horizontal (constant velocity): $t=\dfrac{0.34}{2.5\times10^{3}}=1.36\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}$.

Vertical (starting from zero vertical velocity): $s=\tfrac12at^2$, so $a=\dfrac{2\times0.0040}{(1.36\times10^{-4})^2}=4.33\times10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

Force: $F=ma=6.0\times10^{-7}\times4.33\times10^{5}=0.26\ \text{N}$, and $F=qE$, so $$q=\frac{ma}{E}=\frac{0.26}{7.5\times10^{4}}=3.5\times10^{-6}\ \text{C}.$$

questions.question: A subatomic particle with a charge of $-1.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}$ travels at a speed of $5.3\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ into a perpendicular magnetic field of strength $12.5\ \text{T}$. It follows the semicircular path shown in the diagram below, which has a diameter of $9.96\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}$. Calculate the mass of the particle.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $m=\dfrac{qBr}{v}$.

The path is a semicircle of **diameter** $9.96\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}$, so $r=4.98\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}$.

$$m=\frac{1.6\times10^{-19}\times12.5\times4.98\times10^{-4}}{5.3\times10^{6}}=1.9\times10^{-28}\ \text{kg}.$$

questions.question: The diagram below shows a current-carrying wire ($I=2.5\ \text{A}$, current flowing down and to the left) in a uniform magnetic field of $B=3.6\ \text{T}$ directed to the right. The wire makes an angle of $48^\circ$ with the field and spans $0.82\ \text{m}$ vertically and $0.75\ \text{m}$ horizontally. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the magnetic force acting on the wire in the position shown.
questions.answer:
$F=BIL\sin\theta$ where $L\sin\theta$ is the length of wire perpendicular to the field, $=0.82\ \text{m}$ (the vertical extent): $$F=3.6\times2.5\times0.82=7.4\ \text{N}.$$ (Equivalently, $L=\sqrt{0.82^2+0.75^2}=1.11\ \text{m}$ and $F=3.6\times2.5\times1.11\times\sin48^\circ=7.4\ \text{N}$.)

By the right-hand palm rule (fingers along $B$ to the right, thumb along the current down-left), the force is **out of the page**.

*Note:* using $\cos48^\circ$ or $\sin52^\circ$ gives an incorrect magnitude.

questions.question: A transformer operates from an A.C. primary voltage of $200\ \text{V}$. The primary coil of the transformer has $400$ turns, and the secondary coil has $1200$ turns. Calculate the voltage across the secondary coil of the transformer.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{n_s}{n_p}$, so $V_s=200\times\dfrac{1200}{400}=600\ \text{V}$.

questions.question: A transformer has a primary coil of $400$ turns and a secondary coil of $1200$ turns. Identify if this is a step-up or step-down transformer.
questions.answer: Step-up: the secondary coil has more turns than the primary coil, so the secondary voltage ($600\ \text{V}$) is greater than the primary voltage ($200\ \text{V}$).

questions.question: Explain one method of increasing the efficiency of a transformer.
questions.answer:
One method is to **laminate the iron core** (build it from thin sheets of iron separated by insulating material). This reduces the size of the eddy currents induced in the core by the changing magnetic flux, which reduces the resistive (ohmic) heating and so minimises energy losses.

(Other accepted answers: use lower-resistance (thicker) windings to reduce resistive heating, or use methods that increase the flux linkage between the coils, such as winding the coils closely on a soft-iron core in a closed loop.)

questions.question: A pupil performs the experiments shown below. He puts a solenoid (a coil of wire) on the back of a motion trolley connected to an ammeter and a switch and pushes it towards a powerful fixed magnet at an initial speed $v$. In Experiment 1 the switch is open. In Experiment 2 the conditions are exactly the same as Experiment 1 but now the switch is closed. Describe and explain, in terms of the relevant laws of physics, the observations that he makes of the two experiments. (Ignore the effect of friction on the trolleys.)
questions.answer:
**Experiment 1.** The trolley rolls towards the magnet at a constant speed. By Faraday's law, a voltage is induced across the coil (due to the change in flux as it approaches the magnet). Because the switch is open, no current can flow and so no forces can act between the coil and the magnet.

**Experiment 2.** As with Experiment 1, a voltage is induced. This time, a current can flow in the coil. By Lenz's law, this flows to produce a magnetic field that acts to oppose the change in flux, i.e. to place a north pole on the right-hand end of the solenoid (facing the approaching north pole of the magnet). The trolley experiences a force to the left, which acts to slow it down (kinetic energy is transferred to electrical energy in the circuit).

questions.question: Two spheres A and B are attached to the ends of light inextensible strings XA and XB. They are swung in horizontal circles of radius $0.20\ \text{m}$ (sphere A) and $0.30\ \text{m}$ (sphere B) so that their periods are the same. Determine the ratio $\dfrac{v_B}{v_A}$ of the speed of sphere B ($v_B$) to the speed of sphere A ($v_A$).
questions.answer: $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ and both spheres have the same period $T$ (the same angular velocity $\omega$), so $$\frac{v_B}{v_A}=\frac{2\pi r_B/T}{2\pi r_A/T}=\frac{r_B}{r_A}=\frac{0.30}{0.20}=1.5.$$

questions.question: Two spheres A and B are swung in horizontal circles of radius $r_A=0.20\ \text{m}$ and $r_B=0.30\ \text{m}$ with the same period, so that $\dfrac{v_B}{v_A}=1.5$. Determine the ratio $\dfrac{a_B}{a_A}$ of the centripetal acceleration of sphere B ($a_B$) to the centripetal acceleration of sphere A ($a_A$).
questions.answer: $a=\dfrac{v^2}{r}$, so $$\frac{a_B}{a_A}=\frac{v_B^2/r_B}{v_A^2/r_A}=\left(\frac{v_B}{v_A}\right)^2\frac{r_A}{r_B}=1.5^2\times\frac{1}{1.5}=1.5.$$ (Equivalently, $a=\omega^2r$ with the same $\omega$ gives $\dfrac{a_B}{a_A}=\dfrac{r_B}{r_A}=1.5$.)
