| 2.1 | $-1.02\times10^{-3}$ | $9.996\times10^{-3}$ |
| 2.9 | $-1.43\times10^{-3}$ | $1.401\times10^{-2}$ |
| 3.6 | $-1.86\times10^{-3}$ | $1.823\times10^{-2}$ |
| 4.3 | $-2.15\times10^{-3}$ | $2.107\times10^{-2}$ |

Calculate the gradient of a line of best fit of force against current and use it to determine the strength of the magnetic field. In your response, include any relevant equations.
questions.answer:
$F=lIB\sin\theta$ with $\theta=90^\circ$, so $\dfrac FI=lB$: the gradient equals $lB$. Taking two points on the line, e.g. $(2.0,\ 9.9\times10^{-3})$ and $(4.0,\ 1.97\times10^{-2})$: gradient $=\dfrac{1.97\times10^{-2}-9.9\times10^{-3}}{4.0-2.0}\approx4.9\times10^{-3}\ \text{N A}^{-1}$. Then $B=\dfrac{\text{gradient}}{l}=\dfrac{4.9\times10^{-3}}{0.60}\approx8.2\times10^{-3}$ T (accept about $8\times10^{-3}$ T).

Note: the school's table gave forces about 100 times too small ($5.61\times10^{-5}$ N for the first reading), because the mass readings had been divided by $g$ instead of multiplied. The forces here are corrected, so the field strength in (c) differs from the school's answer ($8.3\times10^{-5}$ T).

questions.question: The Standard Model identifies bosons as responsible for all the force interactions we observe. Outline the role of bosons in our universe.
questions.answer:
Bosons are the force-carrying (gauge) particles of the Standard Model, with integer spin. Matter particles (quarks and leptons) interact by exchanging bosons, which transfer energy and momentum between them.

Each fundamental force has its own boson: the strong force is carried by gluons (binding quarks into hadrons and holding nuclei together); the electromagnetic force is carried by photons (acting between charged particles); and the weak force is carried by the W and Z bosons (responsible for processes such as beta decay). Gravity is predicted to be carried by a graviton, which has not yet been detected. The Higgs boson is a different kind of boson, associated with the Higgs field that gives particles their mass.

questions.question: Students performed an investigation of the photoelectric effect using a zinc cathode. The graph of stopping voltage against frequency was extrapolated to the $y$-axis, where the line of best fit intersects at $-3.74$ V. Calculate the threshold frequency of the zinc cathode.
questions.answer: At the threshold frequency $K_{\max}=hf_0-\phi=0$, so $f_0=\dfrac\phi h$. The work function is $\phi=3.74\ \text{eV}=(3.74)(1.602\times10^{-19})=5.99\times10^{-19}$ J, so $f_0=\dfrac{5.99\times10^{-19}}{6.626\times10^{-34}}=9.04\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$.

questions.question: Students plotted stopping voltage against frequency for a zinc cathode, with the line of best fit intersecting the $y$-axis at $-3.74$ V. The investigation is repeated with a different metal with a greater work function. Describe, with a sketch, how the line of best fit will differ.
questions.answer: $eV_s=K_{\max}=hf-\phi$, so the gradient is $\dfrac he$ (the same for any metal) and the $y$-intercept is $-\dfrac\phi e$. A greater work function gives a line that is parallel to the original and below it, with a more negative $y$-intercept and a greater $x$-intercept (threshold frequency), as shown.

questions.question: In a photoelectric effect investigation, the students noticed that the photoelectrons did not all have the same velocities despite all receiving the same frequency of incident light. Account for this observation.
questions.answer: Light of a single frequency consists of photons that all have the same energy $E=hf$, and each photon transfers all of its energy to one electron. The electron then needs a different amount of energy to escape depending on where it came from: electrons in higher energy levels (and nearer the surface) need only the work function $\phi$, so they leave with the maximum kinetic energy $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$, while electrons in lower energy levels, or deeper in the metal, need more energy to escape or lose energy in collisions on the way to the surface. Their kinetic energy is the energy remaining after this, so it is smaller. Hence the electrons are emitted with a range of kinetic energies and velocities, up to a maximum.

questions.question: A pair of detectors is set up to measure the intensity of a parallel beam of unstable particles. In the reference frame of the laboratory, the detectors are separated by a distance of 45 m and the speed of the particles in the beam is $0.97c$. The intensity of the beam at the second detector is 12.5% of the intensity at the first detector. Calculate the half-life of the particles in the reference frame in which they are at rest.
questions.answer: In the particles' rest frame the detector separation is length-contracted: $l=45\sqrt{1-0.97^2}=10.9$ m. The time between detectors is $t_0=\dfrac{10.9}{0.97c}=3.8\times10^{-8}$ s. An intensity of 12.5% $=\left(\tfrac12\right)^3$ means three half-lives have elapsed, so $t_{1/2}=\dfrac{3.8\times10^{-8}}{3}=1.3\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}$ (13 ns). (Alternatively the lab time is $45/0.97c=1.55\times10^{-7}$ s, and dividing by $\gamma=4.11$ gives the same $t_0$.)

questions.question: In 1864, James Maxwell developed equations to describe the interaction of electric and magnetic fields and suggested that light was an electromagnetic wave. Outline why his work was challenged by physicists of his day and explain the eventual solution in Einstein's Theory of Special Relativity.
questions.answer:
Maxwell's equations described electric and magnetic fields propagating perpendicular to each other as an electromagnetic wave, with a speed fixed by constants of electromagnetism that matched the measured speed of light, so he concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave.

This was challenged because all known waves needed a medium, so physicists proposed a luminiferous aether as the medium for light, and Maxwell's predicted speed was independent of the observer, which clashed with Galilean relativity (the speed of light should vary for observers moving relative to the aether). The Michelson–Morley experiment used an interferometer to look for the change in the speed of light, and hence the fringe shift, expected as the Earth moved through the aether, and found none, so the aether was not detected.

Einstein's solution was to abandon the aether. His postulates were that the speed of light in a vacuum is an absolute constant for all observers, and that all inertial frames are equivalent (the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame). Since the speed of light is absolute, time and length must be relative to the motion of the observer, giving time dilation and length contraction.

questions.question: Describe one experimental evidence supporting Einstein's Theory of Special Relativity.
questions.answer:
Muons are produced in the upper atmosphere by cosmic rays and travel at close to the speed of light. Their half-life is so short (about 1.5 µs) that most should decay before reaching the Earth's surface, but many more are detected than classical physics predicts. This is explained by time dilation: for an observer on Earth, the muons' clocks run slow, so their half-life is longer (equivalently, in the muons' frame the distance to the surface is length-contracted).

(Alternatively, the Hafele–Keating experiment: atomic clocks flown around the world on aircraft differed from a clock on the ground by amounts consistent with relativity's predictions.)

questions.question: A student has a Blu-ray disc (slit separation 0.32 µm), a DVD (0.74 µm) and a CD (1.60 µm), the reflective coating of which is removed so each acts as a diffraction grating. The student also has two laser pointers: A, emitting 445 nm light, and B, emitting 636 nm light. Deduce the combination of disc and laser pointer that will produce the greatest possible number of interference maxima.
questions.answer: From $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$, the maximum order is $m_{\max}\le\dfrac d\lambda$ (since $\sin\theta\le1$), so the number of maxima is greatest when $\dfrac d\lambda$ is greatest: the largest slit separation and the shortest wavelength. This is the CD with laser pointer A: $\dfrac d\lambda=\dfrac{1600}{445}=3.6$, so $m=0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3$, giving 7 maxima.

questions.question: A student uses a CD (slit separation $1.60\ \mu\text{m}$) and a laser pointer B ($\lambda=636$ nm) in fixed positions. The horizontal laser beam is incident normally on the CD, and a diffraction pattern is produced vertically on a circular screen of diameter 30 cm, positioned 15 cm behind the CD. The height of the screen can be adjusted without changing its distance from the CD. Determine the greatest number of bright spots that can be observed on the screen.
questions.answer: $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$. For $m=1$: $\theta=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{636\times10^{-9}}{1.60\times10^{-6}}=23.4^\circ$, so $x_1=0.15\tan23.4^\circ=6.5$ cm from the central spot. For $m=2$: $\theta=\sin^{-1}(0.795)=52.7^\circ$, $x_2=0.15\tan52.7^\circ=19.7$ cm. ($m=3$ is not possible since $3\lambda/d>1$.) The spots are not equally spaced. The spots lie at $0,\ \pm6.5,\ \pm19.7$ cm. A 30 cm screen can span from $-6.5$ cm to $+19.7$ cm (26.2 cm), so it can show $m=-1,0,1,2$ (or $-2,\dots,1$), but the span for five spots would be $39.4$ cm $>30$ cm. The greatest number is 4.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at a speed of $32.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $62^\circ$ above the horizontal. Calculate the magnitude of the initial vertical and horizontal components of the velocity of the projectile.
Which combination of quarks makes up a proton?
questions.answer: A proton has charge $+1$: $u+u+d=\frac23+\frac23-\frac13=+1$ (A). ($udd$ is a neutron.)

questions.question: A person on Earth watches a spacecraft fly past Earth at a speed of $0.85c$. An event on the spacecraft takes 43 minutes to occur as measured by the person on the spacecraft. How long does the event take for the observer on Earth?

The diagram shows the splitting of the four fundamental forces at the beginning of the universe. Formation of particles, nuclei, atoms and stars could not occur until specific forces existed. Gravity causes particles to attract to each other. Which other forces were required to form the following types of matter?
questions.answer: Atoms need the electromagnetic force to bind electrons to the nucleus (and the strong force to hold the nucleus together), so (D). Protons are not held together by the weak force, so C is wrong.
options: Atoms: strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces.
Nuclei: strong nuclear and electromagnetic forces.
Protons: strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces.
Atoms: strong nuclear and electromagnetic forces.

questions.question: The image shows an experiment that helped to understand the structure of the atom. Who performed this experiment and what was the discovery made?
questions.answer: Alpha particles from a source strike beryllium, producing neutral radiation that knocks protons out of paraffin wax: Chadwick's discovery of the neutron (D).

questions.question: The graph shows how the mass of radon-211 in a sample changes over time. Determine the radioactive decay constant for Rn-211.
questions.answer: The mass halves from 12 g to 6 g in about 14.5 h, so $t_{1/2}\approx14.5\times3600=5.2\times10^{4}$ s. $\lambda=\dfrac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}}=\dfrac{0.693}{5.2\times10^{4}}=1.3\times10^{-5}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows the laminated iron core of a transformer. What is the purpose of the laminations in the iron core?
questions.answer: The thin insulated layers limit the size of the eddy current loops in the core, which reduces resistive heating and power loss (B). They reduce, but do not completely prevent, eddy currents (so D is wrong).
options: To make the iron core lighter.
To reduce power loss in the transformer.
To transfer the flux from the primary to the secondary coil.
To prevent the formation of any eddy currents in the iron core.

questions.question: A fan has three points marked on it, X, Y and Z, as shown. As the fan blade spins, the angular speed and linear speed of points X, Y and Z are measured. Rank the angular and linear speed of points X to Z.
questions.answer: All points on a rigid rotating body have the same angular speed $\omega$. Linear speed $v=r\omega$ increases with distance from the axis, and Z is furthest, so $v$ increases from X to Z (B).
options: Angular speed and linear speed both increase from X to Z.
Angular speed is constant, linear speed increases from X to Z.
Angular speed is constant, linear speed increases from Z to X.
Linear speed is constant, angular speed increases from X to Z.

questions.question: Two parallel wires of length 3.5 m carry the same magnitude of current. The two wires are fixed in place, 5.3 cm apart and have a repulsive force of $3.78\times10^{-6}$ N between them. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the current in the wires.
questions.answer: $\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0I^2}{2\pi r}$, so $I^2=\dfrac{2\pi rF}{\mu_0l}=\dfrac{2\pi(0.053)(3.78\times10^{-6})}{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.5)}=0.286$ and $I=0.535$ A. Parallel wires repel when the currents are in opposite directions (D).

questions.question: The diagram shows a fission reactor. What is the role of the moderator and control rods in a controlled nuclear fission reaction?
questions.answer: The moderator slows fast neutrons by collisions so they are more likely to cause further fission. Control rods absorb neutrons and can be raised or lowered to control the rate of the chain reaction (A).
options: Moderator: a substance that slows neutrons via collision. Control rods: moveable rods that absorb neutrons.
Moderator: a substance that slows neutrons via collision. Control rods: moveable rods that slow neutrons through collision.
Moderator: a substance that absorbs and releases neutrons. Control rods: moveable rods that absorb neutrons.
Moderator: a substance that absorbs neutrons via collision. Control rods: moveable rods that slow neutrons through collision.

questions.question: The diagram shows a metal disc that is free to rotate about the central pole and is not in contact with the magnet. When the metal disc is spun and the magnet is not present, the disc takes approximately 45 seconds to come to a stop. When the metal disc is spun at the same initial rate and the magnet is present, it comes to a stop in approximately 10 seconds. What is the reason for the difference in stopping times?
questions.answer: The part of the disc moving through the magnet's field has a changing flux, so by Faraday's law an emf and eddy currents are induced in the disc. By Lenz's law the magnetic fields of these currents oppose the change (the motion), so the disc slows quickly (D). The disc is not in contact with the magnet, so friction is not involved.
options: Friction between the magnet and disc creates a resistive force that opposes the spinning motion.
Eddy currents form in the disc due to Lenz's law, resulting in magnetic fields that oppose the spinning motion.
Eddy currents form in the magnet due to Faraday's law, resulting in magnetic fields that oppose the spinning motion.
Eddy currents form in the disc due to Faraday's Law, resulting in magnetic fields that oppose the spinning motion.

questions.question: Muons form in the upper atmosphere through nuclear reactions and provide evidence of special relativity. Non-relativistic data about muons: distance from formation to Earth's surface 10 km; half-life of muon 2.2 µs; number of muons reaching Earth 0. What is the reason that relativistic data measured about muons differs from the non-relativistic data?
questions.answer: In the Earth's frame the muons' clocks run slow, so humans observe a longer half-life (time dilation). In the muon's own frame its half-life is unchanged but the distance to the surface is length-contracted. So (B).
options: The muons experience a longer half-life due to time dilation. Humans observe muons travelling a shorter distance to the Earth's surface.
Humans observe muons having a longer half-life due to time dilation. The muons experience length contraction of the distance to Earth's surface.
The muons experience a longer half-life due to time dilation. The muons experience length contraction of the distance to the Earth's surface.
Humans observe muons having a longer half-life due to time dilation. Humans observe muons experiencing length contraction of the distance to Earth's surface.

questions.question: The diagram shows examples of a fission reaction and a fusion reaction. Which of the following is true when comparing the two reactions?
questions.answer: In both reactions the products have less mass than the reactants (mass defect), and the lost mass is released as energy ($E=mc^2$) (B). Both also need an initial input (neutron absorption or high temperature and pressure), and A and D are false.
options: Only fusion reactions require energy to start the reaction.
Both fission and fusion reactions have a net release of energy.
Fission reactions have a net release of energy, fusion reactions have a net absorption of energy.
In fission the products have greater mass than reactants, in fusion the reactants have greater mass than the products.

questions.question: The gold foil experiment is shown. In experiments like this, specific observations are used to make a conclusion about the structure. Which of the following observations matches the conclusion?
questions.answer: The few alpha particles deflected through large angles were repelled by a small, dense, positively charged nucleus (C). Most passing straight through shows the atom is mostly empty space, so A and B pair observations and conclusions the wrong way round. Alpha particles are deflected, not refracted (D).
options: Observation: the majority of alpha particles passed through undeflected. Conclusion: the nucleus was in the centre of the atom.
Observation: a small proportion of particles were deflected or reflected. Conclusion: the atom is mostly empty space.
Observation: a small proportion of alpha particles changed course and were deflected. Conclusion: the nucleus had a positive charge causing deflection of alpha particles.
Observation: a small proportion of particles were deflected or refracted. Conclusion: the nucleus had a positive charge causing deflection of alpha particles.

questions.question: The diagram shows Millikan's oil drop experiment where negatively charged oil droplets fall into a uniform electric field directed downwards. The plates are a distance $d$ apart with potential difference $V$. The oil droplets in the electric field are accelerating downwards. Which of the following is the correct relationship to find the charge $q$ on an oil drop that is accelerating downwards?
questions.answer: A negative drop in a downward field feels an upward electric force $qE=\dfrac{qV}{d}$. If it accelerates downwards, the weight exceeds this: $mg>\dfrac{qV}{d}$, so $q<\dfrac{dmg}{V}$ (A). ($q=dmg/V$ would hold if the drop was stationary.)

questions.question: For an object to leave the Earth's gravitational field it must be projected at escape velocity. Which of the following is NOT a consideration in the definition of escape velocity?
questions.answer: Escape velocity is defined by the object just reaching infinity ($r\to\infty$) where its gravitational force (and potential energy) is zero, and $K+U=0$, so $\frac12mv^2=\frac{GMm}{r}$ with $K$ and $U$ equal in magnitude. The acceleration of the object is not a consideration, as it decreases continually (C).
options: The object reaches an infinite distance from Earth.
The Earth's gravitational force stops acting on the object.
The acceleration of the object equals the gravitational acceleration of the Earth.
The initial gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy of the object are equal in magnitude.

questions.question: All motors have a constant top speed that will be reached some time after beginning to rotate. What is the reason for the maximum top speed?
questions.answer: As the coil speeds up, the back emf (which opposes the supply emf, by Lenz's law) increases, reducing the net voltage, current and torque. At the top speed the back emf has reached its maximum value, so the net voltage across the coil (and the torque, which balances friction and load) is constant (C).
options: The back emf eventually equals the supply emf, resulting in a constant net voltage.
The supply emf gradually decreases as the back emf increases, resulting in a constant voltage in the motor.
As the motor increases in speed, the back emf increases to a maximum, resulting in a constant net voltage.
The starting resistance gradually decreases, resulting in a constant resistance that determines the maximum speed of the motor.

questions.question: Two transformers, X and Y, are shown. Which of the following shows a change made to both transformers and the resulting correct change to the output voltage?
questions.answer: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$ is fixed by the turns ratio, so increasing $V_p$ increases $V_s$ in both (C). Changing the frequency does not change the output voltage in an ideal transformer.
options: Change: increase frequency of input AC. Result: increased voltage output in both transformers.
Change: input voltage decreased. Result: output voltage on X will increase, but decrease on Y.
Change: input voltage increased. Result: output voltage on both transformers will increase.
Change: input voltage increased. Result: output voltage on X will increase, but decrease on Y.

questions.question: The following nuclear equation shows the formation of a daughter nucleus and an unknown particle: $^{A}_{Z}X+{}^{1}_{0}n\rightarrow{}^{A-1}_{Z-2}Y+\,?$ What is the other type of particle produced?
questions.answer: Conservation of mass number: $A+1=(A-1)+m$, so the products other than Y total mass number 2. Conservation of charge: $Z=(Z-2)+q$, so total charge 2. This is two protons, $2\,{}^{1}_{1}p$ (D), each with mass number 1 and charge $+1$.

questions.question: Two satellites, A and B, orbit Earth at different altitudes (A: 629 km, B: 7629 km above the surface; Earth's radius 6371 km). Determine the ratio $T_A:T_B$.
questions.answer: $r_A=6371+629=7000$ km and $r_B=6371+7629=14000$ km. Kepler's third law: $T^2\propto r^3$, so $\dfrac{T_A}{T_B}=\left(\dfrac{r_A}{r_B}\right)^{3/2}=\left(\dfrac12\right)^{3/2}=0.354$ (C).

questions.question: The diagram shows a simple DC motor with a single rectangular coil of wire in a uniform magnetic field of strength 4.52 T. The length of side AB is 0.13 m and the length of side BC is 0.057 m. If the current flowing in the coil is 0.48 A, calculate the magnitude of the maximum torque produced by the motor.
questions.answer: $\tau_{\max}=nIAB=(1)(0.48)(0.13\times0.057)(4.52)=0.016\ \text{N m}$ (maximum when the coil's plane is parallel to the field).

questions.question: The diagram shows a simple DC motor with a single rectangular coil of wire in a uniform magnetic field. Justify one change to the motor that would increase the maximum torque.
questions.answer: $\tau_{\max}=nIAB$. Increasing the strength of the magnetic field $B$ (for example, using stronger magnets) increases the torque, because torque is directly proportional to $B$ ($\tau\propto B$). (Equally, increasing the number of turns, the current or the coil area increases the torque in proportion.)

questions.question: A red laser is shone through a double slit with slits $3.50\times10^{-5}$ m apart. The screen is 5.50 m away from the double slit. A student measures the distance between two adjacent bright bands to be 10.0 cm. Calculate the wavelength of the laser light.
questions.answer: For small angles, $\Delta y=\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{d\,\Delta y}{L}=\dfrac{(3.50\times10^{-5})(0.100)}{5.50}=6.4\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}$ (640 nm). (Using $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$ with $\Delta m=1$ and $\sin\theta\approx\tan\theta=\frac{0.100}{5.50}$ gives the same result.)

questions.question: A student measures the distance between adjacent bright bands formed when a red laser is shone through a double slit onto a screen (the measured spacing is 10.0 cm). Outline a limitation of this experiment that impacts the reliability of the results.
questions.answer: The bright bands are wide and fuzzy with no clearly defined edges or centres, so deciding where each maximum is (and therefore the spacing between them) is subjective. Different measurements or different people would give different values (random error), so repeated results are not consistent, which reduces the reliability.

questions.question: An object of mass 5.25 kg moves around a point in a circle of radius 4.83 m. The object has a period of 4.10 s. Calculate the acceleration of the object.
questions.answer: $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi(4.83)}{4.10}=7.40\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. $a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}=\dfrac{7.40^2}{4.83}=11\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ (11.3) directed towards the centre of the circle. (Acceleration is a vector, so the direction is required.)

questions.question: A planet orbits the Sun in an elliptical orbit. The shaded sectors swept out by the line from the Sun to the planet, between A and B (close to the Sun) and between C and D (far from the Sun), have equal areas. Justify whether the planet is travelling faster between A and B or between C and D.
questions.answer:
By Kepler's second law, the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so the planet takes the same time $t$ to go from A to B as from C to D. The arc length AB is longer than arc length CD (AB is closer to the Sun, where the same swept area needs a longer arc), so $v_{AB}=\dfrac{s_{AB}}{t}>v_{CD}=\dfrac{s_{CD}}{t}$. The planet is faster between A and B.

(Equivalently, by conservation of energy: $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ is more negative closer to the Sun, so with $U+K$ constant, $K=\frac12mv^2$ and $v$ are greater between A and B.)

questions.question: Explain why a geostationary satellite in orbit around the Earth has a constant total energy.
questions.answer: A geostationary satellite stays at a constant height in a circular orbit, so its orbital radius $r$ is constant. Its orbital speed $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$ is therefore constant, so its kinetic energy $K=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ is constant, and its gravitational potential energy $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ is constant. The total energy $U+K=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ is therefore constant, as $G$, $M$, $m$ and $r$ are all constant.

questions.question: The graph shows information about the moons of Jupiter (radius$^3$ of orbit, in units of $10^{30}\ \text{m}^3$, against period$^2$, in units of $10^{15}\ \text{s}^2$). Use the graph to determine the mass of Jupiter.
questions.answer: Kepler's third law: $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}=\dfrac{GM}{4\pi^2}$, so the gradient of $r^3$ against $T^2$ is $\dfrac{GM}{4\pi^2}$. Taking two widely spaced points on the line, $(0.5,\ 1.6)$ and $(3.3,\ 10.4)$: gradient $=\dfrac{(10.4-1.6)\times10^{30}}{(3.3-0.5)\times10^{15}}=3.14\times10^{15}\ \text{m}^3\text{s}^{-2}$. Then $M=\dfrac{4\pi^2\times\text{gradient}}{G}=\dfrac{4\pi^2(3.14\times10^{15})}{6.67\times10^{-11}}=1.86\times10^{27}\ \text{kg}$.

questions.question: The diagram shows three possible electron transitions in a hydrogen atom (from $n=4$, $n=3$ and $n=2$ to $n=1$). A photon of energy $1.94\times10^{-18}$ J is released from the hydrogen atom. Which electron transition from the diagram causes this energy photon?
questions.answer: $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{E}=\dfrac{(6.626\times10^{-34})(3.00\times10^{8})}{1.94\times10^{-18}}=1.02\times10^{-7}$ m. The final level is $n_f=1$ in all three transitions, so $\dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)$ gives $9.76\times10^{6}=1.097\times10^{7}\left(1-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)$, so $\dfrac1{n_i^2}=0.111$ and $n_i^2=9.0$, $n_i=3$. The photon is emitted in the transition from $n=3$ to $n=1$.

questions.question: Models of light have changed over time as new experiments have been conducted. Outline a property of light successfully explained by Huygens but not by Newton.
questions.answer: Huygens' wave model explained diffraction and interference of light: waves spread around obstacles and through slits, and overlapping waves reinforce or cancel to form bright and dark fringes (as later shown in Young's double-slit experiment). Newton's particle (corpuscular) model, which treated light as particles travelling in straight lines, could not explain how light bends around edges or produces fringe patterns. (Refraction is another example: the wave model correctly predicts light slows in a denser medium, whereas Newton's model required it to speed up.)

questions.question: Describe a significant contribution that Maxwell made to the classical theory of electromagnetism.
questions.answer: Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism into a single theory, summarised in four equations. He showed that a changing magnetic field induces an electric field (Faraday) and, adding to Ampère's law, that a changing electric field produces a magnetic field. Together, these allow a self-sustaining electromagnetic wave, with perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields travelling through space (even without a medium). He predicted that these waves travel at $c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}\approx3\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, the measured speed of light, and so concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave. Hertz later produced and detected radio waves, confirming the prediction.

questions.question: The graphs show changes in emf generated over time by AC or DC generators. Graph 1 and Graph 3 are produced by the same type of generator. The three graphs show emf (V) against time (ms) produced by AC or DC generators. Graph 1 is a rectified (all positive) sine-wave shape with peaks of 3 V every 15 ms. Graph 2 is a sine wave alternating between +3 V and −3 V with a period of 30 ms. Graph 3 is an almost constant emf of about 4 V with small ripples at a much higher frequency. Justify which structural feature of the generators results in the different shapes of Graph 1 and Graph 3.
questions.answer: Both are DC generators, with a split-ring commutator. The generator for Graph 3 has an armature with multiple coils (for example three or more coils at different angles, each connected to its own pair of commutator segments), whereas the generator for Graph 1 has only a single coil. With several coils, when the emf of one coil falls towards zero another coil is near its maximum, so the combined output stays near its peak value, giving the smooth, almost constant emf with small ripples of Graph 3. With a single coil the emf rises to a maximum and falls to zero twice per rotation, giving the repeated humps of Graph 1.

questions.question: The graphs show changes in emf generated over time. Graph 1 and Graph 2 are produced by generators with different commutators. The three graphs show emf (V) against time (ms) produced by AC or DC generators. Graph 1 is a rectified (all positive) sine-wave shape with peaks of 3 V every 15 ms. Graph 2 is a sine wave alternating between +3 V and −3 V with a period of 30 ms. Graph 3 is an almost constant emf of about 4 V with small ripples at a much higher frequency. Explain how the different commutators result in the shapes of Graph 1 and Graph 2.
questions.answer:
Graph 2 comes from a generator with slip rings, one connected to each end of the coil. Each end of the coil is always connected to the same external contact, so as the coil rotates and the direction of the induced emf reverses every half rotation (the coil cuts the field lines in the opposite direction), the output current alternates direction. This gives a sinusoidal AC emf with positive and negative half cycles.

Graph 1 comes from a generator with a split-ring commutator: a single ring cut into two halves, each connected to one end of the coil. Each time the coil passes the vertical position where the emf is zero and about to reverse, the split gaps swap which brush each coil end touches. This reverses the connection to the external circuit at the same instant as the emf reverses, so the output always has the same polarity. The negative half-cycles are flipped to positive, giving the pulsating DC output of Graph 1, which falls to zero twice per rotation.

questions.question: Explain how the atomic model proposed by Bohr was able to overcome the significant limitation of Rutherford's 'planetary' atomic model.
questions.answer:
In Rutherford's model, electrons orbit the nucleus in circular paths held by the electrostatic force, so each electron undergoes uniform circular motion with a centripetal acceleration. According to classical electromagnetism, an accelerating charged particle emits electromagnetic radiation, so the electron would continuously lose energy, spiral into the nucleus in a very short time and emit a continuous spectrum. Atoms are observed to be stable and to emit only discrete line spectra, so the model fails.

Bohr proposed that electrons can exist in certain stable orbits called stationary states, with quantised angular momentum, in which they do not radiate energy despite their circular motion. Because an electron in a stationary state has constant energy and does not radiate, it cannot spiral into the nucleus, so the atom is stable. Electrons emit or absorb energy only when they move between stationary states, with a photon whose energy equals the difference between the two energy levels.

questions.question: Three polarising filters are set up in a line. Unpolarised light of intensity 100 units is incident on filter 1. The plane of polarisation of filter 3 is perpendicular to the plane of polarisation of filter 1. Both filter 1 and 3 are fixed in place. Filter 2 can be rotated. Identify both positions of filter 2 that will ensure that no light emerges from filter 3.
questions.answer: Let filter 2 be at angle $\theta$ to filter 1. The intensity leaving filter 3 is $I_3=I_2\cos^2(90^\circ-\theta)=I_1\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta$, which is zero when $\theta=0^\circ$ (filter 2 parallel to filter 1, same as $180^\circ$) or $\theta=90^\circ$ (filter 2 parallel to filter 3, same as $270^\circ$). In the first case, filter 3 is perpendicular to the light from filters 1 and 2; in the second, filter 2 is perpendicular to the light from filter 1 and blocks it.

questions.question: Three polarising filters are set up in a line. Unpolarised light of intensity 100 units is incident on filter 1. Determine the intensity of light transmitted from filter 2 when the plane of polarisation of filter 2 is at an angle of $30^\circ$ to that of filter 1.
questions.answer: An ideal polariser transmits half the intensity of unpolarised light, so after filter 1 the intensity is $I_1=50$ units. By Malus' law, $I_2=I_1\cos^2\theta=50\cos^2(30^\circ)=50\times0.75=37.5$ units.

questions.question: Data was collected for Stars A and B by scientists on Earth: a graph of radiation intensity against wavelength (Star A peaks at about 350 nm, Star B at about 660 nm), the stars' spectra compared with a laboratory spectrum, and a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. Star A has a luminosity of 1, while Star B has a luminosity of $10^2$. The two stars undergo different types of fusion in the core. Compare the types of fusion occurring in the core of Star A and B and TWO other features of the stars. You must include information from all three stimulus diagrams in your response.
questions.answer:
**Surface temperature and classification (graph 1 and HR diagram).** Stars radiate as black bodies, so Wien's law $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac bT$ gives their surface temperatures. Star A: $T_A=\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{350\times10^{-9}}\approx8300\ \text{K}$; Star B: $T_B=\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{662.5\times10^{-9}}\approx4400\ \text{K}$. Plotting each star on the HR diagram using temperature and luminosity: Star A (about 8300 K, luminosity 1) lies on the main sequence, in the hot, white (A/F) region. Star B (about 4400 K, luminosity $10^2$) lies in the red giant region, so it is a cool, red-orange (K-type), very large star that has left the main sequence.

**Type of fusion.** Star A is a main-sequence star fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, here by the proton–proton chain, which has a low enough core temperature for this (net: $4\,{}^{1}_{1}\text{H}\rightarrow{}^{4}_{2}\text{He}+2e^{+}+2\nu+\text{energy}$). (More massive, hotter main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen to helium by the CNO cycle instead, which needs a higher core temperature; CNO also does not produce more than helium.) Star B is a red giant, which has finished fusing hydrogen in its core. Post-main-sequence fusion occurs: hydrogen fuses in a shell around an inert helium core, which contracts and heats until helium fuses to carbon and oxygen (triple-alpha process), and in more massive stars progressively heavier elements (up to iron) fuse in shells, layered around the core as each fuel runs out.

**Translational velocity (spectra).** The stars' absorption lines are compared with the laboratory spectrum of the same element, whose lines are at known wavelengths. Star A's lines are shifted only slightly towards the red end, while Star B's lines are shifted more towards the red end. By the Doppler effect, red-shift shows that both stars are moving away from Earth, with Star B moving away faster (greater translational velocity). Because $\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}=\dfrac vc$, the larger shift gives the larger recession speed.

questions.question: A charged particle $q_1$ is projected horizontally into a vertical electric field $E_1$ with an initial velocity $u_1$. A particle $q_2$ of identical charge and mass is projected horizontally into a different electric field $E_2$ with an initial velocity of $u_2$. The physical setup of the two parallel plates, including their length and the distance between the plates, is identical. It is known that $u_1>u_2$ and $E_2>E_1$, and that the particles will hit the bottom plates in both electric fields before leaving the field. A student predicted that particle $q_1$ will travel further than particle $q_2$ before hitting the bottom plate. Analyse the accuracy of the prediction made by the student.
questions.answer:
The particle moves like a projectile: constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration $a=\dfrac{F}{m}=\dfrac{qE}{m}$. Since $q$ and $m$ are the same, $a\propto E$, so $a_2>a_1$.

Vertical motion (starting with zero vertical velocity): $s_y=\tfrac12at^2$, so $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2s_y}{a}}$, and as the plate separation $s_y$ is the same, $t\propto\dfrac1{\sqrt a}$. Since $a_2>a_1$, $t_2<t_1$.

Horizontal motion: no horizontal force, so the horizontal distance (range) is $R=ut$. Since $u_1>u_2$ and $t_1>t_2$, $R_1=u_1t_1>R_2=u_2t_2$.

So particle $q_1$ travels further than $q_2$ before hitting the bottom plate, and the student's prediction is accurate.

questions.question: Hubble's observations provided evidence that the universe is expanding. Describe the observations that led Hubble to conclude that the universe was expanding.
questions.answer: Hubble measured the distances to galaxies (using Cepheid variable stars as standard candles, from their apparent and absolute magnitudes) and measured their velocities from the Doppler shift of the spectral lines in their light compared with laboratory spectra. He observed that the spectral lines of almost all galaxies were shifted towards longer wavelengths (red-shifted), meaning that they are moving away from us, and that the more distant the galaxy, the greater its red-shift and recession speed ($v\propto d$, $v=H_0d$). This pattern, in which everything moves away from everything else faster with distance, is explained by the expansion (stretching) of space itself, which stretches the wavelengths of light.

questions.question: Hubble's observations provided evidence that the universe is expanding. Sketch a graph of the data collected during Hubble's observations and outline how it allows the age of the universe to be estimated.
questions.answer:
The graph of recession velocity $v$ (vertical axis) against distance $d$ (horizontal axis) is a straight line through the origin, with gradient the Hubble constant $H_0$ ($v=H_0d$), as shown.

If the galaxies have always moved at constant speed, the time since they were together at the same point (the Big Bang) is $t=\dfrac dv=\dfrac1{H_0}$, which is the inverse of the gradient. This gives an estimate of the age of the universe (about 14 billion years for $H_0\approx70\ \text{km s}^{-1}\text{Mpc}^{-1}$).

questions.question: Explain how the equations $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$ (proposed by Einstein in the analysis of the photoelectric effect) and $\dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)$ (used by Bohr for the analysis of emission spectra for hydrogen) are BOTH related to quantised energy and are BOTH consistent with the law of conservation of energy.
questions.answer:
**Photoelectric effect: quantised energy.** Einstein proposed that light consists of photons, each carrying a discrete quantum of energy $E=hf$ (the idea of quantised energy introduced by Planck). In $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$, the term $hf$ is the energy of a single photon, which is absorbed by a single electron as a whole, and the work function $\phi$ is the minimum energy to remove an electron from the metal. Energy transfers only occur in whole photons, so emission occurs only if $hf\ge\phi$ (the threshold frequency).

**Photoelectric effect: conservation of energy.** Rearranged, $hf=K_{\max}+\phi$: the energy input (the photon's energy) equals the energy output (the work done to free the electron plus the electron's maximum kinetic energy). No energy is lost: $E_{in}=E_{out}$.

**Hydrogen emission spectra: quantised energy.** Bohr proposed that electrons in hydrogen can only exist in discrete energy levels (stationary states) with energies proportional to $-\dfrac1{n^2}$. In the equation, $n_i$ and $n_f$ are whole numbers labelling these quantised levels, and $\dfrac1\lambda\propto\dfrac{E}{hc}$ is proportional to the energy of the emitted photon ($E=hf=\dfrac{hc}\lambda$), so only certain photon energies (spectral lines of particular wavelengths) are possible, rather than a continuous spectrum.

**Hydrogen emission spectra: conservation of energy.** The bracket $\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right)$ is proportional to the energy lost by the electron when it falls from level $n_i$ to level $n_f$, and $\dfrac1\lambda$ is proportional to the energy of the emitted photon. The equation therefore equates the energy released by the electron to the energy of the photon emitted ($E_i-E_f=hf$), so energy is conserved.

questions.question: Two oppositely charged parallel plates are arranged vertically 8.5 cm apart with 15 000 V between them. A ball of mass 2.7 g and carrying a charge of +69 nC is suspended by a massless string from the top of the positive plate, as shown, and hangs in equilibrium. Calculate the magnitude of the tension in the string. Use $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.
questions.answer: Three forces act on the ball: weight $F_g=mg=(2.7\times10^{-3})(9.8)=2.65\times10^{-2}$ N (down), electric force $F_E=qE=\dfrac{qV}{d}=\dfrac{(69\times10^{-9})(15000)}{0.085}=1.22\times10^{-2}$ N (horizontal, towards the negative plate), and tension $T$ along the string. The ball is in equilibrium, so the tension balances the vector sum of the other two forces: $T=\sqrt{F_g^2+F_E^2}=\sqrt{(2.65\times10^{-2})^2+(1.22\times10^{-2})^2}=2.9\times10^{-2}$ N.

questions.question: A ball carrying a positive charge is suspended by a massless string from the top of the positive one of two oppositely charged vertical parallel plates. Sketch on the diagram the path of the ball if the string was to break. Justify your predicted path. Calculations are not required.
questions.answer: When the string breaks, the ball is at rest and the only forces are its weight (constant, vertically down) and the electric force (constant, horizontal towards the negative plate, as the field between the plates is uniform). The resultant force is constant and is the same as the tension in magnitude but opposite in direction (the equilibrium condition before the string broke), so the ball accelerates uniformly from rest in the direction of that constant resultant force. Since the initial velocity is zero and the acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction, the ball moves in a straight line, down and towards the negative plate, at $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{F_E}{F_g}\approx25^\circ$ from the vertical (along the line of the former string, extended away from the point of suspension), until it hits the negative plate.

questions.question: Two solenoids are positioned close to each other. Solenoid A is connected to a power source. Solenoid B is connected to a cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO) that outputs data showing emf generated over a period of time. An experiment investigates how the CRO output from Solenoid B changes when the current in Solenoid A is changed. Test 1: direct current (DC) of magnitude 1.5 A. Test 2: alternating current (AC) of magnitude 3.0 A. Sketch and explain the observed CRO output (emf against time) from Solenoid B for Test 1 and Test 2.
questions.answer:
**Test 1 (steady DC).** The steady current of 1.5 A in Solenoid A produces a constant magnetic field, so the flux linking Solenoid B is constant. By Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=0$, so the CRO shows a flat line at zero emf (apart from a brief pulse when the current is switched on or off).

**Test 2 (AC).** The alternating current changes continuously in magnitude and direction, sinusoidally, so the magnetic field of Solenoid A and the flux through Solenoid B change continuously. The induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of flux, which is greatest when the current is changing most rapidly (at zero current) and zero when the current is at a maximum or minimum. The emf in Solenoid B is therefore also sinusoidal (alternating) with the same frequency as the current (a quarter cycle out of phase with it). Its amplitude is larger than any emf in Test 1 (the flux changes at a greater rate with the larger 3.0 A current).

questions.question: Projectile A is launched on Earth with an initial speed of $40\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. Projectile B is launched with the same initial conditions on a planet where the acceleration due to gravity is exactly half that on Earth. Projectile B's path compared to projectile A will have:
questions.answer: $H=\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$, so halving $g$ doubles the maximum height. Landing back at launch height, the final speed equals the launch speed by conservation of energy (the horizontal speed is unchanged and the vertical speed is reversed), so it is equal (D).
options: Maximum height: equal; final speed: double
Maximum height: equal; final speed: equal
Maximum height: double; final speed: double
Maximum height: double; final speed: equal

questions.question: Two objects are launched into space from the ground so that they will just escape Earth's gravitational field forever, by being given an initial velocity. Object A had a mass of 10 kg, while object B had a mass of 100 kg. Which alternative is correct?
questions.answer: Escape speed $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}r}$ does not depend on the mass of the object, so the speeds are equal. $K=\tfrac12mv^2\propto m$, so B (10 times the mass) has 10 times the kinetic energy (B).
options: Initial speed equal; initial kinetic energy equal
Initial speed equal; B's initial kinetic energy is 10 times greater than A's
Initial speed equal; B's initial kinetic energy is 100 times greater than A's
B's initial speed is 10 times greater; B's initial kinetic energy is 100 times greater

questions.question: A cyclist tightens a nut with a 50.0 cm spanner, applying a force of 70.0 N at an angle of $70^\circ$ to the spanner, as shown. What magnitude of torque has the cyclist applied to the nut?
questions.answer: $\tau=rF\sin\theta=0.500\times70.0\times\sin70^\circ=32.9$ N m (B). (C and D come from using 50.0 cm without converting to metres.)

questions.question: Two planets, Centaur and Tri, orbit a star. Centaur has an orbital path with a radius that is four times smaller than the radius of Tri's orbital path. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: Kepler's third law: $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}$ is constant, so $T\propto r^{3/2}$. $\dfrac{T_\text{Tri}}{T_\text{Centaur}}=4^{3/2}=8$. Tri's orbit takes 8 times longer (A).
options: Tri would take 8 times longer than Centaur to make a full orbit of the star
Centaur would take 8 times longer than Tri to make a full orbit of the star
Tri would take 64 times longer than Centaur to make a full orbit of the star
Centaur would take 64 times longer than Tri to make a full orbit of the star

questions.question: Ganymede has a mass of $1.5\times10^{23}$ kg and a radius of $2.6\times10^6$ m. Which one of the following is closest to the magnitude of Ganymede's surface gravity?

A charged particle $+Q$ enters a region of uniform electric field $E$ between two parallel plates, as shown, with speed $v$ (the field points from the top plate to the bottom plate). The apparatus is in a vacuum and the experiment is performed in weightless conditions. The particle travels a horizontal distance $D$ before striking the charged plate. What change would result in the particle travelling twice the horizontal distance, $2D$?
questions.answer: Vertically, $d=\tfrac12at^2$ with $a=\dfrac{QE}m$, so $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2dm}{QE}}$ is independent of $v$. Horizontally, $D=vt$, so doubling $v$ doubles $D$ (A). Halving $d$ or $E$, or halving the mass, changes $t$ by a factor of $\sqrt2$ only (so $D$ changes by $\frac1{\sqrt2}$, $\sqrt2$ and $\frac1{\sqrt2}$ respectively).
options: halving the vertical distance, $d$, the particle must move
halving the mass of the particle

questions.question: A ball is attached to the end of a string and rotated in a circle at constant speed in a vertical plane. Ignoring air resistance, which one of the following best represents the forces acting on the ball when it is at the bottom of the circular path and moving to the left?
questions.answer: Only two forces act: the weight (down) and the tension (up). There is no separate 'centripetal' or forward force. At the bottom the net force must point up, towards the centre, so the tension (up) is larger than the weight (down): $T-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}r$ (D).

questions.question: Three metal rods A, B and C carry currents of 3 A (to the right), 4 A (to the left) and 5 A (to the left) respectively. Rod A is 10 cm above rod B, and rod C is 20 cm below rod B. What is the magnitude and direction of the force per unit length on rod C?
questions.answer: Using $\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r}$ ($\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}=2\times10^{-7}$). From B (same direction, so attraction, upwards): $2\times10^{-7}\times\dfrac{4\times5}{0.20}=2\times10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$ up. From A (opposite direction, so repulsion, downwards; $r=0.30$ m): $2\times10^{-7}\times\dfrac{3\times5}{0.30}=1\times10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$ down. Net $=1\times10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$ up (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows a small DC electric motor, powered by a battery connected via a split-ring commutator. The rectangular coil has sides KJ and LM. The magnetic field between the poles of the magnet is uniform and constant. The switch is closed, allowing current to flow, and the coil is stationary and in the position shown. Which one of the following statements best describes the motion of the coil when the switch is closed?
questions.answer: By the motor effect (right-hand push rule), the forces on the sides KJ and LM are in opposite directions and produce a torque in direction B. The split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn, so the torque keeps acting in the same sense and the coil keeps rotating in direction B (C).
options: The coil will rotate in direction A, as shown in the diagram
The coil will rotate in direction B, as shown in the diagram
The coil will oscillate regularly between directions A and B

questions.question: Three identical magnets P, Q and R are released simultaneously from rest and fall to the ground from the same height. P falls directly to the ground, Q falls through the centre of a thick conducting ring and R falls through a ring which is identical except for a gap cut into it. Which one of the statements below best describes the sequence in which the magnets reach the ground?
questions.answer: Q falls through a complete conducting ring, so the changing flux induces an emf and an eddy current. By Lenz's law the current's magnetic field opposes the magnet's motion, so Q accelerates more slowly. The gap in R's ring prevents a current flowing round it, so no opposing force arises and R falls freely like P. P and R land together, then Q (A).
options: P and R arrive together followed by Q.
P and Q arrive together followed by R.
P arrives first, followed by Q which is followed by R.

questions.question: Which line correctly describes the trajectory of charged particles which enter, at right angles, (a) a uniform electric field, and (b) a uniform magnetic field?
questions.answer: In a uniform electric field the force is constant in magnitude and direction, so the path is parabolic (like a projectile). In a uniform magnetic field the force is always perpendicular to the velocity and constant in magnitude, so the path is circular (C).

questions.question: James Maxwell wrote a series of equations that unified electricity and magnetism. Consider the following statements about these equations. I The equations predict the wave-particle duality of light. II The equations predict that electromagnetic waves travel at $3\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in a vacuum. III Radiation from black bodies is emitted in discrete packets called quanta. IV Oscillating charges produce electromagnetic radiation. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.answer: Maxwell's equations treat light as a classical wave: they predict EM waves travelling at $c=\dfrac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$ (II) and that accelerating or oscillating charges radiate (IV). Wave-particle duality (I) and quantised emission (III) came later from quantum theory (C).

questions.question: The Sun produces $5.4\times10^{25}$ J of energy each second by the conversion of mass to energy. How many positron-electron annihilations would need to occur each second for an equivalent amount of energy to be produced (all mass is converted to energy)?
questions.answer: One annihilation converts the mass of an electron and a positron: $E=2m_ec^2=2\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times(3.0\times10^8)^2=1.64\times10^{-13}$ J. Number per second $=\dfrac{5.4\times10^{25}}{1.64\times10^{-13}}=3.3\times10^{38}$ (D).

questions.question: As a star rotates, the observed atomic absorption bands change. When a star is rotating away from an observer, light is X. When the star is rotating towards the observer, light is Y. The Z it rotates, the wider the absorption band will appear in its spectrum. Which row completes the statement?
questions.answer: Light from the side receding from the observer is red-shifted and from the side approaching is blue-shifted (Doppler effect). The faster the star rotates, the larger the range of Doppler shifts, so the wider the absorption line (B).
options: X blue-shifted, Y red-shifted, Z faster
X red-shifted, Y blue-shifted, Z faster
X blue-shifted, Y red-shifted, Z slower
X red-shifted, Y blue-shifted, Z slower

questions.question: In a Young's double-slit experiment, monochromatic light is incident on two narrow slits and the resulting interference pattern is observed on a screen. Which change decreases the fringe separation?
questions.answer: Fringe separation $\Delta x=\dfrac{\lambda L}d$. It decreases if $\lambda$ decreases, $L$ decreases or $d$ increases. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, so $\Delta x$ decreases (C).
options: decreasing the separation between the two slits
increasing the distance between the slits and the screen
using monochromatic light of higher frequency
using monochromatic light of longer wavelength

questions.question: The nuclear fuel, which provides the power output in a nuclear reactor, decreases in mass at a rate of $6.0\times10^{-6}$ kg per hour. What is the maximum possible power output of the reactor?
questions.answer: Mass rate $=\dfrac{6.0\times10^{-6}}{3600}=1.67\times10^{-9}$ kg s$^{-1}$. $P=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}c^2=1.67\times10^{-9}\times(3.0\times10^8)^2=1.5\times10^8$ W $=150$ MW (C).

questions.question: A deuterium nucleus and a tritium nucleus fuse together to form a helium nucleus and a particle X: ${}^2_1\text{H}+{}^3_1\text{H}\to{}^4_2\text{He}+X$. What is X?
questions.answer: Mass number: $2+3=5=4+A$, so $A=1$. Charge: $1+1=2=2+Z$, so $Z=0$. A particle with $A=1$ and $Z=0$ is a neutron (B).

questions.question: On the horizontal axis of a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, what can be plotted instead of temperature?
questions.answer: The horizontal axis shows surface temperature (decreasing to the right), which can be replaced by the equivalent stellar colour or spectral class. Brightness (luminosity) is on the vertical axis (A).

questions.question: When light of a certain frequency greater than the threshold frequency of a metal is directed at the metal, photoelectrons are emitted from the surface. The power of the light incident on the metal surface is doubled. Which row shows the effect on the maximum kinetic energy and the number of photoelectrons emitted per second?
questions.answer: $K_{max}=hf-\phi$ depends on frequency, not intensity, so it is unchanged. Doubling the power doubles the number of photons per second and hence the number of photoelectrons emitted per second (C).
options: Maximum kinetic energy unchanged; number per second unchanged
Maximum kinetic energy doubles; number per second unchanged
Maximum kinetic energy unchanged; number per second doubles
Maximum kinetic energy doubles; number per second doubles

questions.question: A skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a ramp at A and leaves the ramp at B horizontally with a velocity $v=5.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. After leaving the ramp at B, the skateboarder lands on the ground at C $0.42$ s later (B is $1.0$ m above the ground). Find the horizontal distance travelled between B and C.
questions.answer: The horizontal velocity is constant: $x=v_xt=5.4\times0.42=2.3$ m.

questions.question: A skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a ramp at A and leaves the ramp at B horizontally with a velocity $v=5.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. After leaving the ramp at B, the skateboarder lands on the ground at C $0.42$ s later (B is $1.0$ m above the ground). Calculate the vertical component of the velocity immediately before impact at C.
questions.answer: $v_y=gt=9.8\times0.42=4.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (downwards), since the vertical velocity at B is zero. (Using the 1.0 m drop instead, $v_y=\sqrt{2gh}=4.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, was also accepted.)

questions.question: A skateboarder starts from rest at the top of a ramp at A and leaves the ramp at B horizontally with a velocity $v=5.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. After leaving the ramp at B, the skateboarder lands on the ground at C $0.42$ s later (B is $1.0$ m above the ground). Determine the magnitude of the resultant velocity immediately before impact at C.

A small ball of mass 1.8 kg travels in a horizontal circular path at constant speed while suspended from the ceiling by a 0.75 m long string, which makes an angle of $25^\circ$ with the vertical. Use labelled arrows to indicate the two physical forces acting on the ball (describe them).
questions.answer: The two forces are the weight $mg$ (vertically downwards) and the tension in the string (along the string, up and towards the centre of the circle). The centripetal force is not a third force: it is the horizontal component of the tension.

questions.question: A small ball of mass 1.8 kg travels in a horizontal circular path at constant speed while suspended from the ceiling by a 0.75 m long string, which makes an angle of $25^\circ$ with the vertical. Calculate the speed of the ball.
questions.answer: The radius of the circle is $r=0.75\sin25^\circ=0.317$ m. Vertically, $T\cos25^\circ=mg$; horizontally, $T\sin25^\circ=\dfrac{mv^2}r$. Dividing: $\tan25^\circ=\dfrac{v^2}{rg}$, so $v^2=9.8\times0.317\times\tan25^\circ=1.45$ and $v=1.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question: Supertankers float with their centres 100.00 m apart and each has mass $5.00\times10^8$ kg. Calculate the gravitational force between the two supertankers.

The centre of a planet of mass $1.00\times10^{24}$ kg is a distance $d$ from the centre of one of its moons. The gravitational force of attraction between them is: $F$ ($\times10^3$ N) $=37, 32, 23, 17, 11, 6$ for $d$ ($\times10^6$ m) $=3.43, 3.70, 4.34, 5.06, 6.32, 8.45$, so that $\dfrac1{d^2}$ ($\times10^{-14}\ \text{m}^{-2}$) $=8.5, 7.3, 5.3, 3.9, 2.5, 1.4$. Describe the graph of $F$ (vertical axis) against $\dfrac1{d^2}$ (horizontal axis) and the line of best fit that results, and explain the shape using Newton's law of gravitation.
questions.answer: The points lie on a straight line through the origin (directly proportional), as $F=GMm\cdot\dfrac1{d^2}$ is of the form $y=kx$ with gradient $k=GMm$. A line of best fit is drawn passing through (or very close to) the origin and the points, with a rise from about 6 (at 1.4) to about 37 (at 8.5) on the force axis (in $10^3$ N). The plotted graph is shown.

questions.question: The centre of a planet of mass $1.00\times10^{24}$ kg is a distance $d$ from the centre of one of its moons. The gravitational force of attraction between them is: $F$ ($\times10^3$ N) $=37, 32, 23, 17, 11, 6$ for $d$ ($\times10^6$ m) $=3.43, 3.70, 4.34, 5.06, 6.32, 8.45$, so that $\dfrac1{d^2}$ ($\times10^{-14}\ \text{m}^{-2}$) $=8.5, 7.3, 5.3, 3.9, 2.5, 1.4$. The line of best fit has gradient $k$ on the graph of $F$ against $\dfrac1{d^2}$. Determine the gradient of the graph, including units. Show all working.
questions.answer: Using two points widely spaced on the line of best fit (the end points (8.5, 37) and (1.4, 6)): $k=\dfrac{\Delta F}{\Delta(1/d^2)}=\dfrac{(37-6)\times10^3}{(8.5-1.4)\times10^{-14}}=\dfrac{31\times10^3}{7.1\times10^{-14}}=4.4\times10^{17}\ \text{N m}^2$ (the school's value $4.366\times10^{17}$ N m$^2$ is the same to 2 sf).

questions.question: The centre of a planet of mass $1.00\times10^{24}$ kg is a distance $d$ from the centre of one of its moons. The gravitational force of attraction between them is: $F$ ($\times10^3$ N) $=37, 32, 23, 17, 11, 6$ for $d$ ($\times10^6$ m) $=3.43, 3.70, 4.34, 5.06, 6.32, 8.45$, so that $\dfrac1{d^2}$ ($\times10^{-14}\ \text{m}^{-2}$) $=8.5, 7.3, 5.3, 3.9, 2.5, 1.4$. Use the gradient of the graph ($4.4\times10^{17}\ \text{N m}^2$) to help determine the mass of the moon.
questions.answer: The gradient is $k=GMm$ with $M=1.00\times10^{24}$ kg. $m=\dfrac{k}{GM}=\dfrac{4.366\times10^{17}}{6.67\times10^{-11}\times1.00\times10^{24}}=6.5\times10^3$ kg (about 6500 kg).

questions.question: A communications satellite has a mass of 250 kg. The satellite is in orbit around Earth (mass $6.0\times10^{24}$ kg) at an orbital radius of 33 500 km. Determine the gravitational potential energy of the satellite.
questions.answer: $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}=-\dfrac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times6.0\times10^{24}\times250}{3.35\times10^7}=-2.99\times10^9$ J (the radius must be in metres).

questions.question: A communications satellite of mass 250 kg orbits Earth. If the satellite were to move to an orbit of a higher radius, state what would happen to its kinetic energy.
questions.answer: It decreases: orbital speed $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}r}$ is smaller at a larger radius.

questions.question: A communications satellite of mass 250 kg orbits Earth. If the satellite were to move to an orbit of a higher radius, state what would happen to its gravitational potential energy.
questions.answer: It increases (becomes less negative), since $U=-\dfrac{GMm}r$ rises towards zero as $r$ increases.

prev.question: A communications satellite of mass 250 kg orbits Earth. If the satellite were to move to an orbit of a higher radius, state what would happen to its kinetic energy.
prev.answer: It decreases: orbital speed $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}r}$ is smaller at a larger radius.

questions.question: A communications satellite of mass 250 kg orbits Earth. If the satellite were to move to an orbit of a higher radius, state what would happen to its total mechanical energy.
questions.answer: It increases (becomes less negative): $E=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$. The gain in potential energy is greater than the loss of kinetic energy, and energy must be supplied to the satellite to move it to the higher orbit.

prev.question: A communications satellite of mass 250 kg orbits Earth. If the satellite were to move to an orbit of a higher radius, state what would happen to its kinetic energy.
prev.answer: It decreases: orbital speed $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}r}$ is smaller at a larger radius.

prev.question: A communications satellite of mass 250 kg orbits Earth. If the satellite were to move to an orbit of a higher radius, state what would happen to its gravitational potential energy.
prev.answer: It increases (becomes less negative), since $U=-\dfrac{GMm}r$ rises towards zero as $r$ increases.

questions.question: The diagram shows a transformer with an iron core. The primary coil has many more turns than the secondary coil. Identify whether this is a step-up or step-down transformer.
questions.answer: Step-down: the secondary has fewer turns than the primary, so the output voltage is lower than the input.

questions.question: Explain a feature of the iron core of a transformer that would significantly improve the efficiency of the transformer.
questions.answer: The core should be laminated (made of thin sheets insulated from each other). This breaks up the paths of the eddy currents induced in the core, reducing their size and hence the energy lost as heat, so the efficiency improves.

questions.question: Explain why transformers only work continuously when supplied with an alternating current.
questions.answer: A transformer works by electromagnetic induction. An emf is induced in the secondary only while the magnetic flux through it is changing. An alternating current produces a continuously changing flux; a steady direct current produces a constant flux and so no induced emf.

questions.question: The primary coil of a transformer is connected to a 230 V AC supply. The secondary coil has 300 turns and provides an output of 20 V and a power of 65 W. Calculate the number of turns on the primary coil.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}=\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}$, so $N_p=300\times\dfrac{230}{20}=3450\approx3500$ turns (2 sf).

questions.question: The primary coil of a transformer is connected to a 230 V AC supply. If the primary current is 0.30 A, determine the primary power.
questions.answer: $P=VI=230\times0.30=69$ W (compared with 65 W output, so the transformer is about 94% efficient).

questions.question: A rectangular wire loop with dimensions 0.050 m $\times$ 0.035 m is placed between two magnets that create a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.20 mT. The loop is rotated with a frequency of 50 Hz. The ends of the loop are connected to a split ring commutator. State the direction of the induced current through the loop (viewed from above) for the first quarter turn of the loop in the direction shown.
questions.answer: Anticlockwise as seen from above, by Lenz's law (the induced current opposes the change in flux through the loop). The school's diagram shows the current coming out of the page.

questions.question: A rectangular wire loop with dimensions 0.050 m $\times$ 0.035 m is placed between two magnets that create a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.20 mT. The loop is rotated with a frequency of 50 Hz. The ends of the loop are connected to a split ring commutator. Calculate the emf induced in the loop for the first quarter turn of the loop.
questions.answer: Period $T=\dfrac1{50}=0.020$ s, so a quarter turn takes $\Delta t=0.005$ s. In the first quarter turn the flux changes by $\Delta\Phi=BA=0.20\times10^{-3}\times0.050\times0.035=3.5\times10^{-7}$ Wb. $\varepsilon=\left|\dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|=\dfrac{3.5\times10^{-7}}{0.005}=7\times10^{-5}$ V (magnitude; average emf).

questions.question: A rectangular wire loop with dimensions 0.050 m $\times$ 0.035 m is placed between two magnets that create a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.20 mT. The loop is rotated with a frequency of 50 Hz. The ends of the loop are connected to a split ring commutator. What is the effect of using a split ring commutator instead of slip rings in this generator?
questions.answer: It reverses the connections every half turn, so the output current always flows in the same direction: a pulsating direct current (DC) is produced instead of alternating current.

questions.question: A rectangular wire loop with dimensions 0.050 m $\times$ 0.035 m is placed between two magnets that create a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.20 mT. The loop is rotated with a frequency of 50 Hz. The ends of the loop are connected to a split ring commutator. Identify the main energy change that is happening in this generator.
questions.answer: Kinetic (mechanical) energy of the rotating loop is converted to electrical energy.

questions.question: A rectangular wire loop with dimensions 0.050 m $\times$ 0.035 m is placed between two magnets that create a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.20 mT. The loop is rotated with a frequency of 50 Hz. The ends of the loop are connected to a split ring commutator. Describe the graph of the emf produced for one complete cycle of the loop (with a split ring commutator), assuming the loop starts moving from the position shown.
questions.answer: The emf is always positive (never reverses) because of the commutator, and has a series of humps, two per rotation, each shaped like the magnitude of a sine wave, starting at a maximum value at $t=0$ and falling to zero every half turn (every 0.010 s) before rising again. The sketch is shown.

questions.question: The diagram shows the paths of two charged particles entering a magnetic field of strength 1.0 T (directed into the page) from the left. Identify the sign of the charge following path P (which curves upwards).
questions.answer: Positive. The velocity is to the right and $B$ is into the page; the force on a positive charge $\mathbf F=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ is upwards, which is the direction in which path P curves.

questions.question: Explain what happens to the kinetic energy of a charge that follows either path P or path Q as it moves through the magnetic field (strength 1.0 T).
questions.answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed (and kinetic energy) stays constant: the charge moves in uniform circular motion. (In reality an accelerating charge radiates a little electromagnetic radiation, so a very small loss of kinetic energy occurs, but this is normally negligible.)

questions.question: Calculate the size of the magnetic force on a proton entering a 1.0 T magnetic field at $2.4\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (assume the proton enters perpendicular to the field direction).
questions.answer: $F=qvB=1.6\times10^{-19}\times2.4\times10^6\times1.0=3.8\times10^{-13}$ N.

questions.question: The emission spectrum for helium gas has lines at 668, 588, 502, 492, 471, 447 and 403 nm. Which spectral line (in nm) indicates the photon emitted with the lowest energy?
questions.answer: $E=\dfrac{hc}\lambda$, so the lowest energy is the longest wavelength: 668 nm.

questions.question: The emission spectrum for helium gas has lines at 668, 588, 502, 492, 471, 447 and 403 nm. Calculate the frequency of the photon emitted at the 588 nm line.
questions.answer: $f=\dfrac c\lambda=\dfrac{3.0\times10^8}{588\times10^{-9}}=5.1\times10^{14}$ Hz.

questions.question: The emission spectrum for helium gas has lines at 668, 588, 502, 492, 471, 447 and 403 nm. Determine the energy of the photon emitted at the 588 nm line.

In a Young's double-slit experiment, monochromatic laser light is incident on two slits $S_1$ and $S_2$ that are $4.0\times10^{-4}$ m apart. Rays from the slits meet on a screen 2.00 m from the slits to produce a pattern of bright and dark bands. Point C is a bright spot at the centre of the pattern and P is the fourth bright band from C ($1.26\times10^{-2}$ m from C). State the path difference, in terms of integer multiples of wavelength, at P.
questions.answer: P is the fourth bright band from the central maximum, so the path difference is $4\lambda$.

questions.question: In a Young's double-slit experiment, monochromatic laser light is incident on two slits $S_1$ and $S_2$ that are $4.0\times10^{-4}$ m apart. Rays from the slits meet on a screen 2.00 m from the slits to produce a pattern of bright and dark bands. Point C is a bright spot at the centre of the pattern and P is the fourth bright band from C ($1.26\times10^{-2}$ m from C). Calculate the wavelength of the laser.
questions.answer: There are four fringe spacings between C and P: $\Delta x=\dfrac{1.26\times10^{-2}}4=3.15\times10^{-3}$ m. $\Delta x=\dfrac{\lambda L}d$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{\Delta x\,d}L=\dfrac{3.15\times10^{-3}\times4.0\times10^{-4}}{2.00}=6.3\times10^{-7}$ m $=630$ nm.

questions.question: Describe the significance of Young's double-slit experiment in the wider debate about the nature of light.
questions.answer: The experiment produced an interference pattern of alternating bright and dark bands. Only waves can show interference and diffraction, so it provided strong evidence for the wave model of light over Newton's particle (corpuscular) model.

questions.question: A technician on Earth observes a spaceship travelling past at $0.7c$. The spaceship fires a laser light beam forwards. What is the speed of the laser light as seen by the technician?
questions.answer: $c=3.0\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers (Einstein's second postulate).

questions.question: A technician on Earth measures a spaceship travelling at $0.7c$ to be 135 m in length and 35 m in width. What is the length and width of the spaceship when measured at rest on Earth?
questions.answer: Length is contracted only along the direction of motion: $L=L_0\sqrt{1-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$, so $L_0=\dfrac{135}{\sqrt{1-0.7^2}}=\dfrac{135}{0.714}=189$ m (about $1.9\times10^2$ m). The width is perpendicular to the motion, so it is unchanged: 35 m.

questions.question: Is a spaceship travelling past Earth at a constant $0.7c$ an inertial or non-inertial frame of reference? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: Inertial: it moves at constant velocity (in a straight line at constant speed), so it is not accelerating.

questions.question: At the turn of the 20th century scientific thinking about the nature of light underwent significant changes. These changes were heavily influenced by issues scientists were having with successfully explaining black body radiation and the photoelectric effect. Describe the nature of black body radiation and the photoelectric effect and then analyse the problems that the prevailing model of light had with both black body radiation and the photoelectric effect, and how these problems were solved. Make reference to appropriate equations in your response.
questions.answer:
Prevailing model: Light was regarded as a continuous electromagnetic wave (Maxwell). Both phenomena could only be explained by treating light/energy as quantised, leading to the quantum (photon) model, alongside the wave model.

Black body radiation: A black body is an ideal absorber and emitter whose radiation depends only on its temperature. Its spectrum is a smooth curve, with a peak wavelength given by Wien's law $\lambda_{max}T=b$ and total emitted power increasing with temperature. Problem: the classical wave model (Rayleigh-Jeans) predicted that intensity would increase without limit at short wavelengths (the "ultraviolet catastrophe"), implying infinite energy emission, which contradicted the observed curve and conservation of energy. Solution: Planck proposed that energy is emitted and absorbed only in discrete amounts (quanta), $E=hf$, which suppresses emission at high frequencies and reproduces the observed curve.

Photoelectric effect: Electrons are emitted from a metal surface when light shines on it. Problems: the wave model predicted that (i) brighter light should increase the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons, but it depends only on frequency; (ii) electrons should be emitted at any frequency if the light is intense or shone long enough, but below a threshold frequency there is no emission at all; (iii) there should be a time delay while energy accumulates, but emission is instantaneous. Solution: Einstein proposed that light consists of photons of energy $E=hf$, with each photon giving all its energy to a single electron: $K_{max}=hf-\phi$. If $hf<\phi$ (the work function) no electrons are emitted; above the threshold the maximum kinetic energy rises linearly with $f$, and increasing the intensity only increases the number of photons and hence the number (not the energy) of photoelectrons.

questions.question: Electron microscopes use a high-precision electron velocity selector consisting of an electric field $E$ perpendicular to a magnetic field $B$. Electrons travelling at the required velocity $v_0$ hit the aperture at point Y, while electrons travelling slower or faster hit the aperture plate. Show that the velocity of an electron that travels straight through the aperture to point Y is given by $v_0=\dfrac EB$.
questions.answer: To travel straight, the electric force and magnetic force must balance: $qE=qv_0B$, so $v_0=\dfrac EB$ (the charge cancels).

questions.question: Electron microscopes use a high-precision electron velocity selector consisting of an electric field $E$ perpendicular to a magnetic field $B$. Electrons travelling at the required velocity $v_0$ hit the aperture at point Y, while electrons travelling slower or faster hit the aperture plate. Calculate the magnitude of the velocity $v_0$ of an electron that travels straight through the aperture if $E=500\ \text{kV m}^{-1}$ and $B=0.25$ T.
questions.answer: $v_0=\dfrac EB=\dfrac{500\times10^3}{0.25}=2.0\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question: Electron microscopes use a high-precision electron velocity selector consisting of an electric field $E$ perpendicular to a magnetic field $B$. Electrons travelling at the required velocity $v_0$ hit the aperture at point Y, while electrons travelling slower or faster hit the aperture plate. At which of the points X, Y or Z would an electron travelling faster than $v_0$ arrive?
questions.answer: Z. The electric force is independent of speed, but the magnetic force $qvB$ increases with speed. The magnetic force is therefore larger than the electric force, and the electron deflects in the direction of the magnetic force, which is towards Z.

questions.question: In stars, a helium-3 nucleus and a helium-4 nucleus can fuse to produce beryllium-7 with the release of energy in the form of gamma radiation. The masses of the nuclei are: helium-3 3.01493 u, helium-4 4.00151 u, beryllium-7 7.01473 u. Calculate the energy released, in J, when a helium-3 nucleus fuses with a helium-4 nucleus.

In stars, a helium-3 nucleus and a helium-4 nucleus can fuse to produce beryllium-7 with the release of energy in the form of gamma radiation.
